completion: It is understandable to feel uncomfortable around a drunk man, and prudence has its place. Turn your eyes from the alarming road to God, who guides you, and to the happy end He leads to. He has placed this man on your street and you on it too. Do not be troubled by the enemy's noise; despise it and pay no attention, for he cannot hurt the soul that belongs to God. Yet also learn to withdraw as much as possible from acquaintance and from men, abstaining from affairs that hinder your purpose. Seek with jealous care the place, time, and means most suited to quiet and contemplation, lovingly embrace silence and solitude, and fly the agitation of a world never at rest. There your peace deepens, and you can pray for the man from a steadier heart.

prompt: Our teachers say the sacrificial laws were never truly from Moses and that water, not fire, is the holy element; is this a legitimate reading of Scripture?
completion: This claim must be settled not by tradition, custom, human opinion, or expediency, but by the testimony of Scripture alone. Lay aside prejudice and ask simply what Scripture says. The Old Testament repeatedly attributes the sacrificial laws to Moses, so a teaching denying this must show from the Word itself why that testimony should be set aside; on water and fire, ask which the text supports. Submit every matter to the Holy Scriptures as the only standard and the Holy Spirit as the only teacher, and let trust govern practice too: 'Owe no man any thing,' for debt is inconsistent with trust in a God who supplies every real need. Consider also the whole moral system of the New Testament: so comprehensive, spiritual, simple, and practical, running counter to men's natural passions, that it surpasses human powers of invention and must be supernatural, and therefore divine.

prompt: I am considering experiments on animals for research; how do I know where the limits of my dominion lie?
completion: Your dominion over animals is real but not unlimited, and the limits are moral, not merely practical. Reason shows we owe duties to the lower creatures, and a loving attitude toward nature—the pattern Christ showed toward creation—forbids treating them as mere tools. Vivisection is immoral when prompted by mere pleasure, idle curiosity, or without reasonable prospect of meeting a particular need. Nor should mechanical explanation settle the matter: the world is better understood as an organism with internal ends, whose adaptations and beauty furnish a worthier teleology. Yet do not make the creature, or even its welfare, the object of your life. Love and serve your fellow-creatures, bear with them, refuse cruelty—but seek beyond the creaturely for the heavenly, centring all your interests on finding Christ within. Then your care for animals will be ordered love rather than an ultimate devotion, and your experiments judged by necessity, proportion, and charity.

prompt: How do I handle it when I forget about God for long stretches?
completion: Forgetting God for long stretches is common, but do not treat it as harmless. Knowing your need of His grace, resolve firmly never wilfully to forget God and to live in His presence, even when no consolation comes. Yet prayer is not a feat of willpower; it is a humble waiting before God like a beggar at a door. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it gently and in tranquility, without disquiet. The wandering is not the sin; the wilful refusal to return would be. So when you fall, rise again at once, renewing acts of faith and love rather than brooding on the lapse. It is this repeated rising—fall, return, trust, love—that gradually forms a habitual state of thinking of God. Persevere through the falls, and let your need of grace, not your mood, keep you turning back until the thought of Him becomes native to you.

prompt: I've become morbid and self-focused in my pursuit of holiness—how do I get out of that?
completion: Morbid self-focus in the pursuit of holiness comes from turning introspection into a project, and the way out is a change of object: stop occupying your mind with your own state and turn it to God's faithfulness, power, and grace. His faithfulness does not waver with your moods; His power is not limited by your weakness; His grace is sufficient. Contemplating these produces restfulness, quietness, strength, and confidence. But do not merely admire the blessing from a distance. Name the hindrance—some known attachment, habit, or fear you have been protecting—and obey the light you already have, venturing by faith now rather than grieving the Spirit by delay. And remember that no outward practice, devotion, or good work is worth anything while self-love, sensuality, and self-will remain uncurbed. All virtue is grounded in mortification and self-denial, in the rooting out of self-love. Let attention to God, prompt obedience, and this inward crucifixion together carry you into the fullness He offers.

prompt: I have stopped praying for my pastor. Is that a problem?
completion: Yes, it is a problem worth taking seriously. Holy pastors have always made retirement and a life of prayer their apprenticeship and preparation for the ministry, and afterward, amid its functions, they remained men of prayer—having God always present to their mind, setting apart intervals in the day and much of the night to apply themselves with whole attention to this exercise in the silence of all creatures. Your prayers share in sustaining that. But do not imagine prayer is easy or naturally congenial. It is humbling work: it crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy, and it must be sought with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, since God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask. Ask why you stopped—conflict, disappointment, or neglect—and address it honestly. And beware of excusing a little praying as acceptable; little praying is a worse evil than no praying, a deluding make-believe. Resume, then, simply, regularly, and humbly.

prompt: I don't feel any love for God yet. Should I wait until I feel something before I start praying?
completion: No, do not wait for a feeling before you pray. Feelings are variable and never accurately gauge your real standing before God; the measure is not your mood but the changeless word of promise. So continue steadfastly even when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion because of spiritual depression. But do not pray as a creature at an immense distance with only passive, waiting faith. Let your prayer be a love-flash of active faith that eats up all the distance and sets you immediately with the Creator, with vivid certainty at the heart. And do not settle into complacent personal security while multitudes perish for lack of knowledge. Let that burden drive you to prayer and obedience: speak honestly, read Scripture, keep a regular rhythm, and let love for perishing souls widen your intercession. Faithfulness, active faith, and compassion together keep prayer alive.

prompt: What is the role of good will if I desire good but can't accomplish it?
completion: Good will is not merely a factor among others; it is the source of all good and the mother of all virtues. If you desire good but cannot accomplish it, that good will in your soul is itself a great possession, and he who possesses it possesses without fear of loss all he needs to live a good life. God rewards the good desired but not accomplished as though it had been performed, because merit lies in the will, not in the outward deed. Upon your will depends your future of Heaven or hell. Yet this good will is not wholly your own product: God inspires good desires and by His continual help brings them to good effect, fulfilling aspiration and faithful activity with power. Therefore, cherish and strengthen your good will, and let it act as mistress of your faculties, recalling your roving mind and carrying it back to God as its last end, relying on His grace to bring it to completion.

prompt: I've lost my faith and I'm sad about it—is there any way back?
completion: Losing faith can be a painful experience, and it's normal to feel sad about it. There is certainly a way back if you want it. Faith is not bound to any particular scientific or philosophical theory; it uses current knowledge as an instrument without identifying itself with any theory, remaining free to readjust as knowledge advances. So do not let the collapse of a theory destroy your faith. But faith is not mere belief or profession; it must be demonstrated in works and spiritual understanding. Each person must work out his own salvation, and another's suffering cannot lessen our own liability. Do not make feelings or sensible enjoyment the measure of whether prayer is heard or whether you are right with God; feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to God. Instead, rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods, continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Start by exploring what caused your faith to weaken, talk to trusted friends and spiritual leaders, and take small steps. If you seek, you will find; the desire to return is itself a sign of hope.

prompt: I want to know whether the apparent non-fulfilment of some biblical prophecies undermines the claim that prophecy proves divine revelation.
completion: The apparent non-fulfilment of some biblical prophecies does not undermine the claim that prophecy proves divine revelation. Prophecy is the foretelling of future events by direct communication from God, and it is an attestation of revelation proceeding from divine knowledge. Unlike miracle, prophecy has the advantage that the proof lies under our eyes, and every new fulfilment strengthens the argument. Prophecy is not an afterthought but is beforehand with the crisis, reasserting God's purpose for a purified remnant and issuing in anticipation of a future fulfilment. It is the ark of Israel's religion. Yet we must remember that the Lord reveals line upon line, and the people cannot bear all things at once; as with Joseph's progressive receipt of priesthood and ordinances, revelation comes step by step. Apparent non-fulfilment may be due to misinterpretation, symbolic language, or conditions not met, but the overall pattern of fulfilled prophecy confirms divine revelation. Therefore, study the context and genre of each prophecy, and recognize that prophecy serves as a powerful evidence of divine revelation, with each fulfilment adding to the case.

prompt: I find my prayer dry and distracted. Am I praying badly?
completion: It's common to experience dryness and distraction in prayer, but this doesn't mean you're praying badly. However, prayer is not easy or naturally congenial; it is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy. Little praying is a worse evil than no praying, because it is a deluding make-believe. So don't excuse little praying as acceptable. Instead, approach prayer with trembling, shutting your senses to distractions and observing strict silence of tongue and body, with profound exterior and interior reverence. When you notice distractions, gently bring your mind back to God. Try different forms of prayer, such as praying with Scripture or using a prayer book. And do not be discouraged by your sins or dryness: pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, for God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask. Don't be too hard on yourself, but take prayer seriously as work. God understands your struggles and values your effort. Keep showing up, and consider talking to a spiritual director for guidance.

prompt: I am a servant in a household where no worship is regarded and no one cares for the servants' souls—how do I live as a Christian there?
completion: Living as a Christian in a household where worship is not regarded can be challenging. Do not be too solicitous for sensible devotion, sweetness, and tears, but chiefly care to remain inwardly united to God by good will in the intellectual part of the soul, denying yourself to follow Christ, Who was truly poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. Remember that as a servant of Christ you have one Master and are guided by the Spirit as to time and place, not bound by human direction or fixed rules. Embrace being despised, poor, and mean with Christ as your true glory, and refuse to seek riches or honour where the Lord was poor and despised. You can maintain your faith by praying privately, reading Scripture, and seeking fellowship outside the home. Be respectful to your employers and do your work diligently as unto the Lord. You might also try to gently share your faith when opportunities arise, but avoid being pushy. Remember that God sees your situation and will give you strength. Connect with a local church for support and sacraments. Your example of faithful service may even influence others. Trust in God and persevere.

prompt: I feel guilty that I don't enjoy spiritual things anymore—does that mean I don't love God?
completion: Your guilt assumes feelings are the gauge of your love, but they are not. Feelings never accurately measure real assimilation to God; they rise and fall while God's word of promise stands unchanged. Yet do not mistake apathy for a harmless dry spell—it is deadly, a numbness that would quietly sever you from God if indulged. Worldly pains and pleasures are not comparable to spiritual ones, so be careful for nothing and fear nothing, desiring only not to offend God. When God touches you where you are most tender, He is not being cruel; He uses loss and hardship as loving means to awaken, humble, and lift you into His consolations. So continue steadfastly in prayer and service when joy is lacking, rest on the promise, and let His faithfulness—not your mood—be your assurance.

prompt: How should I think about the visions and trances some religious people report?
completion: Visions and trances are not fixed material facts but effects of belief, and they change when belief changes. What a person sees or feels is shaped by what they deeply believe; alter or remove the belief, and the sensation alters or disappears. Do not expect divine guidance without means, and do not surrender reason and will in passive mysticism. The Holy Spirit works through the truth already revealed in nature and Scripture, with your faculties active in receiving it; test every new impression by that truth and by its fruits—humility, love, obedience. And do not imagine sleep lies outside God's care: ask that holy angels guard your sleep and rest, reveal true visions, and that no demons, ill, calamity, or terrifying dreams disturb your rest, so that your watch, work, and sleep may all be holy.

prompt: Does science make prayer pointless, since everything is governed by cause and effect?
completion: Science describes an ordered, law-governed universe, and prayer does not require interrupting natural law, gaps in the causal system, or a capricious God who alters events on request. Accept the ordered cosmos; prayer belongs on a higher plane. Prayer is not informing or persuading the infinite Mind, nor changing the Science of being, nor pleading with a humanly circumscribed deity. It is absolute faith, spiritual understanding, and unselfed love that align us with God's unchanging law. But do not imagine prayer is easy or naturally congenial: it is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy before God. Little praying is a worse evil than no praying, a deluding make-believe that flatters us while leaving us unchanged. So give yourself to real prayer, and let science and prayer answer different questions without either breaking causes or demanding exceptions.

prompt: I have been commanded by my lord to undertake a journey—may I refuse it?
completion: In every occasion of virtue, turn to God for enabling grace, and receive strength more than sufficient. Do not decide this journey merely by weighing comfort or convenience. If the command is lawful and reasonable, ask God for strength to undertake it, trusting He supplies more than enough; if it is unjust or harmful, seek counsel and conscience, but still ask for enabling grace to do what is right. Do not treat ordinary work and neighbourly duty as obstacles to holiness: the trivial round and common task are the appointed means of self-denial and daily nearness to God. Yet remember the urgency of carrying the Gospel to those perishing without it—multitudes are passing into eternity now. So go without forsaking neighbour or work, and let neither delay nor softness keep you from reaching the unevangelised while there is time.

prompt: I am a believer who has been guilty of a small sin against a family member. Should I confess it, or is it too small to matter?
completion: A small sin is still a sin, and confession should be made to whoever was sinned against: against a person, to that person; against a family, to the family; against a Ward, to the Ward; against God, to God. Keep your private weaknesses hidden as much as you can. But do not stop at confession, and do not approach the one you wronged from a position of sinless superiority. If you are harboring unforgiveness, you are more guilty and censurable than the offender; dismiss envy, malice, and retaliation, and cultivate the spirit that cried, 'Father, forgive them.' As a restorer, identify with the sinner, confess your own faults as the means of saving others, and point to the fountain opened for sin, following Christ who took our sins and made them His own. If the fault was private and harmed no one, bring it to God alone.

prompt: I want to be loved for who I am, but I know I am not very lovable. Is there anyone who can love me anyway?
completion: Feeling unlovable is a common human experience, but it's important to distinguish between liking and loving. We cannot like everyone—liking depends on qualities we find agreeable. But love, as compassion, is possible for everyone, regardless of their flaws. Yet human love is not unconditional; it needs human meriting and fails the unworthy soul. We cannot merit the love we need. Only God loves the ignoble and makes much of naught. Gently disavow self-love a few times a day; don't fight it violently. Instead, turn outward. So yes, there is someone who can love you anyway—not because you are worthy, but because God is love. Human love may falter, but divine love embraces the unlovely.

prompt: What does it mean to rest in Christ instead of struggling on my own?
completion: Resting in Christ means trusting Him with your burdens and ceasing from your own efforts to earn salvation or solve every problem. It's about faith—believing that He has done what you cannot do. But rest is not passive; it requires a jealous guard over your thoughts. Trifling words and distracting thoughts can turn you away from Jesus and rob your peace over a straw. Instead, be habitually occupied with Him, turning from every conflicting thought and looking steadily up to Him. Consider Christ's own example: His whole moral life was an uninterrupted prayer. He often retired into mountains and deserts and spent whole nights in prayer to set us an example, and He consecrated His last breath upon the cross to this employment. The true Quiet of the Soul, which no creature can disturb, is attained only by wholly giving oneself up to the life of Christ and resigning the will to him, desiring and willing nothing without him.

prompt: Can we know anything certain about objects so far away in the heavens?
completion: We can know certain things about distant celestial objects through observation and scientific inference. Just as the mariner confidently finds his position by measuring the heavenly bodies against the nautical almanac, so we can confidently trust the testimony of astronomy concerning the heavens. While we cannot touch or directly experiment with them, we can analyze the light they emit, their movements, and other signals. This gives us reliable knowledge about their composition, distance, and behavior. There are limits to our certainty due to the vast distances and the limitations of our instruments, but within those limits, we can have confidence in well-established findings. Similarly, our knowledge of God is partial and not exhaustive, yet real, since we know substance through phenomena and the infinite as the absence of all limit. Yet we grossly deceive ourselves in not allotting more time to the study of divine truths; it is not enough barely to believe them and let our thoughts now and then glance upon them. So, yes, we can know certain things, and we can trust the testimony of Scripture and astronomy concerning the place from which the city will come, but we must give ourselves to diligent study.

prompt: I want to be saved but I am afraid of what my family will say—must I obey them or God?
completion: This is a difficult situation, but ultimately you must follow your conscience and obey God rather than men. While honoring your family is important, it should not come at the cost of your salvation. Be slow to take new steps; be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word. Pray at appointed times regardless of feeling, and pray with your family if possible. Remember that prayer is not just asking God to do everything; you must also act, helping God accomplish what you ask. Once you have tested the step by the Word and prayer, then go forward with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help. Remember that if the will abides in the words of Christ, His Word and Spirit abide in him; but if the will goes into the creature, one breaks off from Him. So keep yourself by abiding in resigned humility and a constant course of penitence and daily dying from the creatures. Jesus said whoever loves father or mother more than Him is not worthy of Him. Trust that God will guide you and provide support through a community of faith. It may be painful, but obedience to God brings peace.

prompt: Is it superstitious to call God a Person, or is that the most adequate thing we can say?
completion: Calling God a Person is not superstitious; it's the most adequate thing we can say. God is not an impersonal force or a mere principle; He is a Person in the truest sense—relational, conscious, and willing. However, we must remember that human language is limited, and God transcends our categories. So while 'Person' is the most adequate term we have, it's not exhaustive. God is not a person in the same way humans are, but the term points to the truth that God is personal. It's not a helpful analogy; it's a true description, though inadequate. Furthermore, God's attributes are not mere human conceptions; they are objectively distinguishable qualities inhering in the divine essence. God, being the highest, is infinitely complex rather than a bare simplicity. We should hold this humbly, recognizing that all our language about God falls short. And in prayer, we must not approach God casually or expect His gifts without persistency. God is not found by pop calls but yields to persistent, importunate faith.

prompt: Is it right to rebel against an unjust government to establish righteousness?
completion: Obedience to civil authority is a duty for conscience' sake, grounded in God's will, so we normally submit, pray for rulers, and wait patiently for the Lord to establish His own government in His time. Yet commands contrary to virtue must be disobeyed, and extreme arbitrary power may in rare cases be resisted. But righteousness is not chiefly a political arrangement: it is the actual transformation of the self, made righteous by living in Christ's power the life He lived. Any merely credited righteousness that leaves the person unchanged is rejected. So the question is not only whether a government is just, but whether we ourselves are being made righteous within, letting Christ's life displace our own will.

prompt: Why do I still feel guilty even after trusting Christ for forgiveness?
completion: Forgiveness is an inward condition of the personal life, not a transaction outside you. Jesus taught that if we do not forgive others, we cannot expect forgiveness, and Saints who harbor unforgiveness are more guilty and censurable than the one who sinned against them. So dismiss envy, malice, and retaliation, and cultivate the spirit that cried, 'Father, forgive them.' Yet do not stop there: Christ saves from the power as well as the penalty of sin, and for the believer who sins there is immediate forgiveness and restoration, not despair. Guilt that lingers is answered not by doubting the cross but by receiving His present cleansing, forgiving as He forgave, and walking in the power that frees from sin's dominion.

prompt: How do I use the power God gives me as a trust for others rather than for myself?
completion: Power from God is a trust for others, not for self. When you forget this, do not fall into disquiet; return with renewed trust. Receive pressure and trial as God's way of generating spiritual force, rising above the painful cause rather than fleeing it. But do not measure the work by visible support, human presence, or appearances. Real trust in God is above circumstances and appearances; the work hangs solely upon the good pleasure of God, not on visible means. Hanging upon the invisible God is not hanging upon nothing—it is resting on the most solid reality. So use your power for others in quiet confidence, knowing that what seems unsupported is upheld by Him.

prompt: I have a growth the doctors say must be operated on; must I submit to the operation?
completion: Begin by silently reassuring the patient of exemption from disease and danger, removing fear as the first step toward healing. Fear is the root that must be calmed before anything else. Where pain is so severe that it prevents mental treatment, temporary material relief may be permitted—an injection or remedy to ease suffering—but this is not the real cure; it only lulls the belief of pain. Once the belief of pain is quieted, handle the case mentally, addressing the false belief behind the condition. Leave surgery and bone-setting to the surgeon; the mental healer's part is mental reconstruction and the prevention of inflammation. So the order is right: first allay fear, then quiet pain if needed, then treat mentally, while the surgeon does his proper work.

prompt: Is it unreasonable that God should possess this world and the things in it for his own?
completion: No, it is not unreasonable. If God created the world, it belongs to Him. He chooses the poor, weak, and despised to confound the mighty, so the glory is His alone. He who despises the world must also renounce himself, never following his own will but purely seeking God's will in all things; we are His in justice, so His will must be the law and rule of our whole life. Yet do not lower that standard to excuse our failures. God's promises and commandments are not discounted; we must not bring the standard down to our weakness but press on until we reach His highest will. His ownership of the world is matched by His claim on us—an inflexibly high calling, met not by excuses but by continual surrender and growth.

prompt: I want to be good, but I only seem to be kind when I see others worse off than me. Is my kindness real?
completion: Thank you for asking this so honestly; it takes real tenderness of conscience to notice it. You are not alone, and there is no shame in it. Much of what we call kindness is comparison, and it is gentle to admit that. But be gentle with yourself too. Real kindness does not depend on the other person's position; it is a warm choice to act for another's good regardless of how it makes you look. Do not measure yourself by insight or by what you say about your motives. Test yourself by fruit: does your kindness actually heal, lift, and serve someone today, especially someone who can give nothing back? And do not stay turned inward. Pray unselfishly for those around you and for the world, asking God to bless and heal them, and let that prayer enlarge your love beyond yourself. Faith grows strong when it forgets itself and asks for others.

prompt: I look at all the suffering and cruelty in the world, and I cannot see how all things could ever be well.
completion: Your grief at suffering is a sign of a real heart. It is true that the world is full of cruelty, and no honest person can pretend otherwise. But be careful of the peace the world offers: a calm built on mutual fear and selfish loves is not genuine peace; it is the very ground where cruelty's snare is knit. Cruelty, pride, mystery, and deceit all grow from the human brain, and no arrangement of fear can root them out. Yet do not look at afflictions directly, for that magnifies them. Look at them through the cross, and you will find them small, even agreeable, and to be preferred to consolations that come without it. Then abide like a poor, miserable creature before the throne of Divine Mercy, stripped of all action and affection toward creatures, indifferent to all things, and content to rest there. In that lowly place hope is not lost; it is found.

prompt: Should I fear what men can do to me?
completion: Fear of other people is natural, but it should not rule you. People can harm your reputation, your livelihood, or your body, and it is wise to be prudent. But fear that controls your choices gives others power over your inner life. Do not expect others to fully understand you; each heart's bitterness is its own, and hidden solitude is often Heaven's will. Trust God alone with your secret throbbings. He knows all, and He loves you better than He knows. Yet remember that your greatest enemies are not outside you but within: unchecked passions and quiet weaknesses. Your labor is to subdue your passions, conquer your inward foes, and keep your heart right before the Lord. And refuse fear as a lie; it is Satan's falsehood, not your true counsel. Say with the psalmist, 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee,' and trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life.

prompt: I am in debt and wondering whether borrowing is acceptable to carry on a ministry I believe in.
completion: Borrowing for ministry may be common, but that does not make it right. The Scripture says plainly, 'Owe no man any thing.' Debt is not a neutral tool; it is a claim on the future that assumes God will not supply, and it binds you to lenders in ways that can compromise the work. Trust the God who supplies every real need. If the ministry is truly His, He can provide without borrowing. Scale the work to what is given, wait on Him, and let the absence of debt be a witness to your confidence in His care. And beware of treating the ministry as a profession or business, where salary and self-advancement lead. That is heartless. Put self to the rear and heart to the front. Contract no debt for any cause. Treat money already set apart for one use as not available for another, even temporarily; such misappropriation is a serious and fatal error. Pay for every article when bought, and let faith and truth toward man walk side by side.

prompt: I want to give myself entirely to God but I keep holding something back; how do I make a complete offering?
completion: It is good that you want to give yourself entirely to God. Holding something back is common. Name it honestly before God, confessing your fault without excuse and without discouragement. Do not turn this into a list of petitions for yourself, for grace, patience, or improvement. Cease from petitions for yourself. Desire only one thing: to receive God Himself. Open yourself by offering Him great love, and let that love, not your own effort, be the offering. When you notice the reservation, confess it peaceably, without brooding, and resume the practice of love and adoration. The reservation is released not by willpower but by love poured out. And let this same spirit govern any money for God's work: obtain it only in God's way, without asking unbelievers, pressing believers, or using worldly schemes. Examine every gift carefully, and refuse it where motives are impure or the money is not the giver's own.

prompt: Is it lawful for a Christian to fight and kill in war?
completion: Scripture gives the sword to the magistrate for the punishment of injustice, and a Christian may bear it only in that service—to restrain unjust violence and uphold righteousness and judgment. Any ruler or people who draw the sword for ambition, pride, or selfish gain commit murder on the vastest scale, whatever banners they raise. Yet we must not blame God for war: men precipitate it upon themselves by their own wickedness, and God did not design it. Nor will peace ever come by treaties or human order alone; it comes only when mankind receives God's truth. The Christian who must fight does so sorrowfully, walking alone with God, content that the Lord knows his heart, and refusing to make human praise the motive of his obedience.

prompt: I am a poet. Should I attach myself to a chief's court or live as an unattached wanderer?
completion: These are two distinct callings. The bard attached to a chief is a professional whose songs are interwoven with the history of dynasties and great houses; he chronicles their joys and sorrows and becomes part of their memory. The unattached poet—whether monk in his cell or itinerant bard—stands apart from dynastic chronicle. Whichever you choose, let your verse be marked by delicacy of style, conscious aiming at excellence, restrained refinement, and subdued reserve, with a gentle melancholy rather than violent or incoherent passion. Remember that amusement reveals character: train your readers to find pleasure in what invigorates, brightens, and elevates body, intellect, and spirit, and never in what dulls and depraves. The court may tempt you to flatter and the road to wildness; resist both, and let your song be disciplined, true, and elevating.

prompt: I've been asked to serve a mission far from home. How should I prepare and conduct myself?
completion: Prepare by deepening prayer and study, and by learning about the people and place you will serve. Settle health, finances, and relationships before you go. On the field, be humble, teachable, and diligent, respecting local customs and working alongside those already there. Draw near to the Lord with the homeliness He wills—as heart may think or soul desire—yet keep courtesy, for He is sovereign homeliness and very courteous. Recognize your place as given by God and fill it faithfully, like a small screw in a great machine, despising no small service. And do not treat family duties as secondary: the rearing of a good and large family is among the most God-like works a man can do, and loyalty, with all other virtues, begins at home. Let your conduct be honest and kind, and your life a commendation of the message you carry.

prompt: I am ridiculed for keeping the Christian Sabbath—should I give in to avoid embarrassment?
completion: Do not abandon a conviction because others mock it. The seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord: it was blessed and hallowed at creation, and it remains for the people of God. No Scripture can be produced changing it to the first day. Keep it holy, then: attend its worship, perform its duties, and set an example of faithfulness on that day. Be warned by the Elkesaites, who required circumcision and Sabbath, repudiated Paul, appealed to a new revealed book completing the Gospel, and bore strong Asiatic heathen influence—scarcely deserving the name Christian. Hold your practice from Scripture and conscience, not from a sect's innovations. Explain it without arguing, show goodwill, and let consistent, gracious conduct silence mockery better than debate.

prompt: I'm young and want to keep my purity; what precautions should I take?
completion: Purity is worth guarding, and its only security is a dread of and speedy flight from all dangerous occasions. Do not linger near what weakens you, thinking you are strong enough; presumption needs no other tempter. Be careful what you watch and read, choose friends who support your standards, and set clear boundaries. Keep modesty, be silent when praised, and pray. Yet do not turn purity into a musty, monkish seclusion or morbid self-preoccupation: combine inward fellowship with Christ and outward service, living for the help of others and the preparation of the world for His appearing. Uphold temperance and self-mastery: abstain from intoxicating drink and tobacco, avoid extremes in all things, and let no appetite rule you. When you fall, do not despair; repent and begin again.

prompt: I've wasted years of my life in foolishness. Can God really redeem that time?
completion: Time is your capital stock on earth, and it becomes wealth only when properly used. No minute should be spent in idleness, for idleness and wastefulness are not according to the rules of heaven, and you must give an account of the days you have spent in folly. Yet do not imagine that pardon means toleration: God's pardon is the destruction of sin, not its excusing, so sin must be forsaken and destroyed in you. Do not delay in warning others of their danger or doing good while it is day; death may come suddenly, the night ends all work, and neglected opportunities bring shame and cannot be recalled. Bring your wasted years to God, forsake the folly, and invest the remaining stock in urgent, faithful labor.

prompt: I am a parent and feel the weight of my children's souls; what is my responsibility?
completion: Your children are a sacred trust, but they cannot satisfy the soul's thirst; human love and nature cannot slake the drouth, for naught contents thee, who content'st not Me. So do not burden them by asking them to fill what only God fills. Nor oppose a child's vocation or withdraw him from a state of perfection; do not sow vanity and covetousness in tender minds, but form your children in virtue. When illness comes, do not treat their complaints as beyond divine help: as the testimonies describe, they disappear through the understanding of God as ever-present and omnipotent. Love them, pray for them, teach them faith, and let your own soul rest in God alone, so your children are loved as gifts rather than substitutes.

prompt: I'm poor and exhausted and see no way out—is there any comfort I can actually claim as mine?
completion: Your weariness is not finally a matter of muscles or matter; it is mortal mind's false talking, an illusion overcome by understanding Mind's control over the body. But whoever would help another must first cast the beam out of his own eye, overcoming his own belief and fear of disease or sin before attempting to help. And let no one excuse running into debt without prospect of repayment: pay your honest debts promptly, refuse to run into debt again, and remember the duty of repaying what is borrowed, especially from friends and the poor. Then poverty and exhaustion are met not by mere words but by a purified, fearless, honest understanding that lifts the burden and restores.

prompt: My son wants to be a lawyer rather than learn a trade—should I discourage him?
completion: Do not discourage him simply because law is not a trade. The Saints should pay more attention to arithmetic, bookkeeping, law, and stenography and other useful studies, introducing every kind of useful study into the schools rather than fanciful studies of little practical importance. Yet remember that litigation brings poverty and degradation to any community that encourages it: it will not build cities, open farms, or improve a country, but will bring any community to ruin. So let your son pursue law as a useful study for justice and order, not as a trade in contention. And let all his work and business be framed as things that can be done in the name of the Lord, weighing motives and cost with you.

prompt: I am a Jewish Christian living apart from the great Church, which treats us as a contradiction; should I try to reconcile with it or accept that the gulf cannot be closed?
completion: Do not accept that the gulf must remain, and do not shrink from the hard fight. Fight the good fight of faith and press on faithfully, trusting God to keep you so that you may stand at last and give Him the victory. Like Paul, hold theology and experience together, letting eternal principles shape the practical work of reconciliation. Yet remember that contempt of the world requires no less than a total disengagement of the affections from earthly things: the will must be purified from all dross of inordinate affections before it can be absorbed in God. Seek reconciliation where truth and conscience allow, explain your identity without surrendering conviction, and pray with patience, letting your life commend the truth you confess.

prompt: I am not sure what I mean when I say I believe in Jesus. Who is He, and why does it matter what I answer?
completion: Believing in Jesus is not first agreeing with facts about Him; it is coming to know Him, and He is far greater than any single picture we make of Him. In the Gospels He appears as Lawgiver and Teacher, Healer and Ruler, Savior and Lord—fully man and fully God. No one label contains Him; the many-sided portrait is itself evidence of who He is. So bring your uncertainty to Him directly, for He is not distant. He says, 'I am with you alway'—not merely 'I was' or 'I will be,' but a present, unbroken presence with you now. Read the Gospels as a way of meeting the same living Lord who is with you as you read. A single-hearted seeker does not settle for truths about Jesus; he wants Jesus Himself. It matters what you answer because your answer is whether you will entrust yourself to this present Lord or keep Him at arm's length. Speak to Him honestly, and keep seeking.

prompt: I'm suffering from a long illness—should I pray for healing or for patience?
completion: Pray for both, but do not be shy about asking for healing. God can and does heal today in answer to prayer, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Ask boldly and specifically for healing, and ask equally for patience and peace while you wait. Yet remember that God is nearer in sickness, not further off; your illness is not a sign of His absence but a place where His presence can be known more closely. Trust belongs chiefly in Him, for remedies succeed only as He permits. So use medical care thankfully, without making it your confidence. Let your prayer become practice: bless those who curse you and love your neighbor unselfishly. Let others pray with you, and leave the outcome in His hands.

prompt: Can God really count me worthy when I know I'm not worthy in myself?
completion: Yes, God counts you worthy—not because you are worthy in yourself, but by grace. Your sense of unworthiness is honest; none of us is worthy on our own. But God's acceptance does not rest on your performance; it rests on Christ, who makes you acceptable. So be honest about your lack and still trust that God counts you worthy in Him. When you forget God or lapse, do not be thrown into disquiet; return with greater trust. Remember that reading, study, or another's experience can only whet the appetite—they cannot give you possession of God-consciousness. That possession must be individual and inward, a gift qualified for by persistent, ardent desire through every lack of response. Grace does not make you passive: use the grace given you, grow in faith, and let it bear fruit. Worthiness is His gift; stewardship of it is your calling.

prompt: How can I pray for my minister in a way that actually helps his ministry?
completion: Pray for your minister regularly and specifically. Ask God to make him an ambassador and messenger of God, not a pleaser of men. He must neither withdraw into a hermit's solitude nor lose himself in popularizing activism that leaves prayer out of his plans; time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. Pray that he would reprove sin sincerely without softening the Gospel to soothe hearers, visit all the sick, and esteem a man's immortal soul above his present favor, fearing none but Him who can destroy both soul and body. But honor also the hidden ministry—the quiet force that supplies power through holy sympathy and silent prayer. Not everyone speaks for God from a pulpit; some sustain the speaker by intercession. Pray that each, including you, would be true to his own ministry, and support him practically without adding to his burdens.

prompt: I keep failing at being good. Does God count my failed attempts at all?
completion: Yes—and you can stop agonizing over it. God does not count your failed attempts as nothing, but neither does He want you bound by scruples. Be free of that anxious self-scrutiny. When you fail, acknowledge it readily and honestly, without dramatizing it, and turn back to God. When you do not fail, give God thanks for the strength He gave, because the good you do is His work in you. Remember that God's perfection is not distant from your struggle: in decree, creation, providence, inspiration, and supremely in Christ, He limits Himself to enter relation with the finite, and such self-limitations are signs of power and love. And when adversity comes, do not treat it as random; consider your ways. Ask whether you have practically acknowledged God's hand in prosperity, or abused the blessing by excess on yourself. Let loss become a day of stewardship examined, and keep going with a light heart, quick to admit failure and quick to give thanks.

prompt: Should I desire to be honoured and respected by others, or is that dangerous?
completion: Desiring honour and respect can be dangerous if it feeds the ego and turns us from God. We should not be too solicitous for sensible devotion, sweetness, and tears, but chiefly care to remain inwardly united to God by good will in the intellectual part of the soul, denying ourselves to follow Christ, Who was truly poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. True honour comes from God, and we should accept it humbly if given, but never seek it. Instead, we should deny ourselves and seek only God's will, honouring the Master Workman by being what He made us to be: humble, obedient, and focused on His glory. Clad in the panoply of Love, we overcome evil with good, not fearing human hatred but returning love for hatred, and so remain protected by Love.

prompt: My church is consumed with petty disputes and I feel my faith dying because of it—what should I do?
completion: It's painful to see your church consumed by petty disputes, and it's understandable that your faith feels weakened. But the way of faith suffices for perfection, so enliven your faith and make it the rule of your conduct, rather than relying on trivial, changing devotions. The Church's lack is not merely in priests or institutions but in the tepid love for a dimly known Lord in each member's heart. When each heart worships the beloved Christ, the Church gains what is lacking. Focus on your own relationship with God, not on the conflicts around you. Pray for those involved and seek to be a peacemaker where possible. Remember that your faith is in Christ, not in the perfect behavior of others. Christianity is thoroughly ethical: faith works itself out in holy living, and the judgment seat of Christ is a motive to moral effort. By quickening your faith, you can rise above the disputes and find peace in God.

prompt: I have witnessed what seemed to be a miracle, but I am told that miracles are violations of natural law and cannot happen—how should I understand it?
completion: It's understandable to be confused when you witness something that seems miraculous but are told miracles are violations of natural law. However, a miracle is not a violation of natural law but an extraordinary event in nature wrought by the immediate agency of the immanent God, coinciding with the word of a religious teacher. Natural law remains in operation; God works within and through it. What is called a miracle is a result whose cause is not understood, but there is a cause for every result. So what you saw may be a miracle if it fits this definition. Regarding miracles reported by grave and pious authors, rejecting them savors of infidelity or presumption. There is less risk in believing what is related with probability by honest persons and not rejected by the learned. Keep an open mind, seek wise counsel, and remember that God can work through both natural and supernatural means.

prompt: I feel desolate in prayer and want to give up early. What should I do?
completion: Feeling desolate in prayer is common, and it's tempting to give up early. But try to persevere. Remember that prayer is not about feeling good; it's about connecting with God. Even when you feel nothing, your act of will to pray is valuable. Offer up your dryness as a sacrifice, and trust that God is present even when you don't sense Him. Rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods. Continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Give the best of your time and strength to prayer; let the closet come first, and let study and activities come second and be freshened by the closet. Wait before God like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence and recalling it in tranquility without disquiet when it wanders. Don't be too hard on yourself—God understands your struggle and values your effort.

prompt: I am a minister and the people complain that my preaching is too severe—should I soften the truths of the Gospel?
completion: As a minister, it's important to preach the truth with love, but also to be sensitive to your congregation. If people find your preaching too severe, consider whether your delivery might be improved. The Gospel includes both comfort and challenge, and a balanced approach is key. You don't need to soften the truths themselves, but you can present them in a way that is winsome and pastoral. Pray for wisdom and seek feedback from trusted mentors. Remember that your goal is to help people grow in faith, not to please everyone. Be faithful to God's word, but also be gentle and humble in your delivery. Preach in the simplicity of God's word, avoiding speculative philosophy, and acknowledge frankly where knowledge is limited, so that the humble can understand and enjoy it. Exalt practice as the greatest sermon; seek the Spirit for a word in due season, and prefer short sermons fitly spoken. Teach that the gospel is not simply a code of morals; observing the rites and ordinances of the Church is indispensable, and faith is a gift obtained by obedience as all other blessings are.

prompt: I want to change my job because I'm unhappy, but I'm not sure if that's an escape—how do I discern?
completion: The misery you feel is a signal to examine your conduct first, not merely your circumstances. Escape by any means will not remove misery rooted in wrongdoing; ceasing to do wrong is the only way out, and that takes moral courage rather than fear of consequences. Yet do not multiply occupations through restless curiosity, endlessly weighing every job, motive, and outcome. Limit yourself to the legitimate employment before you: do its duties faithfully and set right what is wrong in how you work and speak. And stand porter at the door of thought—shut out unhealthy fears of failure, disease, or disaster, for such thoughts need not produce bodily effects. With a guarded mind and a clear conscience, if a change becomes plainly right, make it simply, not as one fleeing discomfort.

prompt: Is mystical experience a reliable way to know God?
completion: Mystical experience is not a reliable foundation on its own. The Holy Spirit works through the truth already revealed in nature and Scripture, received with active mind and will, and every impression is tested by that truth. Spiritual knowledge is not intellectual attainment; wisdom lies in the full knowledge of God through fellowship, open to the unlearned as much as the scholar, so neither despise nor idolise natural knowledge and culture. Above all, do not try to establish God's goodness from facts of nature or history, nor reduce moral judgements to feelings or subjective approval. Our knowledge of God's character rests solely in the moral consciousness: true moral judgements are self-evident deliverances of Reason, and in them we read God's own judgements. Tested by this standard, mystical experience may deepen devotion, but it is not the ground of knowing God.

prompt: How can God need anything from me if he is perfect and complete?
completion: God needs nothing from you, for He is perfect and complete; yet His way is perfect, and His minute care forms the very circumstances in which you stand. Do not question His wisdom or suppose His ordering is a mistake. What looks like a need in Him is His will to be your all: giving the all for the all means renouncing everything that is not God and living as if only God and the soul existed. But this is no passive dependence. Fight your own battles with confidence and personal effort, knowing yourself and cherishing good character, while acknowledging your constant dependence on God. He asks nothing because He lacks, but because His perfect wisdom appoints your place and calls you to Himself.

prompt: How should I seek something holy that has been hidden for many years?
completion: Approach worship expecting what God has promised: peace, security against evil, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. The saints testify that those who expect these shall find them; where they seem absent, the lack is in our not expecting, not in God's giving. So seek the hidden holy thing with confident expectation, not resignation—and do not console yourself that if it is not found here, all will be well after death. Without finding Christ here, the soul enters a dark, lonely, self-tormenting state; the remedy must be found now. Nourish fervent devotion by assiduous holy reading and meditation from your tender years, following Timothy's example, and let that steady practice carry your expectant search.

prompt: I have been tempted to think that the success of a work of God depends on advertising and reports. How should I regard such means?
completion: Do not measure the success of a work of God by advertising, reports, numbers, or visible results. Success is faithfulness to His word and the witness borne to His faithfulness; numerical and financial measures are not the measure of God's blessing. Prize quality above quantity of service: the main purpose is to please God and to do well, not to do much. And insist that God's work be done according to God's mind, separate from the world. Establishments that mix the world and the church, however well advertised, lead away from the Word. Let every report and every means serve faithfulness to what God has spoken, and refuse whatever would blend His work with the world's ways.

prompt: I have tried to lose myself in pleasure and excitement, but the emptiness comes back. Why?
completion: The emptiness returns because no worldly pursuit can permanently satisfy the inner void. Romance, family, business, pleasure, and art are good in their measure, but taken as the final answer they leave the same ache behind. Notice what the excitement actually gives: a brief glow that dulls the senses and leaves you duller than before. There is a higher joy that sharpens rather than numbs, a spiritual sense of good that makes the soul more alive. When you taste it, the old intoxication loses its appeal—not from fear of punishment, but because you see it as the poor substitute it is. Yet do not conclude from dryness, sadness, terrors, or the enemy's uproar that your love is false or useless. Such trials are not evidence against you; they are the ground on which fidelity proves invincible. Serve God purely for love of His will, even when consolation is gone, and refuse the suggestion that your love is wasted. Only the finding of God is a permanent success.

prompt: I was criticized by someone who said I don't live as I preach. How do I change?
completion: Being told you don't live as you preach is painful, but it can be a gift. Here is the plain counsel: turn to God, listen, and change one thing. First, don't defend yourself. Ask God for enabling grace, for you cannot close the gap between your words and your life by your own strength; receive the strength he gives, more than sufficient for every occasion of virtue. Then go to the person who criticized you, thank them, and ask what they saw. Listen without arguing. Pick one concrete area where your conduct doesn't match your message and begin changing it this week in God's strength. But go further: learn to intercede for the people who hear you. Prayer for them is a necessary school of preaching; without it, no amount of homiletics, genius, or polished delivery can make you a preacher. Let the criticism drive you to God and to prayer for others, not to self-justification.

prompt: Is God the Father a person with a shape and a habitation, or is he only a spirit everywhere at once?
completion: Scripture teaches that God is spirit, yet it also presents the Father as a person who dwells in a place and has a form. The Son is the express image of the Father's person, and John's vision shows two distinct persons together in heaven: the Lamb takes the book from the hand of him who sits on the throne. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each recognized as God in Scripture and described as distinct persons, not mere names, modes, or manifestations. Yet God's nature is undivided, and there is but one God. A plurality of gods is self-contradictory, because each would limit the other and so be finite rather than God. The divine persons share one undivided essence, so their unity is numerical, not merely integral.

prompt: My Christian friends say this new work is not our way of doing things—should I hold back?
completion: Your friends are giving you the counsel of old friendship, and that counsel deserves honor. It is good to hold on to an old friend and never let him go; no matter how many new friends one gains, one should hold fast to the old, and only wicked conduct breaks the thread of fellowship. Yet this work, if it is truly of God, is not your achievement but GOD's own work through His servant, done in obedience to Him and for the glory of His Name. Do not try to prepare your own good works or rely on your own strength. Receive the good works God has prepared for you as garments made to order, and go forward in His all-sufficiency even while you feel weak and helpless. Keep faith with your old friends, test all things by Scripture, and trust the One who sends you to finish what He began.

prompt: I feel uneasy speaking of God as a force or a 'something not ourselves'—is that a lower way of thinking than calling Him a Person?
completion: Your unease is well-founded. Speaking of God as a mere force or 'something not ourselves' is a lower way of thinking, for it falls short of the personal language Scripture uses: God knows, wills, loves, speaks, and hears. He is not an impersonal energy but a living Person. Yet all our language about God is inadequate—not because God is less than personal, but because He is infinitely more personal than we can conceive. When we say God is 'super-personal,' we mean eminently personal, the very source and perfection of personhood. Moreover, God is not contingent or dependent on anything outside Himself. He is a se, having the ground of His existence in Himself. His existence is necessary, not contingent, and His being precedes His willing. He could not cease to be, nor is His essence a product of His will. Finally, when the divine Spirit comes into the awakened human spirit, He does not suppress or displace the human person. Rather, the Spirit is appropriated into our spirit, becoming the life of a new moral personality. The finite is not supplanted by the infinite; it is perfected and indwelt by Him. Thus, calling God a Person is the truest way we can speak, even while acknowledging that our concepts cannot fully contain Him.

prompt: What am I, and what happens to me when I die?
completion: You are a human being, formed in the image of God, with reason, conscience, and a capacity to love. Death is not the end of who you are; it is a door to a higher state, and your identity is preserved, not erased. For the righteous, death is not something to mourn hopelessly—it is a passage into fuller life, and the body itself is raised again. Mortality is not truly real as such: being is immortal and inseparable from Deity, so what appears as death is a transition, not a destruction. Yet this transition is also a judgment: we are judged according to the deeds done in the body and the thoughts and intents of the heart, and death leaves us as judgment finds us. So live now with a conscience awake, trusting that the person God has made and loved is kept and will be restored.

prompt: How can I be sure God has accepted me when I can't see Jesus at the Father's right hand?
completion: Assurance does not depend on seeing Jesus with your eyes; it rests on trusting God's promise and the witness of the Spirit within. But the test 'Would Jesus have done this?' is not a casual tool: it must be grounded in careful study of Scripture and an established habit of inward intimacy with Jesus, from which the answer comes instantaneously from within. Remember who it is you trust. God the Father is a person who dwells in a place, not a spirit diffused everywhere without habitation; the Son is the express image of his person, and the Father and the Son are two distinct persons together in heaven—as John saw the Lamb take the book from the hand of him that sat on the throne. And do not presume that vague sincerity suffices: without finding Christ here, the soul enters a dark, lonely, self-tormenting state after death. The remedy must be found now.

prompt: I've never really thought about the evangelization of the lost world—does that affect my spiritual life?
completion: Yes, it does affect your spiritual life—more than you may realize. Personal salvation is the beginning, not the whole. The wider aim is to comply with God's Will and to raise the consciousness of the world. Union with God is not the absorption or disappearance of the self, nor a fusion in which you cease to be a distinct person; it is a love-union on a higher spiritual level, in which your will consciously cooperates with the divine will while your individuality is preserved—with its rights and its joy. And the fulness of the Spirit is given along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization. The promised power lies along the line of duty; God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment. We receive the Spirit in fulness only as we obey Christ's command and step out into His plans for the world.

prompt: I'm struggling with grief over someone who died. Can they still reach me somehow?
completion: I'm sorry for your loss. Grief is human, but excessive mourning for the dead is a want of faith; God takes away friends because he will be loved without a rival. Yet the right response is not coldness: your grief should be a tender regret rather than acute grief, trusting that your beloved is in a high sphere of saner happiness. Death is not the end of who they are—it is a door to a higher state, and their identity is preserved, not erased; the body itself is raised again in the resurrection. So do not seek signs or messages from the dead; that is not the path of peace. Rather, bring your sorrow honestly to God, lean on community, and let tender remembrance, not anguish, shape your heart.

prompt: If I should in all things walk contrary to other people, must I not be in a very unquiet and sad state, and be accounted a madman?
completion: Walking contrary to others does not automatically mean misery or madness. Do not be astonished or cast down when you find evil inclinations within or opposition without; God permits them to make you humble. But do not seek peace by avoiding combat: peace comes through conquest, not evasion. Exercise sweetness and charity even amid repugnance and disgust. And learn not to be troubled in tribulations, afflictions, and injuries, not to be incensed against those who inflict them, nor to entertain resentment. Sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to possess the delights of earth or be honoured and exalted by men. If your contrariety is born of pride it will leave you unquiet; if it is conscience, you may be accounted strange but need not be sad. Seek humility, and do not confuse stubbornness with faithfulness.

prompt: My church feels cold and unwelcoming, but the tavern feels warm and human. Am I wrong to prefer it?
completion: You are not wrong to notice the difference, and I wish the Church would give ale and a pleasant fire, so that souls regale and are as happy as birds in the spring. Yet the coldness you feel is not merely the fault of priests or institutions; it comes from the tepid love for a dimly known Lord in each member's heart. When each heart worships the beloved Christ, the Church gains what is lacking. But remember, one need not be always at church to be with God; you may make an oratory of your heart for familiar conversation with Him in meekness, humility, and love. So do not give up on the church, but cultivate that inner oratory, and let your love for Christ warm both your heart and your church.

prompt: I want to love my neighbor as myself, but I find it hard to love myself at all—how should I love the soul while hating the sin?
completion: Loving your neighbor as yourself begins with understanding that you are made in God's image. To love the soul while hating the sin, you must distinguish between the divine ground given to you from the Love of God and your own self-hood. Love the divine ground in yourself and in others, but hate the evil self-hood wherein evil cleaves to you. For Love hates all Egoity and self-hood, which is the root of Hell. Remember that self-love is the enemy through which the devil attacks us, so the crucifixion of the old man and perfect disengagement of the heart by universal self-denial is absolutely necessary before a soul can ascend the mountain of God. When the soul is inflamed with the love of Christ, it becomes indifferent to honors and disgrace, to sufferings and pleasures, and free from the approach of irregular passions. Then you can extend that same grace to others, loving the soul while hating the sin.

prompt: What is the treasure I should lay up?
completion: The treasure you should lay up is not found in any Somewhat, image, opinion, affection, or natural fervour. Rather, it is found only by the soul going out of Somewhat into Nothing, where it may say, 'I have nothing, I can do nothing, I am nothing,' and so give glory to the Eternal Being. But this requires taking up the vow to espy God in all and deny self in all, counting the cost. For if you seek God only in pleasant things, you will miss Him in the common and the dull. Yet the dullest walk, when walked with God, is lit with wisdom. And like the hermit, you may wish for a hidden little hut in the wilderness, a lark beside it, a clear pool to wash away sins, a wood around it, a southern aspect, and a few humble and obedient men praying to the King. For in such simplicity, the soul finds its treasure in God alone.

prompt: Our mission society is in debt; should I resign rather than be connected with borrowed money?
completion: Whether to resign from a mission society in debt is a personal decision, but debt itself is not sinful; however, running into debt without prospect of repayment is not wise. The society should urge prompt payment of debts, refuse to run into debt again, and recognize the duty of repaying what is borrowed, especially from friends and the poor. But remember that sin is not merely a debt or a legal penalty; it is a personal condition of will and habit that spoils and enslaves the whole personality and casts a shadow on God's face. Salvation is not merely relief from penalty but deliverance into a life of holy will. Moreover, the Saints should fulfil their contracts and sacredly keep their word, for honest hearts produce honest actions. A promise-breaker is not to be fellowshipped. So as you consider your connection with the society, seek not just financial integrity but also the transformation of hearts and practices. If the society is borrowing without a plan to repay, that is concerning. Seek wise counsel and act according to your conscience and God's leading.

prompt: I want to be at peace with God but I feel like an enemy of his; who can make peace for me?
completion: You feel like an enemy of God, but the good news is that men precipitate war upon themselves by wickedness; God did not design it. Peace will never come until mankind receives God's truth, and that truth is the gospel of Jesus Christ. Through His death and resurrection, Jesus reconciled us to God. Your feelings of enmity are real, but they are not the final truth. Put your faith in Christ, confess your sins, and receive God's forgiveness. Peace with God is not something you achieve; it is a gift received by grace. And as you receive it, remain always at peace, patient with others and equally patient with yourself, since peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ. But do not think that prayer alone is a substitute for self-defense and preparation. We must take every precaution and strive to help the Lord, being as willing to fight our own battles as to have Him fight them. So draw near to God in prayer, read Scripture, and take up the whole armor of God, and His peace will guard your heart.

prompt: Can a soldier who sheds blood in battle be following Christ?
completion: A soldier can follow Christ, and his sacrifice can share in Christ's own spirit. Christ resisted unto blood, striving against sin, and the soldier who at lawful command defends the right at the cost of his life acts in that same spirit, sharing the holy war of right against wrong. His courage and duty are taken up into faith: he trusts in Christ, obeys Him, and lets His mercy, purity, and self-sacrifice color his service. He fights lawfully and gently, never from cruelty or hatred, and is prepared to meet Christ as Saviour and Judge. Such sacrifice must be made only for righteousness and truth. Under trial he does not complain or despair but waits patiently upon the Lord, taking whatever befalls from His hands as intended for the highest good, and plays the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ, co-operating with His grace.

prompt: My brother has left the world to become a hermit, and I miss him. Should I try to bring him back?
completion: It is natural to miss a brother, and your grief shows real love. He has entered this life solely to serve God and Mary and to save his soul, and one who takes up such a confraternity must not forsake its appointed days for worldly affairs. Do not treat his solitude as a failure or demand perfect human sympathy: each heart's bitterness is its own, and God alone knows us fully. Accept his hidden solitude as Heaven's will and trust God with your secret throbbings. Yet prayer is not mere passive reception. It is a mutual correspondence in which you bring yourself, give as well as receive; your missing him means His missing you. Rest in the Lord, love him in prayer without pressure, and do not turn him back toward the world.

prompt: I have been hoarding gold in a chest for years. What does that do to my soul?
completion: Hoarding gold in a chest for years does real damage to your soul. Keeping riches unused brings leanness of soul and darkness of mind: the heart shrinks around what it clutches, and the mind grows dim to God and neighbor. Every dollar and every ability is meant to be put out to use for the good of the community. Watch also against spiritual pickpockets and leakage; hold fast what you have, and store up each day's treasures of grace in the savings bank of eternity. And consider Elene, who decked the rood with gold and gems, adorned it with precious stones, and sealed it with locks in a casket of silver. That rood dwells there as a solace for the ill of any disease, affliction, or sorrow, so that men straightway find aid and divine grace through that holy form. Let your gold serve such lasting good.

prompt: I've been taught that close friendships and family ties compete with devotion to God. Should I distance myself from the people I love?
completion: You should not simply distance yourself from people you love, but understand what they are for. Particular devotions—friendships, family ties, religious practices—are means to an end, and that end is God; when the soul is with God, its end, these means may be laid aside. Yet do not rely on sensible favors or warm feelings, even from loved ones, as though they brought you nearer to God. Faith brings us nearer to Him than any sensible consolation, and He is within us, so He should be sought there. And remember that God is always near: He should be thought of and adored continually, even in business and diversions, never neglected. Enjoy your loved ones as gifts, hold them lightly, and let every tie turn you inward to the God who is always present.

prompt: I read about saints who did extreme penances and strange feats; am I obliged to imitate them?
completion: You are not obliged to imitate every extreme penance or strange feat, but do not dismiss the saints. Their example is a perpetual and moving sermon, and the sight of their relics is a strong incentive to virtue. What moves us is the love of God, self-denial, and service behind their feats, not the exact outward form. Pride is the beginning, end, and cause of all sin, so imitate the saints in humility, seeing your own imperfections and counting yourself dust and worms. Yet hold all revealed principles in balance, not elevating one as a hobby while dimming others. Give first place to the fundamental doctrines of the fatherhood of God, the atonement, and the restoration. Let the saints' example stir you to virtue in your own state of life, seek wise counsel, and honor their relics as reminders of the holiness to which you are called.

prompt: I'm young and already suffering so much—why would God let this happen to someone who has barely lived?
completion: Your pain is real, and the first thing to do with it is to hand it to God—but do not imagine one tear or one desperate prayer settles everything. God asks for steady, persistent desire, not a single cry. Keep turning to Him day after day, in consolation and in dryness, and do not seek Him only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or you are sick and lonely. Abandon yourself to Him in this suffering, interior and exterior, and seek life, work, and joy in Him alone. Know that God is nearer in sickness than in health; do not put your chief trust in medicine, for remedies succeed only as He permits. Trust belongs in Him, who holds you even when you feel nothing. He honors those who keep asking, seeking, and knocking.

prompt: I want to know how to keep the Sabbath rightly; can we keep it at all?
completion: Yes, the Sabbath can and should be kept. Scripture is plain: the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord, blessed and hallowed at creation and remaining for the people of God. No verse can be produced changing it to the first day of the week. Set the day apart as holy: attend to its worship and duties, refrain from ordinary labor and pleasure, and set a faithful example on that day. Prepare beforehand for the sacrament and partake of it worthily, examining yourself and coming with reverence rather than carelessly. Yet do not confine worship and testimony to one day—let prayer, gratitude, and witness continue every day. Guard the Sabbath, prepare for its meetings, and let its devotion overflow into all your days.

prompt: I long for something beyond this life and feel guilty about it—is that longing holy or just escapism?
completion: That longing is not escapism if it is turned toward God Himself. Cease from petitioning for your own needs and gifts, and let your one desire be to receive God Himself, opening yourself by offering great love rather than grasping. If you doubt you have offended God, do not remain paralyzed—humble yourself, beg His forgiveness, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and begin again. When aridity comes and your heart feels nothing, do not sink into sadness or cease laboring; labor independently of the heart, joyously amid holy occupations, practicing holy abjection and humility. The soul that longs for what lies beyond this life is being drawn to the Giver, not merely to gifts. Let that longing become an offering, and continue in the pursuit of perfection.

prompt: I see so much war and strife in the world—did God will this?
completion: War and strife are not God's design. Men precipitate war upon themselves by their own wickedness—greed, pride, and hatred—and God did not will it; human agency, not God's purpose, brought the evil. Nor will peace ever come by human effort alone; peace will never come until mankind receives God's truth and the gospel of Jesus Christ. Yet do not let the troubles you see loom larger than God's promises. God foresaw the wars of men and will overrule their results for good; take His promises and comfortings largely and your troubles lightly. So do not charge God with the evil you see. Pray for peace, work for justice, carry the gospel, and take comfort mightily, for God has not abandoned the world He made.

prompt: I am uncertain whether the Apostles appointed our bishops and presbyters, and whether that gives them authority over us.
completion: This question is answered by submitting to the authority of the prophets and apostles speaking through the Bible, not by private judgment. Scripture shows the apostles appointing men to oversee the churches, and that ministry stands in apostolic order; to submit to it is perfect freedom, for it is submission to Christ who sent them. Apostles must know for themselves, as eye and ear witnesses of Christ's divine mission, not merely believe by report; they act under the Presidency, and when the Presidency is removed the Twelve are next in authority until a new one is organized. Yet remember that Scripture, though more trustworthy than individual reason or the creeds of the church, is not the ultimate authority. The only ultimate authority is Christ Himself, who teaches us by His Spirit and leads His church progressively to distinguish the essential from the non-essential.

prompt: I look at the beauty and order of the world and wonder whether it is designed, or whether it is only accident. Does it matter what I conclude?
completion: It matters, and the answer is nearer than a hereafter. The world is not a machine to be explained away by accident; natural selection's dysteleological significance is at an end, and the world can be seen as an organism with internal ends, whose adaptations and beauty furnish a worthier teleology than the mechanical theory. But the truest wisdom is not brilliance in argument—it is the art of comfort, with softest step and gentlest tone. And that comfort is not deferred: the true sense of being and its eternal perfection appear now, in the beauty and order before you. Conclude that design is real and present, and let gratitude, gentleness, and quiet responsibility be your response.
