Recognize that everyone has faults and weaknesses. God loves you unconditionally, and your worth is rooted in being created in His image. However, be aware that pity and mercy are not pure virtues; they exist because somebody was made poor and unhappy. Pity would be no more if we did not make somebody poor. The tree of Mystery and Deceit grows in the human brain, so examine whether your self-image is rooted in truth or in deceptive patterns. Sanctification requires discovering and rooting out habitual disorders, guarding the senses, living in recollection, opening your interior to a spiritual director, and aiming at God's will rather than multiplying external works. Reject discourse, research, and tiresome care of self; confine yourself to the simple view of God and your own nothingness. In that simplicity, you will find peace and freedom from the burden of self-condemnation.

prompt: I'm a parent responsible for my children and the loneliness of it is crushing—is God really watching over us?
completion: Parenting is a demanding and often lonely role, but you are not alone. God is watching over you and your children. The Bible assures us that God cares for the sparrows and will certainly care for you. Your feelings of loneliness are valid, but they don't reflect reality. God is ever nigh, appearing like a father to the lost child, kissing him, and leading him by the hand to his mother. Even when you feel isolated, God is present, ready to comfort and guide you. Lean on Him in prayer, and seek support from your community. Remember that God is always near and should be thought of and adored continually, even in business and diversions, not neglected. Trust that He will provide the strength and companionship you need. You are doing a sacred work, and God sees your efforts. When you face loss or chastisement, see it as the dealing of a loving Father who means to give something better, and who supports with one hand while smiting with the other.

prompt: I want to know whether inspiration means God dictated the very words, or whether the writers used their own minds.
completion: Inspiration means that God guided the biblical writers to record His revelation accurately. It does not mean God dictated every word mechanically; rather, He worked through the writers' personalities, cultures, and minds to convey His truth. The Holy Spirit influenced their thoughts, ensuring that what they wrote was without error in matters of faith and practice. So, the writers used their own minds, but under divine supervision. This view upholds the Bible's authority while respecting human agency. Inspiration is an influence upon the mind, not the body, securing a record of revelation sufficient for its religious purpose rather than a model history or scientific text. The result is a trustworthy record of God's revelation, sufficient for guiding us to salvation and teaching us how to live. However, faith in Christ comes first, and belief in the Bible as inspired follows logically; belief in the Church precedes belief in the Bible. The written Word is an instrument by which the Spirit leads us to itself within us. The Word which teaches must be living in the literal Word and the Spirit of God in the literal sound, or else one is but a Teacher of the Letter.

prompt: I keep a small attachment I know God asks me to give up. What should I do?
completion: It's common to struggle with attachments, even small ones. If you know God is asking you to give something up, the first step is to acknowledge that and bring it to God in prayer. Ask for the strength and willingness to let go. Don't be discouraged if you fail; humble yourself, beg God's forgiveness, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and continue in the pursuit of perfection. Surround yourself with supportive people who can encourage you. Remember that God's commands are for your good, and letting go will ultimately bring freedom. Take small steps, and trust that God will help you. If you stumble, don't dwell on guilt; instead, turn back to God and keep moving forward. Rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods; continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to God. Keep on rejoicing even when it feels ineffectual, counting it all joy in temptations and trusting God to make the reckoning good.

prompt: I am a young woman and my sister mocks my new religion, saying my head is turned—how should I answer her?
completion: When your sister mocks your new religion, it can be hurtful, but try to respond with grace. You might say something like, 'I understand you're concerned, but this faith has brought me peace and purpose. I'm not trying to offend you; I just want to live out what I believe.' Avoid arguing or defending yourself too much. Instead, focus on showing love and respect. Over time, your actions may speak louder than words. Pray for your sister and ask God to soften her heart. Remember that Jesus faced mockery too, and He responded with love. Keep your head up and stay true to your convictions. In prayer, the raised head and uncovered face are forced by a sweet necessity, not by our own intention. Conceal this change from others except in special instances. Mark a long visit, staring, and constant questioning as signs of ill-breeding, and 'perhaps,' 'may be,' and 'I dare say' as false sisters. Development is not mere innovation or heresy, nor a narrowing and hardening of theology by added dogmas; rather, it is the Church standing firm in her old truths while entering into and assimilating the new social and intellectual movements of the age.

prompt: I feel like I'm not doing enough for God and I keep adding more devotions—is that the right approach?
completion: It's natural to want to do more for God, and adding devotions can be good, but the key is that devotion suits every state of life. Whether you're in a cloister or in the world, your heart must remain on God amid exterior business. The spirit of the world must be shunned, so don't let worldly affairs crowd out interior recollection and prayer. In every occasion of virtue, turn to God and ask for enabling grace, for He gives strength more than sufficient. Remember that brief inward remembrances and acts of worship are acceptable prayers that fortify courage, even in danger. So, as you add devotions, ensure they help you keep your heart on God and rely on His grace, and include short acts of worship throughout your day.

prompt: The prophets seem obsessed with social injustice. Is that really central to Scripture?
completion: Yes, social injustice is central to Scripture. The prophets repeatedly condemn oppression and call for justice because God cares deeply about how we treat others. The Bible teaches that true religion includes caring for the vulnerable. This theme is also affirmed in the Book of Mormon, which contains nothing injurious or contrary to the Bible; all its teachings tend to make bad men good and good men better. Moreover, the oppression of the poor, the forcing of their labor to serve another's pomp and vanity, is done to Christ himself and falls under his severe judgment. It works with the Devil against the Kingdom of Christ, which consists only in Love. We must submit every matter to the Holy Scriptures as the only standard and the Holy Spirit as the only teacher, laying aside prejudice and asking simply what the testimony of Scripture is. So, while social injustice is not the entirety of Scripture, it is indeed a central concern.

prompt: Is it wrong to ask God to keep me out of hard trials, or should I welcome testing?
completion: It's not wrong to ask God to keep you out of hard trials. In fact, the cry to be kept from testing is the natural and right shrinking of the tender soul. Jesus himself prayed that the cup might pass from him. However, bitter cups and hard baptisms may be part of the making of character. The Bible says trials produce perseverance. So, while it's okay to ask for protection, we should also be willing to accept trials if they come, trusting that God will use them for our good. In all things, do everything as perfectly as you can for God, then think no more of the finished action but rather of what there is to be done. To discern God's will, ground the test 'Would Jesus have done this?' in careful study of Scripture and an established habit of inward personal intimacy with Jesus, so that the answer comes instantaneously from within. The key is to submit to God's will, whether that means being spared or being tested.

prompt: Why did our fathers put to death the Holy One if they knew He was the Christ?
completion: The fathers put to death the Holy One, but we must be cautious in speculating about their knowledge and motives. We know in part and must not be wise above what is written. God escapes the nets of our syllogisms, and we must keep to Holy Scripture rather than building on isolated texts. The Scriptures testify that the rulers did not understand, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. Yet we cannot fully fathom their hearts. We must be careful not to construct elaborate theories beyond what is revealed. Instead, we should humbly accept the testimony of Scripture and avoid presuming to know more than God has disclosed. Let us set our hope on Christ's return and the final judgment, which is both a motive to holiness and a source of inexpressible joy. And let us live under the holy Cross, drawing breath from above until the likeness of Jesus' death is traced in our lives.

prompt: I have more than I need and wonder whether my spending on myself is excessive—how do I judge my expenses?
completion: To judge whether your spending is excessive, consider that the Lord asks how your wealth was come by and what will be done with it. Greater means bring greater responsibility to spread righteousness and relieve misery. Remember that wealth belongs to the Lord and is uncertain; it must be used for the Gospel and the poor. Ask yourself if your purchases are necessary or just for comfort and luxury. Ensure you're giving generously to God's work and to the poor. Wealth is a tool for good, not an end in itself, and we must warn against covetousness and idolatrous love of property. Embrace self-denial and economy as a privilege that frees resources for the LORD and brings fuller joy. Also, consider whether your spending aligns with your values and brings you closer to God. Seek balance and avoid both extravagance and stinginess. Pray for wisdom and examine your heart.

prompt: I feel like everything I cling to eventually betrays me. Why does nothing hold?
completion: It is painful when what you lean on gives way, but every refuge grasped as a substitute for God will betray you back to Him. Nature, human love, work, pleasure, study—none can shelter the soul from God, for all things are in league with Him and cannot conspire against Him. Yet small capricious vanities are not trivial: a minor indulgence nursed can quietly displace God from the center, and that is where the betrayal begins. God uses no force; He does not compel the will. Your decision is made here, in the world, in your exact circumstances—not in some abstract realm. Keep yourself in His love by constant trust and obedience, and hard things become easy and sorrow is silver-lined with hope. You are not abandoned by the world but pursued by a Father who means your good.

prompt: Should I tell others about the specific answers to prayer in my life, even the very personal ones?
completion: Yes, you may tell of answered prayer—but let prayer itself be the cornerstone, not an afterthought. Prevailing prayer rests on Bible-recorded conditions: humility, forsaking sin, faith, obedience, and asking according to God's will in Christ's name. Examine whether what you would tell was truly sought in Christ's name, or merely a wish fulfilled. Let prayer be unselfish, interceding for others, including those unknown to you, with a sympathy quick, wide, and deep. On your knees, both in secret and in the companionship of believers, prayer is the one great central secret of holy living and serving, the first resort in every crisis great or small. When testimony flows from such prayer, it strengthens faith. Consider your motive—to glorify God or to draw attention to yourself—and share with humility, confiding intimate details with a trusted few.

prompt: What does it mean that the saints are living stones built up into a spiritual house?
completion: The image of living stones built into a spiritual house means believers are joined in Christ as a dwelling place for God, each stone alive and shaped by Him. A house must stand, so the Saints must be self-sustaining: producing what they need to eat, drink, or wear, living within their means, and keeping a year's or two years' provision against a day of scarcity. Yet provision is not the whole building. Amidst weighty employments, the saints reserved time for frequent retirement, conversing with God and themselves, and in their exterior functions raised their minds to heaven with holy sighs and desires, making all their actions in some measure an uninterrupted prayer and exercise of divine love and praise. And because a spiritual house is made of souls, temporal succor must be joined with redoubled labor for spiritual good—seeking the rooting out of sin and the establishment of God's grace in souls—so that the whole building grows holy in Christ the cornerstone.

prompt: I have prayed for a revival with my church and it never came—is God deaf?
completion: It is understandable to feel discouraged when you pray earnestly for revival and see no obvious result, but God is not deaf, nor has He failed. When He seems silent to our cries, it is to grant our main desire by doing what is most expedient for us; His delay is not indifference but a wiser answer. Yet do not conclude He is unwilling or unable to act today: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, and God can and does heal and revive in answer to prayer now. Remember that God, who understands all things, can hear the earnest supplication of the soul and our innermost thoughts—just as human invention enables communication across great distances, so He receives what is never spoken aloud. Therefore ask in faith, nothing wavering, leaving the outcome in His hands, and keep praying while you look for the deeper work He is doing in you and your church.

prompt: If my conscience has grown and changed through history, can it still be a revelation of God's mind?
completion: Conscience can develop as individuals and societies mature, but that does not make it a mere human invention. Still, we must not rest our knowledge of God's mind on moral development or on records alone, nor on a private experience detached from the historical facts. Faith is grounded first in the historical resurrection of Jesus Christ, witnessed and recorded. Then, making trial of that message, the believer comes to know the living Saviour directly: besides the records and witnesses, the Spirit of God bears record in the heart of the living Redeemer, and that witness exceeds all other evidence. And do not wait to feel more, weep more, or gain greater power before you act. This moment you can renounce sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender. A growing conscience may perceive a real moral order, but its surest ground is Christ risen, known through the Spirit within.

prompt: Why is chastity so important, and what are the eternal consequences of impurity?
completion: Chastity matters because the body and soul are meant for God, and impurity disorders both. Scripture warns that the impure shall not inherit the kingdom of God, so the stakes are eternal: unrepented impurity separates the soul from God, while purity of heart opens the way to the vision of God. Chastity is a most precious treasure, to be protected by prayer, by mortification, by modesty of the senses, especially the eyes, and by avoiding the occasions of temptation—for he who loves danger shall perish in it. Marriage is a moral provision, subject to increasing virtue, and chastity is the cement of civilization; infidelity to the marriage covenant is therefore to be condemned. In marriage, chastity is not possessiveness: jealousy and mistrust destroy affection, so spouses should give each other freedom, confidence, and a benevolence that grows more diffusive.

prompt: The Bible seems full of contradictions—how do I handle that?
completion: Apparent contradictions in the Bible usually dissolve on closer study—different authors, genres, purposes, and passages addressing different questions—but the final appeal is never to scholarship, custom, human opinion, or expediency. Submit every matter to the Holy Scriptures as the only standard, and to the Holy Spirit as the only teacher, laying aside prejudice and asking simply what the testimony of Scripture is. Then actually live by it: put its promises and directions to the test rather than merely professing them. Replace error with truth poured in through flood-tides of Love, for Christian perfection is won on no other basis. Where difficulties remain, hold them without fear, obey what is clear, and let the Word prove itself in a life lived by it.

prompt: How do I become one of the 'pattern men' God is looking for?
completion: To become a pattern man, begin with the inner life. Trifling with the objects of imagination and the senses keeps a man within the limits and instincts of his animal nature, shared with brute beasts. But by his intelligence, affections, and will—created in the image and likeness of God—he ought purely and directly to commune with God, to be united to Him, and to cleave to Him. Offer all your desires and liberty to God with a large and liberal heart, withholding nothing; the more liberal one is toward God, the more liberal God will be toward him, and the more fit he will be for greater graces. Finally, let honest self-examination reveal your wretchedness, and so accept troubles, temptations, and contradictions from men as advantageous, bearing them as God pleases. Guard the senses, cultivate prayer, serve others, and let small faithful choices become habitual.

prompt: I'm a mother worried my anxious thoughts are affecting my child. Do my thoughts really shape her?
completion: Your worry is understandable, and it should be taken seriously, because a mother's thoughts do form and mould her child's mind, for good or ill, through divine influence. Children read tone, tension, and atmosphere; anxious thought can shape the home as surely as words do. Much disease is mental contagion, spreading through association and fear, and fearful talk about sickness, fatigue, and exposure only feeds it. So counsel the opposite understanding: God is ever-present and omnipotent, and as the testimonies describe, children's complaints have disappeared through that understanding. Stand porter at the door of your own thought, shut out fear, and let love rather than dread set the atmosphere. Rightly ordered, your mental influence becomes a channel of blessing and healing to your child.

prompt: How may I try all things and hold that which is good, without standing in my own opinion as if I could not err?
completion: Test everything by Scripture and by its fruit, and hold fast only what proves good. The key to not standing in your own opinion is humility—learned in prayer, where you wait before God like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence. When it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. Stand porter at the door of thought: shut out unhealthy thoughts and fears, including thoughts of disease, contagion, and accident, so the body cannot suffer from them. But do not measure progress by claims or words. Test yourself by whether you live the supreme good and demonstrate healing; let fruits prove understanding. Recognize that you can err, seek wise counsel, change your mind when truth warrants it, and hold convictions charitably, distinguishing essentials from preferences.

prompt: I'm jealous of someone and it's poisoning my happiness. How do I deal with this feeling?
completion: Jealousy feels real, but it is a belief in lack—a suggestion that Life is not whole. Do not yield to that illusion or let fear and doubt overshadow your clear trust in God. Cling steadfastly to God and to His likeness, in which you and your neighbor both live, and refuse to accept the picture of sickness or sin as your identity. Where possessiveness or mistrust would confine another within narrow walls, release them into the freedom God gives, and let your care grow more diffusive. Keep on rejoicing even when the first dose of goodwill seems ineffectual, counting it all joy, and trust God to make the reckoning good. With calm trust, know that harmonious Life destroys the belief in what Life is not, and your peace returns.

prompt: I want to enjoy God now, but I am weighed down by the memory of my past sins—how do I set them at nought?
completion: The memory of past sins is serious, not something to wave away; unrepented sin accumulates and dulls the conscience, so let the weight drive you to repentance and reformation. But do not wait to feel more or weep more before you turn—you can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose, and God supplies the strength, with feeling following the surrender. I do not say this from above you: I confess my own faults too, and I stand with you as one who needs the same mercy. Together we look to the fountain opened for sin, following Christ who took our sins and made them His own. As we identify with the erring rather than judge them, the accusing memory loses its grip and we enjoy God now.

prompt: Should I vote, and how should I decide?
completion: Voting is how members in good standing express their true feelings on the propositions before them, and no one should violate conscience. A sister's vote counts equal with a brother's, and presiding officers depend on the voice of the people for their authority. Yet the authorities are presented and members are sincerely requested to act freely and independently: no one is told how to vote, and no one is injured for honest objections. So research the candidates and measures and vote your convictions, abstaining if uninformed. But do not let civic life become an excuse for idleness. Be industrious and thrifty, use your time and resources wisely, and remember that labor is indispensable and the elements of wealth are already around us. Vote freely, then work diligently, supporting yourself and others rather than depending on them.

prompt: I feel guilty enjoying my comfortable church while millions have never heard the Gospel—what should I do?
completion: Your discomfort is a good sign, but examine it: it is easy to enjoy a comfortable church while quietly looking down on those outside, as if we hold the truth and they must come to us. Instead, desire that all honest-in-heart come to know the truth, and share it freely. The Gospel must go to all nations so that every people has the privilege of receiving or rejecting it, leaving the wicked without excuse. Yet remember to distinguish the kernel of the Gospel from the historical forms in which it has been expressed—no single form, not even the earliest or most primitive Christianity, is the final or classic embodiment of the treasure. The vessel changes; the treasure does not. So support mission, welcome newcomers, and share freely, without absolutizing your own tradition, and take one concrete step this month.

prompt: There is a big feast day at the Marian shrine near me, but the crowds get wild and drunken. Should I still go?
completion: It is understandable to want to honor Mary on her feast day, but the servants of Mary should avoid her sanctuaries in times of feasting and excess, and help others avoid them too. When crowds grow wild and drunken, devotion is drowned in noise and disorder. Visit instead when the sanctuary is not thronged—a quiet weekday or early morning—when you can pray undisturbed. Yet do not think of the shrine or of joy as something to be feared: it is the privilege of the Saints to enjoy every good thing, since the earth and its fulness belong to the Lord, who has promised all to his faithful. Saints should be happy and may enjoy wholesome social recreation, keeping all things in moderation and in the Spirit of the Lord. So enjoy the good, avoid the excess, and let your devotion be peaceful and glad.

prompt: Is this war a judgment of God on our nation's sins?
completion: War is not a mere accident or purely a political failure; it is the natural penalty by which evil passions punish themselves under God's righteous constitution of the world. Lusts, covetousness, and injustice—whether in a nation or in individuals—carry their own consequences, and God's righteousness works through these ordinary laws of human nature. When a people give themselves to greed, pride, and oppression, the fruit is conflict and bloodshed. Yet even in judgment God remembers mercy: He will not quench nor slay the afflicted quite, and the wandering are not wholly forsaken. His preserving hand sustains those who suffer, and He asks only that the captive heart feel its woe and burthen and turn to Him. But we must take the Lord's warning to heart first for ourselves, confessing our own share in the sins that bring judgment, rather than standing apart in self-justification. Humble repentance, not blame of others, is the fitting response.

prompt: I am a woman and people say I am fickle. How should I live so that I am not ashamed?
completion: Being called fickle can feel like a heavy label, but it does not have to define you. The first counsel is to keep yourself in God's presence and to avoid hurry and anxiety, for over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Do not strive anxiously to prove others wrong or to remake yourself by force of will. Sanctification requires more than multiplying pious exercises: it requires discovering and rooting out habitual disorders, guarding the senses, living in recollection, and opening your interior to a spiritual director. Cut off irregular attachments, and aim at God's will rather than at multiplying external works. Let your courage be humble courage, grounded in a low esteem of self rather than confidence in your own powers; its greatness lies in humility, not in self-reliance. With patience and freedom from hurry, you can cultivate a faithful and settled character, trusting that God is patient with you and that your worth rests in Him.

prompt: I am a woman in the Church. Can I be baptized for my deceased father, or must a man do it?
completion: Vicarious baptism for the dead is a genuine practice in some Christian traditions, and it rests on the hope that those who died without the Gospel may be brought up into glory through the living. The dead are not beyond help; the living may act on their behalf, and baptism and vicarious ordinances can be offered for them. As for who may perform it, honor the father's presiding authority in the home and consult parents before extending calls to their children. A worthy man's priesthood is not confined to a ward or locality; he has the right to bless when requested in another's home. Distinguish God's once-for-all gift at Pentecost from the believer's personal appropriation of the Spirit by faith: the gift is not repeated per believer, nor does every believer automatically possess the Spirit's enduement without appropriation. Speak with your church leaders, trusting that God's purposes extend to those who have died.

prompt: I find myself despising people whose sins seem worse than mine—what does that say about me?
completion: Despising others for their sins often reveals more about us than about them. It can be a sign of pride, a way of reassuring ourselves that we are better than someone else. But sin is not a mere mistake or social failing; every sin is an insult to God, and its malice is measured by the greatness of God compared with the littleness of man. It is the greatest of evils, to be avoided at any sacrifice. Saints who harbor unforgiveness are more guilty and censurable than the one who sinned against them. We should dismiss envy, malice, and retaliation, and cultivate the spirit that cried, 'Father, forgive them.' Meet evil inclinations without astonishment or being cast down, accepting that God permits them to make you humble. Instead of comparing ourselves to others, measure yourself against God's greatness and recognize your own shortcomings, seeing others as fellow sinners in need of grace.

prompt: I am a widow with property and suitors pressing me to remarry. How should I decide?
completion: This is a significant decision, and it is wise to take your time. Above all, pray and wait on God for guidance, for true godliness is the first and absolutely needful qualification in a companion. Look at each suitor's character, values, and how he treats you and others, and weigh calmly other questions of suitableness. Marriage should be marked by mutual tender love and the bearing of each other's faults; beware of making marriage a matter of traffic or a money job, for unions made for money are warned against. Financial considerations matter, but they should not be the only factor. Let reformation include reparation: make good past wrongs, unpaid vows, or defrauded parties, restoring to the wronged party, or to the Lord where that is impossible. Beginning anew is not enough without making good what was broken. Talk with trusted family, friends, or a pastor who knows you well, and give yourself space to think clearly rather than being rushed by pressure.

prompt: I'm poor and ashamed of it. Does my poverty make my prayers worth less to God?
completion: No—your poverty does not make your prayers worth less to God. Scripture is full of poor people whose prayers were heard: Hannah, the widow with two mites, the beggar Lazarus, and the psalmist who cried out in his distress. God does not measure prayers by wealth but by the sincerity of the heart. Do not turn prayer into a request for riches; wealth is not a proper object of prayer. Pray instead for what you need to keep yourself and your family from want—daily bread, honest work, and strength to endure. Poverty is not degrading; it is no measure of a person's worth. The destitute have a right to food and to fellowship, and persons are esteemed by character, not by wealth or station. Far from being negligible, the prayers of the poor and desolate rise with more than royal pomp and pierce the skies. Bring your need to God honestly, and do not be ashamed.

prompt: I am tempted to compare myself with others and strive to outdo them—is emulation really sinful?
completion: Emulation is not automatically sinful, but it is dangerous. Comparing yourself with others can spur you to grow, yet it easily curdles into envy, pride, and rivalry. The question is what you are aiming at. If you strive to outdo someone so that you may look better than they do, the motive is vanity and the fruit is division. Remember that amusements and recreations reveal character; train yourself to find pleasure in what invigorates, brightens, and elevates body, intellect, and spirit, and refuse what dulls and depraves. If comparison stirs you to diligence, generosity, and usefulness, it can serve a good end. But moral ignorance or sin is never irrelevant to success: it hinders demonstration and must be overcome. Apply this test to every thought, word, and deed: does it render you more humble, more recollected in God, and more strong? If not, fear lest all is not according to God, acceptable to him, or profitable to yourself.

prompt: I'm watching my youth and beauty fade and it terrifies me—how do I make peace with passing like a rose?
completion: What you feel is real and common: youth and beauty do pass, like a rose that blooms and fades. But you are not only a rose. Human life is not merely the life of roses and leaves. Though roses and leaves pass, our life is not theirs, and the longings that Nature moves in us promise their own fulfillment—they are not mockeries but prophecies. Meet this passing in prayer, understood as a humble waiting before God like a beggar. Keep your mind in his presence; when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. And place Jesus crucified before your mind. Measure your present sorrows against his thorns, and you will find that the crosses of this world appear as roses. Turn to what does not wither: character, love, wisdom, and friendship with God. Grieve honestly, but let the passing of beauty teach you to hold lightly what was never meant to be grasped.

prompt: I worry my daughter spends every evening at dances—how many is too many for a Latter-day Saint family?
completion: There is no fixed number of dances that makes a Latter-day Saint family faithful or unfaithful. Saints are meant to be happy, and wholesome social recreation is a good gift, not a sin to be rationed. The question is whether the dancing is kept in moderation and in the Spirit of the Lord. Is your daughter growing in kindness, self-control, and devotion, or drifting from prayer, study, and family life? Is the company wholesome? A rigid rule about evenings will not settle these questions; wise, loving conversation will. Set reasonable expectations, keep the Sabbath and family time sacred, and help her learn moderation. Teach her also to deal honestly and to pay what she owes; one who will not pay is undeserving of the fellowship of the Saints. And let your home be open: invite neighbors in, love your neighbor as yourself, and do not shun the drunken, the weak, or the erring, since they ought to be saved as well as anyone else.

prompt: I pray to Christ as a divine being who stands beside God; am I threatening the monarchy of God by giving him a pre-existence independent of the Father?
completion: No—praying to Christ as a divine being beside God does not threaten God's monarchy. Christian faith confesses Christ as divine, distinct from the Father yet one with him in purpose and honor. A pre-existence independent of the Father need not rival God's rule; it is the Son's own eternal being, subordinate in role but not in nature. Nor confuse God's kingdom with the kingdoms of this world: no present king or ruler has been called of God or lawfully anointed. Their dominion is usurped, and God merely overrules them as he did Nebuchadnezzar and Cyrus. God's kingdom is a literal kingdom on the earth, of living and resurrected saints, with laws and administrators, and Christ will reign over all the earth. Draw confidence from God's revealed names: plead 'the Father of the fatherless' and 'Jehovah Jireh' as his own pledges, and rely on them in need.

prompt: My work keeps me from my family and I see my children growing independent and disrespectful; what is my duty?
completion: Your duty is to provide for your family, but not at the cost of your children's moral discipline. The industrial employment that keeps you from home and undermines parental authority is a danger to domestic duties. As a Christian, you are called to counteract whatever interferes with the rudiments of moral discipline. This means resisting work demands that keep you from your family and actively teaching your children respect and obedience. But do not be behind with the whip; instead, be in advance of your children in mind and affection. Provide innocent amusement and lead them so they delight to follow you. In your trouble, speak to God lovingly and humbly, as a child to its mother. Complain to Him alone, not proudly to others, and trust Him to guide you.

prompt: I'm anxious about the future—how do I trust God with it?
completion: Trusting God with the future means committing your wants to His care without anxious hoarding. Use all proper means diligently—planning, working, and watching—but remember that God is the one living Agent, and all human workers are only His instruments. Cast all your care upon Him, for He cares for you. Anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. Keep yourself in God's presence, and avoid hurry and over-eagerness, for over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. So, do your part, but do not treat your effort as the real support. Pray as if everything depends on God, and work as if everything depends on you, but ultimately rest in His sovereignty.

prompt: I want to obey God's commands but feel I have no power to do so—what does the Gospel offer me?
completion: The Gospel offers you forgiveness and new life in Christ, and it also offers you enabling grace. God's precepts are promises—all He requires He gives. So when you face an occasion of virtue, turn to God and ask for His enabling strength. He promises strength more than sufficient. 'Thou shalt not' becomes His assurance to preserve you from sin as you trust Him. Do not wait for a greater feeling; you can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose. God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender. Through faith in Jesus, the Holy Spirit empowers you. Confess your weakness, ask for help, and trust that God will supply what you need to obey.

prompt: I am more comfortable in my study with books than in my closet with God. Is that a danger?
completion: Yes, it is a danger if your study replaces your closet. The closet is the heart's study, where thought is born and where more is learned about preaching than in libraries. Books can inform, but they cannot substitute for intimate communion with God. If you are more comfortable with books than with God, you may be avoiding Him. Use your study to understand Scripture, but let the closet be the place where your heart is formed. As a Scientist, you are a law unto yourself, so mental malpractice cannot harm you asleep or awake. Measure your ability to stay with God outside the closet by your ability to stay with Him in it. Great waiting in the closet is the source of great victories outside it. Do not settle for hasty visits.

prompt: I say little prayers during the day but they feel empty and mechanical. Is that worth anything?
completion: Yes, little prayers are worth something, even if they feel empty. No true prayer is lost; supplications accumulate as a memorial before God. The longer the answer waits, the larger it becomes. So do not despise your short prayers. Keep praying at appointed times, regardless of feeling, and include family prayer. Remember that prayer is not just asking God to do everything; it is also helping God accomplish what is asked. Be willing to act as He leads. Brief inward remembrances and acts of worship are acceptable prayers that fortify courage, even in danger. Trust that God hears and will answer in His perfect timing. If they feel mechanical, pause to refocus, but do not give up.

prompt: How do I respond when I'm falsely accused or persecuted?
completion: When falsely accused, bring whatever men say before the tribunal of your own conscience. Enter within and judge yourself justly: neither excuse the soul without reason nor accuse it lightly, but examine honestly, so that it neither grows insolent nor loses courage. If conscience truly accuses, amend; if after reflection it does not, then human praise profits nothing and blame loses nothing—it is no loss to be despised without if you are innocent within. Be patient and silent, rejoicing in the Lord. Do not seek revenge or the accuser's punishment; forgo prosecution where you can and desire his repentance and faith, valuing his soul above your name. Pray for him, return good for evil, and leave the outcome to God in peace.

prompt: I'm fighting a temptation nobody knows about and I feel completely alone in it—does God see me in that fight?
completion: God sees you, and you are not alone. He tempts no one, will not allow you to be tempted beyond your strength, and with every temptation provides a way of escape; patient endurance is crowned with life. Distinguish the sources: some temptations rise from your own concupiscence, some from the evil spirit; guard your senses, practise mortification and temperance, and avoid occasions, and you will greatly diminish their force. Yet remember that temptation is not sin but a means of proving virtue and gaining great profit, for the life of man upon earth is a warfare. Light temptations, suspicions, sadness, depression, and pusillanimity are mere nothings—a good will puts them to flight by lifting the soul to God. He sees your hidden fight and is faithful.

prompt: I have an idea of infinity, but is my idea itself infinite, or only finite—and does that matter for proving God?
completion: Your idea is finite, but it can truly intend the infinite God. Do not confuse infinity with the indefinite: God's infinity means no limits at all—transcendent yet present, and intensive, an inexhaustible resource of spiritual life whose glory is its expression. The arguments from change and from order are cumulative probable evidence: they corroborate the intuition of God, proving an indefinitely great cause and an intelligent will, yet they have real defects and cannot by themselves reach personality and righteousness. So apply their results to one personal Cause, Contriver, and Lawgiver, and ascribe infinity and perfection to Him as what the mind cannot but think—while the anthropological argument supplies what they lack. Your finite idea matters because it is the mind's necessary reach toward that one Being.

prompt: I want to be liked and praised for my good works. Is that wrong?
completion: Wanting to be liked is not wrong; you were made to value love and approval. The mistake is straining to be something other than what God made you. Accept your condition and be that well, honoring the Master Workman and seeking to please God's will. To be gentle and kind, modest and truthful, full of faith and integrity and doing no wrong—this is of God, and such goodness sheds a halo of loveliness and makes the countenance beam. Yet do not locate the joy of God's love in your merit, your charitable or social work, your learning, or any arbitrary favouritism. That joy lives in the continually maintained attitude of longing, grateful giving, and receiving Christ. Do your good works honestly, receive praise as a gift, and let your gladness rest on that obedient communion rather than on being noticed.

prompt: I am afraid of death and the dark valley—how can I face it with peace?
completion: Fear is natural, but hear the testimony of the saints: the Lord deals gently with His dying servants. The valley is not dark, because the Lord is there; the sting of death is taken away, and victory is given through Jesus Christ. Peace is not passive—meet sufferings, afflictions, and injuries with a strong will to bear them for God, so that their bitterness remains full of peace and tranquillity. Learn not to be troubled in tribulations, not to be incensed against those who inflict them, nor to entertain resentment. Sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to possess the delights of earth or be honoured and exalted by men. Then dread cannot destroy you, and you walk toward the Lord who is light, and beyond death to resurrection.

prompt: I have a hard time accepting that God allows bad things to happen to good people—how do I trust His will?
completion: It's understandable to struggle, but Scripture calls us to receive all things from God's hand—sweet or bitter—equally, because His love makes them acceptable. Afflictions are not signs of His absence but of His fatherly care. When we see trials as coming from a loving Father, they become consolation, not curse. Moreover, if you love God, all things—even grief and sin—will turn to your good, even when the means are unseen. All evil of whatever kind happens only by God's permission and ever for some good end; it could not be except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him Who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. Therefore commit all things without fear to the Providence of God, trusting that He steadies His own ark and guides His people.

prompt: What does it mean that the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath?
completion: This phrase from Jesus means that the Sabbath was made for man's benefit, but it is not a bondage or a mere Jewish custom. The seventh-day Sabbath is the memorial of creation, given at the beginning, and the sign of the cross, the seal that God sanctifies His people. Jesus spoke these words when His disciples were criticized for plucking grain, showing that human need takes precedence over rigid legalism—yet He did not abolish the Sabbath. Instead, He calls us to trust Him for the cost of keeping it holy. We are to keep the Sabbath holy, attending to its worship and duties, and setting an example of faithfulness on that day. And as we serve, we must remember that God's method is men, not methods, plans, or organizations; the Holy Ghost flows through men, not through machinery. The Sabbath serves our well-being, reminding us that we are not slaves to work but children of God who can trust Him enough to rest.

prompt: What does it mean to live 'in Christ' day to day—how does that change how I face my ordinary tasks?
completion: Living 'in Christ' day to day means recognizing that your life is hidden with Christ in God, and that your hope is anchored in the vision of the Lamb upon the throne—not in calculating times and seasons. That vision grounds Christian hope amid trials and the humdrum. But Christianity is not a religious system or mere imitation of Christ; it is actual union with Him as indwelling life. Christ dwells in you as the life and source of all your experience and work. So as you face ordinary tasks—washing dishes, working at a desk, caring for family—you let Christ be formed in you, living the Christ-life and showing forth His excellencies as a re-living of His life in your place. You rest in His indwelling presence, holding to His person rather than mere theories, and He lives His life through you.

prompt: Can anyone search out the name of the Saviour, or is it beyond all men?
completion: The name of the Saviour is not hidden from those who seek Him with a sincere heart. While it may seem beyond human searching, God promises that those who seek will find. The name of Jesus is revealed in Scripture and proclaimed throughout the world. It is not a secret for the elite but a gift for all who call upon Him. True greatness is not measured by position, wealth, or worldly acclaim but by the number of beings a person loves and blesses and who love and bless him. Like Elene, whose heart mourned until the nails were found, we must seek with longing. Cyriacus bowed his head on Calvary and prayed the Lord of angels to reveal the unknown mystery. Then a sign in the form of fire rose where the nails were hidden, a leaping flame brighter than the sun, and the nails glittered from their burial-place like stars or gems set in gold. The people said with one accord that the miracle is of God, whom they formerly withstood. But remember: whoever wishes to steady the ark of God without being called has a dark spot in him, for God steadies His own ark, dictates His own affairs, and guides His people. So seek the name with humility, not with self-appointed zeal, trusting God to reveal it in His way.

prompt: I have been reading that God cares for the sparrow. How can I apply this to my own fears about my needs?
completion: When Jesus said that God cares for the sparrow, He was teaching that if God provides for small, seemingly insignificant creatures, He will certainly provide for His children. But God is not distant or uninvolved—He knows our needs before we ask, and He numbers the very hairs of our head. You can apply this by reminding yourself that your needs are intimately known to God and that He is faithful to provide. Fear often comes from focusing on what we lack, but faith focuses on God's detailed care. Yet we need His continual help, and that help comes through the holy habit of praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often. Since we must know before we love, such habits deepen our knowledge of Him and cast out fear. And remember that our longing for an enduring home is Nature's own cry in us, not an unholy strife; she who gives wings to birds will find out a way for us. Practical steps include: writing down your fears and giving them to God in prayer, recalling past times when He provided, and trusting that He will do so again.

prompt: I have lost my childhood faith and I want it back, but I don't know how. Can God still find me?
completion: Yes, God can still find you—but the way back is not a technique for managing your feelings. God sometimes hides Himself, and when He does, faith alone supports us and grounds all confidence in Him; yet faith is not a theory or a mood, and it uses prayer, Scripture, and fellowship as instruments without being bound to any of them. More than that, the soul must be converted and become as a child, turning again to God out of whom it proceeded, forsaking its own imaging, its lust, and every self-made centre. Stop curving inward to inspect your faith; turn outward to Him. In that turning, the Divine Vision is restored. Come as a child, trust the Father who seeks you, and let faith—not self-analysis—be your foundation.

prompt: How do I pray when I'm in danger and afraid for my life?
completion: When danger and fear for your life press on you, do not look at the storm or at your own strength—look at Christ, who is the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance. Abide in Him, and remember that you need His continual help, since prayer, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked through holy habit; we must know Him before we love Him. Yet do not think you must pray at length. Brief inward remembrances and short acts of worship—'Lord Jesus, have mercy,' 'You are my refuge'—are acceptable prayers and fortify courage even in danger. A single turning of the heart to Him is real prayer. Keep your eyes on Christ, offer these short acts often, and let His presence, not the length of your words, be your peace.

prompt: Are the saints the temple of God now, or is the temple in heaven something we are being prepared to enter?
completion: The saints are the temple of God now, but they are not the Holy City. The city is prepared for them, and the righteous dead have not yet been caught up; they wait for the resurrection. Believers are being built together as a temple—God's dwelling now—yet this temple is being prepared to enter the city God has prepared. Approach worship expecting peace, security against evil, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit; the saints testify that those who expect these shall find them, and if they seem absent, ask whether we have expected them rather than blaming God. And remember: only the pure in heart shall see God. Set yourself against all licentiousness and every form of impurity, for chastity and purity of heart are not optional but the very condition of seeing Him. Be built together in holiness, and so be made ready to enter the city.

prompt: I do not know what to pray for; how can I pray aright?
completion: Not knowing what to pray for is itself a place to begin—but prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, not an occasional exercise. Pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Bring even the smallest matter to Him, honouring Him by asking His guidance rather than taking any decision out of His hands. And remember that you need His continual help: praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked through holy habit, since we must know Him before we love Him. So make prayer a habit, not a crisis tool. Think on Him often, and you will come to know Him; knowing Him, you will love Him; loving Him, you will pray aright, with your heart searched, reformed, and wholly turned to Him.

prompt: My conscience tells me one thing and my neighbours another—can we both be right?
completion: It is possible for two people to differ in good conscience, but do not treat this lightly. Conscience can be mistaken, and unregretted sin accumulates and destroys the ability to do right; where your conscience accuses you, repent and reform rather than explaining it away. Yet judge your soul justly: neither excuse it without reason nor accuse it lightly or without reflection, so that it neither grows insolent nor loses courage. Bear patiently with the imperfections of others, for such forbearance is a great part of perfection and the practice of love of neighbour. Take your neighbour's view seriously, seek wise counsel, and where Scripture and clear teaching speak, follow them. Repentance for yourself, forbearance toward others, and a just, steady judgment of your own heart—this is the way forward in humility and love.

prompt: Is God a distant and gloomy being, or can I approach him as a father?
completion: God is not a distant, gloomy being to be dreaded. He is our Father, and his children may come to him freely. He listens when we pray and numbers the hairs of our heads, and his service is full of beauty and cheerfulness rather than gloom. Yet he who is united to God is one mind with Him, so out of regard for his sovereign honour we must never think or imagine in his presence what we would blush to have seen before men; we raise all thoughts to God alone and set him before our inward gaze as though he alone existed. Above all, we must not imagine God as the author of sickness, sorrow, or affliction. He is a loving Father who gives only good, and sickness is not his will, as the testimonies confess they had wrongly believed.

prompt: Why do some people respond to the gospel and others don't?
completion: In the simplicity of God's word, the gospel is plain: Christ died for our sins and rose again, and whoever believes is saved. Why some respond and others do not is not fully given to us, and we should say so frankly rather than dress it up in speculative philosophy. The message is simple enough for the humble to understand and enjoy. The first witnesses were competent, honest men whose testimony cost them worldly interests; their voluntary suffering is the strongest evidence of their truth, since imposture must have a motive and they had none. Yet we must never withhold the gospel from any people. It must go to all nations, so that all have the privilege of receiving or rejecting it, leaving the wicked without excuse.

prompt: What does it mean to worship God with my gold and my possessions like the Magi?
completion: The Magi brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the child Jesus, and their gifts show that we honor God with our possessions. Our wealth is not securely our own; it belongs to the Lord and is uncertain, a trust to be used for the Gospel and the poor. We guard against covetousness and the idolatrous love of property, holding our goods loosely for God's purposes. Worth is not measured by public display: hidden Christian worth is precious, and the prayers of the poor and desolate rise with more than royal pomp. Above all, we must not credit the success of God's work to the wealth, influence, or abilities of men. God chooses the poor, weak, and despised things to confound the mighty, so the glory belongs to Him alone, not to human riches or power.

prompt: I believe matter and Spirit both have power in my life. Is it possible to serve both?
completion: You cannot serve both matter and Spirit, for no one can serve two masters. To trust matter as a source of power is to serve mammon, and that must be expelled. Spirit alone is to be trusted and God alone served. We must separate Truth from error and Spirit from matter, denying any copartnership between them; they do not cooperate in man, nor coexist in healing. Material beliefs must be cast out rather than blended with faith. Nor is human will-power a faculty of Soul or a reliable means of governing oneself or others; it has no governing role. Truth and Love are the motive-powers of man. Choose to serve God alone, letting Spirit govern your life, and put away the belief that matter or mere will has genuine power over you.

prompt: Why doth Christ say that what is done to the least of these is done to him, and how doth a man do it to Christ himself?
completion: Christ says that what is done to the least of these is done to him because he dwells really and essentially in the faith of those who yield themselves to him. Christians are branches of the Vine and members of his Body, so what is done or withheld from the least of his brethren is done or withheld from Christ himself. Each of us casts his own burden on the Lord who is within him, and in Christ's strength we also bear the burdens of others, fulfilling the law of Christ. But we must not cling to independence or self-will, or insist on the right to please ourselves. Instead we take the servant's place after Christ's pattern, renouncing self-will and obeying even as Christ became obedient unto death.

prompt: I was punished harshly as a child for asking questions. Was that just?
completion: No, it was not just. A priest who seizes a weeping child and burns him in a holy place betrays God, and we must ask whether such things are done on Albion's shore. Yet I bring this trouble to You, O God, as a child to its mother, complaining humbly to You alone and not proudly to others. You are not the author of that cruelty. Your pattern is always to warn before You judge: You sent Noah before the flood, Abraham's plea before Sodom, and prophets before Jerusalem fell, appealing to man's reason and intelligence rather than striking without word. So the harsh punisher acted against Your manner, which persuades and warns. Teach me to trust Your love, to bring my questions to You, and to hear Your warnings with a reasoning heart rather than fear.

prompt: My faith feels like a very little light in a great night, and I wonder whether it is enough to live by.
completion: A little light is still light, and faith is our measured light in our night, given so that we may live meedfully and earn meed and thanks of God until at the end of woe our eyes are opened in clearness of light. It is not night if Christ be near; ask Him to abide from morn till eve and when night is nigh, for without Him we cannot live or dare to die. Yet this light is not a private feeling only: in mortality the temporal and spiritual are blended and cannot be separated, and the Church is a physical as well as a spiritual organization. So let your little faith be practical faith that practices the principles of the gospel, in ordinary duties and service, and it will be enough to live by.

prompt: What is the difference between ambition and service?
completion: Ambition seeks its own advancement; service seeks another's good. The deeper difference is quality, not quantity: service is measured by its quality and its aim to please God, not by how much is done or how visible it is. A small hidden act done well pleases Him more than a great public work done for notice; the main purpose is to do well rather than to do much. Wealth represents labor and industry, and to take it by force or by legislation is robbery, a principle that would crush all energy and enterprise. And service must be rightly aimed: the three worst services a man can serve are serving a bad woman, a bad lord, and bad land. Fidelity to what is unworthy is not service but complicity. True service honours God, the worker's labor, and worthy ends, and the test is what you would do if no one ever knew.

prompt: How can I know whether a work is really GOD's, if the money always seems to run short?
completion: Short funds are not proof that a work is not God's; many true works have been poor. The work of the Lord is best carried on within the landmarks of His word. The patronage of the world is not to be sought or depended upon, no debts are to be contracted, and all dependence is on God's blessing in answer to prayer. The Living God alone is Patron, and prayer is the only appeal. Ask whether the work is faithful to Scripture, bears good fruit, and trusts God rather than manipulating people. Remember that the work is God's own through many hands: those who pray and sympathize, though they never see the mission field, share in it as truly as the visible worker. Measure it by prayer, honesty, and fruit, not by the bank balance.

prompt: My conscience accuses me and I fear the judgment; is there an advocate who will defend me before Christ?
completion: Yes, there is an advocate: Jesus Christ, who died and rose and intercedes for us. Bring whatever men say or think before the tribunal of your own conscience, entering within to learn the truth, for human praise profits nothing if conscience accuses, and it is no loss to be despised without if you are innocent within. Where accusations are baseless, seek to remove them, reserving the glory of suffering for suffering endured for Christ's sake. But know that abiding in Him is not automatic: if the will abides in the words of Christ, His Word and Spirit abide in him, but if the will goes into the creature, one breaks off from Him. So keep yourself by abiding in resigned humility and a constant course of penitence and daily dying from the creatures, confessing your sin and trusting His mercy, rejoicing in the Lord in patience, silence, and peace.

prompt: What sins have we as a nation committed that brought this war upon us?
completion: This war came upon us in part because of our own sins, and a day of humiliation is fitting. We have shared in the tone of thought and life that produced this catastrophe—the love of gain, the pride of opinion, the neglect of God—and we dare not claim superiority over the enemy. Every sin, ours and theirs, is an insult to God, whose greatness is infinite and whose majesty we have slighted; measured against Him, man is a little thing, and our offenses take their true malice from the greatness of the God we have wronged. So we smite our breasts and pray, 'God be merciful to me a sinner,' watching and praying for the Mind of Christ, doing unto others as we would have them do unto us, being merciful, just, and pure. We hold sin the greatest of evils, to be avoided at any sacrifice, and we trust not in our own righteousness but in the mercy of God.

prompt: I want to know what makes a person truly wise. What should I study?
completion: True wisdom is not the opposite of practical wisdom but its crown. It is our privilege and duty to be as wise in our generation as the children of this world, and even wiser, because we are privileged with superior advantages through faith and obedience to the Gospel. Study scripture and prayer, and also the world God made—its laws, history, arts, and sciences—so that we may know more about all matters than any other people. But wisdom must govern the body too: be moderate in all things, care for your health, eat wholesome food, live much outdoors, take exercise, and feed children properly, in keeping with the Word of Wisdom. Above all, hold to Jesus as your highest sovereign Friend. Fasten to Him homely in whatever state you are, foul or clean, and never flee from Him for weal nor for woe; for to hide from Him because of foulness is the most folly.

prompt: There's constant arguing and division in my ward. How important is it really that we be of one heart?
completion: Singleness of heart is the most necessary condition of faith and true virtue. Constant arguing and division in a ward should trouble you deeply, because without one heart we cannot enter the kingdom of heaven. We must return to the simplicity of little children and cut off the inordinate affections of vice—pride, resentment, the need to be right—that feed division. Yet the cure is not endless self-observation of our own progress; it is keeping the heart occupied with God, the object of its love, delighting in pleasing God above any pleasure in our own performance. The love of God is the soul's home and goal, and the patience of Christ is not passive waiting but active endurance of wrongs for His sake. Christ is both the pattern and the power of that endurance; fasten to Him, and unity will follow.

prompt: I am a slave to habits I cannot break—is there any power stronger than my own will?
completion: Character is not fixed by temperament. Strength of character is the will's power to control one's actions independently of inclinations and of the opinions of men, and it grows by repeated virtuous acts and shrinks by yielding to passion. Each self-victory strengthens the will, and progress is proportioned to such victories. But beware the saying that the best devotion is the constant practice of ordinary duties; some abuse it to excuse a life of dissipation. Every one is bound to live to himself in the first place and to reserve leisure for frequent exercises of devotion. So bridle your tongue, subdue anger, examine yourself daily, and attend to your own duties rather than judging or meddling in the affairs of others. Set aside regular time for prayer, and trust that the power stronger than your own will is the grace of God working with your repeated acts of self-control.

prompt: I am a parent and I have been too lenient with my children's bad habits. What should I do?
completion: Leniency is not cured by harshness. Parents should be in advance of their children, providing innocent amusement and leading them so that the children delight to follow, rather than being behind them with the whip. Win their hearts first: plan good things for them, join in their play, and let them see that following you is pleasant. Be careful, too, about the books they read, for books create feelings for good or bad, and trashy novels are poisonous adders to the soul. Reading is a form of companionship that shapes the heart, so know what enters your home. Never lose control of your children's amusements during their tender years, and be scrupulously careful about the companionship of your young people in places of amusement; do not leave them to find their fun wherever and whenever they can.

prompt: I keep chasing pleasure and it always leaves me empty. Why does the world's joy fade?
completion: Pleasure fades because it was never meant to be your master. Chasing it is a kind of living death: the more you grasp, the emptier you become. Beware of going into debt for fashionable display, and know that the hunt for pleasure leads to cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. Every substitute for God leaves an emptiness unfilled—romance, family, business, pleasure, art may be good, yet none can permanently satisfy; each ends in disillusionment when asked to be what only God can be. Only the finding of God is permanent success. But do not pursue happiness by trying to feel happy; that is another chase. Seek joy instead by being right with God, forgetting yourself in service to others, rejoicing in the Lord above your feelings, and obeying Him faithfully. There the fading of worldly joy gives way to a joy that does not fade.

prompt: I am troubled by conflict between capital and labor; how should a Christian respond?
completion: The conflict between capital and labor is real, but begin with this: your time and your ability to labor are capital entrusted to you by God, and you will give account for how you use them. No act, word, or thought escapes accountability—secret dishonesty, bitter speech, and exploitative schemes will be brought into judgment. Yet the work is GOD's own work through His servants; we do not achieve it, we obey in it, for His glory. So limit yourself to legitimate employments. Refuse the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that multiply superfluous occupations and create more impediments than works. Deal honestly, pay and demand just wages, and refuse the anger that hardens the heart. Both employer and employee are neighbors owed love and stand before the same Judge. Let His glory, not human credit or restless enterprise, be the aim of all your labor.

prompt: My grief for someone I lost feels too calm, almost tender—am I grieving wrong?
completion: A calm, tender sorrow is not a failure—it may be the truer shape of grief. The one you lost is in a high sphere of saner happiness, present with the Lord, beyond the strains and confusions of this life. Trusting that, your grief need not be acute and stormy; it can be a tender regret, a quiet longing that loves without clutching. Do not turn inward to examine and explain the causes of your sadness; patiently endure the aversions and repugnances that come, bearing them as a way of loving Him who suffered. And let your grief become thanksgiving: thank God for giving this beloved, for long sparing them to you, and for taking them to Himself. Rejoice in their gain even while you feel the loss. Grieve as one who loves someone now safer and more joyful, letting tenderness and praise together shape your remembering.

prompt: I'm a parent and I can't decide whether to compel my young child to fast on fast day.
completion: The fast is a reasonable law, observed from evening to evening, with the food or its equivalent given to the poor—but it is left to conscience and wisdom, not imposed as an iron-clad rule. The weak, the sick, nursing mothers, and little children should not be compelled to fast. So with your young child, do not compel; gently include them in adapted ways—simpler meals, prayer, and giving. And remember that parents should never permit themselves to do anything they are not willing to see their children do; demanding good behavior and kind words while scolding in bitterness is inconsistent. Set an example worthy of imitation. Nor lose control of your child's amusements in these tender years: do not let them find their fun wherever and whenever they can. Be scrupulously careful about the companionship of your young people in places of amusement, guiding their pleasures as carefully as their prayers, so that formation in faith comes through imitation, oversight, and love rather than compulsion.

prompt: I wonder whether the bread and wine of the Supper are truly the body and blood of Christ, or only symbols of spiritual blessings.
completion: The bread and wine of the Supper are truly Christ's body and blood, given to be received within us—not mere symbols of spiritual blessings. On the altar is Christ's substantial presence, body and soul, God and Man, present as our helper. This is no human ceremony but a mystery calling for awe, purity, and burning desire for union with Him. The holy Mass is the most powerful prayer, and Holy Communion gives God Himself and increases grace according to our dispositions. So come with reverence, examine yourself, and receive with longing. And remember whose servant you are: the true servant bears in his body the marks of the Lord Jesus, belongs to Christ alone, and owes no allegiance to men, parties, factions, or the flesh. Do not shrink from the shame and branding of the cross, for the One you receive in the Supper is the One you follow in suffering and glory.

prompt: I am rich and wonder what my property demands of me; is private property itself unchristian?
completion: Private property is not itself unchristian, but you are not your own: you were bought with a price. Your time, talents, gold, silver, and all you possess are the Lord's; you own nothing but the talents God has given you to improve. Riches are uncertain, lent for a season for the Gospel and the poor. So hold your estate as a steward, not an owner, and beware hoarding: keeping riches unused brings leanness of soul and darkness of mind, hardening the heart while the money sits idle. Put every dollar and every ability out to use for the good of the community—give generously, deal honestly with workers and tenants, and refuse luxury that breeds covetousness. Ask whether you could lose it tomorrow and still trust God; if not, it has become an idol. Enjoy His gifts with gratitude, but keep them loose in your hand, always ready for His use.

prompt: How can I pray when I have no words?
completion: When words fail, do not fill the silence with activity; take time to be alone with God and His word, for secret prayer and meditation are indispensable to fruitful service, and nothing compensates for the loss of the secret place. Yet prayer is humbling work: it crucifies pride, signs our bankruptcy, and little praying is a worse evil than none, a deluding make-believe. So ask for strength to suffer with courage, humility, and love, and cultivate familiar conversation with God—watchful over your thoughts, words, and deeds. Begin with Scripture; the Psalms give words when yours run out. A few honest phrases, 'Lord, have mercy,' are enough. Guard a daily appointment alone with Him, refuse to let service or fellowship crowd out communion, and if dryness persists, keep the secret place first. Such watchful converse brings the peace of paradise even now.

prompt: How do I direct my heart into the love of God when I feel distant from Him?
completion: Feeling distant from God is common, but the answer is not a vague longing; it is actual fellowship with a personal Friend—the Father we know through His human revelation in Christ. Yet that fellowship requires a heart emptied of all other things, so God may possess it alone and act in it. Do not assume you can find your way home by your own insight: sin has blinded and biassed us, so we cannot arrive without the Lord's guidance. Seek His direction through the Word, the indwelling Spirit, and Providence. Name the distance honestly, clear away competing loves, meditate on His love in the Psalms and the prodigal son, serve others, and confess what has cooled your affection. Distance is a season, not a verdict; keep meeting the Friend who has come near.

prompt: I have great talents and education. Can these alone make my ministry fruitful?
completion: Talents and education are gifts, but they alone cannot make ministry fruitful. Ministry is not a profession or business where salary and self-advancement lead; treated so it grows heartless. Put self to the rear and heart to the front. Holy pastors made retirement and a life of prayer their apprenticeship and preparation—and afterward, amid ministry, remained men of prayer, God always present to their mind, setting apart intervals in the day and much of the nights to attend to God in the silence of all creatures. So make prayer your first preparation. As an ambassador and messenger of God, reprove sin sincerely rather than softening the Gospel to soothe hearers; visit all the sick; esteem a man's immortal soul above his present favor; and fear none but Him who can destroy both soul and body.

prompt: I've had moments in nature or in music where I felt something vast and beautiful beyond words. What is that?
completion: Those moments are real, but beware the seductive inertia of spiritual sensuality—making a pleasant feeling the goal and sinking into passive contentment. The soul's health lies in intense living and activity in connection with the Divine Energy. Nature is not merely material, nor an end in itself: it is the visible demonstration of an invisible Will. So trace the beauty you feel to its Source, and bless God for every beautiful thing, until your days become one long delight. Let awe in nature or music rouse you rather than lull you; ask what it points to, and respond with gratitude, worship, and action. And know that one moment of divine understanding is a foretaste of eternity, bridging even the interval of death—so receive beauty, and press beyond it into lively communion and service.

prompt: What does it mean to be transformed in God, and how do I begin?
completion: Being transformed in God means consenting without protest as He strews your vanities to the winds, breaks your prides, and transfigures your lusts into Holy Love. He transposes your pleasures—removing the guilty and giving blameless ones—and receives you into His transformed world only when you are at peace with yourself and all persons. Begin by offering God your divided heart, receiving His Grace as the Divine Anaesthetic through the pain of the stripping, and keeping prayer, Scripture, and fellowship. Crucially, let no change of place or occupation alter your love or distract you from being equally for God: remain indifferent amid variety, the same in every setting, so that your love and its object never shift. Submit, stay at peace, and be equally for Him in all things.

prompt: I've been disappointed in my career and I'm bitter—how do I keep from letting it curdle into hatred?
completion: Bitterness after career disappointment is real, but do not give up rejoicing because the first dose seemed ineffectual—count it all joy even in these temptations, trusting God to make the reckoning good. Beware the enemy's false dread of wretchedness: it whispers that your disappointment and any fall are his final victory, and would drive you from the blissful beholding of your Everlasting Friend. Refuse that device; stay beholding God, and when you fall, rise by charity and meekness, turning the enemy's gain to his own sorrow. If you counsel others, first know, live, and love this truth yourself—never merely repeat words, for healing comes from truth embodied, not recited. Forgive those you blame, keep gratitude and service, and let joy, not dread, set the tone of your waiting.

prompt: I am a new Christian, and I feel overwhelmed by all the doctrines; do I need to understand them all to grow?
completion: No, you need not master every doctrine to grow—but do not mistake development for mere innovation or for a hardening of theology by piling on new dogmas. True development is the Church standing firm in her old truths while entering into and assimilating the new social and intellectual movements of the age. Begin with the essentials: who God is, who Jesus is, what He did, and how to follow Him. The doctrine of sin rests not on the literal history of Genesis or on external dogma alone, but on Christ's authority verified in Christian moral experience; you are free to treat the early chapters of Genesis as allegorical. And do not think development ended with Christ's teaching: the Spirit continues His work in the Church, and there remains both the right and the duty of further development in Ethics and Theology. Grow patiently through prayer, Scripture, obedience, and fellowship.

prompt: I do good things mainly to be seen by others. Does that cost me anything?
completion: Yes, doing good mainly to be seen costs you something real. When approval is your motive, the deed becomes a performance and your reward is only the praise you get—nothing deeper; you drift toward visible acts and your worth hangs on opinions. But do not measure progress by claims or words. Test yourself by the fruits of living and demonstrating Truth and Love: does your life show the supreme good and bring healing? Remember that every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way, and that we should make ourselves capable of doing at least a little good. And do not see self-denial and economy as loss: they are a privilege that frees your resources for the LORD and brings fuller joy, enabling greater giving. Practice hidden deeds and ask whether you would still do the good if no one knew.

prompt: I have been a faithful minister for years and see little fruit—should I keep laboring in the same place?
