completion: Seeing little fruit after years of faithful ministry is discouraging, and your question is honest. But do not respond by cautiously narrowing your labor. If you are required to do ten pieces of work and only one is necessary for the Kingdom, do all ten—so that you are sure of performing the one the Lord really requires. Yet do not rely on elaborate appeals or human recruitment methods; seek labourers first by earnest prayer to the LORD of the harvest and by deepening your own spiritual life, so that men cannot stay at home. And remember: we have no time allotted to work for ourselves in the narrow, selfish sense. When you labor most fervently for the Kingdom of God, it is all for yourself, since your interest is bound up in that Kingdom. So keep laboring wholeheartedly where you are, and let faithfulness, not visible results, measure your obedience.

prompt: I get jealous when I see others succeed and I hate that about myself—what do I do with this feeling?
completion: Feeling jealous when others succeed is common, and hating it shows a conscience that wants to change. But jealousy and mistrust destroy affection, and possessiveness shrinks the heart. Do not confine the good of others within your own four walls; practice mutual freedom, confidence, and a benevolence that grows more diffusive. This demands absolute self-conquest, not small accommodations: lay aside retaliation and petty aims, and recognize humbly your own smallness and how ineffective your self-control is on its own. Yet do not hurry or fret anxiously over your progress. Keep yourself in God's presence, and treat over-eagerness as the mother imperfection of all imperfections, for anxiety is an obstacle to perfection. Ask what the envy is telling you, pursue it honestly without begrudging anyone, and let gratitude and generosity crowd out envy in God's own time. Be patient, and speak with a trusted friend if the feeling is intense.

prompt: My church seems to care more about its building and budget than about people. How should I respond?
completion: It is painful to feel that your church cares more about buildings and budgets than about people. Remember that church revenues belong to the poor: even sacred vessels may be devoted to those in need, and goods hoarded while people suffer are a scandal. When you hear complaints of impoverishment, answer with confidence that God will provide—providence, not accumulation, is our security. Yet do not blame priests or institutions alone. The Church's lack is found in the tepid love for a dimly known Lord in each member's heart, including your own; the Church gains what is lacking when each heart worships the beloved Christ. Trust that the government of this Church is based upon true principles. People fall out by the way through ignorance, because they do not thoroughly canvass their acts and wisely ponder probable results. So pray, examine your own love, speak calmly and specifically with your leaders, and offer to help connect resources to people.

prompt: Can I be forgiven if I'm still holding a grudge against someone who hurt me?
completion: Holding a grudge after being hurt is understandable, but forgiveness is not a transaction granted regardless of the state of your heart. It is an inward condition of the personal life: it comes naturally to the soul that loves and forgives, and it depends on your own spirit as well as on God. A heart that remains hard and unforgiving cannot simply receive pardon while refusing to give it. As St. Fulgentius teaches, Christians must not seek revenge but forgive injuries. Do not limit forgiveness by a human reckoning of how much the wound deserves. Forgive as you hope to be forgiven, looking to the Lord who resigned all to earn our pardon. Refuse to mete out love by your own narrow rule; be honest with God about the hurt, pray for the person, and let his generous pardon shape yours.

prompt: How can I keep myself aloof from the sin of my people without betraying them?
completion: Wanting to stay aloof from sin without betraying your people is a worthy tension, but beware of approaching others from a position of sinless superiority. You are not a clean judge standing over the guilty; you are one of them. The restorer identifies with the sinner, confesses his own faults, and points to the fountain opened for sin, following Christ who took our sins and made them His own. Before you attempt to help another, cast the beam out of your own eye first: overcome your own belief in and fear of sin, your own hidden faults and fears, or you will heal no one. Then refuse to participate in wrongdoing without withdrawing in pride. Stay in relationship—eat with people, listen, serve—and speak honestly and gently, beginning with your own need for mercy. Ground this in the practical success of the doctrine of sin: faith acting on promised strength overcomes sin, and believing in others enables their recovery. No bad character is beyond remedy.

prompt: I am a parent and wonder whether my prayers and teaching for my children will bear fruit—should I expect present fruit?
completion: It is natural to wonder whether prayers and teaching for your children will bear fruit. Scripture encourages faithfulness in sowing while God gives the growth, yet you may expect present fruit and should pray for it perseveringly and submissively. Do not demand uniformity of knowledge or opinion as the condition of fellowship. The children of God have various gifts and degrees of knowledge, yet all form one Spirit; do not contend about different fruits and gifts, but acknowledge them in one another like children of the Spirit of God. Seek substantial information for them and trust little to so-called learning based on theory; pluck fruit from the tree of knowledge, taste it, and introduce the best books into your home and school. Remember the vast power for good or evil residing in a little child and the eternal consequences of a child rightly trained or neglected. Pray for present fruit in their conversion, teach by word and example, and look for small signs of growth without pressure.

prompt: I am exhausted from trying to be good enough for God. Does He require me to earn His love?
completion: No—God does not require you to earn His love. His love was in Him from without beginning and was never slacked: He loved us ere He made us, and in that love He made all things profitable to us. Love was His meaning in all He shewed. His self-limitation—in decree, creation, providence, inspiration, and above all in Christ—is no denial of His perfection but its expression, a sign of power and love. So do not multiply offerings or fret over distraction; simply do your work for God without anxiety, and when your mind wanders, gently return without disquiet. Your striving cannot purchase what was always yours. Rest in that love, and let obedience flow from gratitude rather than exhaustion.

prompt: I lost something important and I'm panicking—should I pray about it?
completion: Yes—pray, and let prayer be your main assistant in every step, not a last resort. Continual help from God is needed, so let praying, being with Him, and thinking of Him often become a holy habit; for we must know before we love, and knowing Him grows through repeated turning to Him. Come like a beggar and wait before Him, keeping your mind in His presence; when it wanders in panic, recall it gently and without disquiet. Ask Him to enable you to search out and discover your own heart—what fear or attachment is stirred, what is amiss and needs reforming. Let prayer lead your practical steps too: retrace, check, ask for help. He cares for the lost item and for the heart that clutches it.

prompt: What is the Paradise of God, and where is it located?
completion: The Paradise of God is the garden of Eden restored, enclosed within the Holy City, the New Jerusalem, where stands the tree of life and from whose throne flows the river of water of life (Rev. 22:1–2). These are realities of the sanctuary, for this city is God's sanctuary. Yet entering this Heaven is not a journey to a place after death: it is the will yielding to God, whereby the soul is penetrated throughout with the Divine Light as glowing iron is by fire, is held in the hand of Christ, and becomes itself the Heaven of God wherein He dwelleth. For Heaven and Hell are within the soul: Heaven is the turning in of the will to the Love of God, and Hell the turning of the will into the wrath of God. At death the soul needs no going forth; it stands in that which is manifested in it.

prompt: I have been praying for prosperity in my business—will God answer that?
completion: Yes—bring your business to God, and treat prayer as real, expectant business with the living GOD, not a mere sentiment or last resort. He is faithful to answer for souls, for needs, and for protection. Yet remember that our only business is to please God, and all else is folly: so renounce all that is not Him, and trust Him wholly. Ask Him plainly for prosperity, with expectation, but also for wisdom and integrity, holding the outcome in His hands. Consider those who gave themselves and their goods to God's work without salary, believing He would supply all their need—such cheerful, self-denying service is the pattern of faith. Let your business be held in that spirit, in perpetual remembrance of Him.

prompt: Can I believe in the objectivity of duty without believing in God?
completion: Obey God in this question, and hold one Mind. You cannot finally separate the objectivity of duty from God, for duty is real because He is real; but do not let the argument become a transfer of evil suggestions between mortals. Love your neighbor as yourself, and refuse to receive or pass on suggestions that deny the one Mind. In every occasion of virtue, turn to God and ask for enabling grace, receiving strength more than sufficient for what is set before you. Take the attitude of faith: having asked, act and pray as though the blessing were already given, leaning your weight on God for what you have claimed. Do not ask and then live as though you had not received. Stand in the truth that there is one Mind, and in that Mind your duty and His will are not divided.

prompt: Why does religion often seem so melancholy and forbidding?
completion: Religion seems melancholy when we keep it indoors as our own feelings and thoughts about ourselves—our guilt, our anxious self-examination, our resolutions. But religion is not our feelings about God; it is the love of God, objective to our hearts, as near as the open air and as free as the sunshine. The leal love of God is every day. We must not imagine a safe middle way, serving God and the world together as a happy compromise; that half-way stopping brings gloomy wretchedness. Follow Christ all the way, that He may complete His process in us. And reject immoderate sadness, for sadness is the enemy of devotion; console your soul in the service of Him who is our joy forever, and it will grow like an olive-tree green in God's house.

prompt: How should I share my faith so that people are actually convicted of sin?
completion: Sharing faith so that people are convicted of sin does not begin with standing above them as a sinless judge. The restorer must identify with the sinner, confessing his own faults, and point to the fountain opened for sin. We follow Christ, who took our sins and made them His own. We must not excuse or minimize small sins, nor delay confession; rather we promptly confess and forsake even the smallest, abandon questionable practices at once, and give thanks for every mercy of God. And we must watch and pray for the Mind of Christ, doing unto others as we would have them do unto us, being merciful, just, and pure in all our dealings. That pattern of obedience, gratitude, and prayer makes our witness credible, so the other is drawn toward the fountain rather than pushed away by our superiority.

prompt: I feel like angels and principalities are watching my every step—how should that change how I live?
completion: Feeling that angels and principalities watch your every step should not lead you to passive waiting or to asking God to do what lies within your reach. It is inconsistent to pray for God to do all when remedies within our knowledge are available. Apply every remedy within your knowledge—diligence, honesty, prayer, and practical care—and ask your Father in Heaven to sanctify the application. Only when nothing is within reach should you ask the Lord to send an angel to heal. Yet prayer is a humble waiting before God like a beggar: keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. Do not be absorbed in observing your own actions; keep your heart occupied with God, the object of your love, delighting in pleasing Him above any pleasure in your own performance.

prompt: I have suffered from rheumatism for years and been told it is inherited; can I be freed?
completion: Rheumatism that has lasted for years and is said to be inherited is a belief that must be examined. Hereditary disease is not real as a transmission through matter, for matter cannot transmit good or evil intelligence. The belief in hereditary disease must be destroyed, not indulged. Drugs, hygiene, and animal magnetism may bring temporary relief, but they are not healing; healing belongs to divine Mind alone. So do not mistake relief for cure. Refuse the belief that matter carries disease from parent to child, turn to the divine Mind as the source of your being, and trust God to sanctify whatever remedies you use. Yet never coerce a patient to stay with mental treatment against his wishes; release such cases freely, letting the invalid learn from his own experience rather than being compelled.

prompt: How can these two subsist together, that a person should both love and hate himself?
completion: Loving and hating oneself at the same time is not a contradiction when we rightly divide what is given from what is our own. We are to love the divine ground in ourselves, the good given us from the Love of God, and to hate only that which is our own wherein evil cleaves to us. Love hates all Egoity and self-hood, for self-hood is the root of Hell. But we must not mistake self-seeking love for love: love seeks not itself to please, does not bind another to its delight nor rejoice in another's loss of ease. As the clod of clay sings, love gives its ease for another and builds a heaven in hell's despair. And when faced with human hatred, do not meet evil with evil; overcome evil with good at all times, clad in the panoply of Love, which is your sure protection.

prompt: I see cruelty and terror in my own heart and I'm ashamed. Does that make me evil?
completion: Seeing cruelty and terror in your own heart should not be softened into a harmless sign of sensitivity. In the new light the Spirit of Love sheds, evil shows its true complexion: disease, misery, imprisonment, and death. Yet do not mistake doubtful dread for humility. Despairing self-condemnation is a foul blindness and weakness against the truth, coming subtly of Enmity to keep you from Love. And do not imagine your cruelty is only a vague inward shadow: Cruelty has a human heart, and Jealousy a human face; the human heart can be a hungry gorge, and the human dress is forged iron. Seeing that face is the beginning of truth. Turn the bitterness of doubt into the sweetness of love by the knowing of love, for the light that shows you the disease is the light that shows the Healer.

prompt: I want to know what God's secret plan is for the world and for the souls of those who die outside the faith; should I keep pressing to understand it?
completion: It is right to press toward understanding, but not as idle curiosity about hidden secrets. Scripture prays that we be filled with the knowledge of God's will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, and this is the secret of true living. Yet be slow to take new steps: presumption is not faith. Be willing to have no will of your own, ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word, and then wait with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help. And do not hold back your desires or your liberty from God. Offer them all with a large and liberal heart, for the more liberal you are toward God, the more liberal He will be toward you, and the more fit you will be for greater graces.

prompt: What is the place of Israel in God's plan?
completion: Israel's place cannot be read as mere human history or as a contest of opinions. God is at work in the history of men and nations, guiding and judging them by it. Israel was chosen to bear His oracles and to be the channel of the Messiah, and the partial gifts of the peoples are appointed by Him and fulfilled in Christ. Nor are the holy things separate: the Holy City, the New Jerusalem, the tabernacle of God, the bride the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, and the sanctuary are one city coming down from God out of heaven to dwell with men. And the afflicted are not wholly forsaken: God will not quench nor slay them quite, but preserves them in mercy. Ask only that the captive heart feel its woe and burden, and that mercy be found.

prompt: I am terrified of the dangers of missionary service; how do I face the possibility of death or persecution?
completion: Fear of danger and death is a normal human response, but the missionary must be sent out rightly. Start with clean hands and pure hearts: you need a testimony and must keep the Word of Wisdom, for these are not optional for the one who carries the gospel. Teach in simplicity, humility, and love, avoiding contentious argument and debate. Do not look at the storm for comfort; fasten your eyes on Christ Himself, who is the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance. Live so as to enjoy the Holy Ghost every day, seeking His continual guidance, and return as pure as white paper. Abide in Him, and in His presence you will find the remedy for trouble and the substance of all you need.

prompt: I have neglected my prayers for a long time and feel far from God; is there still a way back for me?
completion: Yes, there is a way back, and nothing you have prayed is lost. No true prayer is wasted; your supplications have accumulated as a memorial before God, treasured at His throne until the due time, and the longer the answer waits the larger it may become. So return by waiting before God like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence and recalling it in tranquility without disquiet. But do not imagine prayer is easy or naturally congenial. It is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs your bankruptcy before God. Little praying is a worse evil than no praying, a deluding make-believe. Begin again honestly, with few words if need be, trusting that God is already waiting for you.

prompt: How can I repent when I feel more angry than sorry?
completion: Feeling more angry than sorry does not excuse you, for sin is doing wrong when you know and can do better. If you now see the wrong, refrain immediately and forever; the sin of ignorance God winks at, but knowledge binds you to forsake it at once. Abiding repentance means leaving all things that love and entertain the will, all visibles and sensibles that delight the appetite, and loving that which hates thee, embracing the reproach of the world and the cross of Christ. But know that anger itself must never be permitted to rise in your bosom, and angry words must never pass your lips. Keep an even temper at home and abroad, holding angry feelings as one holds a wild horse until the good Spirit moves your tongue to kindness. Confess plainly, make restitution, and let the cross be your daily exercise of penitence.

prompt: I am a chief and my people look to me. What are my duties at a feast?
completion: As a chief, remember first that you are not your own. Make it your first business each morning to be truly at rest and happy in God, reading and studying the Scriptures with much prayer, especially early, for a chief who has not met God cannot rightly lead. Keep yourself free for whatever service the LORD may require, binding yourself by no commitment as though your time and person were your own. Then at the feast preside with dignity: greet guests warmly, seat elders and visitors first, speak briefly and graciously, keep order, and settle disputes quietly. Honor the duties of the housewife and the labor of the women who prepare and serve; let all dress modestly, and let the feast include the service of Relief Societies in caring for the poor and needy. Show generosity, model hospitality and restraint, and listen to your people, remembering that your authority exists to serve them and that the feast is only the overflow of a heart already fed by God.

prompt: I am a laborer with no property. How can I put my hands out to usury instead of hiding my one talent in a napkin?
completion: As a laborer with no property, do not hide your talent, but neither run frantically after wealth. Be calm, contented, and patiently diligent, saving a little from your wages and using it honestly. Attend your meetings, pray, read the Scriptures, and meditate, keeping your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. In dealings with neighbors, remember that circumstances easily deceive; do not rashly judge or privately condemn, for judgment belongs to magistrates and private persons should vindicate rather than condemn their neighbors. Remember that it is all the Lord's and we are only his stewards; the faithful steward puts in ten dollars where he takes one out of the treasury, and pays his tithing before any other claim. Avoid debt and speculation, learn your trade, keep honest records, and trust God to multiply the labor of patient hands.

prompt: I've been told that doctrine divides and that tolerance is the highest virtue. Should I tolerate teaching that seems to excuse immorality?
completion: Tolerance is sometimes a virtue and sometimes a deadly sin. To tolerate teaching that excuses immorality is not charity but complicity, for the letters to Pergamum and Thyatira rebuke churches that tolerated false teaching and moral laxness. Proper tolerance bears patiently with persons and differences of opinion, but it does not treat every doctrine as equally true or every practice as harmless. This matters most in the home: do not indulge children's appetites for amusement, but give them spiritual and moral education, teaching obedience to the moral law and restraint of indulgence, so that they grow in the understanding of man's higher nature. When a matter has been decided by the council or conference, uphold that decision; a minority may withdraw conscientiously, but it may not wage internal war against the Church's decisions or break its working harmony. Weigh every teaching against Scripture; if it plainly excuses what is wrong, refuse to accept or promote it, and warn others gently, never calling indifference to evil a virtue.

prompt: I have a chance to escape a difficult and dangerous mission—should I take it?
completion: Do not wait to settle every question before you act, for such waiting is itself a decision to drift, and do not merely chat about difficulties when the hour calls for action. Cut the Gordian knot with the sword of decision: take the light you have and launch out into the deep with a bold plunge, leaving the speculations to Christ. Remember what you are choosing: the wisdom of the gospel is to flee the dangers of the world and secure your one necessary affair, for the gate of life is narrow and the multitude perishes on the broad way. Do not trust the crowd or the easy path, and do not rely on your own powers. Say with the apostle, "I will do much; not I, but the grace of God which is within me." Pray briefly, seek one wise counsel, and then act courageously in that grace.

prompt: I do good works quietly and no one notices. Does it count if no one sees?
completion: Yes, it counts, and the quietness of it may be doing more than you know. Begin by checking your words, for if you gain power to check your words you will then gain power to check your judgment and thoughts. Stand porter at the door of thought, shutting out unhealthy thoughts and fears so the body cannot suffer from them. But do not argue with temptation or attend to it; never answer it nor appear to hear the enemy. Instead prostrate yourself before God and remain at His feet while the enemy makes noise. Do not measure the work by witnesses, and do not condemn on rumor; wait until heaven clearly indicates the fault. Unseen good is real because it is done before God, and a guarded, humble mind keeps it clean.

prompt: I am a Gentile with no Jewish background—can I be saved the same way as Abraham, or is there something more I must do?
completion: Yes, you may be saved the same way Abraham was, but first let your eyes be opened to sin and to the danger of it. Repentance comes before faith, not after; the sinner must see the peril and turn from it. Only then direct the penitent to believe on the Lord Jesus Christ. Understand too what Israel was for: a preparation and vantage-ground, a people through whom universal truths were preserved, though Judaism had no promise or power of expansion in itself, and those truths could only be made available by a power beyond Israel's own forces. Do not imagine salvation is available outside the way God has pointed out; there is no hope of everlasting life but through obedience to the law affixed by the Father of life. Your Gentile background is no barrier.

prompt: I want to write poetry but I'm afraid my passion is too raw and incoherent—should I restrain it?
completion: Yes, restrain it—but understand restraint as the aim, not merely a technique. Verse should be marked by delicacy of style and a conscious aiming at excellence, with restrained refinement, subdued reserve, and a gentle melancholy rather than violent or incoherent passion. Do not linger in the cheerless tomb of passion or glamorize its storm; when the storm is laid, mark the silent growth of grace and light in the soul. Remember that Nature is too beautiful for your strains to surpass. Do not crave silence, and do not seek Autumn or eternal sleep, for they come soon enough without your calling. Follow the fair goddess while green remains, and let your song be delicate, deliberate, and humble before what it cannot outshine.

prompt: I'm a member who has been asked to vote against a proposition in conference but I feel uneasy about it. Must I vote with the majority?
completion: No, you need not vote with the majority, and you should not assume you were instructed to. The authorities are presented to the Saints, and members are sincerely requested to act freely and independently in voting and speaking; no one has been told how to vote, and no one is injured for honestly stating objections. Come with a heart full of wisdom. If you discern any lack of judgment or failure in the authorities, do not withhold it and do not broadcast it: come to them individually and let them know, for they would exchange a thousand errors for one truth. Remember that the Saints are to be good citizens, loyal to the Constitution and laws of the land, and that the Church is not partisan in politics. Weigh the proposition on its merits and vote according to honest judgment.

prompt: I want to know whether the great Church's victory over paganism came from its organization, its dogmas, or its ability to unite the faith of the learned and the simple; which should I value most?
completion: The victory came from all three working together, but understand the Church rightly: it is a visible, unified body, not a merely invisible or private affair. It witnesses to central truths with authority and allows freedom on points not central. Yet do not confuse Christian religion with outward observance, opinion, or speculation about God. All Christian Religion is learning to know ourselves: how we were in the Unity in Adam, how we are now in dissension and contrariety, whither we go when we pass out of this condition, and how we come forth from disunion into that one Tree, Christ in us. And do not measure the Church by personal success or national expansion. It cares only that the individual be pure in heart and the nation honourable, indifferent to both success and expansion, and ready to suffer for that testimony.

prompt: I long for a real union with God, not just pardon for the past. Does the Atonement offer me anything more than forgiveness?
completion: The Atonement is not merely a legal transaction that secures pardon for past sins; it is the means by which God reconciles us to Himself and brings us into union with Him. But forgiveness is not a transaction granted regardless of our inward condition. It is an inward condition of the personal life, coming naturally to the soul that loves and forgives. We cannot be forgiven while remaining hard and unforgiving, for the same Spirit who pardons also softens the heart. Therefore, we must promptly forgive and reconcile, returning meekness and kindness for insults, and warning that refusal to forgive endangers the soul. Yet the Atonement does not stop at what is done for us without us; it works in us an actual deliverance and new creation. As we cooperate with the Holy Spirit, He transforms us into Christ's likeness, enabling us to participate in the divine life. Forgiveness is the beginning, but the goal is union with God, which is realized as we grow in faith and obedience. The Atonement provides both the pardon that clears our guilt and the power that enables us to live in fellowship with God, so yes, it offers much more than forgiveness alone.

prompt: I feel like I'm not advancing spiritually—what should I do?
completion: Feeling stagnant in your spiritual life is common, but don't be discouraged. The foundation of all progress is self-renunciation: be slow to take new steps in self-will, willing to have no will of your own, and ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word. Confess your utter insufficiency, for apart from Christ you can do nothing; the conviction of helplessness is the condition of receiving His all-sufficiency. Take firmly hold of Him by a faith that will not accept less than all. Then, with watchfulness, humility, and compunction, lay this foundation before any exterior practices. Only then should you move forward with earnest, patient, and believing expectation of His help. Examine your habits: are you praying daily, reading Scripture, and participating in community? Begin with small, consistent steps, but always in dependence on God. Set specific goals, like a few minutes of prayer each morning or reading a chapter of the Bible, but hold them loosely. Also, consider serving others; acts of service can reignite your sense of purpose. Remember that growth is often gradual and not always visible. Don't compare yourself to others. Seek accountability from a trusted friend or mentor who can encourage you. Finally, be patient with yourself; God is faithful and will complete the work He began in you.

prompt: I'm facing prolonged trials and feel like giving up—how do I find the patience of Christ?
completion: Prolonged trials can be exhausting, and it's normal to feel like giving up. But do not give in to impatience or complaint. Instead, wait patiently upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls you from His hands as intended for the highest good. Be patient with your trials, accepting them as God's permission to reveal what you are when left to yourself. Become indifferent to serving Him amid thorns or roses, for His service is not dependent on circumstances. Extend patience universally to all God sends or permits, bearing ignominious and honorable trials with the same evenness of temper. Play the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ, co-operating with His grace. Start by acknowledging your feelings to God in prayer, but then surrender them to Him. Remember that Jesus Himself faced trials and endured them with patience, relying on the Father. Draw strength from His example and from the promise that He is with you. Break your trial into manageable parts and focus on getting through one day at a time. Seek support from fellow believers who can pray with you and encourage you. Also, practice self-care: rest, eat well, and take breaks. Don't be afraid to seek professional help if needed. Finally, hold onto hope that God is working through this trial, even if you can't see it now. He will give you the strength to endure.

prompt: I am afraid of being thought a fanatic if I spend hours in prayer. What should I do?
completion: It's understandable to worry about what others think, but prayer is essential to your relationship with God. Do not treat prayer as a small duty fitted into leftover time. Instead, give the best of your time and strength to prayer, with the closet first and study and activities second and freshened by the closet. Approach prayer as a humble waiting before God, like a beggar before a generous king. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. Pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, for God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask. Do not be discouraged by your sins, but seek His grace boldly. You don't need to spend hours in prayer to be faithful; even short, consistent prayers are valuable, but they should not be an excuse to neglect extended time with God. Start with a manageable routine, like 10-15 minutes a day, and gradually increase as you feel comfortable. Remember that prayer is about connection with God, not about impressing others. If you're concerned about being seen as a fanatic, you can pray privately and discreetly. Jesus often withdrew to solitary places to pray, so follow His example. Ultimately, seek to please God rather than people, and trust that He will guide you.

prompt: I had a powerful spiritual experience once and have never been able to repeat it. Was it real? Should I try to get it back?
completion: It's common to have a powerful spiritual experience and then wonder if it was real or if you can get it back. Such experiences can be genuine encounters with God, but they are not meant to be repeated on demand. Accept spiritual experiences only as God chooses, without praying for or secretly desiring them, in total submission without questioning, fear, or curiosity. Instead of trying to recreate the experience, focus on the fruit it produced in your life—did it draw you closer to God, increase your faith, or change your behavior? If so, it was likely real. Trying to get it back can lead to disappointment and distract you from the ongoing work of God in your life. Instead, cultivate a daily relationship with God through prayer, Scripture, and community. Seek strength with all the saints to grasp the breadth, length, height, and depth of the divine love by spiritual insight, in the wider fellowship of believers. Remember that the Holy Spirit comes in power and love, gentler than the morning gale, lighting crowns on sainted heads and proclaiming life to come. Trust that He is with you even when you don't feel His presence strongly. He is more interested in your faithfulness than in repeating past experiences.

prompt: How do I keep my heart from being defiled by the images of this world?
completion: Live as though your mind were in heaven and your body in the tomb, gently withdrawing your heart from amusements and vanities that turn you from blessed eternity. The text gives a fivefold method. First, strictly guard the senses—eyes, ears, tongue—since images enter through them. Second, practice recollection: return often to God's presence in silence. Third, be candid with a spiritual director, hiding no failure. Fourth, watch the enemies of purity of intention—vanity, pride, sensuality, interest, and aversions—naming them honestly. Fifth, replace what you renounce with prayer and pious reading. Do all with the softest step and gentlest tone, for the noblest art is skill in comfort; purity grows gently, not by anxious force.

prompt: I want to be a good person but I keep failing—why does sin seem to have such power over me?
completion: Sin seems powerful, but the doctrine of sin is verified by moral triumph, not despair. Faith acts on promised strength: God does not command what he withholds power to do. Believe, and let others believe in you, for believing in a person enables recovery. See too that sin confers no real pleasure—its sweetness is counterfeit—and this knowledge strengthens courage to master evil. Yet do not treat sin's harm as final. The tender word of the Thirteenth Revelation is that sin is behoveable, taken up into a greater good, and that all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. So rise quickly, keep prayer, confession, and good company, and trust that grace finishes what your effort begins.

prompt: I want to be a good person, but I'm not sure why—is it because it makes me happy, because it's useful, or because God is holy?
completion: All three motives can work together, but the joy of God's personal love is not earned by merit, charitable work, or cleverness. It lives in a continually maintained attitude of longing, grateful giving, and receiving Christ. Keep the order right: moral attributes rank above natural ones, and within them holiness is supreme; love is under bonds to holiness, not the reverse. Yet do not be merely righteous and hard like a granite mountainside. Be good as God is good—clothed with kindness, affectionateness, sympathy, and active benevolence toward others. Happiness and usefulness follow as byproducts. Root yourself in that maintained posture of giving and receiving, so that when goodness costs happiness or utility, you keep going—gently, warmly, and toward real people.

prompt: I am tempted to impurity. What means should I use against it?
completion: Keep yourself in God's presence, and let nothing be done in a hurry. Guard your senses and remove access—eyes, phone, company—but without anxiety, for over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections and the great obstacle to perfection. When temptation comes, turn quietly to prayer, activity, or a friend; despise it rather than fear it, since a temptation that displeases you is harmless and its suffering merciful. Do not arm yourself with jealousy or mistrust, which destroy affection; cultivate mutual freedom, confidence, and a benevolence that grows more diffusive. Confess regularly to God and a trusted person. If you fall, rise calmly, learn your triggers, and continue. Grace is available, and gentle patience does more than frantic force.

prompt: I am a parent and my child has become serious about religion while I remain ignorant—should I listen to her?
completion: Yes, listen—but listen as one responsible for her formation. Her seriousness about religion is not a threat but an invitation. Remember that the chief purpose of our being here is personal connection with God; teaching children to prize holidays, parties, and career success above this is a mistaken basis. So commend obedience to the moral law, restrain indulgence, and let her grow in understanding man's higher nature. You need not pretend to know what you don't; honesty about your ignorance is fine. Ask her questions and speak with a pastor. And take up the charge laid on parents and pastors: guard the young from corrupting books and supply pious ones, so her reading feeds rather than undermines her faith. Let her seriousness draw you both toward God.

prompt: I've been praying for something for years and God hasn't answered—should I stop asking?
completion: It's understandable to feel discouraged when prayers seem unanswered, but we are called to pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, not our own. God offers grace at each action, and we receive it when we ask. So do not stop asking; instead, ask with the confidence that Christ has made the way open. Yet we must also acknowledge that God may deny a request in kindness, for He knows what is best for us. We should resign our will to His, trusting that His denial can be better than the thing we ask for. At the same time, we should watch our prayers, using the light God has given, and not ask God for what we should do ourselves in ordinary wisdom. Our confidence rests not in the strength of our asking but in the merits of Christ, who intercedes for us. So keep asking, not with discouragement, but with the assurance that God is ready to give grace, and that even His denials are expressions of His love.

prompt: Is it wrong to be wealthy?
completion: Wealth itself is not inherently wrong, but we must remember that it belongs to the Lord and is uncertain. The Bible warns against covetousness and the idolatrous love of property. Wealth is not securely our own; it is entrusted to us for a purpose. We should use it for the Gospel and for the poor, not hoard it or treat it as an end in itself. However, we must also recognize that wealth represents labor and industry. Taking it by force or legislation is robbery, and such a principle would crush all energy and enterprise. Yet the danger is not only for the very rich. A moderate income brings within reach distractions that drown the voice of conscience, base comforts in whose lap duty is forgotten. Comfort makes us thoughtless, and thoughtlessness is the parent of every cruelty. So, being wealthy is not wrong, but we must hold it loosely, recognizing that it is the Lord's and should be used for His kingdom. Seek first the kingdom of God, and use your resources generously, while respecting the rights of property and the fruits of labor.

prompt: How should I understand the cross—as something done to satisfy God, or as something showing me God's love?
completion: The cross is not a new thing detached from the old pieties; rather, it is the putting of the love of God into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart. In Jesus, the dearest truths about God are realised in Himself: that God is love, that He is deeply interested in our life, and that He assumes responsibility for its eternal issues. The cross reveals the infinite degree of God's interest in us and His commitment to our eternal well-being. So, when we look at the cross, we see not a distant transaction but the very heart of God, who in Christ takes upon Himself the burden of our sin and death. Moreover, the sign of the cross is an impregnable rampart against the devil, to be made with great faith and devotion rather than by mere custom. Yet we must also accept being fashioned by whatever means God pleases, desiring that the cross be wholly the cross of Jesus Christ, not a cross of our own choosing. Thus, the cross is both satisfaction and revelation, and its sign is a powerful weapon for the believer.

prompt: Is there mercy for one who has many times transgressed against the Lord?
completion: Yes, there is mercy for those who have transgressed many times. The Lord of all is merciful if we straightway purge ourselves of our evil deeds and cease again from the unrighteous act, though we have many times transgressed against Him and wounded Him with our sins. We should never offer scorn, blasphemy, or wrathful opposition to the Son of God, that we may deserve eternal life in heaven. Moreover, we should trace God's goodness and mercy through every trial, recording His dealings with thanksgiving and offering continual praise, finding mercies even in the dust of sorrow. We must also hope in the divine mercy which restored more by grace than the devil robbed by Adam's sin, and acknowledge that we fall into sin only by our own malice. The key is genuine repentance and turning away from sin. God does not delight in the death of the wicked but desires that they turn from their ways and live. So, no matter how many times you have sinned, if you come to God with a contrite heart, He will forgive. His mercies are new every morning. Don't despair; turn to Him and receive His mercy.

prompt: I am drawn to missionary service, but my family opposes it and I fear losing their support. How do I know whether to go?
completion: Discerning a call to missionary service while facing family opposition is challenging. First, pray earnestly for guidance and wisdom. Seek counsel from mature Christians, especially those with missionary experience. Consider your motives: are you driven by a genuine love for God and people, or by a desire for adventure or escape? Also, examine your qualifications and the needs of the field. Family opposition is significant, but Jesus said that anyone who loves family more than Him is not worthy of Him. This doesn't mean disregarding family, but it does mean that following Christ may sometimes require painful choices. As you go, remember to speak well of predecessors who did their best, to invite others without urging, and never to compel anyone. Let your motive be a passion for human beings as human beings, with respect for peoples and their growing independence, rejecting the Jonah-like conception of truth as the property of one nation. Moreover, ground your hope for fellowship among nations in the Church's spiritual society, recognizing that political machinery may presuppose but cannot replace that common membership in Christ. Trust that God will provide support, perhaps through a church community. Ultimately, step out in faith, knowing that God is faithful and will equip you for the work He calls you to.

prompt: I have hurt people I love by my distance and secrecy. Can I be forgiven?
completion: Forgiveness is an inward condition of the personal life, coming naturally to the soul that loves and forgives. Yet do not heal from a place of self-condemnation or doubt. The healer must work with the moral might of Mind and firm trust in Truth, not from guilt. If you hold unforgiveness, you are more guilty than the one who sinned against you; Saints must forgive as Christ did. So dismiss envy, malice, and retaliation, and cultivate the spirit that cried, 'Father, forgive them.' Let your own spirit be truthful and soft, willing to make amends, and let God's mercy meet you there. Forgiveness depends on God and on your willing spirit—on forgiving as you have been forgiven—and it is received with confidence, not with fear.

prompt: My husband and I disagree about trusting God for our finances. How should I respond?
completion: Begin by listening calmly, remembering that God is the one living Agent and all human workers are only His instruments. Cast all your care upon Him, and treat anxious self-reliance as distrust. But know that God remains unchangingly faithful even when your faith fails; His faithfulness does not depend on the strength of your belief. Unbelief still brings loss—it closes the hand that would receive—so let your faith grow. Do not treat sacrificial giving as unrealistic: Scripture records helpers who gave themselves and their goods without salary, believing God would supply all their need. Commend that spirit, and be willing to serve and give cheerfully and self-denyingly, trusting Him who supplies all your need.

prompt: Was the garden of Eden a literal place, and where did it go after the fall?
completion: Eden is presented in Scripture as a real garden, and its deepest reality is preserved in the sanctuary. The Holy City, the New Jerusalem, encloses the garden of Eden—the Paradise of God—with the tree of life and the river of water of life issuing from the throne; these are realities of God's sanctuary, not mere figures. After the fall the way to the tree of life was guarded, yet the garden is kept in the city of God. Do not think of heaven as elsewhere and the earth as abandoned: the meek shall inherit the earth, the Saints will reign on the earth with Christ, and the New Jerusalem will come down to a purified earth. And do not excuse Eve: she confesses that she plucked the apple and robbed her children of Heaven, that by rights she should have gone upon the cross, and that there would be no hell, sorrow, or fear if it were not for her.

prompt: I feel no assurance that my prayers are heard; how can I have confidence before God?
completion: Do not be discouraged. God offers grace at each action, and it is yours to ask for. Pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, not your own worthiness. God, who understands all things, can hear the earnest supplication of the soul and our innermost thoughts—just as human invention enables communication across great distances, so much more does God hear the secret prayer. Ask in faith, nothing wavering. Yet do not pray in hurry or anxious fretting; over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Keep yourself in God's presence, calm and attentive, setting anxiety aside as an obstacle to perfection. Bring your sins to God, ask for the grace He is already offering, and rest your confidence on His merits rather than your feelings.

prompt: If right and wrong are real whether I think so or not, where does that moral law exist?
completion: If right and wrong are real whether you think so or not, the moral law cannot be mere social approbation or subjective feeling. An objective moral law must exist in a mind, and the idea of duty implies the idea of God. Duty binds absolutely, as a law we did not invent. Yet the question is not whether the law should be kept but how: it is holy and binding, not done away, and its righteousness is fulfilled in us by the Spirit through faith. Nor may we excuse ourselves by heredity or circumstance. A man's moral constitution, though defined by heredity, is his heritage for which he is responsible; guilt may be minimized but not denied. So the law exists in God, and we answer for how we keep it.

prompt: What is the purpose of my existence on this earth?
completion: The purpose of your existence is to praise, reverence, and serve God, and by this means to save your soul. You were created for this end, and all other things on earth were created for you to help you attain it. This longing for enduring life that you feel is not an unholy strife but Nature's own voice within you; she who gives wings to birds will find out a way for you to reach your true home. Therefore, you should be indifferent to health or sickness, riches or poverty, honor or dishonor, and long or short life, desiring and choosing only what most leads to the end for which you were created. This indifference concerns what is left to your free will and not what is forbidden.

prompt: What does it mean to grieve or quench the Holy Spirit?
completion: To grieve or quench the Holy Spirit means to wound the jealous, loving Friend who dwells within you. The Spirit loves you to jealousy and longs for your undivided affection. When you divide your heart between God and the world, you grieve Him, for friendship with the world is enmity with God. Quenching the Spirit is resisting His promptings and stifling His work. Therefore, yield to the Spirit of prayer: bring each burden to God and pray it out in wordless prayer before acting it out in life. Be faithful to His faintest whisper. Remember that the Spirit is the life of the Spirit-bearing body, consecrating nature and working gradually and socially while intensifying personal character. So do not separate the Spirit's work from the Church, nor set spirit against matter or nature against grace, but honor His presence in the community of faith and in the sacraments, cultivating a lifestyle of prayer and obedience that honors Him.

prompt: I feel the Holy Spirit is jealous over me—is that a good thing or something to fear?
completion: Feeling that the Holy Spirit is jealous over you is a good thing, for it reveals the jealous, loving Friend who dwells within you. The Spirit loves you to jealousy and longs for your undivided affection. When you divide your heart between God and the world, you grieve Him, for friendship with the world is enmity with God. Therefore, do not fear His jealousy as though it were petty, but meet it with unbounded love, turning away from worldly attachments and giving Him your whole heart. Remember that the Holy Ghost is the principal agent of sanctification, pouring charity into your heart and giving His gifts, yet He requires your co-operation; no grace fails of its effect except through your fault. So co-operate with His grace, and claim the filling of the Holy Ghost as a command and privilege, bringing an empty, honest, trusting heart to be filled for purity, victory, and power. His jealousy will then lead you to deeper devotion.

prompt: I have been taught that God sends sickness to draw us to Him; is that true?
completion: The idea that God sends sickness to draw us to Him contains a truth: God is nearer in sickness, and He uses it to call us to Himself. However, sickness, sin, and death are unreal errors presupposing the absence of Truth, Life, or Love, and are no part of God's creation. God is a loving Father who gives only good, and sickness is not His will, as the testimonies confess they had wrongly believed. So sickness is not sent by God as a punishment; rather, in His providence He permits it and draws near to us in it. Our trust should be in Him, not chiefly in medicine, for remedies succeed only as He permits. So, while we may use medicine, we must ultimately rely on God, who is present in our suffering and desires to draw us closer to Him. Trust in Him above all.

prompt: What is an Angel or a human Soul, that they can be manifested either in God's Love or Anger, in Light or Darkness?
completion: An angel or a human soul is a spiritual being created by God with free will, capable of choosing love or rejecting it. When aligned with God's will, they manifest His love and light; when turned away, they experience His anger and darkness. But even afflictive circumstances are not merely wrath or punishment; Love can transform them into an angel entertained unawares. Entering Heaven is not a journey to a place after death but the will's yielding to God, whereby the soul is penetrated throughout with the Divine Light as glowing iron by fire, is in the hand of Christ, and becomes itself the Heaven of God wherein He dwelleth. Yet this transformation is not achieved by effort or sentiment alone; it comes by living under the holy Cross, drawing breath from above until the likeness of Jesus' death is traced in the life. So the soul's state depends on its response to God's love, which can turn even darkness into light.

prompt: I want to protect the innocent and vulnerable, but I don't know how. Where do I start?
completion: Here is where to start: name evil plainly, refuse silence, and act. Learn the local resources—trusted authorities, charities, and church groups. Speak up with facts when you witness harm, and stand with the vulnerable even when it costs you. Guard your soul: refuse bitterness, anger, hatred, envy, and malice; be filled with love for God and neighbor, do good to all, and keep your covenants. Trust God to stand by you, and do not let fear delay you. That is enough to begin; say it, do it, and stop there.

prompt: I long to see God face to face and to be freed from this life; is this longing itself a sin?
completion: This longing is not a sin; it can be holy. But examine why you long: do not seek God merely for His consolations or to escape hardship, but because it is His wish, because Perfection calls and love answers love. A soul inflamed with the love of Christ is indifferent to honors and disgrace, to sufferings and pleasures, and free from irregular passions. Meekly acknowledge your sin and feebleness before God, without overdone self-accusation or indiscreet sorrow, and trust His courteous excusing. Remain faithful in present duties, and let hope draw you toward holiness and obedience.

prompt: What is the Christian attitude to slavery and other accepted evils of the past?
completion: The curse is disobedience, and Christ was made a curse for us on the tree, loosing us from sin so we need not sin any more. This rests on history: the resurrection is a fact to examine, and making trial of that message you come to know the living Saviour directly. Past evils such as slavery were transgression, and the church's complicity was sin; repent honestly and work for justice now. Remove baseless accusations against the name of Christ, and do not treat suffering as heroic in itself: the glory of suffering belongs only to suffering endured for His sake. Live in the liberty He bought—freedom from sin, not freedom to disobey the law.

prompt: When opposition and persecution arise, does it mean I have mistaken GOD's will?
completion: Opposition does not mean you have mistaken God's will. Hindrances and persecution are not misfortunes or signs of abandonment; they are divinely ordered links in providence, often opening wider service. Yield completely to God's will, without exception, accepting to be struck where and as He pleases, even in repugnant events. Do not dispute about God's Being or Will from images and self-opinion; such disputation is carried on without God and shows that one has not felt Him. Instead, be humble, love, and try things one with another. Examine your motives, seek counsel, and keep serving.

prompt: I am afraid I will not persevere to the end and will fall back into sin; how can I be sure of final perseverance?
completion: Your fear is understandable, but do not rest on past beginnings. It avails nothing to have begun unless the course is finished well; look not to how far you have run but to what remains. Keep pressing forward in prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and fleeing temptation, and when you fall, repent and return. The author teaches that those who persevere in true devotion to Mary until death may securely trust their salvation is certain. Yet remember: every blessing is predicated on obedience to law, and one who sins in youth and repents late has lost something never regained, though he may be forgiven.

prompt: What does it mean to love God with all my heart, soul, and might in wartime?
completion: Loving God with all your heart, soul, and might in wartime means living in the atmosphere of Christ's love, which was in Him from without beginning and was never slacked. He loved us ere He made us, and in that love He made all things profitable to us. Divine love infuses a spirit of mortification, patience, obedience, humility, and meekness, with a love of sufferings and contempt, in which consists the sweetness of the cross. But this is not grim duty; it is a response to His eternal love, believing He ever loves you and claiming His sweet approval and tender regard. In wartime, you endure hardships as sharing His cross, yet with confidence that He loves you. Love was His meaning in all He shewed. This love is shown in humble obedience, meekness toward enemies, and patient endurance, all under the sweet awareness of His loving gaze.

prompt: I am afraid of dying. How can I prepare my soul?
completion: Fear of death is natural, but prepare your soul by keeping yourself in God's presence and avoiding all hurry and anxiety. Over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Patiently wait upon the Lord and take all that befalls from His hands as intended for your highest good. Play the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ, co-operating with His grace. Remember that death is certain, but its time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain. Therefore, make now the changes you would wish to have made when death is near. Examine your life, repent, and receive the sacraments, but do so with patience, not anxiety. Cultivate prayer and detachment, serve others, forgive, and make amends. Trust that God uses every trial, including the fear of death, to purify you. Your preparation is not about achieving perfection but about faithful co-operation with God's work in you, enduring trials with patience and hope.

prompt: I have been driven from my home and robbed of my property. Was this for my righteousness or as a chastening?
completion: Being driven from home and robbed is a painful trial. It may be a chastening from God for sins, or a test of righteousness like Job. Examine your conscience: if you find unrepented sin, repent. If not, trust God's purposes. Do not become bitter; forgive. Remember that your true home is in heaven, and earthly possessions are temporary. But beware: hoarding gold or property brings leanness of soul and darkness of mind. Put every dollar and every ability out to use for the good of the community. Reformation includes reparation: make restitution to the wronged party, or to the Lord where that is impossible. Do not merely begin anew; make good past wrongs, unpaid vows, and defrauded parties. And when restoring others who have fallen, do so in meekness, first examining yourself lest you be tempted. The work of the Gospel is to save the straying rather than to condemn them. Use this trial to grow in faith and detachment, seeking support from your community and continuing in prayer.

prompt: I want to know God, but he seems distant and abstract—how can I find him?
completion: Feeling that God is distant is common, but the search is double: your quest for God is grounded in experience and matched by the Divine Companion's quest for you. God is seeking you and spares no cost to bring you into fellowship. The one Door through the dividing wall is Jesus Christ. God is found by first finding Christ within your own heart. Our knowledge of God is partial and not exhaustive, yet real, since we know substance through phenomena and the infinite as the absence of all limit. To find Him, seek sincerely. Read Scripture, pray, and engage in community worship. Practice silence and meditation to become aware of His presence. Reflect on experiences of beauty, love, and goodness as glimpses of God. Ask God to reveal Himself. Remember that He promises to be found by those who seek Him. Be patient and persistent; faith is a journey. Serve others and you will encounter God in them.

prompt: I feel like God is deaf to my cries right now; how should I understand this?
completion: Feeling that God is deaf to your cries is a common experience, but it is not indifference. When God seems deaf, it is to grant your main desire by doing what is most expedient for you. He hears all prayers, even if the answer is not immediate or what you expect. Receive all from God's hand, sweet or bitter, equally, for afflictions seen as from a loving Father become consolation. Do not make feelings the measure of whether prayer is heard or whether you are right with God; feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to God. Rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods. Continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Use this time to draw closer to Him, examining your motives and aligning your will with His. Trust that He is working for your good, even when you cannot see it.

prompt: I keep returning to old sins even after I've repented. Will Christ keep taking me back?
completion: Christ will keep taking you back, and you need not wait to feel more or weep more before returning. This very moment you can renounce the sin in will and purpose—surrender it to God—and He supplies the strength to do what you cannot. Feeling follows surrender, not the reverse. Understand the older teaching: in Clement, Barnabas, Polycarp, and Ignatius, forgiveness was a single remission at baptism, and righteousness was identical with virtue—a life actually lived in obedience. So do not treat repentance as a revolving door of washings, but as a call to put on virtue. Yet do not expect a life free of temptation: temptations increase with grace, but never exceed your capacity, and when they would, a way out is found by the return of Grace. Confess, rise, and walk in righteousness, trusting Him to make it real.

prompt: I want one constant theme for my life through time and eternity; what should it be?
completion: The one constant theme for time and eternity is the cross of Christ. I will glory in nothing else: Jesus tasted death for me, and that is my ground of glory now and forever. The present truths the literature commends—the Sabbath, the law, righteousness, and the Lord's coming—are matters to be studied and shared, read in the light of that cross. Nor are the visible works of God unreal or worthless: study them with love. Observe the equal care in the humblest and the proudest, and consider with love that God fashioned our eyes to see and enjoy them. So let the cross be your theme, the present truths your study, and creation's works your delight, all anchored in the death He died for the sinner. When everything else shifts, this theme remains.

prompt: I'm young and my songs feel small and dated—is there any worth in them at all?
completion: Yes, there is worth in your songs. Songs of vanished love and fleeting joy—bidding adieu to what has passed—are still worth while and retain a haunting power that still thrills the reader. They are not mere practice pieces; they carry real feeling. And remember: human life is not merely the life of roses and leaves. Roses and leaves pass, but our life is not theirs, and the longings Nature moves in us tell of their own fulfillment. Nor is faith impossible amid crowded city life or worldly labour: Love can bless even in crowded loneliness, and hidden souls carry a holy strain through the wrangling mart of daily tasks. So keep writing, and let that larger hope sound through your songs, even in the noise and hurry of the city.

prompt: My family keeps asking the elders to administer to my sick mother again and again. Is repeating the ordinance appropriate?
completion: It's understandable that your family wants your mother to receive every blessing, but administration by anointing and laying on of hands is an authoritative ordinance, too sacred to be repeated loosely. Once the blessing is pronounced, give time to prayer and thanksgiving rather than unwarranted repetition. This reflects a wider order: the family is patriarchal, and Church officers must consult the father before calling a young man to any Church duty—ordination, mission, or calling—while children honor and consult their parents throughout their lives. And remember that it is every Elder's right to enjoy the Holy Ghost and know his own duties by the Spirit, but not his right to dictate his superior in office or give him counsel unless he is called upon, and then only to make suggestions. So let the family receive the blessing with gratitude and honor the order of counsel.

prompt: I am a simple believer who cannot follow the philosophic exercises of the learned; where can I find the way to the highest good that they say is hidden from people like me?
completion: You don't need to master philosophy to find the highest good. All Christian Religion is learning to know ourselves: how we were in the Unity in Adam, how we are now in dissension and contrariety, whither we go when we pass out of this condition, and how we come forth from disunion into that one Tree, Christ in us. The greatest lesson one can learn is to know oneself—and when we know ourselves, we know how to deal with our neighbors—yet no one can thoroughly know himself without understanding the things of God. The way is not rapid progress through the letter alone, but to study the letter, imbibe its spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the divine Principle. Start where you are, and God will meet you there.

prompt: I keep excusing my sensual habits by saying they are natural to me—how should I understand what I am doing?
completion: Calling a habit "natural" can quietly become a way of avoiding the deeper question: what is my soul actually reaching for? The body's pleasures are not the measure of what is good for you. Rather than studying the sensation, turn your attention to Truth and Love, and learn the discipline of sometimes forgoing even innocent, lawful pleasures so that your soul takes its pleasure only with God. But such resolve is not enough by itself. Divine truths must be seriously and frequently meditated upon—chewed, digested, and turned into the nourishment of your affections—before they can become powerful and operative enough to change those affections and produce the necessary fruit in your life. So take one truth, such as "my heart is made for God," and return to it often until it feeds you. Ask not "how do I manage this feeling?" but "to what is my heart devoted?" Let that question lead you outward, away from preoccupation with the body and toward the One who is Truth and Love.

prompt: How do I handle a task I'm naturally bad at and dread doing?
completion: Begin by slowing down. Over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections, and anxiety is a great obstacle to perfection. So keep yourself in God's presence: breathe, be still, and remember you are not alone. Then stop talking about how hard the task is and act. Do not merely chat about difficulties or lean on your own powers; say with courage, "I will do much; not I, but the grace of God which is within me." And do the work for the love of God, praying for grace as you go—for labor done for His love, with prayer, becomes easy. What dread made heavy, love makes light. Take it up calmly, one portion at a time, without fretting over speed or mastery. When anxiety rises, pause and return to His presence. Work quietly before God, letting love and prayer, not fear, set your pace.

prompt: I've been toiling for a long time without seeing fruit and am tempted to think it's in vain—what should I do?
completion: Long toil without visible fruit is discouraging, but the temptation to think it is in vain often comes from wanting to see your own results. Ask instead whether you are willing to be hidden in Christ and to serve unseen. Let others be more prominent, and hold up their hands by the silent ministry of love and prayer. When Christ seems absent from your perception, do not conclude you are abandoned: His absence is characteristic of temptation, and temptation faithfully borne becomes a means of mounting. Yet do not settle for comfort alone. Seek substantial information; trust little to that so-called learning based on theory. Pluck fruit from the tree of knowledge and taste it for yourself, and put the best books into your schools and hands. Let your perseverance be fed by real knowledge, not slogans, so that your labor is grounded in truth and not merely in endurance.

prompt: I rise late and rush into the day without seeking God. How does that affect my ministry?
completion: Rising late and rushing into the day without seeking God shapes your ministry more than you might realize. But the answer is neither to withdraw into private devotion and neglect people, nor to throw yourself into popular work with prayer left out of your plans. Time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. So begin the day with Him, then carry that presence into your work. When obstacles arise, do not meet them with anxiety or self-willed scheming; wait meekly before God with your hands off the scales, trusting Him to remove them in His own way and time. Yet do not assume events will unfold slowly as in former times: trust that God will cut His work short in righteousness. Avoid date-setting, and instead prepare yourself for events that are hastening. Make small, sustainable changes—a modest wake-up time, preparation the night before, ten quiet minutes—and let your planning rest on His timing rather than your own.

prompt: I feel nothing in prayer anymore. Have I been abandoned by God?
completion: Feeling nothing in prayer does not mean you have been abandoned. Feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to God; the changeless word of promise does not rise and fall. So do not measure your standing by your mood, and continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, refusing to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Yet do not conclude that prayer does nothing: valid prayer has real effects, and there is a genuine incoming of energy from beyond the margin of the normal self, ordered within the life of the spirit rather than in capricious interruptions of nature. Understand, too, that prayer is not easy or naturally congenial. It is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs your bankruptcy before God. Little praying is a worse evil than no praying, because it is a deluding make-believe. So keep praying with simple words and Scripture, attend to health and community, and rest on the promise rather than the feeling.

prompt: What should I do when I feel spiritually dry and my senses incline to evil?
completion: Spiritual dryness is common, but do not let it soften your view of evil. Seen in the new light that comes when the Spirit of Love descends, sin is not an attractive option or a harmless feeling: it is disease, misery, imprisonment, and death. When your senses incline toward evil, name it truly and turn from it, because it destroys what God loves. Do not fear that another's sick thoughts can force their way into your mind; virtue and truth are a strong defence, and evil finds no lodgment in a mind kept by truth and love. Yet when you would help someone who has strayed, do so in meekness, first examining yourself lest you also be tempted. The work of the Gospel is to restore the fallen, not to condemn them. Ask the Spirit of Love for clear sight, keep prayer and fellowship, and be patient in dryness, knowing faithfulness in the dark is still love.

prompt: I've stopped feeling horrified by a sin I once hated—is that a warning sign?
completion: Losing horror at a sin you once hated is worth taking seriously. The remedy is not to manufacture dread or punish yourself into feeling rightly, for mortification without love cannot efface sin. The pardon of sin is to be expected without anxiety from the Blood of Jesus Christ, while you endeavor to love Him who shed it. Yet do not mistake mercy for permission to drift: unregretted sin accumulates, dulling the conscience and destroying the ability to do right. So repent and reform now. If God seems distant or stern, remember that the chasm and the stern face are the shadow cast by your own deed in you; God's own attitude remains love. The change needed is in you, not in Him. Return to Him, ask for a heart that hates the sin because it grieves the One you love, and let gratitude for His Blood draw you back.

prompt: I'm anxious about the future and whether God really knows what I will freely choose.
completion: Anxiety about the future and about God's knowledge of your free choices is understandable, but take comfort mightily in God's promises and hold your troubles lightly. The Bible gives no neat philosophical formula, yet it shows a God who knows you intimately and cares for you personally; His promises are far larger than your fears. Do not imagine He may abandon you to trouble without giving courage: the eternal Father who cares for you today will care for you tomorrow, either withholding the trouble or giving you invincible courage to bear it. So do not anticipate future accidents with fear. Await them with perfect hope, trusting that God, whose child you are, will deliver you according as they come. Pray honestly about your fears, make your choices responsibly, and let the mystery draw you toward trust rather than paralysis.

prompt: I keep putting myself in situations that tempt me. Is that a problem?
completion: Yes, repeatedly placing yourself in situations that tempt you is a real problem, because it makes giving in far more likely. But address it with self-control, not self-loathing or anger. Begin with honest self-examination: identify the situations and what draws you to them. Then make concrete changes: avoid the places, people, or times that set you up to fail, and build in accountability with someone you trust. Bridle your tongue, subdue your anger, and attend to your own duties rather than judging others. When you slip, confess it, learn, and get up again. Do not give up rejoicing because the first attempt seemed ineffectual; keep on rejoicing and count it all joy, trusting God to make the reckoning good. And where a matter lies within God's purpose and only time and patience can solve it, it is no discredit to say 'I don't know.' Undue impatience and gloom are nearly unpardonable, especially in those who lead; waiting may need as much courage as acting.

prompt: I am a poor laborer and want to know how to see God in the fields where I work—can nature teach me anything of grace?
completion: Yes, nature can teach you much about grace if you look with attention. The seed that dies and rises, the rain that falls on good and bad ground, the patient growth that cannot be rushed—all picture how God works quietly and generously. As a laborer you see daily how life comes from the ground only through care and waiting. Do your work for the love of God, praying for grace as you go, and the labor becomes easy, for love makes the burden bearable and grace supplies strength. Read the word of God upon your knees, turning its promises, precepts, warnings, and counsels into supplication, and expect that such use of Scripture will give insight, self-searching, and acceptable prayer. Yet remember that God is the one living Worker and all human workers are only His instruments. Cast all your care upon Him; anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. Let the fields remind you that He is patient and abundant, and let your work become prayer.

prompt: I want to be humble but I also want people to respect me—how do I deal with that tension?
completion: The tension eases only when you humble yourself profoundly before God, acknowledging that you depend on Him for every good thought and deed. Humility is your shield: it guards devotion from becoming display. So do not pursue virtues on your own strength, and do not seek to be humbled only in visible ways. Desire rather the humiliations no one sees, for the keenest are the least visible. Love lowliness and even abjection as the highest humility, since greatness lies not in confidence in your own powers but in a lowly heart that rests wholly on God. Respect may come or go; what matters is that lowliness keeps you fixed on Him rather than on being seen.

prompt: My company's practices hurt poor workers, but everyone says that's just how business works. What should I do?
completion: "That's just how business works" is a slogan, not an argument. Do this unwelcome task as God's business, without uneasiness: document what you know, raise it plainly in writing, ask what policy governs it and what remedy exists, and get advice before whistleblowing. Yet the deeper answer is character. Saints should increase in goodness until their mechanics are so honest and reliable that employers prefer them for engineers, watchmen, clerks, and managers; if they are not so preferred, it proves they do not live their religion. So be scrupulously honest and dependable yourself, and require the same even-handedness of the poor: those helped must be honest, thankful, and frugal, for coveting another's goods is as wicked as miserly hoarding. Advocate fair wages without teaching envy, and let your reliability itself be a rebuke to unjust practice.

prompt: What does it mean to be delivered from the power of evil if the enemy is really inside me?
completion: The enemy is inside you, part of your own self—habit, fear, self-will—so deliverance is a siege, not a magical rescue from outside.
