God and man together batter the citadel of evil within, and you must bring your own resolve: name the impulse, pray, confess, submit to accountability, retrain desire through small faithful choices. When pressed to extremities, do not despair; they are God's challenges pushing you into His best, and though walled in you can always get out at the top. But do not merely manage or tolerate the evil within. Resist it of every sort, firmly, to the end, for error is opposed to Life and will flee before Truth. Freedom grows as the inner citadel is taken room by room, your will joined to His, refusing compromise.

prompt: My brother was stoned for his faith—how should I think of his death?
completion: Your brother died for his faith, and that is both grief and honor. But never let your soul live in sadness, bitterness, or scrupulous fear; these are not the Christian's home. The soul's business is persevering in God's presence by simple attention and fond regard—a silent, secret conversation with Him beyond obliged forms. Yet do not ground assurance in your brother's faithfulness, your feelings, frames, or worthiness; looking at self only clouds the view. Rest wholly on Christ—his sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. His promises leave no room to doubt his power and will to save. Keep the secret conversation going through grief, and let the altogether lovely Saviour, not self, hold your sorrow and your hope.

prompt: I have been asked to state my needs to a wealthy inquirer who wants to help. Should I tell him how much I need?
completion: Answer honestly, but consider first what the Lord asks of wealth: not how much a man holds, but how it was come by and what will be done with it. Greater means bring greater responsibility to spread righteousness and relieve misery. State your needs plainly—no inflation, no pretending you need nothing—and say what you will do with any help. Yet do not solicit or collect; lay the matter before him and leave him burdened to ask God what he would have him do, trusting unsolicited giving. And resign your will to God, who may deny a request in kindness: his denial can be better than the thing asked for. A denied petition is not proof that prayer fails but a Father's loving answer, so ask, then leave the outcome to Him.

prompt: I feel like my life has cracked and gone up in smoke. Is there anything left to salvage?
completion: Your feeling that life has cracked and gone up in smoke is real, but it is not the truth of your being. In Truth, there is no real relapse; what seems like collapse is a call to meet the cause mentally and courageously. Fear would have you believe the wreckage is final, but fear is a liar. Face the cause squarely—not as a victim, but as one who can conquer fear by refusing to accept its verdict. Do not settle for a middle way that tries to serve both God and worldly interests as a safe compromise; that path leads to gloomy wretchedness. Instead, follow Christ all the way, allowing Him to complete His process in you. Victory over lower passions is not achieved by unaided human will or mere self-discipline, but by a Living Power within us, slowly transforming us from fleshly to spiritual and teaching us higher pleasures so we are not left comfortless. Nothing is truly lost except what you consent to lose. Stand in the truth that your life is not defined by smoke and ashes, but by the unbroken core within you. Meet this moment with courage, and you will find that what seemed like an end is actually a beginning. There is everything left to salvage, because the Real cannot be destroyed.

prompt: Is it wrong to plan my own life instead of leaving it open to God's leading?
completion: Planning your own life isn't inherently wrong—God gave you wisdom and responsibility to make choices. But leaving it open to God's leading means inviting Him into those plans, holding them loosely, and being willing to change direction if He prompts you. The key is not whether you plan, but whether you plan with a heart open to God. You can set goals and make decisions while still praying for guidance and being attentive to His voice. Often, God leads through the very process of planning, giving clarity and peace along the way. So don't be afraid to plan, but plan prayerfully, submitting your plans to God and trusting that He will direct your steps as you acknowledge Him. Moreover, this life is not the complete end of the world; belief in a righteous God gives ground for expecting continuance after death, for His purpose for the higher spirits is not exhausted by this life. Immortality is a corollary of that belief. Yet do not busy yourself with the hidden lot of another soul; leave another's calling and end in Christ's high hand, asking only that love for Christ endure, and turn to follow Him. The high ideal of walking worthy of the Lord is not impossible or a mere ideal; it is realisable, since God's commands always imply promises. Trust that He who calls you will also enable you.

prompt: Will there be a river and a tree of life in the city, and what do they mean for us?
completion: Yes, the Bible describes a river and a tree of life in the New Jerusalem. The Holy City, the New Jerusalem, encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the river of water of life issuing from the throne. These are not mere figures but realities belonging to the sanctuary. For us, they mean that in God's presence, there is continual nourishment and restoration. The river represents the Holy Spirit and the life He gives, while the tree represents Christ and the healing He brings to the nations. Together, they show that God's ultimate plan is to dwell with His people and provide for their every need, offering eternal life and wholeness. They invite us to hope in the fullness of life that awaits us in God's city. However, entrance into the city is not open to those who do not keep God's commandments; only those who do His commandments have right to the tree of life and enter through the gates into the city. Nothing that defiles, works abomination, or makes a lie shall enter it. Our longing for an enduring home is Nature's own cry in us, not an unholy strife, and she who gives wings to birds will find out a way for us.

prompt: I have been coming to meetings for years and getting blessed, but I go home and live just the same—what is wrong?
completion: It sounds like you're experiencing a disconnect between your spiritual highs at meetings and your everyday life. That's not uncommon. The blessings you receive at meetings are meant to strengthen you for daily living, but if you're not intentionally applying them, they can fade. Perhaps you need to focus on integrating your faith into your routine—praying throughout the day, finding a community for accountability, and serving others. Also, consider whether you're truly engaging with the messages or just passively listening. Transformation often requires active participation and a willingness to change. Don't be discouraged; growth is a process. Start with small, practical steps to live out what you're learning, and ask God for the strength to follow through. Remember that membership in the Church is a real bond carrying personal obligation, not a loose affiliation. Yet the Church's divisions have made it less actual and less powerful than the nation, which may explain some of your struggle. Join diligent work with earnest believing prayer, trusting not in the work but in the Lord who alone gives the increase. And remember that you need not be always at church to be with God; you can make an oratory of your heart for familiar conversation with Him in meekness, humility, and love.

prompt: Is it true that morality would collapse if religious belief disappeared?
completion: That's a complex question. Many people argue that religion provides a foundation for morality, offering a sense of absolute right and wrong and a motivation to be good. Without it, they fear a slide into relativism or chaos. However, others point out that morality can exist independently of religion—secular ethics, human empathy, and social contracts can guide behavior. History shows both religious and non-religious people capable of great good and great evil. So it's not clear that morality would collapse entirely; it might change shape. But religion does offer community, purpose, and a framework for moral education that many find valuable. Yet we must ensure that our idea of God commends itself to the highest known morality, and that religion and morality strengthen one another rather than being set against each other. A God who is truly good will not conflict with what we know to be right. Moreover, the misconduct of preachers does not excuse us from obeying a message that comes from God; obedience is owed to God's message regardless of the preacher's example, as the Epiphany discourse teaches. The Christian doctrine of sin is verified by moral triumph: faith acting on promised strength overcomes sin, and believing in others enables their recovery. A bad character is not beyond remedy.

prompt: Is this earth my final home, or am I destined for some far-off heaven?
completion: The question of whether earth is our final home or if we are destined for heaven is one that touches the core of our existence. According to the text, we are not meant to find our ultimate rest in this world. Instead, our longing and seeking are our common working until we reach fulfillment in Heaven. This earth is not our final home; we are pilgrims and strangers here, looking for a city whose builder and maker is God. While we may experience moments of joy and peace, the fullness of rest is reserved for the life to come. Therefore, we should hold onto our longing for heaven as a sign of our true destination, not as a fault to be cured, but as a guide that leads us onward. Moreover, we must weigh the passing pain of sacrificing our self-will against the deepest pain of descending to the grave without the Saviour. The fear of temporary discomfort should not deter us from the sacrifice of will that leads to eternal life. In Christ, we find the track that leads us home. He is the way, the truth, and the life, and through Him we can become the most perfect worshippers of God. Indeed, the end we propose is to be the most perfect worshippers of God in this life as in eternity, and this is the goal toward which all our longing and seeking should tend.

prompt: I feel called to ministry—how do I know if it's really God's call?
completion: Discerning a call to ministry is a significant step. First, consider whether you have a strong desire to serve God and others. Look for confirmation from your church community and leaders. Pray about it and seek wise counsel. Also, examine your gifts and abilities—do you have the skills needed for ministry? Finally, consider the needs of the world and where you can best serve. If you feel a persistent pull toward ministry and others affirm your gifts, it may be God's call. But remember, ministry is not just about preaching; it's about serving. So, start serving in small ways and see if it leads to a larger role. Trust that God will guide you as you seek Him. However, beware of two extremes: the hermit's withdrawal from people and the popularizer's prayerless activism. Time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. So, balance prayer and action, and let your time with God fuel your service to others. Furthermore, do not rely on your own abilities or on orthodoxy alone. All life-giving power comes from the Spirit of God upon the preacher and the word. Truth unquickened by the Spirit deadens rather than gives life. Therefore, seek the Spirit's anointing and depend on Him to energize both you and your message. Finally, before you undertake exterior labors for others' salvation, mortify the deeds of the flesh and acquire charity, humility, and holy joy. Interior virtue and self-denial must precede and accompany your ministry. Only then will your service be fruitful and pleasing to God.

prompt: I feel like I'm failing the tests God puts before me—does that matter for my eternal future?
completion: It's natural to feel discouraged when you think you're failing God's tests, but remember that God is merciful and forgiving. Your eternal future is secure if you have faith in Jesus Christ. While our actions matter, they don't determine our salvation—grace does. So, don't be too hard on yourself. Instead, focus on growing in your relationship with God and learning from your mistakes. God knows your heart and your struggles. He doesn't expect you to be perfect. Keep trying, and trust that God's grace is sufficient for you. If you're struggling, talk to a pastor or trusted friend. You're not alone in this journey. However, recognize that life's experiences are tests watched by God with jealous love. Every step is decisive for your eternal future. God is looking for tested pattern men, and all experiences come as tests. So, rather than disappointing your watching Father, strive to overcome each test, knowing that He is cheering you on and that your response matters for eternity. Yet, do not engage in anxious self-inspection to determine your own perfection or imperfection. Instead, humble yourself over faults found and go on with simplicity and confidence, trusting in God's grace and guidance. Finally, do not rely on baptism or the name of Christian, or the mere fact of dying, to guarantee paradise. Death works no miracle; we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. The Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. So, ensure that love is cultivated in your life now, for that is what determines your eternal progress.

prompt: I'm exhausted all the time and blame my heavy muscles—but is it really my body that's tired, or my thought?
completion: It's common to feel exhausted and attribute it to physical factors like heavy muscles. However, fatigue can also be influenced by mental and emotional states. Stress, anxiety, and negative thinking can drain your energy just as much as physical exertion. So, while your muscles may feel heavy, it's worth considering whether your thoughts are contributing to your tiredness. Are you dwelling on negative thoughts or worrying excessively? Sometimes, addressing mental patterns can alleviate physical fatigue. It's also important to rule out medical causes. A balanced approach—attending to both body and mind—is best. If fatigue persists, consult a doctor. But don't overlook the power of your thoughts in shaping how you feel. In truth, fatigue is often a mental illusion, a false talking of mortal mind. By understanding Mind's control over the body, you can overcome it. So, rather than blaming your muscles, examine your thoughts and realize that your true being is spiritual and not subject to weariness. Remember that Mind is causation, and the body expresses mortal mind. Therefore, impress thoughts of health, not sickness, upon your body. As you hold to the truth that Mind governs the body, fatigue will dissipate. Moreover, consider that a soul devoted to God should sometimes deprive itself of innocent lawful pleasures, taking pleasure only with Him. This discipline can free you from dependence on bodily sensations and align you with divine Love, bringing true rest.

prompt: What shall I do to come to Rest, when I have tasted the Divine Sweetness and it is gone from me again, and I am deserted within and scorned without?
completion: When you have tasted the Divine Sweetness and it seems to have vanished, leaving you deserted within and scorned without, it's important to remember that such experiences are common in the spiritual life. The return of temptation and doubt does not mean that your earlier experience was false. Instead, it may be a test to refine your faith. To come to Rest, focus on trusting God even when you don't feel His presence. Continue in prayer, seek support from fellow believers, and recall the times you have felt God's closeness. Avoid isolating yourself. Remember that God's love is constant even when our feelings fluctuate. Rest will come as you persevere in faith, knowing that God is with you always. Indeed, after tasting the Divine Sweetness, the soul is assaulted from without by the World's reproach and from within by temptation and doubt. The Divine Light retires as fire raked in embers, yet the burning Fire of Love sown in it keeps a continual hunger and thirst after the Divine Sweetness. Therefore, stand firm and shrink not, for this is the trial by which you are refined. However, do not seek rest through your own reason, self-direction, or creature comforts. The true Quiet of the Soul, which no creature can disturb, is attained only by wholly giving yourself up to the life of Christ and resigning your will to him, desiring and willing nothing without him. Finally, if you would help others who have fallen, restore them in meekness, first examining yourself lest you be tempted. The work of the Gospel is to save the straying rather than to condemn them. So, in all things, seek the meek restoration of the erring and the quiet rest that comes from surrender to Christ.

prompt: I feel weary of time and long for something beyond this world. Is that longing wrong?
completion: Your longing is not wrong, and it is not an unholy strife. The spirit's thirst for enduring life is Nature's own voice in you, the cry of the one who made you for an enduring home. She who gives wings to birds will find out a way for you, so have no care for the morrow: think only of doing well today and trust the eternal Father's care for tomorrow, neither dreading nor forecasting troubles. But this longing must become steady, persistent desire, not a single cry, a moment of disappointment, or a few tears of self-pity. God is not to be sought only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or you are sick and lonely. Seek him always, and let the longing make you faithful today.

prompt: I want to love God and my fellow-Christians, but I do not understand what charity truly is in me.
completion: Charity is not first your effort or feeling. Charity unmade is God himself; Charity made is your soul in God; Charity given is the virtue by which God dwells in you. This Charity keeps you in Faith and Hope, and Hope leads you on in Charity, until all shall be Charity. Yet do not rest in a blessing about Christ—doctrine, joy, church, or friends—but in Christ himself, united to him who is the fountain of all blessings and the unfailing one when all else withers. And charity does not flatter: it faithfully and lovingly reproves a brother's sin, going to him directly rather than speaking evil behind his back, as Paul rebuked Peter and Christ rebuked his own.

prompt: How can I find real community?
completion: Real community is built when people are organized for industry, faithfulness, and prudence: every person industrious, faithful, prudent, never wanting what they cannot get, living within their means, making what they wear and raising what they eat, so that in time they prosper. But order alone gives the world no inducement; the community must live a true and pure Christian life whose victorious example attracts, so that others say, 'If that is the religion of Jesus Christ, I want it.' Historically, too, the Christian community's detachment from the Jewish Church and its development within Græco-Roman culture made the Hellenising of the Gospel necessary, drawing the material of its doctrine from Greek culture—not a mere accident but a consequence of that breach.

prompt: I have been robbed and know who did it; should I prosecute, or seek the thief's salvation?
completion: Your first aim should be the thief's repentance and faith, not punishment or revenge. Go to him privately, seeking his soul and valuing it above the loss, and forgive personally. But keep proper ward over your own mind: dwell on good, and exclude false beliefs as you would exclude thieves, not letting thought grow familiar with evil. If restitution can be made without harm, receive it, but never let goods matter more than the man. And walk in the light of Love, excluding all that defiles or makes a lie, for nothing unclean belongs in the spiritual city; let mercy and truth together govern the whole matter.

prompt: I have a sick family member and have prayed for healing; should I ask Mary for health or leave it to God's will?
completion: Ask Mary for health, and do not set her intercession against God's will. Her prayers have the force of a command with her Son, and it is impossible for her not to be heard. She is prompt to aid those who invoke her, anticipating their prayers with compassion and never sending away unconsoled anyone who calls upon her. So bring your sick family member to her with confidence, asking her to obtain health, while entrusting manner and timing to God. Yet do not treat the sick as helpless victims: they are not unable to resist disease, and can resist it as positively as they resist sin. Join prayer with that resistance, using medical care, rest, and support, and pray with faith rather than anxiety.

prompt: How do I keep my faith when so many young lives are being destroyed?
completion: It is heartbreaking to watch young lives unravel, but do not let grief become an excuse to drift from God. He has promised never to forsake us unless we first forsake Him; the danger is ours, not His. So fear to leave Him and remain always with Him. Trust Him with all your heart and refuse to lean on your own understanding or on the wisdom of others, for such dependence hinders faith. Bring your lament to Him honestly and stay close to His people. Then act: parents and pastors especially are charged to guard the young from corrupting books and to supply them with pious reading. Mentor, serve, and pray—not as a substitute for God but as a way of abiding in Him who first abides with us.

prompt: I have been given great wealth. What should I do with it?
completion: Great wealth is a responsibility, but do not respond with frantic hurry. Counsel yourself to calm, contented, patient diligence: attend your meetings, pray, read the scriptures, and meditate, keeping your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Understand what wealth truly is—not gold or money, but skill to organize the elements and produce conveniences and comforts. Well-directed labor is the true power that supplies human wants, and it deserves honor. Wealth so understood represents labor and industry; to take it by force or legislation is robbery, and such a principle would crush all energy and enterprise. Steward your own honestly, give freely, refuse coercion, and let money serve God's purposes rather than master you.

prompt: Our congregation seems to follow the leader's every word, and it worries me. How should a leader actually govern the Saints?
completion: Your concern is understandable, but the remedy is not suspicion. Each member should seek a living witness by the Holy Ghost of whether the leaders are walking in the Lord's path, trusting that the Lord will not suffer His Church to be led astray. Leaders should govern by persuasion, transparency, and service, inviting questions and explaining decisions. Members should weigh what they hear prayerfully and speak up respectfully. Remember also that the Saints are to be good citizens, loyal to the Constitution and laws of the land; the Church is not a partisan political body. And government must protect the Saints' religious rights equally with other denominations, molesting no one in the free exercise of worship. Trust is confirmed by the Spirit, not demanded by men.

prompt: I don't understand the Holy Spirit. Is he just a force or influence, or something more?
completion: The Holy Spirit is not merely a force or influence; He is a divine Person, co-equal with the Father and the Son. Jesus promised the Paraclete, the Comforter, who would teach, guide, and remind. The Spirit speaks, commands, and leads, and can be grieved—signs of a Person, not an impersonal power. He works personally and gradually in the Church; imperfection in the Old Testament or in the Church does not disprove real inspiration. Understand too that the human spirit naturally loves truth and virtue, yet it must be enlightened by the Holy Ghost to overcome the flesh and the power of the Devil. So relate to Him as a Person: listen, obey, and do not resist His promptings. He is God with you, sent by Christ to dwell in His people.

prompt: I have been treated with ingratitude by people I helped—should I stop helping?
completion: Being met with ingratitude is painful, but before you judge the ones you helped, cast the beam out of your own eye. The healer must first overcome his own belief and fear—his own fear of disease or sin—before helping another. Examine whether you help from fear, pride, or a need to be appreciated, and deal with that first. Remember that ingratitude is no small thing: failing to acknowledge God and His hand in all things is one of the greatest sins. The world wrongly credits its discoveries and success to itself rather than to God; do not imitate that spirit. And do not ask God to do all while neglecting remedies within your knowledge. Apply every remedy within reach and ask your Father in Heaven to sanctify it to the healing of body and soul; only when nothing is within reach ask the Lord to send an angel to heal.

prompt: I feel like God has abandoned my church—everything seems dark and faithless. How do I hold on?
completion: I hear your pain. When a church feels dark and faithless, it's natural to feel abandoned by God. But remember that God has not abandoned you. You need not be always at church to be with God; you may make an oratory of your heart for familiar conversation with Him. In meekness, humility, and love, you can converse with God wherever you are. Yet the Church is not merely invisible; it is a visible, unified body witnessing to central truths with authority, while allowing freedom on non-central points. Hold on by cultivating that inner oratory, but also remain connected to the visible community where possible. However, beware of establishments that mix the world and the church in their conduct of God's work; God's work must be done according to God's mind, separate from the world. Such mixing leads to departure from the Word. Pray, read Scripture, and seek support from trusted friends. The church is made of imperfect people, and sometimes we need to step back and find God in other ways. Don't give up on faith; God is still working, even in the darkness. Consider talking to a pastor or counselor about your feelings. You are not alone.

prompt: I keep going back to old habits I thought I had left—why do I love the chains that bound me?
completion: It's common to return to old habits even after trying to leave them. You might love the chains because they are familiar and provide comfort, even if they are harmful. But do not despair. Daily contrition and compunction wash off the stains we discover in our souls and incite us to repair past sloth and barrenness by a fervent and fruitful following life. Yet one renewal of fervor is not enough, for our fallen nature constantly draws us down. The soul is like a clock that needs repeated winding. So each day, practice contrition: acknowledge your faults, ask for forgiveness, and resolve to amend. If we do not renew our fervor at the proper time, God may do it by more painful means. Remember that temptations increase with grace but never exceed our capacity; when they would exceed it, a way out is found by the return of Grace. Try to identify triggers and replace the habit with something healthier. Seek support from friends, a support group, or a counselor. Keep persevering, and celebrate small victories. You are not alone in this struggle.

prompt: I keep trying to outdo the beauty I see around me and it's exhausting me—should I just stop?
completion: It's understandable to feel exhausted from trying to outdo the beauty around you. The pressure to constantly compete with others can be draining. But consider that every trait of goodness or beauty in creatures is a faint reflection of an infinite perfection in God. Instead of trying to outdo, let the beauty you see raise your heart to God and elicit acts of love for Him. When any creature delights you, turn that delight into love for the Creator. Look away from the body to Truth and Love; hold your thought steadfastly to the enduring and good. Do not seek happiness in bodily conditions or present contentment, but in the unchanging Truth and Love of God. Be a medium reflecting Christ's light and love, showing forth His excellencies rather than any beauty of your own. Take breaks, practice gratitude, and find contentment in God alone. Remember that your worth is not determined by how you compare to others. Seek activities that rejuvenate you in spirit and let go of the need to outshine. You are not enough in yourself, but in Christ you are complete.

prompt: I keep hearing about secret combinations and deceptive spirits. How do I protect my family from them?
completion: It's wise to be concerned about secret combinations and deceptive spirits. To protect your family, first counsel each other to withdraw from secret organizations and to seek first the kingdom of God, which provides all that such societies offer. Educate yourselves about these dangers. Strengthen your family through prayer, scripture study, and open communication. Set clear boundaries and teach children to recognize deception. Build a strong support network with trusted friends and church leaders. Remember that confidence is built from small beginnings: a child's little chest is as sacred to him as a man's is to him. Husbands and wives should never search each other's boxes without consent. Respect each person's property, and never open a spouse's or child's things without consent. Understand that the spirit world is here on this earth, and good and evil spirits dwell together. The Gospel is preached to the spirits in prison. If you suspect influence, seek professional help. Remember that God is more powerful than any evil, and faith in Him is your greatest protection. Stay vigilant and united as a family.

prompt: I am a Gentile Christian attracted to the ascetic life of the Jewish Christian teachers—vegetarianism, celibacy, daily washings; is this a higher path or a departure from the Gospel?
completion: The ascetic practices you mention—vegetarianism, celibacy, and daily washings—have been part of some Christian traditions. They are not essential to the Gospel, but they can be a helpful discipline when rightly motivated. Asceticism is not about treating the body as evil or liberating the spirit from it; rather, it is about restoring the whole nature to its true law. The body is kept under only to be offered at last as a living sacrifice of rational service. However, be aware that some groups, like the Elkesaites, required circumcision and Sabbath, repudiated Paul, appealed to a new revealed book that completes the Gospel, and bore strong Asiatic heathen influence. They scarcely deserve the name Christian. Also, note that the term 'Jewish Christianity' should be applied only to Christians who maintained Jewish national and political forms and literal Mosaic observance as essential, or claimed a Jewish prerogative. It is contrasted with the universalistic Christian religion rather than with Gentile Christianity as such. Consider your motivations and whether these practices draw you closer to God or distract you. The Gospel is about grace, not works. You are free in Christ to adopt or not adopt such practices, as long as they do not become a means of earning salvation. Seek wise counsel and follow your conscience.

prompt: If God is love and love requires sacrifice, does that mean there is sacrifice within God Himself?
completion: God is love, and love gives itself. Within the Trinity there is eternal self-donation among Father, Son, and Spirit, overflowing in the incarnation and cross—self-giving, not need or deficiency. For us, no one is saved or grows in holiness without self-denial; we advance in proportion to the violence done to our own will, and such sacrifice must be cheerful, for God loves a cheerful giver. Yet we should not ask only what sacrifices are bound, but what we can offer in gratitude for Christ mocked, scourged, crowned with thorns, and dying for our sins. This sacrifice takes concrete shape in worship: the spiritual worship of God was realized in definite institutions, and the Supper appeared as the sacrifice of thanksgiving of the community. There our grateful self-offering is joined to Christ's once-for-all sacrifice, so that love's sacrifice is not vague sentiment but embodied praise.

prompt: Should I follow a strict method or rule for my devotions?
completion: A rule can help establish habits, but it must serve communion with God rather than replace it. Beware a common abuse: the saying that the best devotion is the constant practice of one's ordinary duties is sometimes used to excuse a dissipated, prayerless life. Every person is bound first to live to himself and to reserve leisure for frequent exercises of devotion. Yet particular devotions are means to an end; when the soul is with God, its end, they may be laid aside. So hold your rule loosely. The same principle applies to devotion to Mary: true devotion means honoring and invoking her, trusting her intercession, imitating her virtues, and intending to amend one's life—never presuming on her mercy. Let every method, Marian or otherwise, serve the relationship with God rather than eclipse it, and let the means always point beyond themselves to the end, who is God Himself.

prompt: How does the Lord actually guide a person—through feelings, through Scripture, through circumstances?
completion: God guides through Scripture, His Spirit, and providence, but the heart of guidance is meek waiting before Him. We cannot find our way by our own insight: sin has blinded and biassed us, so we cannot arrive without the Lord's direction. He gives means—His Word to instruct, the indwelling Spirit to incline the heart, and providence to open and close the way. When you face a decision, lay it before God with hands off the scales. Do not scheme, and do not let apparent hindrances make you anxious; they are often occasions for God to interpose. He sways the judgment quietly and removes obstacles in His own way and time. Remember that the servant of Christ has one Master: you are guided by the Spirit as to time and place, not bound by human committees or fixed rules. Pray, search the Scriptures, attend to providence, and follow the Spirit's leading, trusting Him to guide a heart that knows its own blindness.

prompt: I feel no desire to pray in the morning. What does that say about my heart?
completion: Feeling no desire to pray in the morning is common, but do not excuse it—morning listlessness is an index of a listless heart. Prayer should not be a small duty fitted into leftover time. Give the best of your time and strength to it: let the closet come first, and let study and activity come second, freshened by the closet. Prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress. Pray specifically that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Early seeking is the mark of a soul following hard after God, so do not separate the discipline of early prayer from the ardor of the heart—let the one kindle the other. Don't wait for desire to strike; often desire follows action. Ask God for help, and arrange your schedule so prayer gets your best, not your remains.

prompt: I'm going through a terrible loss—someone I loved more than anything. Why would God take that from me?
completion: I'm so sorry for your loss. Grief is real and heavy, and God is near to the brokenhearted. Yet everything comes from God's hand, sweet or bitter, and both should be received equally. This loss did not slip past His love; it came from a Father who loves you, and seen as from Him, affliction becomes consolation. Abandon yourself to God in this interior and exterior suffering; do not seek life, work, or joy outside of Him, but live and work and even rejoice in God. At the same time, let your grief be moderated. Excessive mourning is a want of faith and confidence in God. He takes away friends because He will be loved without a rival—He wants your heart wholly for Himself. Bring your questions to Him, lean on your community, and let this sorrow draw you deeper into the God who does not abandon you.

prompt: Is it wrong to want to feel devotion and sweetness in prayer, or to want tears of compunction?
completion: Wanting devotion and tears of compunction is not wrong, but feelings must not be the measure of prayer. Feelings never accurately gauge our real assimilation to God. The changeless word of promise is our foundation. When joy is lacking, continue steadfastly; do not abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Yet the soul's need of God is not a delusion. Our native yearning is evidence of a real Other who answers; the search implies something to be found. Devotion suits every state of life, not only the cloister. Amid exterior business, the heart must remain on God, and the spirit of the world must be shunned. So desire devotion, but rest on God's promise, not on moods, and keep your heart recollected in Him.

prompt: I keep telling myself I'll change later—am I deceiving myself?
completion: You are deceiving yourself if you think change means swapping one set of works for another. Sanctification does not consist in changing works but in doing common works for God's sake. The mistake is to make means the end. Your ordinary tasks can be offered to God as they are. Do not wait for some future dramatic change. Begin now by doing your daily duties for God's sake. But beware: a passing fear or a short-lived fit of fervor is not sufficient conversion. Transient glances effect not a change of heart. Penitents must be brought to a sincere and perfect change of heart. Yet do not be astonished at finding miseries in yourself, for the work is never done. Always begin anew with a good heart, and offer your works to God sincerely.

prompt: I am a student of theology, and I find that the more I study, the less I pray; how do I keep my study from killing my devotion?
completion: Give the best of your time and strength to prayer, making the closet first and study second. Begin each day with prayer before study, letting study be freshened by the closet. But do not abandon prayer after delay. Be patient, believing, and importunate. Continue until the blessing is granted, without prescribing to God the time or manner of the answer. Expect the answer while waiting. Long-continued petition is not pointless; it is the way of faith. Approach prayer with trembling, shutting your senses to distractions and observing strict silence of tongue and body. Profound exterior and interior reverence must accompany your prayer. So keep praying with reverence, and let study follow.

prompt: I am angry and want revenge on someone who wronged me. What does my faith require?
completion: Your faith requires you to forgive and not seek revenge. St. Fulgentius teaches that Christians must not seek revenge but forgive injuries. So put away the desire for revenge. Instead, be patient and forgive, as Christ forgave you. This does not mean the wrong was okay, but it means you entrust justice to God and release your claim. Pray for the person who wronged you. Ask God for the grace to forgive. And when you lapse in remembering God, do not be disquieted. Return with greater trust. Lapses in remembrance are met without disquiet and with renewed trust. If pain prevents mental treatment, temporary material relief may be permitted, but it is only a lulling of belief, not the real cure. Once the belief of pain is lulled, handle the case mentally. So keep forgiving and keep returning to God.

prompt: I am a young person at a funeral and feel strangely moved—what should I do with this impression?
completion: That strange feeling at a funeral is a call to remember that you too must die. Count yourself as already dead, and have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over, regret, and detest your offences and faults. It is not now the time to rejoice but rather to lament with all sincerity of heart. So let this impression lead you to repentance and sorrow for sin. But beware: a passing fear or a short-lived fit of fervor is not sufficient conversion. Transient glances effect not a change of heart. Penitents must be brought to a sincere and perfect change of heart. And remember that God watches over all the dead, even those who perish at sea, as fondly as the churchyard grave. So turn to God with a contrite heart, seeking a sincere and lasting change.

prompt: I'm overwhelmed by too many responsibilities and I feel like I'm failing at all of them—how do I find peace?
completion: Feeling overwhelmed is a signal to slow down, not speed up. Begin by becoming quiet in God's presence; peace is not the reward for finishing your list but a gift received now. Over-eagerness is the mother of many imperfections, so refuse hurry. Take up the next duty plainly before you and do it calmly. Watch your tongue, subdue anger before it speaks, examine your own heart rather than measuring others, and mind your own duties instead of meddling. When anxious fretting rises, return quietly to His presence. And do not quit: having done all, stand. Keep trying even when the work seems to fail; apparent defeat is no reason to abandon the cause. Faith works steadily and never gives up, trusting God with the outcome.

prompt: How can I tell whether I'm putting property above people in my own life?
completion: One test is to notice what you protect most fiercely: do you grieve more over a scratched car than a wounded relationship? Remember that temporal possessions are a shadow and a dew; trusting in them brings disappointment, and worldly riches are not true riches. Confidence is built from small beginnings: a child's little chest is as sacred to him as a man's is to him, so never open a spouse's or child's things without consent. Yet go deeper still: you are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Your time, talents, gold, and silver are the Lord's, and you own nothing but the talents God has given you to improve. You are only a steward of what is lent to you. Ask whether your calendar and money treat people as owners under God or as rivals to your goods.

prompt: Why does the Lord's Prayer have no 'I' or 'me' in it—what does that say about how I should pray?
completion: The absence of 'I' and 'me' shows that prayer is not a solitary transaction but a shared life before God. To say Father to God is to say brother to one's fellows; love of God and love of neighbor cannot be separated. Prayer is simple, natural, constant asking—a child speaking to a parent—not a complicated procedure governed by human rules, and God as Father delights to be sought for everyday needs. Yet prayer must also be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress. Pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and to reform whatever is amiss in it. Pray plainly and often within the living group of faith, carrying others' needs, and let prayer accompany and shape every advance you make.

prompt: How should I regard Saul, who persecuted the followers of Christ and later became Paul?
completion: Regard Saul as Zaccheus taught Judas: Saul in enmity doomed many a follower of Christ, yet the Lord showed mercy unto him so that he became a solace for many men. His name was changed, and he was called Saint Paul, and no man or woman born was ever better than he beneath the span of the heavens. Honor the divine idea set before us by God's messenger; to dismiss or abuse it is to betray ignorance of Principle. And see why such mercy is possible: the Lord who met Saul on the road is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. His saving work is intelligible only on that view of his person—not a mere prophet, but the one in whom all things hold together. Let Saul's life make you humble in judgment and hopeful in God.

prompt: I have been invited to join in Christian work alongside unconverted people—is that acceptable?
completion: Be clear on first things. Members should withdraw from secret organizations, whose oaths and secrecy divide their interests from the Church and from plain loyalty to Christ. Seek first the kingdom of God, which provides all that such societies promise—fellowship, purpose, and security—without compromise. Open, honest work alongside unconverted people can be acceptable, but remember that the work is not chiefly yours: it is GOD's own work through His servants, done in obedience to Him and for the glory of His Name. And do not refuse a task merely because it is unwelcome. Even distasteful business, undertaken as God's business, is to be done without uneasiness, trusting Him with the outcome. Ask what the group expects, be honest about your faith, keep accountability to your church, and decline only what requires secrecy or compromise.

prompt: I keep seeking happiness in things that pass away. Why can't I be satisfied?
completion: Your desire for happiness is God-given, planted in you by the One who made you for Himself, and God is to be found here in this world—the touchstone and finding-place for Him. Understand why you are unsatisfied: every substitute for God leaves an emptiness unfilled. Romance, family, business, pleasure, and art are good gifts, but when we ask them to do what only God can do, they end in disillusionment. Only the finding of God is permanent success. And beware the middle way—trying to serve God and the world together as a safe compromise. Stopping half-way brings gloomy wretchedness. Follow Christ all the way, that He may complete His process in you and fill you wholly with Himself.

prompt: I want to serve God but I have no money and no help. Can I still go forward?
completion: It is good that you want to serve God, and your lack of money and help need not stop you. Remember those who offered themselves and their substance for God's work without salary, believing God would supply all their need. Their spirit is the one to imitate: cheerful, self-denying service that trusts God rather than waiting for security first. You can go forward by offering what you have—your time, strength, and willingness—trusting Him to provide. All honest work and business can be done in the name of the Lord; no labor is outside His service when offered to Him. And you need not leave your ordinary life for a cloistered or conspicuously pious existence. The ordinary man or woman in usual everyday work or leisure can find God—without a life apart, without conspicuous piety, and without leaving undone duties to those dependent on you.

prompt: How large is the New Jerusalem, and is there room in it for everyone who is saved?
completion: The New Jerusalem is a vast city, measured as a cube roughly 1,500 miles on each side, with walls and gates. We should not treat the city, the bride, the tabernacle, and the sanctuary as separate things. They are one: the Holy City, the New Jerusalem, is the tabernacle of God, the bride the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, and the sanctuary—one city coming down from God out of heaven to dwell with men. Its size speaks of sufficiency: there is room for all who are saved. We should look with goodwill for the Jews' gathering and redemption by God's power, not claiming human preaching alone will convert them. And we should not soften the judgements of the last days: they are God's means of purging wickedness and preparing the earth for the reign of Christ, who will rule the nations with a rod of iron.

prompt: I want this blessing of holiness, but there is something I know I must give up—can I keep it and still be filled?
completion: It is understandable to hesitate, but consider honestly what you are holding back. Scripture urges us to examine our possessions and to part with what others could use. Unneeded possessions can hinder both your own blessing and the spread of the Gospel. This is a habit of mind—holding things loosely and giving freely—that brings blessing. And in every occasion of virtue, do not rely on your own strength; turn to God and ask for enabling grace, receiving strength more than sufficient. When dryness or bitterness of heart tempts you to withdraw from Holy Communion, do not draw back. Approach boldly, seeking strength and union with the spirit of meekness, for there you are met and filled.

prompt: Why should I do what I believe is right when everyone around me disagrees and it costs me everything?
completion: Doing what is right when everyone disagrees is one of the hardest things a person can face. Truth is not decided by majority vote; if you are convinced something is right, follow your conscience. But do not make human support a condition of obedience—be willing to depend wholly on God, who is faithful even when every human prop is removed. Remember how high councils ought to act: they should find out the truth and facts, judge according to them, and always temper judgment with mercy, love, and kindness, aiming to build up and save rather than tear down and destroy. And never imagine you can gain by injuring another: wrong done to another returns upon the wrong-doer, while right adjusts the balance.

prompt: Where is heaven, and where will the saints reign with Christ?
completion: Heaven is not a distant place to escape to; the meek shall inherit the earth, and the saints will reign on the earth with Christ. The New Jerusalem will come down from God to a purified earth, making it the eternal inheritance of the faithful. Christ suffers in His least saints, feeling each wound given to them, and He values even a drop of water given for love's sake. Amidst weighty employments, the saints reserved time for frequent retirement for conversing with God and themselves, and in their exterior functions they raised their minds to heaven with holy sighs and desires, making all their actions in some measure an uninterrupted prayer and exercise of divine love and praise.

prompt: Should our church follow a majority vote on important decisions?
completion: Majority vote can be appropriate, but each member should vote according to conscience, expressing true feelings without violating conscience. A sister's vote counts equally with a brother's, and presiding officers depend on the voice of the people for their authority. The presiding president should share responsibility with his counselors, acting as they agree and as the Spirit manifests, for the Lord never intended one man to have all power. The Saints are to be good citizens, loyal to the Constitution and laws of the land, and the Church is not partisan in politics.

prompt: I'm facing tremendous pressure and just want God to remove me from it—is that the right prayer?
completion: Instead of praying for removal, pray for strength and patience to bear the pressure as from God's hand. See your trial as allowed by God for your refinement, and ask Him to help you endure it with faith, not to take it away. Even brief inward remembrances and acts of worship are acceptable prayers that fortify courage, even in danger. Stop praying so much for yourself and begin to ask unselfish things for others and the world, for faith is strengthened by unselfish prayer.

prompt: I'm told to just accept my illness calmly. Is calm submission the right response, or should I resist it?
completion: During a crisis, treat the mental disturbance of chemicalization, not the disease itself. Insist that God is all and there is no disease, and calm your thought by understanding that chemicalization is not producing real pain but is a mental disturbance to be overcome. You are not a helpless victim; you can resist disease as positively as you resist sin. The healer must work from the moral might of Mind and firm trust in Truth, not from self-condemnation, guilt, or doubting trust.

prompt: Can Heaven and Hell both be here present where we are now sitting?
completion: Heaven and Hell are within the soul, not places we go after death. Heaven is the turning of the will into the Love of God, and Hell is the turning of the will into the wrath of God. At death, the soul needs no going forth but stands in that which is manifested in it. If the will goes forth from the creatures, they are forsaken and dead in it and cannot touch the soul, so one may walk with God in heaven while the body lives in the world among creatures. Spiritual consciousness and the cessation of sorrow and pain are a present possibility, for the kingdom of God is within.

prompt: My joy feels fragile, like it could be brushed away at any moment. Why bother being happy?
completion: Your longing for joy is God-given, and God is to be found here, in this world, the touchstone and finding-place for Him. But that joy is not won by a single cry or a moment of disappointment; God asks steady, persistent desire, and He is not to be sought only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or you are sick and lonely. Beware the tempting middle way of serving God and the world together, for stopping half-way brings gloomy wretchedness. Follow Christ all the way, letting Him complete His process in you, and the joy He gives will prove sturdier than the moods that brush it away.

prompt: I feel that my prayers are only words and that I am a hypocrite; does God accept the good will even when I feel nothing?
completion: Feeling like a hypocrite does not mean God rejects you, but prayer is more than words: gratitude is shown through action and daily watchfulness, and the habitual struggle to be always good is the truest prayer. Do not assume God must grant every request as asked; a father may deny a child in kindness, and His denial can be better than the thing we sought, so resign your will to His. Above all, do not let variable moods measure whether prayer is heard. Rest on the changeless word of promise, continue steadfastly when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Feelings never accurately gauge your real assimilation to God.

prompt: Where does the State's authority come from?
completion: The State's authority is sacred and of God, yet its deepest source is Christ himself, who teaches us by his Spirit; Scripture is more trustworthy than individual reason or the creeds, but all power is answerable to Him. Justice is valuable chiefly for the liberty it makes possible, and liberty is self-control, which law fosters as self-discipline. Yet the State is limited: it works by coercive force and can secure only a minimum of morality. It cannot supply the higher motives. Therefore the Church supplements it, appealing to duty and love and holding up the ideal of perfection, while the State keeps order and the Church calls souls beyond mere legality.

prompt: My servant stole everything I owned; how should I respond as a follower of CHRIST?
completion: This is a painful betrayal, and as a follower of Christ you are called to forgive injuries after the example of the good thief and of Christ on the cross, becoming a true imitator of Christ and heir of his disciples' privileges. Do not ask only what you can do in your own strength; Christ dwells within you and can conquer what you never could, so do all things through Him who strengthens you. Yet let your forgiveness reshape your use of goods: whatever is beyond necessity belongs to Christ in his poor by right. To spend on superfluities what the poor need is to rob them. Pursue lawful remedy without malice, and let mercy govern both your heart and your purse.

prompt: I was raised in sin and feel stained from birth—can I still hope that God loves me?
completion: Being raised in sin and feeling stained from birth is a heavy burden, but it does not place you beyond God's mercy. Do not doubt God's loving look: He looks upon you with love, as He looks with love upon the most terrible sinner who has any true desire to be converted. Trust His goodness toward the repentant, and be assured that if you love God, all things—even grief and sin—will turn to your good, though the means are unseen. Yet do not seek only cleansing and shrink from the fire that makes white. Accept the fiery trial that purifies, letting God burn out sin and burn in His glory, preparing you for the Lord's coming.

prompt: What happens to the soul immediately after death?
completion: At death the body returns to the dust, but the soul of the believer is with Christ in Paradise, blessed and at rest; the body will rise again at the last day, and the reunited saints shall be for ever with the Lord. Death only separates spirit and body; the spirit lives on in the spirit world, conscious and held in God's keeping, and the faithful there are beyond Satan's power. Yet do not seek comfort by your own power, by grief, or by self-torment. Do nothing of yourself, but forsake your own will, that the creatures lodged in you may die, and sink down into the One Thing from which you sprang. There God meets you with His Love manifested in Christ Jesus, and there your soul finds true rest.

prompt: I am a monk and I live with a woman as a spiritual sister. Is this pleasing to God?
completion: Living as a monk with a woman as a spiritual sister requires prayerful waiting on God for guidance. True godliness must be the first and absolutely needful qualification in any companion; beyond that, calmly weigh other suitableness—temperament, calling, and the counsel of your abbot. Rejoice in the monastic state itself: the monk surpasses the greatest monarch in honor and happiness, because he rules his passions and possesses God. Parents should rejoice when a child embraces the religious state. Remember that the love of pleasure weighs the soul down, while compunction gives her wings to rise above created things; blessed are those who mourn for sin. If this sister helps you toward that, it may be acceptable; if it clouds your vocation, it should be reconsidered.

prompt: I am a ruler and I lose my temper with my subjects. Am I fit to govern?
completion: Losing your temper with subjects is a serious matter, for no man will rule judiciously on the earth unless he first learns to rule and control himself. Only then is he capable of governing a family, a neighborhood, or a nation. Authority must be exercised with humility, meekness, and tender entreaty rather than imperious command; anger disguised as zeal disqualifies a governor. So bridle your tongue, subdue your anger, and examine yourself before you reprove others. Attend to your own duties rather than judging or meddling in the affairs of others. Let your commands be as tender entreaties, your reproof in the spirit of meekness, your firmness against evil. Place yourself in spirit beneath all your subjects, and ask God for self-control.

prompt: Our worship services feel plain and even ugly, and I've been taught that eloquence and beauty are suspect in religion. Is that right?
completion: There is a real tension here, but the answer turns on what beauty is for. Eloquence and beauty are not suspect in themselves; they become problematic only when they draw attention to the performer rather than to God. Worship is not to claim beauty as its own, but to be a medium reflecting Christ's light and love, showing forth His excellencies rather than any beauty of its own. Do not doubt God's loving look: He looks upon you with love, as upon the most terrible sinner who truly desires to be converted. Remember that the Church is of necessity visible and one, a visible body representing the Incarnate Lord; the ideal is the actual basis of the real. To stress an invisible Church so as to discredit the visible one lowers the demands of holiness and brotherhood. The visible Church is the home of the lonely and the school of brotherhood.

prompt: I have been accused falsely and I want to defend myself loudly. Should I?
completion: Being falsely accused is painful, and the urge to defend yourself loudly is understandable. But bring whatever men say or think before the tribunal of your own conscience. Enter within yourself and learn the truth there: human praise profits nothing if conscience accuses, and it is no loss to be despised or persecuted without if you are innocent within. Judge your soul justly, neither excusing it without reason nor accusing it without reflection, so that it neither grows insolent nor loses courage. Rejoice in the Lord in patience, silence, and peace. Do not abandon your witness: submit quietly to authorities, and persevere in testimony and preaching whenever opportunity allows. A calm, factual clarification may be wise if your reputation is seriously harmed; otherwise, let your conduct vindicate you over time.

prompt: I want to offer God something beautiful, but I have so little. Is my small gift worth anything?
completion: Your small gift is precious to God when it flows from a heart that first gives love to Jesus, makes a home for Him in your heart, and sets your heart upon God. Before you bring any offering, give Him your love, your devotion, and your heart's home. Then your gift, however small, becomes beautiful because it is a response of love. God doesn't measure by amount but by the love behind it. Offer what you have as an act of love, and He will receive it. But ensure that any gift for God's work is obtained only in God's way: do not solicit funds from unbelievers, do not press believers to give, and do not use worldly schemes to raise money. Carefully examine the giver's motives and whether the money is rightfully theirs; refuse gifts where motives are impure or the money is not the giver's own. Remember that the more generous you are toward God, the more generous you will find Him toward you, and the more fit you will daily be to receive in greater abundance His graces and spiritual gifts. So do not withhold; be generous according to your ability, and God will pour out His blessings upon you.

prompt: I feel condemned by the law and see no way out—what is the law for, and can it give me life?
completion: The law condemns us because we cannot keep it perfectly, but it is holy and binding. Its purpose is to show us our sin and lead us to Christ, who fulfilled the law for us. The question is not whether the law should be kept but how. Through faith in Jesus, the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in us by the Spirit. The law cannot give life; only the Spirit can. So do not discard the law; instead, learn how to keep it through the power of the Holy Spirit. The law remains our guide, and by walking in the Spirit, we fulfill its righteous requirement. Moreover, mortal life is a school of experience and probation. We are here to learn and improve, not to wish life away. Embrace each day as an opportunity to grow in grace and knowledge, continually increasing in faith and obedience. Do not passively endure life; actively engage in the learning and progression God intends for you. As you do, heed the counsel of Church leaders with cheerful, intelligent obedience, given and received in the spirit of love rather than coercion. Their guidance helps you apply the law wisely and grow in grace.

prompt: I left home for a big city and a career and now I wonder if I'll ever see my family again—did I make a mistake?
completion: It's natural to feel uncertain after such a big move, but consider that there is no substitute for the home. The home is a divine institution of stability and love, and no genuine happiness exists apart from it. The disposition to move about restlessly should be discouraged in favor of permanent homes. Leaving home for a career may forfeit genuine happiness if it means abandoning the home. You can still stay connected with your family, but prioritize returning to or establishing a permanent home. Pray for guidance and trust that God can use this season for good, but remember that family bonds are best nurtured in a stable home. Seek balance and make time for your loved ones. God is with you wherever you go, but He calls you to honor the home. Moreover, honor the rearing of a good and large family as among the most God-like works a man can do. Loyalty, with all other virtues, begins at home. So do not treat family duties as secondary to public or Church work; rather, let your family be your first priority, for it is the place where loyalty begins. Finally, let the Father fit you now for the place He has prepared, becoming a vessel of mercy prepared unto glory. Live each day with eternity in view, allowing God to shape you for your heavenly home.

prompt: I am tempted by impurity and wonder if chastity really matters.
completion: Chastity matters because it is a most precious treasure. Impurity damages your relationship with God and others, so you must protect this treasure by prayer, mortification, and modesty of the senses, especially the eyes. Avoid the occasions of temptation, for he who loves danger shall perish in it. Do not expose yourself to temptation, thinking you can withstand it. Instead, flee from it and draw near to God. Pray for strength, practice self-denial, and guard your eyes. Remember God's grace is sufficient, and with His help you can pursue purity. Focus on positive relationships and activities. God loves you and wants the best for you. Keep fighting the good fight. But also remember that people must be chastened according to the spirit in them. Some are tender as infants and must not be chastened severely; others may be talked to all day without understanding. Treat each person as they are, with patience and wisdom, and do not impose heavy burdens where gentleness is needed. Finally, understand that man took a body for exaltation through Christ's redemption and for propagating a pure seed. Purity of body is therefore of the greatest importance. Your body is not your own; it is for the Lord, and in it you are to glorify Him and raise up a godly seed.

prompt: My family has kept the law of our fathers since the first believers; are we the true descendants of the earliest Christians, or have we fallen away?
completion: It's commendable that your family has kept the law of your fathers since the first believers. To determine whether you are the true descendants of the earliest Christians, we must apply sound principles of documentary evidence. Ancient documents in proper custody are presumed genuine, and the burden of proof lies on the objector. The Christian Scriptures, having been preserved in proper custody, are therefore to be presumed genuine. We should not be prejudiced against them merely because their story is sacred. Instead, we should examine them fairly. If your family's traditions align with these documents, you may well be true descendants. But if they diverge, you may have fallen away. Examine your beliefs and practices in light of Scripture, and be open to correction. The important thing is to follow Christ faithfully, wherever that leads. Additionally, be aware of the dangers of industrial employment of women and children to domestic duties and parental authority. Christians must counteract whatever interferes with the rudiments of moral discipline, especially in the home. Finally, consider the New Testament's moral system: it is comprehensive, spiritual, simple, and practical, surpassing human powers of invention. A moral system so pure and perfect, running counter to men's natural passions, must have had a supernatural and therefore divine origin. This attests to the truth of the Christian faith and the reliability of its documents.

prompt: I wonder whether the Resurrection really happened in the body, or whether it is only a beautiful spiritual symbol. Does the difference matter?
completion: It matters, but the difference is not between a physical fact and a spiritual symbol, as though we had to choose. Resurrection is the spiritualization of thought: the yielding of material belief to spiritual understanding. Yet this is not the improving of the old nature but a death and a resurrection; the old man is crucified with Christ, and the life we now live is the new creation, a supernatural life received from God that lifts us into Him. Nor does death end the believer's hope. The dead in the Lord are blessed; the departed soul is with Christ in Paradise, and the body will rise again at the last day, when the reunited saints shall be for ever with the Lord. So the empty tomb, the present newness of life, and the final resurrection are one hope, and our belief in matter yields to the Life that cannot be entombed.

prompt: How do I deal with scruples and constant self-doubt about my sins?
completion: Scruples are a heavy burden, but the cure is not to excuse yourself or to wave guilt away. Face justice and truth honestly: name your sins before God without concealment, neither exaggerating nor minimizing them, and do not deny the truth of what you have done in order to feel better. But go deeper than surface faults. Self-denial is not the lopping off of a few branches while self-will, self-seeking, and self-glory remain at the root; the axe must be laid at the root of the tree of self, and the cross taken up voluntarily for Christ's sake, not as a forced trial. And do not treat unrepented sin lightly: unregretted sin accumulates, hardening the heart and destroying the ability to do right, and a guilty conscience is not a small thing. Let honest repentance and reformation of life be your answer, so that conscience is healed by truth and by a life genuinely turned from self to God.

prompt: I long for peace of conscience but my past still weighs on me—where does that peace come from?
completion: Peace of conscience comes from God's forgiveness, but do not treat your past lightly. Unrepented sin accumulates, hardening the heart and destroying the ability to do right, so begin with honest repentance and reformation of life. Yet beware of two errors. The moralists—Clement, Barnabas, Polycarp, Ignatius—narrowed the religious sense, making forgiveness a single remission at baptism and righteousness identical with virtue, which leaves the baptized sinner either presumptuous or despairing. Instead hold both together: dread of the unsureness of ourselves, as a matter of meekness against presumption, and the blessed Shewing of Love, as true comfort and joy against despair. Let the sight of your sin keep you humble, and let the sight of His mercy keep you from sinking. Peace comes not from your virtue but from His love, received by the repentant heart.

prompt: I am a pastor and I am paid a salary. Does that make my ministry professional and heartless?
completion: A professional, salary-centered ministry is heartless, and you should reject it. The ministry is not a business or a career; when salary and self-advancement lead, the heart goes out of the work and people become clients. Put self to the rear and heart to the front. But do not imagine that a warm heart or correct doctrine gives life: all life-giving power belongs to the Spirit of God, energizing the preacher and the word, and truth unquickened by the Spirit deadens rather than gives life. Avoid both extremes. Do not withdraw from people into a hermit's seclusion, and do not become a popularizer whose activism leaves prayer out of your plans. Time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. So pray for the Spirit, keep your heart toward the flock, and let your salary support a ministry that spends itself for others.

prompt: I feel completely apathetic about spiritual things and I can't seem to care. What is happening to me?
completion: Apathy in spiritual things is deadly, not merely a lack of feeling to be managed. Do not treat spiritual experience as something you can manufacture by returning to basics until feelings follow; accept experiences only as God chooses, without praying for them, secretly desiring them, or approaching them with curiosity, and submit without questioning or fear. Yet submission is not repose: allow no slipping back in the spiritual ascent, but go forward like a mountain-climber until the goal is reached, for desires turning aside after lower objects cause distraction and loss of the way; withdraw from worldly distractions into the one unchangeable Good. And understand that God often touches us where we are most tender—through loss and hardship—not as cruelty but as His loving means to awaken, humble, and lift us into His consolations. Name the apathy, keep climbing, and trust His hand.

prompt: I want to be recollected in God but my mind keeps wandering—what should I do?
completion: Think of prayer as a beggar waiting at a door: you have nothing but your presence, and God is already looking at you with kindness. When your mind wanders, do not turn to examine yourself. Turn simply to Him, your love and delight, and rest in His presence again—no fuss, no disquiet. Your joy is not in how well you pray but in pleasing Him. And remember: the mind you guard during the day is the mind you bring to prayer. If outside prayer you keep your thoughts gently in God's presence, refusing idle distraction, your mind grows calm and comes to prayer already recollected. So let your heart be occupied with God at all times, content to be before Him, trusting that He keeps you even when your attention slips. Return in peace, as often as needed.

prompt: I'm reading a lot of dark, realistic fiction and it's making me despair about humanity—is that the whole picture?
completion: Dark fiction can show real suffering, but it is a selection, not the whole picture. Much of what passes for peace in this world is built on mutual fear and selfish loves—and that is precisely where Cruelty's snare is knit. Cruelty, Humility, Mystery, and Deceit grow from the human brain. But see evil in its true complexion: it is disease, misery, imprisonment, and death, not glamour or harmless shadow. The spiritual man sees this by the new light created when the Spirit of Love descends. The Christian faith does not explain away the dread meeting with the Lord; it keeps that expectation alive, and the Apocalypse is a vision of final triumph in Christ. So read with that horizon open: the darkness is real, but it is not the last word. Let the stories deepen compassion, and let your hope rest in the triumph of Christ.

prompt: How can God be love if he was alone before creation and had no one to love?
completion: God's love is not a mere feeling or an abstract attribute. It is rational, voluntary self-communication: God freely gives Himself and seeks the true good of what He loves, and this love is regulated by and subordinate to holiness. Within the Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit give and receive eternally. This is the love that was in Him from without beginning: He loved us before He made us, and His love was never slacked. In that love He made all things profitable to us, and Love was His meaning in all He showed. So do not let fear govern this question. Meet the trial with stronger faith and purer love, for perfect Love casts out fear. 'God is love' means He freely communicates His goodness, holy and never indifferent to sin, seeking our true good from before all time.

prompt: I have spoken badly about a colleague. What must I do?
completion: Speak little, and speak well—and when you speak, speak plainly. First, be silent: do not repeat or spread what you said. Then go to your colleague and say plainly what you said and that it was wrong, so they can hear and understand you without guessing. If others heard you, correct the record in plain words. Say what you have to say, then stop; do not darken counsel by many words. Meanwhile, compel your heart to suffer tranquilly. You will feel rebellious murmurings and sudden impatience; do not let them govern your dealings with your neighbor. Remain kind despite them, praying quietly for the one you wronged. A few honest words, gently and frankly spoken, are better than many. Be patient; trust takes time.

prompt: I have been a light and trifling person and heard serious conversation at a funeral—can that begin a real change in me?
completion: Yes—but let it be something deeper than a mood, and do not mistake a passing stirring for conversion. Count yourself as already dead, since you must die some day. Have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over, regret, and detest your offences and faults; it is not now the time to rejoice but to lament with all sincerity of heart. And as you stand among mourners, remember that the dead beloved is in a high sphere of saner happiness; your grief for them should be a tender regret, not acute grief. Beware: superficial conversions made under fear of calamity rarely bear the characters of sincerity. Transient glances effect not a change of heart. Let this stirring bring you to a sincere and perfect change of heart, not merely a short-lived fit of fervor.

prompt: I keep thinking about my past sins and can't forgive myself—how do I move on?
completion: A guilty conscience is not a small thing to be soothed away. Unrepented sin accumulates; each time you excuse it, the heart hardens and the power to do right weakens. So begin with honest repentance: name your sins to God, grieve them, and turn toward a reformed life, making amends where you can. Confessing your faults and humbling yourself quiets the wandering mind, for pride scatters the thoughts while humility gathers them; in prayer, avoid heaping up many words, which only multiplies distraction. But go deeper than lopping off a few branches. Lay the axe at the root of self: deny not merely this indulgence or that habit, but self-will, self-seeking, and self-glory. Take up the cross voluntarily for Christ's sake—not as a forced trial but as a chosen renunciation—and let each day's conduct show that grace is at work.

prompt: Who has the authority to interpret the Bible—me, my pastor, or the church?
completion: The final interpreter is not a lone individual, nor a pastor alone, nor a formal organization, but the composite judgment of the whole body of believers, checked by the authority of the prophets and apostles speaking through the Bible. Scripture is proved sacred through its use by the congregations, yet the church's judgment stands under the text. Beware traditionalism, which lets custom override Scripture, and institutionalism, which narrows the church to an official body. Yet even Scripture is not the ultimate authority: authority resides in Christ himself, who teaches us by his Spirit, and that Spirit leads the church progressively to distinguish the essential from the non-essential. So read personally, submit to the apostolic word, and above all to the living Lord who speaks through it. Such subjection is perfect freedom, freeing you from private whim and human custom alike.

prompt: Why does doing good seem to cost so much, and why do others have to suffer for my goodness to reach them?
completion: Doing good costs because it asks for sacrifice, and those near us often share the cost. Be good as God is good: clothe your goodness with kindness, affectionateness, sympathy, and active benevolence, so that it reaches others warmly rather than as a granite mountainside. Do not despise the suffering that comes with it—the virtues born amid afflictions are strong and firm, and to carry the cross after Christ is an honor, not a misfortune.
