Yet do not measure your service by how much you do, how visible it is, or what results it yields. The main purpose is to please God and to do well rather than to do much. Prize quality above quantity; a small deed done well and for God's sake outweighs a great deal done for display. Let your aim be to please him, and leave the amount and the outcome in his hands.

prompt: I am asked to reveal a secret I have sworn to keep—what should I do when threatened with death?
completion: This is a serious dilemma, but you are not required to master its hidden outcome. There are two parts to truth: what is open to you and what is hidden in God's counsel. Occupy yourself with what is open—keeping your oath with integrity and acting honestly—and commit the hidden Deed to God's goodness, not treating that hiddenness as a failure of faith. Make no account of the judgments or good opinion of men; endure them silently and find interior peace in that endurance. But do not rely on outward faithfulness alone. Secret prayer is indispensable: public prayer cannot make up for closet communion with God. Keep praying and reading the Word even when enjoyment is gone, for faithfulness in the dark is itself the trust you are called to. Let your hidden life with God sustain your open conduct before men.

prompt: I am a minister, and I have been tempted to soften my message to please the main contributors to my support. What should I do?
completion: This is a real temptation, and you should resist it—but resist it by trusting God rather than by managing your supporters. Preach the whole counsel of God, not what flatters those who fund your ministry. Do not build your work on pressure, solicitation, or guaranteed incomes; depend on voluntary contributions sent freely and without asking, and testify that GOD supplies all your need. In this occasion of virtue, ask God for enabling grace and receive strength more than sufficient, for he does not command faithfulness and leave you alone. And be careful for nothing: cast your anxious care about provision and outcomes upon him, making your requests known to God with thanksgiving, and take his Almighty care in exchange for your worry. Then you will speak freely, fearing neither the loss of contributors nor the displeasure of men.

prompt: I am afraid that if I let God in, He will take away my freedom. Will He?
completion: It's natural to fear that letting God in will cost you your freedom, but the truth is that God's will is never for your harm. He does not wish to take away your freedom but to free you from everything that enslaves you. The unreserved resignation taught by the saints is this: yield completely to God's will without exception or limitation, accepting to be struck where and as He pleases, even in the most repugnant events. Yet even in high contemplation, we must always keep the knowing and sight of our sin and feebleness, for without it there is no true meekness, and without meekness no salvation. And remember that light not used is withdrawn: to him that hath shall be given, and from him that hath not shall be taken away. So obey promptly the truth you know, and trust that He who permits no suffering without a good end will never abandon you. His service is perfect freedom.

prompt: How do I deal with fear when I'm facing a mob or real danger?
completion: When facing a mob or real danger, do not let fear govern you. Fear is not helpful; it must be cast out and replaced by trust in God. In the testimonies of healing, fear was overcome before the healing appeared. So when danger threatens, fasten your eyes on Christ Himself, who is the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance. Abide in Him, and you will find in His presence the remedy for trouble. Do not look at the storm or the circumstances for comfort, but look to Jesus, the author and finisher of your faith. And if you feel alone, accept hidden solitude as Heaven's will, trusting God alone with your secret throbbings and resting in the Lord who knows all yet loves us better than He knows. In Christ you are safe, for He is your refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.

prompt: Who may enter through the gates into the city, and who will be shut out?
completion: The Bible says that those who do His commandments have right to the tree of life and may enter through the gates into the city. Nothing that defiles, works abomination, or makes a lie shall enter it, but only those written in the Lamb's book of life. The city is not the saints themselves, but it is prepared for them; the righteous dead have not yet been caught up, but they wait for the resurrection. So the saints are being built together as a temple, and they will enter the city when it comes down from heaven. And this preparation is not apart from ordinary life: the trivial round and common task are the appointed means of self-denial and daily nearness to God. So do not forsake neighbour or work, but in them learn holiness, for without holiness no one will see the Lord.

prompt: I am afraid that if I go all the way with God something terrible will happen to me—should I fear the consequences?
completion: Do not be afraid to go all the way with God, for He is good and loving, and He does not wish to harm you but to do you great good. Love Him fervently and without servile fear, trusting that His plans for you are for welfare and not for harm, to give you a future and a hope. Remember that all evil of whatever kind happens by God's permission and ever for some good end; it could not be except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him Who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. Yet suffering and evil are not directly God's design or displeasure, but come from human agency, indiscretion, or ignorance. So commit all things without fear to the Providence of God, knowing that He who calls you is faithful and will do it.

prompt: Can I believe in a good God and still believe that death is the end of me?
completion: No, you cannot consistently believe in a good God and hold that death is the end of you. Belief in a righteous God gives ground for expecting continuance after death, for His purpose for the higher spirits is not exhausted by this life. Immortality is a corollary of belief in a righteous God. Death is not the end of identity but a door to a higher state. For the righteous dead, we do not mourn hopelessly, but we are comforted by the promise of resurrection and the preservation of identity. The body will be raised, and we will be with the Lord forever. Yet death does not automatically improve our character or bring us nearer to God; this world is the place to find Him. The remedy must be found here, for this is where we can most easily and quickly find God. So, if you believe in a good God, you have every reason to expect that death is not the end, but you must seek Him now.

prompt: Will I see my family and children again in the world to come?
completion: This hope rests on what God has promised about the earth itself. The world to come is not the annihilation of creation but its restoration: God will renew the earth to its Edenic state, remove the curse, and restore man with it, so families and children belong within that restored order. Between death and that renewal, the spirit world is not idleness or oblivion; all go there, and the faithful continue their labors with the same Priesthood and identity they had in mortality. Yet you need not forecast or dread tomorrow. Think only of doing well today, and trust the eternal Father's care for what is to come. He who restores all things holds your family in His hands; leave the morrow with Him and live faithfully now.

prompt: Is it wrong to use written prayers or liturgy in worship?
completion: Written prayers and liturgy are not wrong; indeed the spiritual worship of God was realized in definite institutions, not left to private impulse. Do not wait for the spirit of prayer before praying: pray at appointed times regardless of feeling, keep family prayer, and act so that God may accomplish what is asked rather than expecting Him to do all. Prayer on the knees, secret and in the companionship of believers, is the one great central secret of holy living and serving, the corner-stone on which all life-work is built, and the first resort in every crisis. In the Lord's Supper the ruling idea is sacrifice, and the Supper appears as the sacrifice of thanksgiving of the community. Set forms serve this worship when the heart is engaged, and liturgy thus becomes devotion rather than a substitute for it.

prompt: Why doesn't God just take me out of this sinful world instead of leaving me here?
completion: The longing to be free of sin and its misery is good, but there is only one way out of misery: cease to sin. God does not take you out of the world because the world is where that victory is won; removal would not cure the heart. This calls for moral courage, not fear of punishment. Yet do not fall into overdone self-accusation or indiscreet sorrow: meekly acknowledge your sin and feebleness, and trust God's courteous excusing. Then abandon yourself to God without exception or reserve. Ask Him to tear and wrest from you all that burdens your heart, and to wrest you from yourself, so that nothing is held back. Bring your weariness to Him honestly, and let Him do in you what you cannot do alone.

prompt: I have been a member of an orthodox church but was never satisfied; will this teaching answer my questions?
completion: It may well, but only if the teaching leads you to the true Christ. The test of orthodoxy is this: Jesus is the only-begotten Son, God manifest in the flesh, omnipresent, omniscient, omnipotent, our living Lord and Judge, in whom all the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily. Any teaching that makes him merely a moral teacher, or divine only as we are divine, fails that test. Do not make your private interpretation final; final interpretation belongs to the composite judgment of the body of believers, and the Scriptures are proved sacred through their use by the congregations. Guard against traditionalism, institutionalism, and narrowing the church to a formal organization. Settle nothing by tradition, custom, or expediency. Lay aside prejudice, submit every matter to the Holy Scriptures as the only standard and the Holy Spirit as the only teacher, and ask simply what the testimony of Scripture is.

prompt: How am I to wait for the rising of this glorious Sun and seek in the Centre this Fountain of Light?
completion: Begin by lifting your gaze above the world's uncertain haze to the bright fields beyond the sky. Waiting is not passive idleness but attentive expectation, like watching for dawn; it is preparing the Lord's way of mercy in your own heart. Keep the childhood's star in view through all of life, and do not let it be buried by the glare of earthly day. Follow its waymarks until all your hopes and thoughts are led to the Saviour's lowly bed. Yet do not strain and drive yourself; seek instead the quiet inner chamber and the rest of Christ's flock at noon. There rest in His exclusive love, which each heart may possess wholly. Gathering your thoughts in quiet, prayer, and Scripture, let go of anxiety and wait patiently, trusting that the light rises for those who lift their eyes.

prompt: I was told my natural desires are sinful. Should I suppress them?
completion: Sin is not a real pleasure but a form of insanity, and sickness is error, not a condition to be accepted. The testimony of the corporeal senses is untrue of man and his Maker; therefore, do not be deceived by apparent desires that would lead you astray. Meekly acknowledge your sin and feebleness, trusting in God's courteous excusing, but know that sin confers no real pleasure—it is a false belief. Strengthen your moral courage by understanding this truth, and master evil by denying the senses' testimony. God loves you and wants you to live in freedom, not in slavery to false pleasures. Stand firm in the truth that man is spiritual and perfect, and reject the illusion of sinful desires.

prompt: I am young and I fear I have wasted my youth; will God count the years I gave Him?
completion: God does not overlook the years you gave Him, even in youth. Every willing service, every moment offered freely, is thanked and rewarded by God, as the Sixth Revelation shows. Do not fear that your youth was wasted; rather, trust that God counts and treasures the time you gave Him. Yet know that your soul is stripped piece by piece, its harness hewn away, its dreams failing; you stand naked and defenceless before God's uplifted stroke. Even so, God's worshipful thanking means nothing offered in love is lost. In this age, real prayer is scarce, and the greatest work you can do is to help restore preachers and the Church to prayer. So bring your regret to God, offer your time and service willingly, and labor to bring prayer back to its rightful place.

prompt: What is the root of the unrest among working people?
completion: The root of unrest among working people is a lack of justice in economic life. Justice requires recognizing workers as persons, not instruments, with a voice in the conditions that govern them. Economic liberty is as essential as political liberty; without it, justice is incomplete. Workers feel marginalized when they are treated as mere cogs in a machine, leading to frustration and agitation. To address this, we must ensure that workers have a say in decisions that affect them, fair wages, and dignified conditions. Recognizing personality in economic life means honoring the inherent worth of every worker and allowing them to participate fully in the fruits of their labor. Moreover, the greatest wealth we possess is knowledge of how to direct our labors rightly, spending every hour advantageously for the benefit of our wives, children, and neighbors. And let oppressors beware: the sighs and groans of the poor are arms more powerful than magistrates, piercing the heavens and drawing down divine vengeance on those who oppress them.

prompt: I am afraid to commit to a long engagement because I do not know when GOD may call me.
completion: It's understandable to feel uncertain about committing to a long engagement when you don't know God's timing. However, fear should not paralyze you. Make a definite, once-for-all committal to the engagement, trusting that God guides those who seek Him. Once you have committed, stay put through the season of establishing and testing until the new relationship becomes a permanent habit. Continual help of God is needed, so cultivate the holy habit of praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often, for we must know before we love. Strenuously lift your heart to God's goodness and exult in it, for that is the only safe temper for tempted men. Seek His loving-kindness in all the breadth and open-air of common life—in whatsoever things are true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—while not missing behind them the greatest Reality, God Himself.

prompt: I am terrified of death and of being judged. How can I prepare for a good death and not despair at the end?
completion: It's natural to fear death and judgment, but as a Christian, you can find hope in God's mercy. To prepare for a good death, focus on living a life of faith, love, and repentance. Remember that judgment is according to deeds done in the body and the thoughts and intents of the heart; death leaves us as judgment finds us. Death is certain, but its time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain. Therefore, make now the changes you would wish to have made when death is near. When you stumble in small faults, do not be terrified; quietly humble yourself before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Trust in His grace and don't despair. God's mercy is greater than your sins. Keep your eyes on Jesus and the promise of eternal life.

prompt: Should I pray for my dead brother, and if so, what should I ask for?
completion: Yes, pray for your dead brother, but bring even this smallest matter to God and ask His guidance rather than deciding it yourself. Commend him to God's mercy: ask that he be acquitted at the great Day, attain perfect consummation and bliss, and be raised at the resurrection of the just. Do not suppose a gradual purification Scripture has not disclosed; leave the unseen to God's wise judgment. Let your love seek Christ first and then go to win an erring brother, giving wreaths of hope rather than fading memorials. Ask God to show you how to grieve, how to live, and how to love, honoring Him by seeking His guidance in all things rather than taking the matter out of His hands.

prompt: I am a young man and I want to be a warrior. What habits should I form?
completion: Wanting to be a warrior is worthy, but know that your first enemy is within yourself. Conquer yourself first and submit to the Father's will before you set out to oppose error and evil around you. Form Cormac's habits: listen in the woods, be blind to secrets, mild in the mead-hall and stern in battle, gentle to allies; do not deride the old, do not speak of anyone in his absence, and give rather than ask. Add faith in Christ, trusting and obeying Him, so your courage is colored by His mercy and self-sacrifice. Then oppose evil by persuasion, patience, and love unfeigned—without violence and without interfering with the agency of others—prepared to meet Him as Saviour and Judge.

prompt: I want to see a miracle to confirm the truth. Is it wrong to require a sign before I believe?
completion: It is not the way of honest faith to require a sign. Miracles are for the consolation and confirmation of the Saints, and no good, honest person requires one to believe. Do not speculate about mysteries that God has not revealed; leave hidden things to Him. Instead, learn to see God's providences as miracles—His daily care and guidance are wonders enough. Ask God in the name of Jesus, and seek the witness of the Holy Ghost within, which cannot be mistaken. That inward witness, not signs and wonders, is the true assurance of the Gospel. Pray honestly, ready to obey what He shows you, and ground your faith in the Spirit rather than in signs.

prompt: I am a teacher and want to make the Bible come alive for my students—how should I present it?
completion: To make the Bible come alive, do not rely on the letter alone; seek and strive for the spirit of Truth and Love. Prepare and explain the text, but let your teaching flow from prayer and love for your students. Teach that when the soul is purified of earthly images and unified and tranquillized in God with loving confidence, the Holy Spirit Himself teaches the love of God and of neighbour, so that study and reading are no longer needed to learn that love—while the Holy Scriptures remain the presupposed foundation of belief. Emphasize present salvation and everyday religion: urge your students to live faithfully today and let the Millennium take care of itself, enjoying the Spirit now rather than merely preparing for a distant future.

prompt: I keep studying to make my sermons eloquent, but few seem converted—what am I missing?
completion: It sounds like you are working hard at eloquence, but conversion is not the fruit of technique. All conversion is the work of the almighty power of the HOLY GHOST, and your great need is to know GOD. Learn intercession for the people: pray for them by name and let that school of prayer shape your preaching, for without it no homiletics or genius can make a preacher. Then learn God's will through the ministers He has appointed, abolishing self-confidence and presumption; do not despise the guides He has given. Let your sermons flow from communion, prayer, and humble obedience, and the same Spirit who called you will work through your words, changing hearts by His power rather than yours.

prompt: I'm drawn to drama and strong feelings rather than quiet growth. Is that a spiritual problem?
completion: You are right to suspect something here, but do not imagine you can diagnose and repair it yourself. The craving for strong feeling is a symptom of a helplessness we cannot cure by insight or effort. Confess that plainly, and take hold of Christ's all-sufficiency with a faith that will accept nothing less than all. Do not pray for dramatic experiences or secretly desire them; accept whatever God gives or withholds, without questioning, fear, or curiosity. And when prayer is dry and irksome—when nothing stirs—do not flee to sensation. Stay there. That dryness is a trial of love, and in it you may make effectual acts of resignation: 'Lord, I will this because you will it.' Such acts, made faithfully in aridity, greatly advance the soul. Quiet growth is not the absence of drama; it is love proved in the ordinary.

prompt: I have doubts I am ashamed of; what should I do with them?
completion: Doubts are common, and shame about them makes them worse. Do not rush to resolve them: over-eagerness is the mother of many imperfections, and anxiety is an obstacle to perfection. Keep yourself in God's presence and bring your doubts there without demanding they be settled today. But go deeper than managing a few anxious habits. Lay the axe at the root of the tree of self: the real issue is self-will, self-seeking, and self-glory, which want certainty on their own terms. Self-denial is a voluntary renunciation of self, taken up for Christ's sake, not the lopping off of a few branches. And be plain with yourself. A long visit, staring, and constant questioning are signs of ill-breeding, not devotion; 'perhaps,' 'may be,' and 'I dare say' are false sisters. Speak simply, act simply, and let your yes be yes.

prompt: I feel like a bridegroom standing before a life that's welcoming me—how do I measure my strength against such a future?
completion: What a striking image. The honest question is not whether you feel strong enough but what strength actually is. Strength of character is the will's power to control your actions independently of your inclinations and of the opinions of men. It is not fixed by temperament and not excused by 'that's just how I am.' Character is formed by habits, and habits by repeated acts; progress is proportioned to self-victories. Yet strength is not for domination: each nation and person needs the others, and needs them free, so fellowship is the first duty. And do not think ideas or aspirations will carry you. They strain as much as they lift, and reverence alone never saved a soul in the storm of life. What preserves you is One by your side, in trust, sympathy, and comradeship, fighting with you in the ranks—by whom your strength is thrilled and your right hand kept fresh.

prompt: I have forgotten the people who helped me when I was young and poor. Does that matter?
completion: Yes, it matters, but the deeper truth is often inverted. The poor are your 'masters': they have great interest in the court of heaven, and their intercession makes almsgiving the best provision a person can make. Remember your helpers with gratitude and honor them by giving generously now. Do not be paralyzed by the fear of giving to the unworthy: it is better to give to ten beggars and be sure of helping the one truly needy. Give with a single eye to assist the needy, and the blessing is yours regardless. But never support in idleness the one able to work—set such a person to work. Relieve present want, then help the poor help themselves.

prompt: I wonder whether the moral teaching of Jesus can be separated from his person, or whether the two are inseparable.
completion: They are inseparable, but the reason is often misstated. The early church did not begin with a doctrine of two natures. Two Christologies stood beside each other: the Adoptian, in which the man Jesus has become a God, and the pneumatic, in which a Divine being appeared in human form. Neither was affirmed as two natures; the pictures simply stood together. The teaching is inseparable from the person because the person is inseparable from the divine life that acted in him. His works demonstrate an ever-operative divine Principle, and his followers have a present duty to heal the sick and cast out error. Yet do not shrink him to a figure small enough to be fully comprehended. The manifold Gospel picture is a self-evidencing fact: Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, man and God, in the richness of his mysterious person.

prompt: If the Old Testament shows development in revealed truth, why can't I expect new revelations added to the New Testament?
completion: The Old Testament shows development, and the New Testament is no mere anthology: though its books differ widely, they share an essential unity and divine authority as God's voice to us. Revelation has always come step by step, line upon line, because people cannot bear all things at once, as with Joseph's gradual receipt of priesthood and ordinances. Yet the goal of that unfolding is not humanity climbing toward divinity but God showing us Himself. In Christ we see God, and God is like Christ; the Old Testament's foreshadowings are gathered up in him. Honoring Jesus' real humanity, we still receive in him the full revelation of God's character, so we need no new revelation beyond knowing him more deeply.

prompt: How can I think of God even during meals and conversations with others?
completion: God is always near, so He should be remembered and adored continually, not only at meals or quiet moments. Give thanks before eating, and keep a silent sense of His presence during conversation, letting attention to others be an act of love toward Him, since business and diversions are not outside His care. When you notice you have forgotten Him, do not be disquieted; return with greater trust, as a child returns to a Father who never left. Yet during a retreat, deep recollection matters: avoid unnecessary intercourse with the world, keep 'God and I' as the only objects of thought, and let even meals and necessary speech be simple and recollected, so nothing needless scatters the heart.

prompt: I have peace with God but still feel anxious day by day—what is the peace of heart I'm missing?
completion: You already have peace with God through Christ; what you're missing is the peace of God, which passes understanding and rests on His changeless word of promise, not on variable moods. Feelings never accurately gauge our real assimilation to God, so do not measure your standing by them. When joy is lacking, continue steadfastly in prayer and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Remain at peace, patient with others and equally patient with yourself, since peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ. Yet the deeper secret is to cease from your own works and striving, receiving the peace of God and letting God work His own divine works in you.

prompt: I prepare my sermons carefully but my heart is cold. Which should I prepare first?
completion: The great need is the preparation of the heart, and a prepared heart is better than a prepared sermon, because it produces one. Begin with morning meditation, and let the passage first search and comfort your own soul. When your heart wanders in prayer, do not be distressed or use violence; gently bring it back to its Master and lay it tenderly at His feet. In all your reading, implore divine light, and season your studies with aspirations to God, resolving your doubts at the foot of a crucifix. Studies without humility, simplicity, and prayer nourish vanity and error rather than virtue; so let prayer shape the study, and let the study flow from a warmed heart.

prompt: I'm trying to serve God and also keep my old life and pleasures. Why do I feel so miserable and divided all the time?
completion: You feel miserable because half-way service is wretched: trying to serve God and the world together divides the heart and brings gloom, not peace. The answer is not a safe middle way but following Christ all the way, letting Him complete His process in you. Keep both beholdings at once: the higher keeps you in solace and enjoying in God, while the lower keeps you in dread and shame of self, yet hold much more in the higher. And do not fear self-denial or economy as loss; they are a privilege that frees your resources for the LORD and brings fuller joy, since a whole heart given to Him is not diminished but enlarged.

prompt: How do I accept adversity as coming from God's hand rather than resenting it?
completion: Accepting adversity as from God's hand requires first examining your own ways. Consider whether in times of prosperity you acknowledged God's hand or instead abused His blessings by excess on yourself. When loss comes, ask: Have I practically recognized God as the source of all good? Have I clung to gifts rather than the Giver? Repent of any self-indulgence that made a god of comfort. Then, with a humble heart, receive adversity as a corrective and refining providence. Even in the horrors of war, God did not ordain the wickedness; men's agency brought the evil, yet God foresaw it and will overrule its results for good. Moreover, do not be surprised at opposition, for the adversary's attack is a token of your salvation. Claim the double blessing, victory, and power that come through resistance, knowing that power is developed by resistance. Trust that He disciplines those He loves, turning even the worst to deeper dependence on Him. In this way, resentment gives way to surrender and peace.

prompt: I'm tempted to give up fighting my own faults because I can't understand why evil exists at all—what's the point?
completion: It's understandable to feel discouraged when you can't grasp why evil exists. But seeking an intellectual solution to the problem of evil won't cure it—only God's goodness can. Instead of dwelling on sin, which intoxicates the will and paralyzes it with despair, turn your gaze to the universal goodness of God. Reduce the cruel facts of experience to their proportion against His infinite love. Recoil from the study of sin and exult in God's goodness. This disengages your will from evil and gives you a new temper for the contest. Yet do not flatter virtues while concealing the foe in ambush. Evil is real and seeks to deceive; warn yourself of its snares and risk displeasure for the sake of doing right. Pain and sin are real evils, not mere aesthetic additions, and can only be accounted for as necessary means to a greater good. God's Omnipotence is limited only by His own nature, so He cannot call evil good or be beyond good and evil. You don't need to understand why evil exists to fight your faults; you need to trust that God's grace is sufficient. Keep pressing forward, not in your own strength, but in the power of His might.

prompt: I have a friend who says all religions are equally true paths to God; how should I respond without being arrogant?
completion: Respond with humility and respect. Acknowledge that you understand your friend's perspective and that you value the conversation. However, as a religious, you must uphold that the vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience remove every obstacle between God and the religious. Yet you must also examine whether you are a religious in truth or only in name, lest by will or desire you cling to the creature rather than the Creator. So share your belief that Jesus is the way, the truth, and the life, but do so with a heart that has renounced all things. In every occasion of virtue, turn to God for enabling grace, asking and receiving strength more than sufficient. Do not approach God with casual or hasty prayers, but with persistent, importunate faith, for He is not found by pop calls but yields to those who keep asking, seeking, and knocking. Avoid arguing; instead, ask questions and listen genuinely. Emphasize that you're both seeking truth and can disagree without being disagreeable. Focus on building the relationship rather than winning a debate. Pray for wisdom and let your life reflect the love of Christ.

prompt: I suspect a coworker of bad motives without evidence. Is that a sin?
completion: Suspecting a coworker of bad motives without evidence is a sin that must be confessed and forsaken, not covered or excused. It violates the command to love your neighbor and to think the best of others. Honesty is required for scientific demonstration in Christian Science, so we must be honest about our own sinful suspicions rather than concealing them. Moreover, harboring unforgiveness makes you more guilty and censurable than the one who sinned against you. Saints must forgive as Christ did, dismissing envy, malice, and retaliation and cultivating the spirit that cried, 'Father, forgive them.' Refrain from slander, gossip, backbiting, and fault-finding against neighbors or Church leaders. Mind your own business and seek and speak of the good in others. Instead of harboring suspicion, pray for your coworker and seek to understand their actions in a charitable light. If you have concerns, address them directly and respectfully. Remember that we all have blind spots and that only God knows the heart. Cultivate a habit of assuming good intentions until proven otherwise, and ask God to purify your thoughts.

prompt: I am a minister and a parishioner asks me to bury her sister though I am not her parish minister—should I comply?
completion: As a minister, you should consider the pastoral needs of the parishioner and the circumstances. While you are not her parish minister, you can still offer comfort and support. However, it is important to respect the role of the parish minister and coordinate with them. If the parish minister is unavailable or if the family specifically requests you, it may be appropriate to comply, provided it does not cause confusion or conflict. Yet, be mindful that clergy living under the same roof with deaconesses or spiritual sisters is condemned as an occasion of evil and a scandal, even where the persons claim security. So avoid any appearance of impropriety. Also, remember that a faithful servant of Mary who honors her and desires to amend cannot be lost, while neglect of her service endangers salvation. Entrust the situation to her intercession. Furthermore, if you are a member of a confraternity, recall that you joined solely to serve God and Mary and save your soul, and you must not forsake its appointed days for worldly affairs. Ultimately, seek to act with compassion and wisdom, and pray for guidance. The priority is to minister to the grieving family and honor the deceased.

prompt: I feel distant from God when I'm busy with work and family—does that mean I'm not faithful?
completion: Feeling distant from God during busy seasons doesn't mean you're unfaithful. Real trust rises above circumstances and appearances; it hangs solely upon the good pleasure of God, not on visible supports or human reassurance, and hanging upon the invisible God is not hanging upon nothing. Yet faith must be shown in works and spiritual understanding, each working out his own salvation, since another's devotion cannot lessen your liability. Do not multiply explicit offerings or grow anxious about distraction during necessary work. Rather, do all your actions for God—cooking, working, tending family—without fretting that busyness separates you from him. Simplicity in his presence means the ordinary task itself is offered, not a pile of added religious exercises. Rest in the unseen God who holds you.

prompt: How was the canon of the New Testament decided, and does it matter?
completion: The New Testament canon emerged as early churches recognized writings carrying apostolic authority and read in worship, with criteria including apostolic connection, widespread use, consistency with the rule of faith, and reception; councils later ratified what was already widely accepted. It matters because, though the books differ widely, they possess essential unity and divine authority as God's voice to us. Christ's use of the Old Testament appeals to its abiding spiritual testimony to Himself, independent of questions of authorship and date, without implying any fallibility in Him. Far from being late second-century productions, the books were cited early: Clement of Rome, Ignatius, Polycarp, Papias, Justin, and Irenaeus attest them, and the Muratorian Canon and Peshito Version show they were received as genuine before the close of the second century and were written in the first.

prompt: Is Jesus just a good moral teacher, or is he somehow the revelation of God himself?
completion: Jesus is more than a good moral teacher: the New Testament presents him as the definitive revelation of God, in whom God's character is fully shown, and his resurrection vindicated that claim. Christianity is not mere belief or admiration; his healing works demonstrated an ever-operative divine Principle, and his followers are called to heal the sick and cast out error today. We do not prove God's goodness from Nature or History, nor reduce moral judgements to feelings; our knowledge of God rests in the moral consciousness, where true judgements are self-evident deliverances of Reason revealing God's own. Yet Christian ethics rests not on abstraction but on the personal and ethical God, on man's conscience and freedom, and on Christ himself—both the pattern of recreated character and the source who recreates it.

prompt: Two ways are set before me, life or death—how do I choose the better?
completion: Choosing the better way begins with honest self-examination and a daily turning toward life—obedience, love of God, and love of neighbor. The better way starts lower than we like: count yourself as already dead, since you must die some day, and have no other consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over and detest your offences, since it is not now the time to rejoice but to lament with sincerity of heart. Yet death is not the end of identity; it is a door to a higher state, and the righteous dead are preserved and will be raised. So do not seek bodily health through mere material regimen. Spiritualize thought; forsake the mortal sense of things for Truth, and bodily improvement follows the renewal of the mind.

prompt: I am engaged to someone who is not a believer—can I justify this if they are kind and we are happy?
completion: This is a hard situation, and kindness and happiness are real goods—but they are not the first qualification in a spouse. True godliness must be the first and absolutely needful qualification; beauty, wealth, age, mental powers, and present compatibility are secondary and can mislead. Scripture warns against being unequally yoked, so wait prayerfully on God for guidance, calmly weighing other suitableness while holding godliness as non-negotiable. If this engagement brings pain, do not read it as God sending affliction; the pains of sense are salutary when they turn the affections from matter to Soul. And guard against envy or rivalry in God's work. Like George Muller, accept obscurity and humiliation without resentment, prefer others in honor, rejoice in the gifts and success of fellow laborers, and trust God to exalt in His own time.

prompt: I have been avoiding prayer because I am angry at God. Is it wrong to run from Him?
completion: Your anger is real and God is not shocked by it, but avoiding prayer lets the distance grow. Pray at appointed times whether or not you feel like it, keep family prayer, and act with God on what you ask rather than expecting Him to do it all. Yet go deeper: God's promise to hear prayer is His promise to give Himself. He is not chiefly offering relief, explanations, or even the resolution of your anger—He is offering Himself, and in His promises He desires to bestow Himself on you. If you ask only for comfort or vindication, you ask beneath Him, and you hurt yourself by preferring a creature to the One who made it. Bring your anger to Him, but ask for Him. Any restraint you practice should rest on hope that your endurance proves redemptive; where it does not, admit it honestly. Seek Him first, and the rest will be added.

prompt: I feel like God is silent and I haven't seen an answer to prayer in months. What's wrong?
completion: Seasons of silence are common, but do not measure prayer by what others see or by quick results. Prayer often rises unseen like a rill that runs underground and still reaches the sea; God hears what no congregation hears and accepts every heart that fears Him and works righteousness, whatever the nation or station. Yet prayer is not easy or naturally congenial. It is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy; little praying that flatters us into thinking we have done our duty is a deluding make-believe, worse than none. Take heart: God understands all things and can hear the earnest supplication of the soul and the innermost thoughts, just as human invention lets us speak across great distances. So ask in faith, nothing wavering, and let the silence press you into deeper, humbler trust rather than despair.

prompt: What are the many mansions Jesus said he was going to prepare for us?
completion: When Jesus spoke of many mansions in His Father's house, He was not describing scattered rooms but the one dwelling of God with His people. Scripture joins these pictures: the Holy City, the New Jerusalem, the tabernacle of God, the bride the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, and the sanctuary are one city coming down from God out of heaven to dwell with men. The many mansions are the many places within that one city, room enough for all who come. This hope is also a motive: the Lord promises to return personally, and that promise calls us to readiness and faithful stewardship now. And stewardship is concrete. God requires one-tenth of the whole person—brain, heart, nerve, muscle, sinew, flesh, and bone—for building temples, sustaining the ministry and missionaries' families, and feeding and gathering the poor, the aged, the halt, and the blind. The mansions are prepared for a prepared people, and preparation includes what we do with all He has given.

prompt: I have come near to this blessing many times and drawn back; can I still enter in?
completion: Yes, you can still enter in, but stop straining and start watching. Much of what holds you back is not doubt but possession—things kept that you do not need, which hinder both blessing and the spread of the Gospel. Make it a habit of mind to look over what you have and part with what others could use. Yet the intense tension of straining itself binds you against the blessing God waits to give; move from asking to receiving, step into the will of God, and take the water of life freely. Then guard what you receive. Watch against spiritual pickpockets and leakage, hold fast what you have, and store up each day's treasures of grace in the savings bank of eternity. Drawing back many times does not disqualify you, but do not let the enemy steal what you are finally ready to receive.

prompt: Is it base to hope for a future life, or is that hope a proper part of trusting God?
completion: Hoping for a future life is not base; it is a proper part of trusting God. But let that hope rest on the right foundation. Join an intimate conviction of your own inability with firm confidence in God's power: all human learning and skill cannot convert or sanctify a single soul, so we trust supernatural means—His Word, His Spirit, His grace. Do not settle for a bare minimum of knowledge either; seek to be filled with the mature knowledge of His will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, which is the secret of true living. And when God hides Himself, as He sometimes does, do not panic or grasp at substitutes. Then faith alone must be your support and the foundation of all your confidence in God. The future hope is not base because it rests on Him who hides and reveals, and who keeps His promise even in the dark.

prompt: Why do the righteous suffer while the wicked prosper?
completion: The question of why the righteous suffer while the wicked prosper is a deep mystery that we cannot fully comprehend. Rather than seeking quick answers or demanding resolution, we are called to abide peacefully in our misery and abjection, trusting that God will raise us in His own time. In our weakness and imperfections, we wait patiently, not murmuring against God but submitting to His will. The prosperity of the wicked is fleeting, and their apparent success is not our concern. Our focus should be on remaining faithful in suffering, knowing that God sees and will act. Moreover, our sufferings, even those we cannot understand, store up spiritual force for the benefit of others. We must not murmur or complain, for that would sap the power of our suffering. Instead, we are to endure victoriously, so that from our victorious suffering we may help others. The source of helping others must be victorious suffering rather than a whining, murmuring pang. We must also value the virtues born amid afflictions as strong and firm, accepting the honor of suffering much and carrying the cross after Christ. For in carrying the cross, we are united with Him and share in His glory.

prompt: How can our prayer meeting be more alive and Spirit-led?
completion: To make your prayer meeting more alive and Spirit-led, begin by recognizing that prayer must be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress. The key is to pray that God would enable us to search out and discover our own hearts and reform whatever is amiss in them. This means that before praying for outward needs, we should focus on inward examination and repentance. Encourage participants to come prepared to confess and seek God's transforming work in their own lives. Then, as hearts are aligned with God, prayer for others flows naturally. Incorporate times of silent self-examination, guided by the Holy Spirit, and corporate confession. Vary the format to include Scripture reading, worship, and intercession, but always with the underlying goal of heart-reformation. However, we must also affirm that valid prayer effects are real and that there is an incoming of energy from beyond the margin of the normal self. These effects, though, occur within the ordered life of the spirit rather than in capricious interruptions of nature. So, expect God to work, but not in sensational or disorderly ways. Furthermore, remember that God, who understands all things, can hear the earnest supplication of the soul and our innermost thoughts, just as human invention enables communication across great distances. Therefore, we must ask in faith, nothing wavering, trusting that God hears and answers according to His will. This will lead to genuine spiritual vitality.

prompt: I'm surrounded by people with needs and I feel too exhausted to help—what should I do?
completion: When you feel exhausted by the needs around you, the first step is to examine your own heart. Jesus commanded us to cast the beam out of our own eye before attempting to remove the speck from another's. So, before you try to help others, you must first overcome your own belief and fear of disease or sin. Take time to search your heart for any fear, unbelief, or sin that may be draining your energy. Pray that God would reveal and remove these beams. Once you have dealt with your own issues, you will be better equipped to help others from a place of spiritual strength. However, you cannot see another's woe without sorrow. The Maker sits by us and moans till our grief is fled and gone. He is near to those who sigh and weep. Therefore, do not ignore the grief of others; instead, let your heart be moved with compassion. Then, you can set healthy boundaries and prioritize self-care, but always after ensuring your own eye is clear and your heart is tender. Moreover, support the sick person's trust in the power of Mind, telling him that his strength is in proportion to his courage. Do not undermine his faith by suggesting he has more courage than strength; rather, affirm that as he trusts in Mind, his strength will match his courage.

prompt: I'm trying to raise my children well, but I worry I'm spoiling them. What matters most?
completion: What matters most in raising children is to prepare them to live, not to die. The exhortation in this Church and Kingdom is not to prepare to die but to prepare to live. Therefore, we should teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. This means prioritizing their physical, mental, and spiritual well-being from an early age. While love and discipline are important, the primary focus should be on instilling habits that lead to a long, healthy life. Teach them gratitude, delayed gratification, and hard work, but always with the goal of preparing them to live fully. Avoid overindulgence, but more importantly, avoid neglecting their health and constitution. Seek support from community and parenting resources that align with this vision. Moreover, do not linger among the slain or hold converse with ghosts. The slain warrior warns us to betake ourselves home and carry off the bequest. So, focus on the living, not the dead, and carry away the spoils bequeathed to you. Finally, remember that the safest place is the path of duty. God must come first, and children can be safely trusted to God wherever He leads. Do not avoid a clear duty out of fear for safety or family, or place personal comfort above obedience to God's leading.

prompt: How may I arrive at the Unity of Will and come into the Unity of Vision, when I feel two Wills and two Eyes in me set against each other?
completion: To arrive at the Unity of Will and Unity of Vision, you must recognize that the will is the mistress of the faculties. When you feel two wills and two eyes set against each other, it is because the mind is roving and not fixed on God. The will must recall the roving mind and carry it to God as its last end. Begin by exercising your will to direct your thoughts toward God. Whenever you notice your mind wandering, gently but firmly bring it back. This is not a passive process but an active discipline. Through consistent practice, the will gains strength and the mind becomes habitually focused on God. Prayer and meditation are tools, but the key is the will's decision to govern the mind. Over time, the divided will and vision become unified as the will takes its rightful place as mistress. Furthermore, remember that acts of the will—love and delight in God—are all-important, while acts of the understanding are of little value. So, focus on loving God and delighting in Him, rather than on intellectual understanding. Love is the key to unity. Finally, do not let the presence of creatures in the body convince you that the soul cannot walk with God. If the will goes forth from the creatures, they are forsaken and dead in it and cannot touch the soul. Thus, you may walk with God in heaven while the body lives in the world among creatures.

prompt: I see beauty in simple things—a flower, a bird—but others say I'm naive. Am I?
completion: No, you are not naive. The beauty you see in a flower or a bird is a faint reflection of an infinite perfection in God, and when a creature delights you, let it lift your heart to Him in love. Do not arm your delight with thorns and threats: the lily is white and delights in love, with neither thorn nor threat staining her beauty bright. Yet this does not mean God is merely soft or distant. He is reverend and dreadful in His majesty, and also marvelously homely and courteous to simple souls who come to Him. So keep your wonder, let it become worship, and approach Him with both holy dread and childlike trust, for He welcomes the simple heart.

prompt: I feel alone in my faith, cut off from other Christians; does my private experience separate me from the Church?
completion: Feeling alone does not cut you off from the Church, but your private experience is not meant to remain vague. Prayer is actual fellowship with a personal Friend, the Father we know through His revelation in Christ, and in Him you are joined to every believer. Do not let public prayer or Christian conversation replace secret communion; public prayer cannot make up for the closet, and when enjoyment is gone, keep praying and reading the Word. Yet remember that God reveals His will for the Church through the legally appointed channels of the priesthood. Claims to revelation outside that order, and self-appointed revelators, are to be rejected. Stay rooted in secret devotion and in the ordered fellowship of the Church, and your loneliness will not separate you from the body.

prompt: What makes a man's opinion carry weight with me—his office or his character?
completion: Character should carry more weight than office, and character is formed by repeated acts: strength of will controls action independently of inclinations and human opinions, growing with each self-victory. But the deepest standard is individual responsibility before an All-seeing God, the first and highest standard of correct living; a man should be good for the truth's sake and not depend on changeable public sentiment. So judge a man's opinion not by the outward appearance or greatness of his deeds, but by the God who commands them. Look past the appearance of the task to Him who commands it, trusting that God can work His glory through trifling things. Office deserves respect, but the character that carries weight is one that answers to God in great things and small.

prompt: I have a chance to study medicine cheaply but must be apprenticed for years—should I bind myself?
completion: Binding yourself for years is serious, but do not let frantic hurry after wealth decide for you. Counsel calm, contented, patient diligence: attend meetings, pray, read, and meditate, keeping your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Do not forbid all temporary material relief; when pain prevents mental treatment, a temporary relief may lull the belief of pain, but it is not the real cure—once the belief is lulled, handle the case mentally. Above all, remember what constitutes a physician: a complete cure, leaving no blemish behind, and a painless examination. Let that standard, not the cheap price or the length of years, guide whether you bind yourself.

prompt: I keep meaning to visit a church dedicated to Mary, but my schedule is full. How important is it to visit her images and churches?
completion: Visiting a church dedicated to Mary is more important than a busy schedule might suggest. The servants of Mary should often visit her images and churches, for these are devotions pleasing to her and cities of refuge from temptations and from the punishments merited by sin. Make room for them as you would for a refuge in a storm. Yet remember that the Church serves the world because it first worships; its service flows from its foretaste of eternal life. And do not think you must always be at church to be with God. You may make an oratory of your heart, where you converse with Him in meekness, humility, and love. So visit her churches when you can, and let your heart remain a place of familiar conversation with God wherever you are.

prompt: Is there a purgatory where souls are purified after death?
completion: Scripture does not reveal a place of gradual purification after death, so we keep our prayers within its limits: commending the departed to God's mercy, praying for their acquittal at the great Day, their perfect consummation and bliss, and their resurrection. Nor should we picture Heaven and Hell as local places to which the soul travels; they are conditions within the soul, Heaven being the will turned in to the Love of God and Hell the will turned in to his wrath. At death the soul needs no going forth but stands in that which is manifested in it. Therefore regard the body as though the soul were already freed from it, thinking only of eternity and the one thing necessary, and count whatever happens inwardly or in the body as little as though it had befallen another person.

prompt: I am old and people mock me. How should I respond?
completion: Mockery of the old is wrong and should be named plainly: it is shameful for a youngster to mock an old man, for the robust to mock an invalid, and for the wise to mock a fool. Yet honour what is truly fair: good manners, skill, and wisdom are fair things that hide ugliness. Look upon others simply, kindly, and amiably, gathering honey from all flowers and refusing to dwell on their imperfections. Do not accept decrepitude as a lawful necessity of nature; the mental state governs the body, and man reflects eternal Life. Answer scorn with dignity and gentle honesty, setting boundaries if cruelty persists. Your worth is not measured by others' mockery, and patience joined with self-respect often wins the respect that ridicule denied.

prompt: I want to improve myself and learn, but I feel too poor and uneducated. Is there hope for me?
completion: Yes, there is hope. Poverty and lack of formal schooling are obstacles, but they do not close the door to learning: libraries, free courses, and willing mentors remain open. Yet the chief purpose of our being here is personal connection with God, and prizing holidays, parties, and career success above this is a mistaken basis for life. The great need is the education of feeling and character—reverence, self-control, and sobriety of judgment—not merely intellectual training. So proceed with calm, contented, patient diligence, not frantic hurry after wealth. Attend your meetings, pray, read the scriptures, and meditate, keeping your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Shame about your background is unhelpful; what matters is a teachable heart turned toward what is highest.

prompt: I am unsure whether to demand that new believers adopt all my customs—what is essential and what is not?
completion: This is an important question. Distinguish essentials from customs: faith in Christ, repentance, and love of God and neighbor are essential, while dress, music, and local traditions are secondary and should not be imposed as tests of fellowship. Do not treat believers' baptism and the breaking of bread every Lord's day as optional; these are scriptural practices to be embraced on the authority of the Word, even when obedience brings loss or reproach. Share the knowledge of the work's needs with fellow laborers that they may join in prayer, faith, and self-denial, while withholding such knowledge from outsiders lest it be construed as an appeal for human aid. Above all, remember that true satisfying religion is not external observance, doctrine, or feeling, but Christ recognised, known, adored, and living within the soul—the New Life and New Birth.

prompt: I have been told that the poor are a burden on the church. Is that true?
completion: It is not true that the poor are a burden on the church. Church revenues belong to the poor, and even sacred vessels may be devoted to those in need; complaints that this impoverishes the church are answered by confidence that God will provide. Yet charity should not encourage idleness or pauperism: men and women should have a self-sustaining spirit willing to labor in exchange for aid, and the Church's plan is to relieve present wants and then put the poor in a way to help themselves. Nor should we blame the Church's failings solely on priests or institutions. The lack lies in the tepid love for a dimly known Lord in each member's heart, and the Church gains what is lacking when each heart worships the beloved Christ.

prompt: Someone wronged me and I want to hold onto my resentment. How do I let it go?
completion: Holding onto resentment may feel like a way to seek justice, but the law of divine justice assures us that wrong done to another returns upon the wrong-doer. You do not need to carry resentment to see balance restored. Instead, trust that right adjusts the balance. If you have forgotten God's presence in your hurt, do not be disquieted; rather, return with greater trust. Learn not to be troubled in tribulations, afflictions, and injuries, not to be incensed against those who inflict them, nor to entertain resentment. Sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to possess the delights of earth or be honoured and exalted by men. In this humility, you will find peace and release from resentment.

prompt: I want to pray but feel my prayers are weak; what is the privilege of prayer?
completion: Prayer is a privilege because it connects us with God. Even if your prayers feel weak, pray at appointed times regardless of feeling, and include family prayer. Remember that prayer is not about eloquence but sincerity. God hears even the simplest words. Also, prayer should not be a one-sided request; it's a conversation. Be willing to act on what you pray about—if you ask for patience, look for opportunities to practice it. The principle is to help God accomplish what is asked rather than expecting God to do it all. Moreover, prayer should be unselfish and sympathetic, interceding for others including those unknown to us, with a sympathy that is quick, wide, and deep. Prayer is not informing or persuading God, but unselfed love and spiritual understanding that align us with God's unchanging law. Deny that prayer informs the infinite Mind or changes the Science of being. Don't wait for a special feeling; pray anyway, and trust that God is listening.

prompt: I'm afraid that if I face the truth about the world, something lovely in me will die—is that a real risk?
completion: It's understandable to fear that facing harsh truths might diminish your innocence or joy. However, truth itself is not destructive; it is ignorance and falsehood that harm. Facing reality can actually deepen your compassion and strengthen your character when you rely on Truth and Love, not on human will-power. The 'lovely' qualities in you—kindness, empathy, hope—are not fragile; they can grow through understanding. Yes, you may need to grieve certain illusions, but that grief can lead to a more mature and resilient love. Silence human will and rely on Truth and Love, which quiet fear and heal. Remember that the cheerful hearth and present love are a powerful charm against every ill, even death. Turn from the storm to the bright hearth and to love's embrace, a charm of might against every ill. Commit yourself to GOD's protection in danger and find His Word sweet and sufficient in peril. So, while it may feel risky, embracing truth with a supportive community and self-care can protect and even enhance the beauty within you.

prompt: I'm curious about the darker side of city life and want to see it for myself—is that harmful?
completion: Curiosity about the darker side of city life is natural, but it can be harmful if it leads you to places or situations where you are exposed to danger or tempted to participate in harmful activities. However, remember that those who live up to the best light they have are safe, and condemnation comes from rejecting light that has come to them. Instead of condemning those in difficult circumstances, recognize that sin lies in rejecting the light one has received. Consider channeling your curiosity into learning about social issues through books, documentaries, or volunteering with organizations that help those in need. This way, you can satisfy your curiosity while contributing positively. Always prioritize your safety and well-being, and avoid glamorizing or seeking out danger for thrills. Deny disease mentally without audibly naming it to the patient, avoiding any fearful diagnosis that would deepen the wrong mind-picture. Moreover, remember that ease and enjoyment must not be the end of Christian retirement, but penance, labor, and assiduous contemplation; without great fervor and constancy in these, close solitude is the road to perdition.

prompt: I am a teacher trying to explain the history of Christian doctrine to students; how do I avoid presenting the development as a simple unfolding of ideas?
completion: To avoid presenting the history of Christian doctrine as a simple unfolding of ideas, emphasize the messy, contingent, and conflict-driven nature of its development. Show how doctrines emerged from debates, power struggles, and cultural contexts. Use primary sources to let students see the arguments and personalities involved. Highlight that what became 'orthodox' was often one option among many, and that alternative views were suppressed. Encourage students to question the narrative of inevitable progress and to consider how social and political factors shaped theological choices. Treat honest doubt with sympathy, substituting for the unreasoning faith of childhood the profound convictions of maturity through an orderly presentation of the facts. Moreover, argue that no mere human genius, and least of all Jewish fishermen, could have originated the gospel portrait of Christ; it must be a photograph from real life. The portrait of Christ, free from the puerility and self-contradiction that mere imagination produces, can only be explained by granting his person and character were historical realities. Finally, ensure that the doctrine of sin rests on Christ's witness verified in Christian experience, allowing liberty to treat the early chapters of Genesis as allegorical rather than historical. This approach will help students appreciate the complexity and human element in doctrinal history.

prompt: I want to believe, but I am told that dogma is a cage for the mind and that honest thinkers must reject it. Is that true?
completion: The claim that dogma cages the mind sounds plausible but rests on a confusion. Dogma, so far as it coincides with truth, cannot limit the mind, because truth liberates thought from error. What people fear as a cage is authority without truth, or submission without understanding. The dogmatic Church, rightly understood, encourages the fullest inquiry, holding that faith and reason serve one truth. It also helps to see how dogma actually formed. Its presuppositions were not simply a continuation of New Testament theology as a whole, nor the whole richness of early Christian preaching. They were the fundamental motives of the Gospel, the common preaching concerning Christ, the Christian use of the Old Testament, and the Greek spirit. Dogma changed and developed not by some abstract impulse unfolding itself, nor by a hypostatised ecclesiastical spirit, but through the actual historical conditions, needs, and conflicts of living, believing men who struggled to state their faith. Recognizing this, the honest thinker should ask whether a teaching is true and whether inquiry is welcomed, rather than rejecting dogma wholesale.

prompt: I'm getting older and feel I've wasted my life—is it too late to start?
completion: It is not too late to start, and the feeling you describe should be met with a different exhortation than the one you may have heard. In this Church and Kingdom the call is not prepare to die but prepare to live. We should teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. Nor should we accept decrepitude and decay as a necessity of nature or law. The mental state governs the body, and man reflects eternal Life. Yet do not expect romance, family, business, pleasure, or art to fill the inner emptiness you feel. Every substitute for God leaves an emptiness unfilled and ends in disillusionment; only the finding of God is a permanent success. So begin now to build habits of life and to seek God, and take the first step today.

prompt: Can I have real peace with God while being at odds with fellow believers?
completion: Real peace with God and peace with fellow believers are closely connected, but we must be clear about where conflict comes from. Men precipitate war upon themselves by wickedness; God did not design it. So when believers are at odds, the cause lies in human sin rather than in God's will. Peace will never come until mankind receives God's truth, and that truth is the gospel of Jesus Christ. Reconciliation with a brother therefore belongs to the life of prayer and worship. When you meet sufferings and tribulations, meet them with a strong will to bear them for God, so that their bitterness remains full of peace and tranquillity rather than turning to resentment. And in every occasion of virtue, do not rely on your own strength: turn to God and ask for enabling grace, and receive strength more than sufficient. Examine whether the quarrel is about truth or pride; seek honest conversation, forgive where you have been wronged, and repent where you have wronged others.

prompt: I want my preaching to be heart-preaching. How does prayer make that happen?
completion: Heart-preaching begins with the preacher's heart, and prayer is how that heart is kept warm. It is not the head that makes the preacher but the heart. Prayer puts the heart into the sermon and the sermon into the heart. It keeps you aware of the weight of what you are handling and of your dependence on God. Do not treat prayer as a small duty fitted into leftover time. Give the best of your time and strength to prayer; let the closet come first, and let study and activities come second and be freshened by the closet. And do not seek mere circumstantial relief, but hearts comforted in the full sense: strengthened, courageous, and consoled. That is the supreme need for facing all things. Ask God to give you love for the people you will address, and let your study serve that love, so that your words carry the weight of a life lived before God.

prompt: I'm afraid of God's will for my life—I imagine it as a path of thorns. Will it always feel like that?
completion: Fear of God's will is understandable, especially if you have been taught to see it as a harsh path of thorns. But it may help to move from fear to longing conformity. What you fear is often a picture built from anxiety, not from knowledge. God's will is not primarily about suffering; it is about your good and your growth in trust. As you come to know it, you find it to be a great Balm and immense security, even amid temporary trials. Nor should you take temptation as proof of ruin. God permits evil inclinations to humble us; despise the temptation while embracing the tribulation it brings. Above all, love God fervently and without servile fear, trusting that He does not wish to harm you but to do your soul great good. Many people find that what they dreaded becomes the place where they meet God most deeply. Bring your fear honestly to God in prayer, and ask for the trust you do not yet have.

prompt: What is the difference between loving God and merely doing religious duties?
completion: Loving God differs from mere religious duty because love is a relationship with the living God, not a transaction. God is not a distant spectator; his holiness is grieved by sin and his love moves to provide atonement. The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world expresses an eternal fact in God's nature: holiness requires atonement and love provides it, under the control of his blessedness. Yet love is not mere sentiment. God's love is rational, voluntary self-communication seeking the true good of its object, regulated by and subordinate to his holiness. And this love is learned: spiritual habits begin with definite acts of will and steady obedience, and the Holy Spirit establishes them until obedience becomes spontaneous delight. So do not wait to feel loving before you obey. Begin with deliberate acts of trust and duty, and ask the Spirit to confirm them until love flows freely.

prompt: I feel far from God and my prayers feel empty—why?
completion: Feeling far from God is common, but the longing behind it is not a delusion. The soul's native yearning for God is evidence of a real Other who answers, because the environment has always produced the appetite and the search implies something to be found. Your empty prayers are not just a subjective mood; they are the cry of a creature made for communion with its Maker. Yet prayer is not naturally easy or flattering. It is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy before God, and little praying is a deluding make-believe, worse than no praying at all. But do not measure prayer by feelings, for moods never accurately gauge real assimilation to God. Rest on the changeless word of promise. Continue steadfastly when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression.

prompt: I want to know whether the Spirit is a person I can grieve and resist, or just an influence.
completion: The Holy Spirit is a person, not an impersonal force. Scripture speaks of grieving the Spirit and resisting him, which only makes sense if he is a personal being with will, intelligence, and emotion. He teaches, guides, comforts, convicts, and distributes gifts as he wills. So when you sin, you resist a person who loves you, and when you disobey, you grieve someone who cares. Our own spirit naturally loves truth and virtue, but it cannot overcome the flesh and the power of the Devil without being enlightened by the Holy Ghost. The interior spirit consists in directing all acts to the glory of God, so beware of acting for human praise, from mere natural impulse, or in routine without supernatural intention. And remember that the fulness of the Spirit is given along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization. God will not give his power for selfish enjoyment; we receive the Spirit in fulness only as we obey Christ's command and step out into his plans for the world.

prompt: I find it hard to forgive someone who hurt me. How should I pray?
completion: Forgiveness is hard, and it is honest to tell God so. Begin by praying for the person who hurt you, asking God to bless them and to soften your own heart. Ask God to help you release the debt and to heal the wounds the injury left behind, for God can and does heal in answer to prayer today, since Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, though the outcome and timing remain in his hands. Pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, because God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask; do not be discouraged by your sins, but keep asking. Remember that forgiving enemies is the best revenge: by bearing injuries patiently you gain grace and the pardon of your sins without trouble or expense. So confess bitterness, ask God to replace it with compassion, and refuse retaliation.

prompt: I am a dying believer and want to know whether I should ask my minister to bury me and to remember my aged parents after I am gone.
completion: Yes, it is appropriate to ask your minister to bury you and to remember your aged parents after you are gone. But choose your minister with care, because a prayerless ministry is not merely less effective; it is a funeral and an undertaker for God's truth and Church, however adorned it may be. A minister who prays will bury you as a witness to the resurrection and will remember your parents before God. Ask him to commend you to God's mercy within the limits of Scripture: praying for your acquittal at the great Day, your perfect consummation and bliss, and your resurrection, while avoiding any supposition of purification after death. And remember that parents bear responsibility to teach and watch over their children in the gospel and to guard them from the wickedness of the world. Speak with your minister soon, put your wishes in writing, and involve your family.

prompt: I'm afraid to speak up about my faith because I don't want to be mocked—how do I handle that fear?
completion: Your fear of mockery is honest, and honest fear deserves sympathy rather than shame. Many hesitate because childhood faith feels fragile when challenged, and it is right to want the settled conviction of maturity. But that conviction does not come chiefly from weighing evidence with our own understanding; leaning on human wisdom hinders faith. Trust God with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. He has not asked you to verify His truth before trusting Him, but to commit yourself to Him. Here is the ground of courage: God never forsakes us until we first forsake Him. So the thing to fear is not mockery but leaving Him, and the remedy is to remain always with Him. Stay in His presence, and His faithfulness, not your own boldness, will carry you.

prompt: My denomination claims to have the correct interpretation. Should I trust it?
completion: It is reasonable to ask whether a denomination's claim is well grounded, but the question should be approached with a fair rule of evidence. Ancient documents preserved in proper custody are presumed genuine, and the burden of proof lies on the objector, not on the documents. The Scripture witnesses should not be treated as suspect merely because their story is sacred; that is prejudice, not evidence. Yet orders and interpretation should not be judged as a mechanical validity apart from the Church's living whole. There is no abrupt choice between a perfectly true church and none; rather there are degrees of approximation to the whole historic life of the Body. Finally, do not measure a church's success by numbers, finances, or visible results, but by faithfulness to God's word and the witness it bears to His faithfulness. Trust where those marks are present.

prompt: What does it mean that God's love reaches even the most lost and scarred wanderer—can it reach me?
completion: Yes, God's love can reach you, no matter how lost or scarred you feel. Scripture says nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus. The lost sheep, the lost coin, the prodigal son all show God seeking the lost. The deeper way into that love is not only to beg Him to come down; it is the constant endeavour to enter up into His estate and offer Him love. And do not picture yourself alone in a lonely fen. The Father is ever nigh, appearing like a father to the lost child, kissing him, and leading him by the hand to his mother. Nor can your fear keep Him out: Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue. Love meets you at every cross-road and by-path and gently turns you back. Offer Him love, and you will find Him already near.

prompt: I am like a man in a desert with a loaf and a stone before me—how do I know which to take?
completion: The choice before you is real, and it is set before you as two ways, life or death, whichsoever you shall please to choose. Think of the desert wayfarer: a loaf and a stone lie before him. He who takes the stone and forsakes the loaf turns to want, but he who chooses the better when both are before him does wisely. So the question is not whether you are free; you are. The question is whether you will refuse the worse and choose the better. Honest self-examination reveals our wretchedness and shows how often we grasp the stone; when we see that, troubles, temptations, and contradictions should be submitted to and borne as advantageous, as God pleases. And remember why we have a body at all: man took a body for exaltation through Christ's redemption and for propagating a pure seed. Purity of body is therefore of the greatest importance. Choose the loaf, and keep your body in purity.

prompt: I have been asked to give up a cherished possession for God's work. How do I know whether this is His will?
