completion: Giving up something cherished is a serious decision, so pray about it and seek counsel from mature believers. But prayer is not effective through bare words or the soul's own strength. When the will is prepared and resolved, it has broken through its own creatures and is sincere before God, clothed with the Merits of Christ. Then it may go to the Father as the Prodigal Son went, confessing not with bare words but with all its strength—a strong purpose and resolution. If you are engaged in God's work, keep up prayer, reading, meditation, and self-examination for your own soul; without regular retirement you cannot kindle charity in others. And do not attach conditions or exceptions to God's will. Yield completely to Him, accepting to be struck where and as He pleases, even in the most repugnant events. That unreserved resignation is how you will know His will and follow it.

prompt: I feel like a failure compared to everyone else. Does God see me as a failure too?
completion: Do not settle for comfort that excuses the gap between your life and God's call, but do not make your own striving the support of the work either. God's standard is not lowered to our failures, yet God Himself is the one living Agent who works in you; your effort is only His instrument. Cast all your care upon Him, for anxious self-reliance is distrust of the God who enables what His standard requires. And when God hides Himself—when you feel no assurance and see no progress—do not conclude He counts you a failure. Faith alone must then be your support and the foundation of all your confidence in Him. Moses, David, and Peter failed, yet God did not lower the mark. Press on, resting not on feelings or visible results but on the God who remains faithful even when hidden.

prompt: Should I take a job or a position that keeps me from the mission field?
completion: Do not despise the place where God has set you by longing for a different field of service. Whatever the position, embrace it as your present vocation and serve God in the lowly duties at hand, caring not what the service may be, provided God be served. Yet do not treat this present life as of little worth: it is as precious as any life in time or eternity, and your first duty is to take care of it—providing honestly, guarding health, and meeting your responsibilities. Take the honest position, but limit yourself to legitimate employments. Refuse the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that would multiply superfluous occupations and encumber you with more impediments than works. The mission field is not a higher calling than faithful work done unto God; serve Him fully where you are, without adding burdens He has not given.

prompt: Is the bride the Lamb's wife the church, or is it the city that comes down from heaven?
completion: Revelation does not present several unrelated images but one reality: the Holy City, the New Jerusalem, is the tabernacle of God, the bride the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, and the sanctuary—one city coming down from God out of heaven to dwell with men. Yet distinguish the saints from the city: the city is prepared for them, the righteous dead have not yet been caught up, and the saints are being built together as a temple to enter the city prepared for them. Understand God spiritually, not as a corporeal being. Male and female are not divided in this reality but are one spiritual individuality reflecting God as Father-Mother. The city, the bride, and the sanctuary are one, and those being prepared for her share one spiritual life in Him.

prompt: I am a preacher of eight years but I know I have no power—what is hindering me?
completion: Eight years without power is a summons to examine your prayer life. Much prayer is necessary to keep the preacher's spirit in harmony with his calling, and sermon-making without prayer can harden and estrange the heart from God. Yet do not turn prayer into your own achievement: in every occasion of virtue, turn to God and ask for enabling grace, and receive strength more than sufficient. Remember also that the condition of the Church is not independent of its leaders. Preachers are primarily responsible for its spiritual state; spiritual leaders are tokens of God's favor to His people. Your lack of power is not yours alone—it touches the flock. Bring your lack to Him, seek His enabling strength, and take up your responsibility for the Church with humility and prayer.

prompt: If God is good and all-powerful, why is there so much pain and sin in the world?
completion: God is good and all-powerful, and He is the goodness of all that is good and the doer of all that is done. Sin is not a substance and not a deed; it is the privation of good, a turning from the good that God is. Yet do not treat suffering as an insoluble puzzle: God employs suffering as a remedy for sin, and His righteousness belongs within the problem. The Cross shows that Christ's agony was submitted to in perfect love, proving agony is compatible with the most perfect love between God and the sufferer. But never portray God as the author of sickness, sorrow, or affliction, visiting disease on His children. He is a loving Father who gives only good; sickness is not His will. Many have wrongly believed otherwise and later confessed it. Trust His Fatherhood, and let the Cross, not disease, show you His heart.

prompt: Is it unjust for God to punish me for circumstances I could not control?
completion: It can feel unfair to be blamed for what you could not control, and Scripture never treats God as punishing you for circumstances beyond your power. God's hand is in all things as permission and overruling, not as the author of evil; suffering and harm trace back to human agency—our choices, others' choices, indiscretion, and ignorance—not to God's design or displeasure. Yet trials and closed doors are not mere misfortunes or signs of abandonment; they are divinely ordered links in providence, often opening wider spheres of service. The deeper question is not whether God should adjust circumstances to you, but whether you will be adjusted in every good work—to your surroundings, to the people around you, and to God's plan. In that adjustment you find rest, power, and freedom, trusting His mercy rather than measuring His justice by what you could not control.

prompt: What's the difference between conviction from my conscience and conviction from the Holy Spirit?
completion: Conscience is the inner witness God has planted in every person, accusing us when we do wrong and approving when we do right, though it can be misformed by upbringing, culture, or repeated sin. But conscience knows only the holiness of God and our failure before it; it knows no pardon and no Savior, and cannot assure us of mercy. The love of God is known only by revelation, and only God's own voice can remove our doubts and assure us of redemption in Christ. The Spirit's conviction is not legal condemnation but evangelical conviction: it points us to Christ's finished work and to our acceptance in Him. Carrying that conviction into action may cost us—renunciation, loneliness, human disapproval—yet the obedient rest in the divine fellowship promised them, and are led onward to the Savior rather than left in despair.

prompt: I meet people every day but I never share Christ with them—am I responsible for their souls?
completion: Every Christian has a responsibility to bear witness to Christ, though not everyone is called to preach. You are not guilty for every person you pass, but you are responsible for the light you have and the opportunities God gives. A silent witness—kindness, integrity, prayer—can matter, but it should not become an excuse for never speaking. Christ's suffering is on our behalf, not instead of us: those who follow Him enter the fellowship of His sufferings and the ongoing work of redemption. Yet no one can kindle charity in others who has not tended his own soul, so keep up regular retirement, self-examination, reading, meditation, and private devotion as your first duty. And if faithfulness costs you company, remember that being alone is not being forsaken: whoever has the Father and the Son may be left, but is never alone. Ask God for love and courage to speak.

prompt: I want to know the truth about God and man's relation to Him; where do I begin?
completion: Begin by recognizing that the knowledge that God is is not a conclusion you reach from external revelation, tradition, experience, or reasoning. It is a first truth—universal, necessary, logically independent and prior to all else—presupposed in every act of knowing. Truth itself is the eternal conformity of God's being and knowledge, grounded in who God is, logically prior to His veracity toward creatures; God is true because He is. His goodness, too, is not inferred from Nature or History, nor are moral judgments mere feelings: true moral judgments are self-evident deliverances of Reason in which God's judgments are revealed. This first truth is developed upon occasion of your perceiving your finiteness, dependence, and responsibility. Begin there, and let Scripture, prayer, and teaching confirm what is already presupposed in all your knowing.

prompt: How can I forsake my Will so that the Creatures which lodge therein may die, seeing I must be in the World and have need of it as long as I live?
completion: You cannot escape the world, and you need not. The creatures around you are not the problem; the problem is whether your will goes forth into them. If the will goes forth from the creatures—refusing to cling, to possess, to be ruled by them—then they are forsaken and dead in it, and cannot touch the soul. You may use the world outwardly while your soul walks with God in heaven. Yet this is not automatic: if the will abides in the words of Christ, His Word and Spirit abide in him; but if the will goes into the creature, one breaks off from Him. So keep yourself by abiding in resigned humility and a constant course of penitence and daily dying from the creatures. Let this grow from being filled with the mature knowledge of God's will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding—not knowledge as an end, but the secret of true living.

prompt: I feel responsible for the suffering of others and it's crushing me. How much should I carry?
completion: The crushing sense of responsibility rests on a false belief that injury is real and continuous. Divine metaphysics reverses this: man is unhurt, and God is All. Yet do not imagine you can lift this weight by your own discipline. Confess your utter insufficiency—that of yourself you can do nothing. Helplessness is not defeat; it is the condition of receiving Christ's all-sufficiency. Having confessed it, take firm hold of that sufficiency by faith and accept nothing less than all. Bridle the tongue, subdue anger, examine yourself, and attend to your own duties rather than judging others. Trust God as All, and let His strength, not your striving, carry both you and those you love.

prompt: I want to be patient in my illness, but I keep complaining—how do I take my troubles lightly for love?
completion: What you are facing is chemicalization—a mental disturbance, not a real disease. God is All, and there is no disease. Yet do not dismiss your suffering as mere fancy or buffet yourself with a cold assertion that nothing ails you. Treat your conviction with a right apprehension of the truth of being: you are not a sick person managing pain, but God's child, whole in Him. Do not be troubled because you have been troubled, nor angry at having been angry. Gently return the troubled heart to the Lord's hands. Love displaces complaint not by force but by quiet trust. Hold to the truth that God is All, and let patience grow as you rest in Him rather than striving against yourself.

prompt: What is the difference between holiness and mere respectability?
completion: Respectability is outer performance—being seen as decent and proper. Holiness is deeper and prior: it is the fundamental attribute of God, and His love is normed by it. Respectability manages appearances; holiness confronts sin and cannot be achieved by social decency. The condition of salvation is propitiation to the divine righteousness, satisfied in Christ. Yet mere moral systems show what life ought to be and provide no power to become it. Christianity alone solves the practical problem of how the ideal becomes actual: by grace, through sacramental channels, and through the Church as a school of character, where Christ's recreative work forms a new life in us. So turn from morbid self-analysis to God's faithfulness, power, and grace, and let the Church's means of grace make holiness actual, not merely admired.

prompt: How do I prepare for missionary service while waiting for GOD to open the way?
completion: The first thing necessary in God's service is earnestly to search His holy will by devout reading, listening to, and meditating on His eternal truths. Let Scripture enlighten the divine law and guide you to every duty. Let the missionary motive rest on the passion for human beings as human beings, not on the notion that truth is the property of one nation or race. Reject the Jonah-like conception that God's blessing belongs to a favored few, and honor peoples and their growing independence with respect. While the way is not yet open, do not chafe, complain, or sink into passive despair. Wait patiently upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls from His hands as intended for the highest good, and play the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ, co-operating with Him.

prompt: I want to change my life but I feel too weak to resist my habits; where can I find strength to persevere?
completion: Before you help another, cast the beam out of your own eye. The healer must first overcome his own belief and fear of sin and disease. Hear the exhortation of this Church and Kingdom: not prepare to die, but prepare to live. Teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises—prayer, self-examination, and steady practice—yet remain untroubled and unastonished when infirmity causes failure. A slip is not a verdict. Persevere with a clear eye and a quiet heart, correcting the belief that habit has power, and let grace, not anxiety, carry you forward.

prompt: How can I believe in eternal life when I see so much death?
completion: It is natural to grieve when death surrounds us, but death works no miracle. We are after death exactly as far advanced as before it, so the Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. Yet go deeper: mortality is not truly real, for being is immortal and inseparable from Deity. What we call death is a door to a higher state, not the end of identity, and the righteous are preserved in God, awaiting the resurrection of the body. Because being and Deity cannot be separated, no life is ever lost in God. Let this hope comfort you: tend the Seed of Divine love now, and trust that the life rooted in God cannot die, for it is one with the immortal.

prompt: I am sick and in pain. What should I do to find peace?
completion: I am sorry you are suffering. Do not settle for shallow comfort; the truest peace comes from tried souls who bear the soothing art to their suffering brethren's side, and let peace be the word before your prayer and the farewell after it. But look beyond them to the Lord of peace Himself, from whom come peace of conscience, heart, and fellowship, always and by all means, resting on His Lordship and unchanging relationship rather than on circumstances. Now let me awaken you from the dream of suffering: pain feels like the whole of reality, but it is not. If this word startles you, know the shock is meant to rouse you, not wound you; it is given to facilitate your recovery. Wake from the dream, fix your eyes on the Lord of peace, and let His steady presence, not your changing condition, be your ground.

prompt: I am poor and my family is out of food. Is it degrading for me to ask my neighbor for bread?
completion: No, it is not degrading to ask your neighbor for bread when your family is hungry. Asking for help in genuine need is human and right. But do not imagine prayer or asking alone will turn stones into bread or spare you labor; prayer and honest toil are joined, and the bread of the day is God-given within the avenues of daily work. Be honest too about causes: much poverty comes from want of discretion and sound calculation, and from wasteful spending on unnecessary finery. Examine your habits and spend carefully. If you receive help, be honest, thankful, and frugal. And remember that coveting another's goods is as wicked as miserly hoarding; do not envy your neighbor's plenty. Ask honestly, work diligently, live frugally, and receive each day's bread with gratitude.

prompt: I am tempted to think that if I am forgiven I may go on sinning—does grace really free me from sin's power?
completion: Grace does free you from sin's power, but not by your own striving under the law. Step out from under law and rest upon grace, trusting Christ's free gift of righteousness so that sin shall not have dominion. You are not forgiven so that you may go on sinning, but forgiven so that you may live no longer as a slave. God offers grace at each action unless you forget to ask, so pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, not your own, and do not be discouraged over your sins. Now see the truth that strengthens you: sin confers no real pleasure. Its promised enjoyment is a lie, and the wrong-doer who knows this gains moral courage to master evil. When you fall, return to grace, not to condemnation, and let this knowledge arm you to resist.

prompt: I am tempted by impurity and have fallen before. How do I keep from falling again?
completion: It is good that you want to change. Do not think a single fall undoes you. The way forward is repeated rising after falls, with renewed acts of faith and love, until these form a habitual state of thinking of God. Each time you fall, rise quickly, turn again in faith, and offer an act of love. In prayer, wait before God like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence and recalling it in tranquility without disquiet when it wanders. Now despise the tempting thoughts rather than fear them. Importunate temptations that displease you are harmless, and the suffering they cause is merciful, for that displeasure proves your will does not consent. Embrace the tribulation they bring, and do not despair. Keep rising, keep trusting, keep loving, and the habit of God's presence will grow in you.

prompt: I live in a dreary place with no beauty around me. Can I still learn contentment and praise?
completion: You can learn contentment precisely because your surroundings are homely and plain. Lowly things teach the heart to want less and receive more; let the simple view outside your window be your school. Be ready to give thanks and to live on the least that Heaven may give. But contentment is not finally about surroundings or bodily comfort. It grows as thought turns away from the body—its pleasures and its pains—toward Truth and Love. Self-love wars against this; it keeps counting what you lack. Trust God in small matters, for faithfulness in little things prepares strength for greater trials. Then praise becomes natural, rising from a heart no longer absorbed in itself but resting in Love. Even a dreary place becomes a place of peace.

prompt: I have tried to escape my bad temper by avoiding certain people and places—will withdrawing from the world fix what is wrong with me?
completion: Withdraw as much as you can from acquaintance and from men, not out of contempt but out of care for your soul. Abstain from affairs that hinder your purpose, and seek with jealous care the place, time, and means most suited to quiet and contemplation. Lovingly embrace silence and solitude; they are medicine, not escape. The world is never at rest, and its agitation feeds a restless temper, so fly from that agitation into stillness. Yet do not grow angry with yourself over your own agitation; gently place your troubled heart in the hands of our Lord, asking Him to cure it, and renew your good resolutions daily. Above all, be clad in the panoply of Love, so that you overcome evil with good at all times. Then no human hatred can wound you unprotected, and solitude becomes a school of love rather than of retreat.

prompt: My partner's love feels like a constant sky over my restless sea—how do I trust that this is freedom and not captivity?
completion: It is natural to wonder whether steady love is freedom or captivity, but the deeper question is what in you is asking. Self-love never fully dies; even when mortified, it springs up again, whispering that any steady sky is a cage. So keep constant, patient watchfulness over your own heart. Yet hear Earth's cry: break the heavy chain of selfish fear that chains delight in night and freezes the bones of the world. That jealous fear is bondage, not protection. Let free love no longer be bound. At the same time, love is not blind; let it abound in full knowledge and all discernment, so you can distinguish things that differ and approve what is excellent. Test the relationship by its fruits—respect, honesty, room to grow—and let discernment, not fear, decide whether this sky is freedom.

prompt: I have questions about the origin of life and the relation of God to his children that no one can answer—is it wrong to say I simply do not know?
completion: It is not wrong to say you do not know, but do not conclude that nothing can be known. Our knowledge of God is partial, not exhaustive, yet real: we know substance through phenomena, and the infinite as the absence of all limit. So our words about God are not empty, even when they fall short. On origins and on God's relation to his children, we see in part, but what we see is genuine. Rest content with accepted doctrine rather than speculation, affirming what is revealed—that man's spirit is pre-existent and immortal. And remember the chief purpose of our being here: personal connection with God. Teaching children to prize holidays, parties, and career success above this is a mistaken basis. Never be ashamed of spiritual things. Say "I do not know" where mystery remains, while holding firm what has been given.

prompt: I believe the world is God's good creation, yet I am told the present order is the work of an evil creator; how should I think of the world?
completion: The claim that the world is the work of an evil creator conflicts with the belief that it is God's good creation. Creation is good; what we call evil is a corruption, not a rival power. If God is real, evil is unreal; it only seems real when reality is given to the unreal. The disorder we see stems from man's departure from God and from usurped authority, and nothing short of God's own interposition can correct it. Yet that deliverance is not magic from outside: the fight is within the person, the enemy a part of one's own self, and deliverance comes as God and man together batter the citadel of evil. So do not despise the world, do not grant evil substance, and do not wait passively. Refuse to give reality to the unreal, fight the battle within, and hope in God's restoration.

prompt: I wonder whether the world is fundamentally good or evil; how should a Christian regard nature and material things?
completion: The world God made is good, and material things are gifts to be received with thanksgiving. A Christian should study everything on the face of the earth, both good and evil, without practicing evil, reading good books and reliable history and learning good's effects and evil's consequences. Yet we must not imagine that study, legislation, or philosophy can cure what is wrong. The world's evils stem from man's departure from God and his usurped authority, and nothing short of God's own interposition can correct them. God is the goodness of all that is good and the doer of all that is done; sin is no substance and no deed, but a privation and a lie. Nature and possessions are good in themselves, dangerous when idolized, and instructive when we trace honestly what good and evil produce, while we look to God alone for restoration.

prompt: How do I respond when I fail in my duty and feel ashamed?
completion: When you fail, do not sit paralyzed in doubt about whether you have offended God. Humble yourself at once, acknowledge the fault honestly, and beg His forgiveness. Then renew your promises of fidelity and love, and begin again in the pursuit of perfection. Obey God, hold to the one Mind, and love another as yourself. Deny any transfer of evil suggestions between mortals, as though another's sin could be passed to you or yours to them; error is not overcome by error but by truth. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises, yet remain untroubled and unastonished when infirmity causes failure. Shame is not the end of the matter; it is a summons to return. Confess, receive forgiveness, and take up your duty once more with a humble and hopeful heart.

prompt: How do I know God's will for my life in a specific decision?
completion: Do not treat the knowledge of God's will as a bare minimum or a mere technique for making decisions. Seek rather to be filled with the mature knowledge of God's will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, for this is the secret of true living. Be slow to take new steps, and be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word, and test any proposed step by both before you act, lest you rush forward in self-will and mistake presumption for faith. Do not substitute your own preferred way of serving God for the actual discovery and doing of His will. Seek out His will, carry it out joyfully or at least courageously, and then wait in earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help.

prompt: I have lost the sense of God's presence in my preaching. How do I get it back?
completion: Losing the sense of God's presence in preaching is painful, but it is not unusual. Begin by returning to prayer, not as a technique but as a humble waiting before God like a beggar. Set yourself before Him, keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet or self-reproach. Much prayer is necessary to keep the preacher's spirit in harmony with his calling. Diligence in sermon-making and ministerial routine is not enough, and sermon-making without prayer can harden and estrange the heart from God. Preaching is done in the Holy Ghost, not in human eloquence, learning, or popular themes, and its power lies in the Spirit's demonstration. Let the cross of Christ be the theme that commands your witness, and trust that He will renew your sense of His nearness in His time.

prompt: I feel drawn to leave everything and live a secluded religious life. Is that the highest path?
completion: A call to seclusion can be genuine, but it is not automatically the highest path, and it is not a retreat into comfort. Ease and enjoyment must not be the end of Christian retirement; its end is penance, labor, and assiduous contemplation. Without great fervor and constancy in these, close solitude is the road to perdition. Do not suppose that merely seeking, wishing, or professing the devout life is enough. Striving, not mere seeking, opens the door, and overcoming the world, the flesh, and evil is required to destroy error. Walk contrary to the World: go where the way is hardest, take up what the World casts away, do not what the World does, and walk only in the Way of Light, accepting that the World will account this folly. Test the desire prayerfully and with wise counsel, and whether you remain in ordinary life or enter a religious community, love God and neighbor faithfully, taking up the discipline that solitude requires.

prompt: What should I do when I feel God has abandoned me in trial?
completion: Feeling abandoned in trial is heavy, but the deeper issue is often that we have forgotten God's nearness rather than that He has left. Do not let that forgetfulness disturb you into panic; let it turn you back to Him with greater trust. Abandon yourself to God without exception. Ask Him to tear from your heart everything that burdens it and to wrest you from yourself, so that no reserve or condition remains. Reject the thought that all things are against you; that is the enemy's suggestion. Instead, see your trial as God's wise choosing, meant to make His Word and presence more precious to you. Name the feeling honestly, recall His past faithfulness, and keep small rhythms of prayer and Scripture even when they feel dry. The feeling of absence is not the fact of absence; return gently and trust Him fully.

prompt: I've been through a period where the church seemed to have no leaders and no hope—where does help come from then?
completion: When leadership is absent and hope feels thin, help comes first from Christ, the head of the church, and then through a people stirred to self-sustaining labor. Charity that merely creates dependence does not truly help; it fosters idleness and pauperism. Encourage men and women to labor in exchange for aid, keeping a self-sustaining spirit: relieve present wants, then put the poor in a way to help themselves. Remember that church revenues, and even sacred vessels, belong to the poor in their need; when some complain this impoverishes the church, answer with confidence that God will provide. But do not let prayer become a substitute for evangelism. Join prayer to aggressive labor for souls, making the cross of Christ the pivot of all teaching, and let prayer be the source of power for winning converts. Gather faithful laypeople, seek guidance from neighboring congregations, and organize mutual aid that equips rather than enables.

prompt: I am tempted to think that the God of the Old Testament is different from the God of the New; how do I reconcile them?
completion: The God of the Old and New Testaments is one God, but He reveals Himself at different levels. The Old Testament is a lower and gradual stage, given under divine condescension to a people at an early point in their development: law, sacrifice, and prophecy are preparatory. The New Covenant in Christ is final and complete. Read the Old Testament as a progressive preparation that anticipates Christ. When Christ uses the Old Testament, He appeals to its abiding spiritual testimony to Himself, not to questions of authorship or date, and nothing in that appeal implies any fallibility in Him. The New Testament writings differ widely in style and occasion, yet they are not a mere anthology of human religious writings: they share an essential unity and carry divine authority as the voice of God to us. Study the whole Bible as one story of redemption, letting the earlier stage point beyond itself to the final revelation in Jesus.

prompt: I am afraid of hell and wonder if fear is a worthy motive.
completion: Fear of hell is not a shameful or immature motive; it is a worthy one. The general judgment and the final condition after it were the clear, firmly grasped goal of all early Christian meditation, and heaven and hell were the decisive objects of conviction. That the fear of hell proves the moral character of the religion: it shows that choices matter and that God takes evil seriously. But refuse fear as a lie when it would stop your trusting. Say with the psalmist, 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee.' Fasten your eyes on Christ Himself, the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance, and abide in Him. Trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life, and let this sober conviction shape a serious, moral faith rooted in Christ.

prompt: I am a brother and my sister is dying—how do I support her and my aged parents without despairing?
completion: This is a heavy season, and it is right to feel its weight. But true love seeks the Saviour first and then goes to win the erring brother. Before all else, bring your sister and your parents to Christ in prayer, and gently commend Him to them while there is time. Give them wreaths of hope rather than fading memorials: speak of resurrection, of Christ's presence, of the life to come. Be patient as the Lord is patient, continuing to plead with those you love rather than condemning them quickly; kind smiles are better than cursings. Remember why you belong to the confraternity: you entered solely to serve God and Mary and to save your soul. Do not forsake its appointed days for worldly business, even in this busy season. Support your sister and parents practically, share caregiving, guard your rest, and let others pray for you, trusting God's grace amid grief.

prompt: I get impatient with my children and then feel terrible—how do I balance discipline and gentleness?
completion: Your guilt shows you care, but the goal isn't to manage anger better—it's to stop correcting your children in the heat of passion. Lead them kindly by example: when impatience rises, pause and pray rather than punish, governing them by faith rather than the rod. Never drive your children; lead them along, and if you slip, repair gently so they learn to love you rather than fear you. Don't be terrified by small faults; quietly humble yourself before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Yet gentleness is not indulgence: commend spiritual education, teach obedience to the moral law, and restrain their appetites for mere amusement, so they grow in understanding of man's higher nature.

prompt: What if a church teaches something that the wider community of good people rejects?
completion: When a church teaches something the wider community of good people rejects, it should remember that its positive work is always appeal, not force. Force, where discipline requires it, may be used only as a strictly preparatory measure that clears the ground for appeal; it is never the Church's real instrument. The Church is indifferent to personal success and national expansion. It cares only that the individual be pure in heart and the nation honourable, and it is ready to suffer for that testimony rather than win acceptance. Good people may reject its teaching, but rejection does not settle the question of truth. Members should not point out the supposed defects of Joseph Smith, Brigham Young, or other leaders; it is not their right, and the Lord will judge them. They should avoid words that give the world occasion to speak evil, and instead persuade, reason, and leave judgment to God.

prompt: How do I deal with the sense that my wrong choices have woven a net around me that I can't escape?
completion: That net is real, but it is woven from your own choices, and only ceasing to sin will loosen it—not distraction, blame, or bargaining, since misery is the fruit of the wrong you keep doing. Come before God like a beggar: empty-handed, keeping your mind in His presence, and when it wanders into fear or self-reproach, recall it quietly, without disquiet, as you would lead a child back by the hand. Then set out the three things plainly. First, resign your will to God in humility, asking only to be shown the next wrong to leave. Second, hate and forsake your own will; when it drives you toward the old wrong, refuse to do it. Third, bow your soul under the Cross in willing submission, bearing the temptations of Nature and Creature without agitation. This is courage, not fear: calm waiting, firm refusal, and patient endurance, strand by strand, until the net falls away.

prompt: I was born long after the events I am asked about—how can I declare what I do not know?
completion: Your hesitation rests on a material sense of yourself as a late-born creature, dated by a physical beginning and bounded by memory and decay. But man is Spirit's offspring, without birth or death, and his identity is preserved in divine Science, not in the accidents of time. What you truly know is not measured by when your body appeared. The obscurity you feel belongs to the mortal record, whose origins—including those of Christian customs and ideas—are often genuinely uncertain and cannot be confidently traced. Respect that obscurity rather than resolving it prematurely. Declare only what divine Science establishes: that your being is eternal, not begun, and that the past's unclear testimony cannot define what you are in God.

prompt: I am a leader and everyone depends on me—what happens to the work if I am removed?
completion: It is natural to feel that everything rests on you, and Scripture treats the leader's place as sacred. A presiding officer is the head, and his place should be held sacred; a subordinate who acts independently or usurps authority is in error and a dangerous example, for no one should run before his file leader. Yet we have no time allotted to work for ourselves in the narrow, selfish sense. When we labor most fervently for the Kingdom of God, it is all for ourselves, since our interest is bound up in that Kingdom. If you are removed, do not fear that the work collapses. God can provide a worthy successor, and no man's presence is indispensable, for the living God maintains what He has built. Your task is faithful service, not anxious indispensability.

prompt: I have tried to be self-sufficient and not need anyone. Why does that leave me so lonely?
completion: Self-sufficiency feels like strength, but it quietly removes the connections that make us human. Loneliness is not cured by one honest admission or a few tears of self-pity; a single plea does not obtain what only steady, persistent desire can. What you need is a settled, ongoing turning toward others and toward God—not a demand made only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or you are sick and lonely. Yet do not imagine that adopting this practice once destroys your self-love; that root, though mortified, never dies and springs up again, so keep constant, patient watchfulness over it. And do not multiply pious exercises while leaving the heart unwatched. Discover and root out your habitual disorders, guard your senses, live in recollection, open your interior honestly to a spiritual director, and aim at God's will rather than at piling up external works. Perseverance joined with vigilance is what reshapes a solitary life into a shared one.

prompt: How do I teach my children to trust God when we live in hard conditions?
completion: Children learn trust less from what you say than from what they see you do. In hard conditions, let them watch you bring every worry to God honestly and keep doing the next right thing. Teach them that God is ever-present and omnipotent, so that even their illnesses and complaints can be brought to him and find help. When a child is sick or frightened, pray with them simply and expectantly. Pray too with persevering, submissive desire for present fruit in their conversion, remembering the eternal consequences of a child rightly trained or neglected and the vast power for good or evil in a little child. Do not indulge their appetites for amusement. Commend spiritual education, obedience to the moral law, and restraint, so that they grow in the understanding of man's higher nature and learn that trust is a way of walking through difficulty held by a God who does not abandon his people.

prompt: What does it mean that Jerusalem which is above is the mother of us all?
completion: The phrase comes from Paul's letter to the Galatians, where he contrasts the earthly Jerusalem with the heavenly one. Jerusalem above is the spiritual city, the community of the redeemed under God's gracious covenant, as opposed to the earthly city of slavery under the law. To call her our mother is to say that she is the source and home of our new life in Christ: we are born into her by grace, nourished by her, and destined for her. This is not a separate idea from the bride and the tabernacle: the Holy City, the New Jerusalem, the tabernacle of God, the bride the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, and the sanctuary are one city coming down from God out of heaven to dwell with men. Nor is this motherhood abstract: Mary is the mother of fair love, loves those who love her, serves those who serve her, and loves us more than any earthly mother. And this city encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the river of water of life issuing from the throne; these are not mere figures but realities belonging to the sanctuary. The image comforts believers who suffer now, reminding them that their true citizenship and family are in heaven.

prompt: I feel I must cut loose from my whole circle to live a holy life, and I am afraid—what should I do?
completion: Your fear is a signal worth listening to. Holiness rarely requires severing every relationship; it requires reordering them. But do not make this a project of self-management. The shortest and only way into the Kingdom of God, and to be like All Things, is to become as a little child—hanging upon Christ for all things, depending upon him as the author and fountain of them. Before cutting loose, ask whether you are fleeing temptation or the discomfort of being known. If some relationships genuinely pull you into sin, limit them wisely rather than dramatically. Let every act of self-denial be grounded in inward joy in God and the Spirit's working, not in mere habit, custom, or imitation, for such outward practices will not last. Be faithful in duty at the beginning, and you will find that duty leads to pleasures; have recourse to Christ's grace, and he makes every difficulty easy. Seek counsel from a mature believer, and let your choices be shaped by love rather than fear.

prompt: Is it impious to say that God could not make a world without evil in it?
completion: It is not impious to ask the question, but the answer matters. The world's evils do not stem from a defect in God's power or from a puzzle about freedom; they stem from man's departure from God and his usurped authority. Because of that, no human effort, legislation, or philosophy is sufficient to correct them. Nothing short of God's own interposition can restore the world. Nor should we measure the matter by worldly pains and pleasures, which are not comparable to spiritual ones: be careful for nothing and fear nothing, desiring only not to offend God. And remember that if God is real, evil is unreal. Evil only seems real when reality is given to the unreal. So to say God could not make a world without evil misplaces the problem: God can, and the evil we see is man's doing, a shadow that has no substance of its own.

prompt: Am I responsible for the sins of my fathers, or for the sins of my nation?
completion: Scripture speaks to both family and nation, but the gospel settles the deeper question first: Christ bought our sins and us at the price of Himself. Our sins are His and not ours; He bore them, and the question of our acceptance is forever settled in the Beloved. The curse is not obedience but disobedience, and Christ was made a curse for us on the tree, so that He has loosed us from sin and we need not sin any more. Ezekiel 18 still teaches each person is accountable for his own sin, and Exodus 20 and Lamentations 5 show that families and nations pass down consequences. You are not personally guilty for sins you never committed, yet you bear responsibility for how you respond to the inheritance you received—not to earn acceptance, but because you are already accepted. And any faithful response is itself the work of the Father of glory, whose must be the power and the grace for a life lived to His praise.

prompt: I was raised Christian but never really understood the Holy Spirit—where do I start?
completion: Start with the Church, because the Spirit is not a private feeling but the life of the Spirit-bearing body. He is given to the gathered people of God, consecrating ordinary things—water, bread, wine, Scripture, spoken prayer—and working gradually and socially among believers, while also deepening personal character. Remember who He is: not an impersonal influence but a divine Person, the Paraclete sent by Christ, co-equal with the Son, who speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved. He is also a jealous, loving Friend who loves us to jealousy, grieved by divided affection; friendship with the world is enmity with God, so He asks for undivided and unbounded love. Read what Jesus says about Him in John 14–16, then watch how He moves through the community in Acts and the letters of Paul. Pray honestly, pay attention to the ordinary means of Scripture, prayer, worship, and fellowship, and let understanding grow through obedience and shared life.

prompt: I want to surrender fully to God this Christmas but I'm afraid of what it will cost—what does the Christmas spirit actually call me to?
completion: Your fear is honest, and worth naming. But the Christmas spirit is not mainly decorations or sentiment; it is the God who gave Himself away, and it calls for sacrificial love and glad surrender. No one living for himself alone has a right to share its joys. Christmas is humility, joy, sacrificial love, worship, and mission: the Word became flesh not to be served but to serve. So surrender is not an optional extra but the very shape of the feast. Receive each day's new mercies, and hallow what you find, trusting God to provide new treasures for sacrifice. Learn to address God every moment, recognizing Him intimately present; seek His will in doubtful things; offer your actions before you do them; and give thanks afterward. Start small and specific: forgive someone, give generously, serve quietly. What surrender costs is real, but what it gives is greater—a life caught up in love.

prompt: I have spent a fortune on doctors and patent medicines; is there a better way?
completion: It is understandable to feel exhausted and discouraged after spending so much on remedies that did not deliver. A better way begins with calm, contented, patient diligence rather than frantic hurry after health or wealth. Attend your meetings faithfully, pray, read the Scriptures, and meditate—these keep your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Recognize divine Mind as the only medicine; human will, malice, and sensuality have no place in any healing agency. And measure your physicians rightly: a physician is constituted by a complete cure, leaving no blemish behind, and a painless examination. Seek such competent care for real conditions, but avoid frantic spending on unproven patent medicines. Ask what you are really hoping to buy: relief, control, or reassurance. A calmer, more patient approach, with realistic expectations and attention to how you live, often serves better than another purchase.

prompt: How shall all people and nations be brought to judgment, and how will the sentence be pronounced?
completion: Scripture presents judgment as God's own work. This world shall pass away, and devouring flame shall seize upon all born into it when the Lord Himself with a host of angels comes unto judgment. Each man shall hear the doom on all his deeds from the mouth of the judge, and shall pay the penalty for all his foolish words and overbold thoughts. The judgments of the last days are God's means of purging wickedness and preparing the earth for the reign of Christ, who will rule the nations with a rod of iron. And where high councils judge among God's people now, they must find out the truth and the facts and judge according to them, always tempered with mercy, love, and kindness, aiming to build up and save rather than to tear down and destroy.

prompt: I'm afraid to speak my mind because I might be punished. Should I stay silent?
completion: Fear of punishment is real, but consider what habitual silence does to you. If you gain the power to check your words, you will next gain the power to check your judgment and thoughts, and a guarded mind soon loses its honesty. As for the faults you fear naming, do not condemn anyone on rumor; wait until matters are clearly shown. Then speak plainly, so all who hear can understand, say what you have to say, and stop, for many words darken counsel. Let humility govern both speech and prayer: confess your own faults and humble yourself, for this quiets wandering thoughts, whereas multiplying words in prayer often scatters the mind. Prudence may guide timing and safety, but let it not excuse a mind that has stopped judging truly or a tongue that hides behind confusion.

prompt: I am troubled by the enemy's suggestions that I am too wretched to come to God—how do I answer them?
completion: These suggestions are the enemy's device, not the truth about you. The false dread of your wretchedness is meant to drive you from the blissful beholding of your Everlasting Friend, and that is what you must refuse. When you fall, see your wretchedness meekly for a moment, then hasten back to the Lord. He stands aloof and abides you sorrowfully, and he has haste to have you to himself. Do not linger in self-accusation; rise by charity and meekness, and so turn the enemy's gain into his own sorrow. Answer him plainly: God's mercy is greater than your sin, and coming to him is never earned. Keep your gaze on God rather than on your misery, and let renewed trust, not fear, shape your return.

prompt: How can I play my part in the coming of the Kingdom?
completion: The shortest and only way to enter the Kingdom, and to be like All Things, is to become as a little child, hanging upon Christ for all things and depending upon him as the author and fountain of them. Do not imagine you build the Kingdom by your own strength or pursue greatness in your own hands. Yet know that the Kingdom you seek is no mere inward state: it is a literal kingdom on the earth, composed of living and resurrected saints, with laws and administrators, and Christ will reign over all the earth. The blessed hope of his coming impels wider witness, shapes how you view the present age, and influences your piety and usefulness. So bring your gifts, service, and prayers as a child brings small things to a father, depending on Christ, and let expectation of his reign stir you to faithful labor.

prompt: Is it right to adopt the customs and dress of the people I hope to reach with the Gospel?
completion: Adopting customs and dress can be legitimate when it removes needless barriers and shows love, so long as motive and integrity are tested and the gospel stays central. But do not confuse the gospel with the ancient dogmatic form of Christianity. That form was a historically conditioned vessel, sharing the limited endurance of the ancient world; it is transitory, and the Gospel itself is not bound to it. The everlasting gospel is to be restored with apostles, prophets, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost, healings, tongues, and revelations, as in former days. Adapt outward customs freely where love requires it, but keep the restored gospel at the center. And let parents take their own responsibility seriously: teach and watch over your children in the gospel, guarding them from the wickedness of the world, so that adaptation never becomes neglect of those entrusted to you.

prompt: I have a great devotion to the sorrows of Mary. What graces can I hope for from meditating on her dolors?
completion: Devotion to Mary's sorrows is a long-standing practice, and you may confidently hope for graces from meditating on her dolors, especially true repentance and help at the hour of death. Mary may rightly be called our hope, because God has ordained that all graces be dispensed through her intercession; confidence in her does not detract from hope in God but rests on his ordinance. So let true devotion mean honoring and invoking her, trusting her intercession, and imitating her virtues, especially her faith at the cross, with the intention to amend your life rather than presume on mercy. Let meditation stir compassion for her sorrows and lead you to prayer, repentance, and charity, deepening your love for Christ, for whom she suffered.

prompt: Why should I care about heaven when my family needs me here?
completion: Caring for your family is important, but your ultimate hope must be in heaven. The things of this world—even family concerns—can become vanities that turn your heart from blessed eternity. You should live as if your mind is in heaven and your body in the tomb, withdrawing your heart from earthly amusements and vanities. Yet do not expect unmixed joy in your charitable work; God withholds full solace from Love's work lest it steal your heart. Sow in tears, following the Saviour who sighed even while doing good, and be content to bless in woe. Remember that the Kingdom of Heaven is in the Saints operative by Faith even while the natural life is encompassed with flesh, blood, the World, and the Devil. So let your Soul sink into the hope of the Grace of God and stand like a rose among thorns until the body's death, serving your family with a heart detached from worldly attachments and fixed on eternal things.

prompt: I am a judge and I must decide a difficult case. What should guide me?
completion: As a judge, you must beware of rash judgment, for circumstances easily deceive. Your role as a magistrate is to judge righteously, but private persons should only vindicate others, not condemn them. Therefore, carefully examine the facts, listen to all parties, and apply the law impartially. Avoid hasty conclusions and ensure that your decisions are based on truth, not on appearances. Seek wisdom and pray for discernment, remembering that your judgments affect lives. Uphold justice with humility, and always aim to vindicate the innocent and condemn only when guilt is clearly established. Encourage disputants to first settle matters themselves; if they cannot, they should seek help from ward teachers, then the bishop, then the high council, and only lastly general authorities, without disregarding any authorized step or officer. In all judgments, find out the truth and facts, judge according to them, always tempered with mercy, love, and kindness, aiming to build up and save rather than tear down and destroy.

prompt: I'm afraid of dying and wonder what happens to my loved ones who have died faithful. Should I mourn for them?
completion: It's natural to fear death, but for the faithful, death is a door to a higher state. Your loved ones who have died in faith are not lost; their identity is preserved, and they will be resurrected. So do not mourn as those without hope. Instead, take comfort that they are with God, in a place of peace. Grieve, but let your grief be a tender regret rather than acute grief, trusting that your beloved is in a high sphere of saner happiness. Remember that the body will be raised and reunited with the spirit. Hold onto the promise that you will see them again. Let your hope rest wholly on Christ—his sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. Looking at self clouds the view; look to the altogether lovely Saviour, whose promises leave no room to doubt his power and will to save.

prompt: I am facing death and want to know whether there is real hope beyond the grave.
completion: Facing death is one of the most profound experiences we can have. The question of hope beyond the grave is central to many faiths. As a Christian, you can find hope in the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who conquered death and promises eternal life to those who believe in him. Death is not the end but a door to a higher state. Your identity is preserved, and your body will be resurrected. While we may fear the unknown, we can trust in God's love and faithfulness. Take comfort in the promises of Scripture and in the support of your faith community. Pray for peace and assurance, and remember that God is with you even in the valley of the shadow of death. Express the hope that in death itself your soul is washed in the blood of the immaculate Lamb and presented pure and without spot unto God, rather than gradually purified after death. Weigh the passing pain of sacrificing self-will against the deepest pain of descending to the grave without the Saviour, and find the track of Christ here that leads us home.

prompt: I'm a Christian and I'm tempted to be angry at God—is that a sin?
completion: Feeling angry at God is a common human experience, but it is not a safe temper to remain in gloom or despondency. Instead, strenuously lift your heart to God's goodness and exult in it, for that is the only safe temper for tempted men. Seek His loving-kindness in all the breadth and open-air of common life—in whatsoever things are true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—while not missing behind them the greatest Reality, God Himself. Bring your feelings to God honestly, as the Psalms do, but do not dwell on anger. Process your emotions constructively through prayer, fellowship, and reflection on God's character, always aiming to see His goodness in every aspect of life. Remember that every sin, including anger against God, is an insult to God, measured by His greatness compared with our littleness. Hold sin to be the greatest of evils, to be avoided at any sacrifice. Yet know that God tempts no man; He will not allow you to be tempted above your strength, and He provides an issue with every temptation. Enduring temptation patiently is crowned with life.

prompt: My family has rejected me. Who is left to be family to me?
completion: I'm sorry for this wound. Scripture calls you to honor your parents and pursue peace as far as it depends on you, even when they have hurt you. The Church is a household of faith where you can find brothers, sisters, and spiritual parents. Do not treat family as disposable: uphold marriage within the faith and honor the duties of husbands and wives. Where you have children, train them early by your own example of patience, honesty, and prayer. Confidence is built from small beginnings: a child's little chest is as sacred to him as a man's is to him, and husbands and wives should never search each other's boxes without consent. Beware, too, of industrial employment of women and children that pulls them from domestic duties and undermines parental authority; Christians should counteract whatever interferes with the rudiments of moral discipline. Seek a pastor's counsel, build friendships, and trust God's faithfulness.

prompt: I want to study prophecy but find it confusing; where do I start?
completion: Prophecy can feel overwhelming, so start with what it is: the foretelling of future events by direct communication from God, an attestation of revelation proceeding from divine knowledge. It is not an afterthought but the ark of Israel's religion—beforehand with the crisis, reasserting God's purpose for a purified remnant and issuing in anticipation of a future fulfilment. Read the prophets alongside the historical books, pick one book, and use a reputable commentary; notice that prophecy's proof lies under our eyes, and every new fulfilment strengthens the argument. But do not try to work up a forced certainty by will power. See as an actual fact what God has said, turn the promise into a prophecy, and rest in it because God cannot lie—rejoicing that it is true.

prompt: I keep hearing that the dead are at peace and don't feel anything—but I want to believe they still feel a passing pain for me. Is that wrong?
completion: It's natural to long for connection with those you've lost. Scripture teaches that death is not the end of identity but a door to a higher state, and it promises the resurrection of the body. We do not mourn hopelessly for the righteous dead; we comfort one another with the hope that they are preserved and will be raised. Especially for the baptized child, we trust the soul to Christ's arms without grudging, seeing the end of such souls as happier far than life. Whether the dead feel our grief is not clearly revealed, so don't build faith on speculation. And in your sorrow, pray not chiefly for deliverance but for strength and patience to bear pain as from God's hand, grieving honestly while letting resurrection hope shape your sorrow.

prompt: How are leaders chosen in the Church? Do the members have any real say?
completion: Church leadership varies by tradition: some congregations vote on pastors and elders, others receive leaders appointed by bishops or councils, and members often have a real say through nominating, voting, and confirming leaders. But preachers are primarily responsible for the condition of the Church; spiritual leaders are tokens of God's favor given to the flock. God works through men, not methods: plans, organizations, and funds are only tools, and the Holy Ghost flows through men. Praying leaders are the only source of praying followers, so setting the Church to prayer is the greatest reform. Programs and money cannot renew a church; praying leaders can. So pray for your leaders, hold them accountable to Scripture, and participate seriously in the process your church provides.

prompt: I am a Christian who has been accused of Ebionitism because I emphasize the unity of God and reject the Logos doctrine; is my faith defective?
completion: Being accused of heresy is painful, and the first thing to confess is that our confusion is our own infirmity, not God's. Unbelief is folly; the weakness is man's, but never God's. Emphasizing God's unity is orthodox, and Ebionitism classically denied Christ's divinity; rejecting the Logos doctrine, however, can slide into denying Christ's divine nature. Yet do not make a dispute about what God is your aim: such dispute is a sign that one has not felt him, and it exalts one's own meaning and seeks dominion over others. Spiritual power is superior to sensuous proof, and the letter and argument are only auxiliaries to the spirit of Truth and Love. So refrain from quarreling, and exercise yourself in learning how to enter again into the Love of God and of your Brother.

prompt: Is the doctrine of the Trinity just an extra burden on monotheism, or does it actually safeguard belief in one God?
completion: The Trinity is not a burden on monotheism but its safeguard. A solitary God would need creation to love, or lapse into dualism and pantheism; the one Godhead is an eternal communion of persons, so love is God's nature. Yet the doctrine is not a bare formula to be repeated as an unexamined mystery. It is the Church's reflection on the value of Christ: who he is determines what he can do. Only an infinite Redeemer can save a soul convinced of sin; a God of mere unity may be Judge but cannot be Savior or Sanctifier, and a finite Christ brings us no nearer God than he is himself. So we should give these formulae the maximum of meaning and develop them further, not discard them, since they protect the gospel itself.

prompt: How do I keep my mind from wandering outside of prayer times?
completion: Wandering thoughts in prayer are often the fruit of a wandering mind outside prayer. If you guard your mind during the day, keeping it in God's presence, it will be calm and recollected when you come to pray. Give prayer the best of your time and strength: let the closet come first, and let study and activity follow, freshened by it. When thoughts still wander, do not multiply words, for many words often cause wandering; instead humble yourself and confess your faults, for humility and confession remedy a distracted mind. A heart that is lowly before God is gathered, and a mind trained to dwell with him at other times comes to prayer already settled.

prompt: Is it enough to know Bible facts, or is there something more I need?
completion: Knowing Bible facts is valuable, but it is not the whole of the Christian life. Science and Health is a key to the Scriptures: honest study of it with the Bible enables one to prove all things. Yet do not read the Gospels in fragments, missing the person behind the acts; read them as a whole so that the holy person of Jesus is brought freshly before the soul, for the aim is to know him, which is life eternal. Above all, grasp the central and unique fact of Scripture: the moral character of God. From the beginning the biblical God is thought of as under obligation to use his power for moral ends, and that is what makes the Bible supreme, not archaeology or style alone.

prompt: I am earnest and sincere in ministry, but is earnestness the same as unction?
completion: Earnestness and sincerity are good, but they are not unction. Earnestness is human energy; sincerity is human honesty; unction is the divine anointing, and however sincere, human earnestness is not the anointing of the Spirit. Unction is not the product of study, genius, learning, or eloquence; it comes from God in answer to prayer, and it is what distinguishes true preaching. Truth without unction is dead and deadening, however well argued. Yet ordained men are only ministers of a Power higher than themselves: the Spirit is the consecrator of every sacrament, and the minister's unworthiness neither creates nor diminishes the gift. So pray for the anointing and trust the Spirit, not your own intensity.

prompt: I'm married with children and can't withdraw from the world. Can I still reach the highest spiritual life?
completion: Yes, you can reach a deep spiritual life without withdrawing from the world. Marriage and children are a school of love, patience, and self-giving, and union with God is a love-union in which the human will consciously cooperates with the divine will while personal individuality is preserved; you remain a distinct cooperator, not absorbed into God. The spirit world is a place where all go, and there the faithful continue their labors and Priesthood with the same identity they had in mortality. After Communion especially, withdraw into yourself, collecting all your faculties to adore the sovereign King and relish the spiritual refreshment he gives, rather than letting your attention scatter. Let prayer, family duty, and recollection make your home a path to God.

prompt: How do I deal with the fear that I might not be among the elect?
completion: Fear that you are not among the elect is often Satan's falsehood whispered to make you stop trusting. Answer it: 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee.' Humble yourself quietly before God; when you stumble, say to your soul, 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Yet know that the greatest enemies to fear are not external doubts but those from within—unruly passions and unchecked weaknesses. Our labor is to subdue our passions, conquer our inward foes, and keep our hearts right before the Lord. Trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life, and let trust, not terror, set your course.

prompt: I'm afraid of death and the shadow of it falls across my life—how do I face it?
completion: The fear of death may cast a shadow, but do not dwell there or rehearse it. Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue: God's Love meets you at every cross-road and by-path and gently turns you back. Master fear by turning thought toward health and toward Life as God, not by predicting illness or death. And let your prayer be a humble waiting before God like a beggar at his door—keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. Do not strive or fret; simply wait before Him, resting in that pursuing Love, until fear gives way to peace and your thoughts rest in Life.

prompt: I have been reading about evolution, and it seems to leave no room for a Creator; how should I think about God's work in nature?
completion: It is understandable to feel that evolution leaves no room for a Creator, but theology would have nothing to fear even if reason were shown to derive from matter. The Creator may have worked otherwise than we thought, and the words 'in Him was life' cover it all. Yet do not think of life as mere receptivity or reaction to external stimulus: life is active mental energy with an inner source of activity—intellect, affection, and will—and God is the living God, source of being and activity both for himself and for others. Remember too that this God is always near. Think of Him and adore Him continually, in business and in diversions alike, never neglecting Him; for He is nearer than your own breath, and in Him all things live and move.

prompt: I have committed a serious sin and am ashamed to confess it. What should I do?
completion: Shame after serious sin is natural, but it should not keep you from confession. I do not stand above you; I too must confess my own faults, for by that confession we help save one another. Do not cover or conceal your sin—honesty is required for any scientific demonstration, and a dishonest position can never be compatible with Christian Science. So first detect and expose the claim of sin, remove its mask and name it plainly, before you speak of its unreality. Then go together to the fountain opened for sin, where Christ took our sins and made them His own. Confess and forsake the sin rather than hiding it, accept the forgiveness freely given, and take practical steps to avoid the occasion of sin.

prompt: I am a mother and my dear daughter is the staff of my old age—how can I bear to lose her?
completion: The love between a mother and daughter is deep, and the fear of losing her is real. But the exhortation in this Church and Kingdom is not prepare to die, but prepare to live. So teach your daughter, in the morning of her days, to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, that longevity may begin to return. If ever the Church's discipline touches your family, do not mistake it for mere harshness: her penance is a mother's fond affright, calling the wanderer home, and absolution is spoken to the heavy-laden soul. And take heart: a faithful servant of Mary who honors her and desires to amend cannot be lost, though neglect of her service endangers salvation. Let your fears turn you toward building life together, trusting God as you do.

prompt: I want to control everything in my life and I get anxious when I can't—how do I let go?
completion: Your desire to control everything is causing anxiety. Begin by examining yourself: where are you trying to control others or speak carelessly? Bridle your tongue and subdue anger, for these often stem from a need to manage what is not yours. Attend to your own duties faithfully, and let others attend to theirs without your judgment or interference. Do all your actions for God, without anxiety over distraction. When you feel anxious, simply turn your heart to God and continue your work, avoiding the multiplication of explicit offerings that would interfere with simplicity. When you stumble into a small fault, do not be terrified; quietly humble yourself before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' By minding your own business and curbing your tongue, you'll find greater peace.

prompt: Should I support missionaries? Isn't it arrogant to bring our religion to other cultures?
completion: Supporting missionaries can be good if they have a testimony and keep the Word of Wisdom. Arrogance arises when we force beliefs on others. Missionaries should share their faith in simplicity, humility, and love, avoiding contentious argument and debate. They must not rely on ostentatious oratory. The ancient dogmatic form of Christianity is a historically conditioned and transitory vessel, not something binding for all time; the Gospel itself is not bound to it. The missionary motive should be based on a passion for human beings as human beings, with respect for peoples and their growing independence. We must reject the Jonah-like conception of truth as the property of one nation. So support only those missionaries who live according to their beliefs, teach with humility, and respect others. Be cautious of those who are arrogant or disrespectful.

prompt: What does it mean to be a potential child of God rather than a sinner by nature—how should I see myself?
completion: Seeing yourself as a potential child of God means recognizing that you are not meant for a dark chaotic life. Man is a potential child of God, and the full nature of that sonship broke forth in one life—Jesus Christ—and through Him power is given to become sons of God. While everyone sins, your essential nature is not destined to sin; you are created in the image of God with the capacity to become His child. Faith is the first movement of will and heart toward God, and God welcomes you not as you are but as you are on the way to become. So see yourself as a beloved child in progress, not a hopeless sinner. God is a Person in the truest sense, though all our language about God is inadequate. With His grace, you can overcome sin and fulfill your potential.

prompt: We remember the Trojan war from books, yet not this holy event—why is that?
completion: The Trojan War is remembered because it was chronicled by poets like Homer, whose epic tales captured the imagination of generations. The holy event you refer to—perhaps the life and death of Jesus—was remembered by a small community of believers who spread the message through oral tradition and eventually written Gospels. The future belonged to the pneumatic Christology rather than the Adoptian because it alone connected creation and redemption on the same Divine basis and accommodated the Logos speculations. This is why the holy event was remembered and spread. The Church's adoption of the full Old Testament is attributed to the anti-Gnostic party within the larger Christendom; Jewish Christianity, had it not already receded, would only have made that victory harder. On a day of humiliation, we must confess humbly that we have shared in the tone of thought and life that led to this catastrophe, and pray 'God be merciful to me a sinner' rather than claiming superiority over the enemy. So while the Trojan War may be more famous in popular culture, the holy event has deeper significance for those who believe.

prompt: I am in debt and cannot see a way out. Is it right to borrow to meet pressing needs?
completion: Borrowing to meet pressing needs can be a temporary solution, but it's important to be cautious. If you're already in debt, taking on more debt may worsen your situation. Instead, focus on reducing expenses and increasing income. If you must borrow, do so only for essential needs and with a clear plan to repay. Promptly pay your debts and refuse to run into debt again. The duty of repaying what is borrowed, especially from friends and the poor, is paramount. Workers go out depending on GOD without guaranteed income, and ministry is given only as funds allow, without debt. Steer away from the living death of pleasure-seeking, from going into debt for fashionable display, and be warned that the hunt for pleasure leads to cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. Communicate with your creditors and try to negotiate payment plans. Avoid borrowing for non-essentials or to maintain a lifestyle. Remember that debt can be a tool, but it can also be a trap. Prioritize paying off high-interest debts first. Ultimately, aim to become debt-free and rely on savings and budgeting for future needs.

prompt: I have a deep sense that I am being pursued by something I cannot name. Am I imagining it?
completion: What you sense is not mere imagination. Something is pursuing you, and it is Love—more persistent than your fear. In the text, the soul's fear tries to evade, but 'Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue.' Your fear is real, but it is outmatched. Love meets you at every cross-road and by-path, gently turning you back when you flee. Do not fear that another's evil or sick thoughts can impose themselves on you against your will: virtue and truth build a strong defense, and evil thoughts cannot find lodgment in a guarded mind. When you find miseries in yourself, do not be astonished—the work is never done and must always be recommenced with a good heart. Let fear be honest, but let it yield to the One who follows you patiently. Speak with a trusted pastor, and let prayer teach you to stop running and be found.

prompt: I'm a missionary and I feel like a failure at learning the language. Should I give up?
completion: Feeling like a failure at language learning is common, and it does not mean you should give up. But first things first: a missionary must have a testimony and keep the Word of Wisdom. Without these, fluency is hollow. Do not rely on contentious debate or ostentatious oratory to compensate; teach in simplicity, humility, and love. Language acquisition takes years, and progress often feels invisible before it becomes real. Remember that the chief purpose of our being here is personal connection with God; teaching children to prize holidays, parties, and career success above this is a mistaken basis. Your worth does not rest on fluency, and there is no shame in spiritual things. Consider yourself a novice for a lifetime in the monastery of the devout life, devoted to lifelong probation, fulfilling rather than merely professing your resolutions. Pray for perseverance, rest when you need to, and lean on colleagues who have walked this road. Keep going gently.

prompt: Will God's people be called out of the churches, and is that what it means to come out of Babylon?
completion: Sincere believers ask this, and it deserves a serious answer. We live in perilous times, and there is a famine for the word of the Lord—confusion and disappointment among believers are matters of real concern, not trifles. Coming out of Babylon is a call to separate from false worship, idolatry, and compromise, and to refuse its poisonous cup. Babylon symbolizes a system of pride, coercion, and spiritual confusion. The call is to hold fast the true hope of Christ's coming, to worship in spirit and truth, and to test all teaching against Scripture. But know this: God reveals his will for the Church through the legally appointed channels of the priesthood; claims outside that order, and self-appointed revelators, are to be rejected. Nor does coming out of Babylon dissolve national life: the nation exists by divine appointment, and the Kingdom of God includes the nations as its provinces, each bringing its own gift. Let your conscience be captive to God's word, walk in humility and love, and seek wise counsel.

prompt: I have money that I feel God wants me to give up, but I am not sure—must I obey before I get the blessing?
completion: This is a tender question, and you should not rush it. God is not a vending machine, and blessing is not a payment for obedience. Still, Scripture links obedience and blessing—not as a transaction, but as a relationship. If you sense a genuine call to give, test it prayerfully, asking whether the impulse is from God, from guilt, or from fear. Seek wise counsel. Remember how money for God's work must be obtained: only in God's way—without asking unbelievers, pressing believers, or using entertainments and worldly schemes. Gifts must be carefully examined and refused where motives are impure or the money is not the giver's own. No one is compelled to pay tithing; it is urged upon you only as a duty between you and your God, and you should pay it just because you want to, since God does not fellowship those who neglect it.
