Do not hoard a reserve for future want as though prudence required it; live from day to day upon the Lord's bounty, treating hoarded provision for the future as a snare, and make one investment in His work and the poor. Pray, wait, and act when your heart is settled.

prompt: What does it even mean to call God omnipotent—could He make two and two equal five?
completion: Calling God omnipotent means He can do all that is an object of power—everything genuinely possible. It does not mean He can do nonsense. 'Two and two equal five' is a contradiction, not a feat; absurdities and things contrary to His nature are not objects of power. Nor is omnipotence a necessity compelling God to do all He can: He has power over His power and can limit Himself freely. As for God's unity, it need not exclude internal personal distinctions; the integration of finite consciousnesses in one divine consciousness, and of subordinate consciousnesses in man, makes a triple consciousness in one divine essence credible rather than incredible. And God is not subject to time: His eternity is the timeless possession of His whole life at once, and time is a relation of finite existence that He Himself causes, though He truly recognizes the successions of history. So no, God cannot make two and two equal five—not from weakness, but because the statement describes nothing.

prompt: Why were whole nations and cities destroyed by God in ancient times?
completion: The destruction of nations and cities in ancient times, as recorded in the Bible, must be understood in light of God's sovereignty and human responsibility. God foresaw and will overrule the results of war for good, but the evil that brought destruction was the result of human agency, not God's design. While the Bible often attributes events to God's judgment, this language reflects the ancient understanding that God is ultimately in control. However, the wickedness that led to destruction—such as violence, oppression, and idolatry—was chosen by humans, not ordained by God. God's foreknowledge does not make Him the author of evil; rather, He permits human freedom and works through history to bring about His purposes. Yet God is also a God of deliverances, who keeps His people in answer to prayer. His purposes are fulfilled in the death of some as in the deliverance of others, and He remains faithful even in martyrdom. We must grieve over the refusal to let Christ keep the souls He died to win, and resolve to hate in thought, word, and deed what made Him mourn. Thus, these events serve as warnings against sin and reminders of God's justice, while also demonstrating His power to redeem and restore.

prompt: Does the Holy Spirit still guide missionaries today the way he did in the book of Acts?
completion: Yes, the Holy Spirit still guides missionaries today, though perhaps not in the same dramatic ways as in the book of Acts. In Acts, we see the Spirit directing Philip to the Ethiopian eunuch, preventing Paul from going to Asia, and sending Peter to Cornelius. Today, the Spirit guides through prayer, Scripture, and the inward witness of the Spirit, but we must leave the conduct of believers' assemblies to the Holy Spirit's ordering, recognizing His distribution of gifts to all believers for common profit. We should speak well of predecessors who did their best, recognizing that God has used many faithful servants throughout history. When inviting others to join the mission, we should invite without urging and never compel anyone, respecting their freedom to respond to the Spirit's call. The same Spirit who guided the early church is still at work, and missionaries should seek His guidance daily. We must affirm the Spirit's personal and gradual working in the Church, allowing for imperfection in the Old Testament and the Church without denying real inspiration. The Spirit works progressively, leading believers into all truth, and we must avoid binding the assembly to human rules.

prompt: I want to make my heart a nest for the Holy Spirit—what does that look like practically?
completion: Making your heart a nest for the Holy Spirit involves recognizing that the Holy Spirit in this present stage seeks a home and nest in our hearts. Practically, this means cultivating a life of prayer, obedience, and openness to God. Set aside daily time for prayer and Scripture reading, confess sin, and seek to align your life with God's will. Be sensitive to the Spirit's promptings and respond in faith. Surround yourself with a community of believers who can encourage and challenge you. Engage in acts of service and love, which are fruit of the Spirit. Remember that the Holy Spirit is a person, not a force, so relate to Him personally. Welcome the Dove to a nest within you, offering Him a resting place. But beware: the Holy Spirit is a jealous, loving Friend who is grieved by divided affection. Friendship with the world is enmity with God. Therefore, meet the Spirit with undivided and unbounded affection, turning away from worldly attachments. Be filled with the Spirit through surrender and faith, expecting repeated fillings as need arises. Do not treat being filled as a one-time event; instead, continually seek His fullness. Ultimately, it's about surrender—letting go of your own agenda and embracing God's. As you do these things, your heart becomes a welcoming place for the Spirit to dwell.

prompt: I'm afraid of the dark and of unseen dangers at night. How do I overcome this fear?
completion: Fear of the dark and unseen dangers is a common experience, but as a Christian, you can overcome it by trusting in God's presence and protection. The Bible assures us that God is with us always, even in the darkest night. Psalm 139 says that darkness is not dark to God. Practically, you can pray for peace, recite Scripture, and remind yourself of God's faithfulness. Avoid dwelling on fearful thoughts; instead, fill your mind with truth. It may also help to have a nightlight or to listen to calming music. Remember that perfect love casts out fear. Ask God to fill you with His love and to help you trust Him. Over time, as you practice these things, your fear will diminish. If it persists, consider seeking support from a pastor or counselor. However, we must deny disease mentally without audibly naming it, avoiding any fearful diagnosis that would deepen the wrong mind-picture. Yet we must also warn of the danger of evil and expose it, refusing to be an unfaithful steward. Do not be ignorant of Satan's devices, but resist him, firm in your faith. Above all, confess that it is not night if Christ be near. Ask Him to abide from morn till eve, and when night is nigh, for without Him we cannot live or dare to die.

prompt: How can the Divine and the Natural Light operate in their several spheres without interfering with each other?
completion: To understand how the Divine and Natural Light operate without interfering, we must first gain a correct sense of the highest visible idea, which is the way to understand the divine Principle. The Divine Light pertains to spiritual truths and revelation, while the Natural Light concerns reason and empirical knowledge. They do not interfere because they address different aspects of reality. However, they can overlap when natural reason examines spiritual matters, but divine revelation supersedes where they conflict. To avoid interference, we must recognize the limits of each: reason cannot fully comprehend divine mysteries, and revelation does not contradict true reason. Thus, they work harmoniously when kept in their proper domains, with faith and reason complementing each other, and with the highest visible idea guiding our understanding of the divine Principle. We must adhere strictly to the rules of divine metaphysics and rest demonstration on this sure basis, not on guesswork. Furthermore, we affirm the Dynamical theory of inspiration, which rejects both the naturalistic Intuition-theory and the mechanical Dictation-theory. Inspiration is neither natural, partial, nor mechanical but supernatural, plenary, and dynamical, with God working from within man's soul while man remains in conscious exercise of his own powers.

prompt: I feel like I've lost my innocence and can't get it back. Is there hope?
completion: There is hope, and it begins not with forcing yourself but with waiting humbly before God like a beggar—empty-handed, asking for what you cannot give yourself. The misery of guilt is not escaped by managing feelings or by fear of punishment; it ends by ceasing the wrong itself, and that takes moral courage, not dread. But do not imagine you must fix yourself by effort alone. Come before God with your longing for innocence, and keep your mind in His presence. When your thoughts wander—and they will—recall them gently, without disquiet or self-reproach, and return to Him in tranquility. Innocence and Truth, the Lamb of Love, meet you there. Your part is not to overpower guilt but to wait faithfully, to turn from the wrong, and to let Love restore what you could never reclaim by force.

prompt: I feel abandoned by God in this darkness; is He still with me, or has He left me to myself?
completion: Your feeling is real, but do not let it become your master. Abandon yourself to God in this darkness: He has not left you. If you have forgotten Him, do not be disquieted; return to Him with greater trust. Hand Him your suffering, your work, your joys, and your very self, holding nothing back, and let Him be your life in the dark. When you are troubled over your sins or your devotion, do not lean on your own efforts or feelings; faith alone sustains the soul through such troubles. Rest in Him who is faithful even when you are not, and let that faith give way to profound inward peace. He is with you, and He will not forsake you.

prompt: Is it right to require someone to give up his own tradition in order to unite with us?
completion: No, it is not right to require someone to abandon his tradition as the price of union, for unity purchased by disowning one's spiritual ancestry is conquest, not fellowship. The guilt of division is shared: every body has contributed to separation, and each has a positive gift the others need. Particular devotions are means to the end of being with God; when the soul rests in that end, the means may be laid aside without betrayal, so customs may be yielded where they obscure God while the heritage that formed us is honored. Yet such fellowship cannot rest on goodwill or political machinery alone. It is secured by the Church's spiritual society, the common membership in which nations are already one; political and legal arrangements presuppose that unity and serve it, but they cannot replace it.

prompt: I want to be a missionary but my parents neither encourage nor discourage me—how should I proceed?
completion: Since your parents are neutral, the decision is largely yours, but first examine yourself. A missionary must have a genuine testimony; without one, wait and seek it through prayer, study, and counsel with church leaders. Keep the Word of Wisdom and live worthily. Then teach in simplicity, humility, and love, not with contentious argument or showy oratory, letting your motive be love for human beings as human beings, respecting peoples and their growing independence, and rejecting any Jonah-like idea that truth is one nation's property. Parents and pastors bear a duty to guard the young from corrupting books and to supply pious reading; ask your parents to help you prepare with sound literature and counsel. Their neutrality gives you room to seek guidance and prepare prayerfully rather than rushing ahead.

prompt: I am scrupulous and tormented by doubts about my salvation; is there comfort for me?
completion: Your scruples reveal a tender conscience, but the torment is not from God. When you fear you have offended Him, do not stay paralyzed: humble yourself, acknowledge your fault, beg His forgiveness, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and begin again as often as you fall. Guard against presumption and despair alike. Let unsureness of yourself be meekness, keeping you low and dependent on God; and let the blessed Shewing of Love be your true comfort and joy, for His mercy is greater than your weakness. Then move beyond fear of His Will into longing conformity to it. What once seemed a harsh path of thorns becomes a great Balm: His Will is your immense security, and even temporary trials serve your growth in trust. Continue patiently in the pursuit of perfection, and let peace grow as you walk forward.

prompt: How do I face the possibility of my own death in battle?
completion: Count yourself as already dead, since you must die some day, and have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over, regret, and detest your offences and faults; it is not now the time to rejoice but to lament with all sincerity of heart. If wounds or sickness come, receive them as a school of virtue and a true martyrdom, a time of great merit; do not give way to impatience or wish for death merely to escape suffering. And when comrades fall, do not mourn without measure, for excessive grief for the dead is a want of faith and confidence in God, who takes away friends because he will be loved without a rival. Trust His fatherly purpose, and let hope steady your sorrow.

prompt: I am a host and I want my feast to go well. How should I arrange it?
completion: Arrange your feast by a different pattern than the world's: the world gives its cloying first bowl, but the Saviour keeps the good wine until now; trust His word and keep your best till last, beginning simply and letting the richest dish come at the end. As servants of Mary, give alms in her honor, especially on Saturdays, and perform works of mercy, which are pleasing to the mother of mercy. Yet be careful for nothing. Make your requests known to God with thanksgiving, and exchange your anxious care for His Almighty care, so that the feast is ordered in trust rather than in worry, and your guests see a host at peace.

prompt: I want to bless my enemies but I don't know how. What does that look like in practice?
completion: Begin with yourself, for the text says, 'bless yourselves': bless others by actively doing the will of God, since we are right only when we do His will. Pray for enemies by name, refuse to speak ill, and do good quietly, for woe comes when men bless you, and those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps. Yet do not moan over your unworthiness or wait to become more righteous before blessing God. Rise up now and bless Him with all the love you have, keeping none back for yourself or creatures. Bless Him from sickness as fully as in health, and let that full-hearted blessing overflow into how you treat your enemies.

prompt: I'm planning my future and making business plans. How should I think about my plans in light of God's will?
completion: In light of God's will, remember that love and delight in God—acts of the will—are our only real business, while mere understanding is of little value. The most excellent method is to do your common business purely for the love of God, without regard to pleasing men, so that meetings and transactions become worship. And let prayer be real, expectant business with a prayer-answering GOD, not a mere sentiment or last resort. Bring Him your plans, your needs, your workers, and your protection, asking with thanksgiving, and trust His faithfulness to answer for souls, needs, and safety. Plan diligently, but transact your deepest business with Him.

prompt: I want to be honored and respected by others. Is that desire wrong?
completion: The question is not first whether the desire is wrong but whether you are straining to be something other than what God made you. Accept your own condition and be that well, honoring the Master Workman, and seek only to please God's will. Be willing to decline available human support where doing so enables a fuller dependence on GOD's faithfulness. Yet do not locate the joy of God's love in your merit, your charitable work, your learning, or any supposed favoritism. That joy lives in the continually maintained attitude of longing for Him, grateful giving, and receiving Christ. Keep that attitude, and honor from others becomes secondary—received with thanks, released without bitterness, because your joy rests in Him alone.

prompt: I'm afraid of growing old and losing my joy in God. Does faith fade with age?
completion: Your fear is honest, but God never forsakes us unless we first forsake Him, so fear only the turning away and stay close to Him. Yet staying is not a single resolve but a daily holding fast, with confidence firm to the end, following faith with perseverance until the blessing comes. And faith must be shown in works and spiritual understanding, not mere feeling: each person must work out his own salvation, and no one else's faithfulness can carry you. So let your years be spent in obedience, prayer, and understanding, trusting that He who is faithful will keep you, and that joy borne of endurance will not fade.

prompt: I keep hearing that Jesus tasted death for me—how should that change what I talk about every day?
completion: Hearing that Jesus tasted death for you should turn your eyes from yourself to Him. Your assurance rests not on how worthy or steady you feel but wholly on Christ—His sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the Father's right hand. Looking at self clouds the view; looking at the altogether lovely Saviour leaves no room to doubt His power and will to save. Never let your soul dwell in sadness or scrupulous fear; ground your consolation in the goodness and sweetness of Him who died to give you life. And measure your own sufferings against Jesus crucified, covered with wounds and despoiled of everything—yours can in no way compare with His. Let your daily talk flow from that.

prompt: I'm frightened of dying before I've loved enough—how do I face that fear without despair?
completion: That fear is understandable, but it should not govern you. Fear must be cast out and replaced by trust in God, as in the testimonies where fear was overcome before the healing appeared. Do not imagine your fear is a successful defense: it cannot outlast His love. As the old word says, Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue—His love meets you at every cross-road and by-path and gently turns you back. So do not fret or hurry as though you must prove enough love before dying; over-eagerness is the mother of many imperfections. Keep yourself in God's presence, free from anxiety, and let love grow quietly in the next small act before you.

prompt: Is there any way to be saved other than the way God has pointed out?
completion: No—there is no salvation but in the way God has pointed out, and no hope of everlasting life except through obedience to the law affixed by the Father of life. Jesus is that way: the truth and the life, and no one comes to the Father except through Him. But salvation is an individual operation: each must receive or reject it for himself, and no one is saved by another's righteousness. So do not merely assent to facts about Jesus. First let your eyes be opened to sin and its danger, let that sight lead you to repentance, and only then, as a penitent, believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and walk in the way He has shown.

prompt: I am tempted to think that since grace abounds, I may sin freely; how does the tradition answer this?
completion: The tradition answers this temptation by pointing away from self-effort and toward Christ. Grace is not permission to sin but power to overcome it; Paul asks, 'Shall we sin because we are under grace? By no means!' The curse is disobedience, not obedience—transgression, not the law itself. Christ was made a curse for us on the tree, bearing that curse in our place, and has thereby loosed us from sin so that we need not sin any more. So stop fighting sin under the law by self-effort and condemnation; step out from under law and rest upon grace, trusting Christ's free gift of righteousness. Under grace, sin shall not have dominion over you.

prompt: I am afraid of death and of judgment; what does the gospel teach about the end of my life?
completion: The gospel teaches that death is certain and that after death comes judgment according to deeds done in the body, including words and thoughts and the intents of the heart. Death works no miracle; we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. The mere name of Christian, or baptism, or the fact of dying, does not guarantee paradise. The Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. Yet our assurance does not rest on our feelings or worthiness, for looking at self clouds the view. It rests wholly on Christ—his sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. His promises leave no room to doubt his power and will to save. Therefore, turn from self to the altogether lovely Saviour, who has borne the penalty for sin and offers forgiveness and new life now. By turning to Him in repentance and faith, we receive a new heart and a new obedience, and the Seed of Divine love grows in us.

prompt: What's the point of set prayer times if I'm supposed to be with God always?
completion: Set prayer times are not merely helpful reminders; they are essential to private communion with God. While we are to live in constant awareness of God's presence, the secret of prevailing prayer is much time alone with God. Short prayers can be powerful, but their efficiency comes from long seasons spent with God. The estimate a preacher places on prayer is measured by the time he gives to it. Great praying is the sign of God's great leaders. Therefore, give the best of your time and strength to prayer. Let the closet come first; let study and activities come second and be freshened by the closet. Do not treat prayer as a small duty fitted into leftover time. The goal is to cultivate a habit of prayer that spills over into all of life, but that habit is built on deliberate, extended times with God. Without those times, our brief prayers become shallow.

prompt: I'm clever and well-educated but feel spiritually dull—why is that?
completion: Feeling spiritually dull despite being clever and well-educated is not uncommon because spiritual knowledge is not the same as intellectual attainment. Wisdom and revelation come from the full knowledge of God through fellowship with Him, not from scholarship alone. Natural knowledge and culture are not evil; they can be useful servants, but they must not be idolized. Spiritual perception is available to the unlearned as well, for God reveals Himself to the humble and childlike. Your dullness may come from relying on your intellect rather than on the Spirit. The letter and mental argument are only auxiliaries to the spirit of Truth and Love; they are not the healing power itself. Spiritual power is superior to sensuous evidence. Therefore, turn your thought away from the body, its pleasures and pains, toward Truth and Love, for self-love wars against spirituality. Seek God Himself, not just information about Him. Cultivate fellowship with God through prayer, obedience, and love, and ask the Holy Spirit to give you spiritual understanding.

prompt: How do I obtain the unction you speak of? Can study or learning produce it?
completion: Unction is the divine anointing that distinguishes true preaching. It cannot be produced by study, genius, learning, or eloquence. Unction comes from God alone, in answer to prayer and a life surrendered to Him. It is a gift of grace, not a result of human effort. To obtain it, you must seek God earnestly, humble yourself, and ask for the Holy Spirit's filling. Truth without unction is dead and deadening; it has no life-giving power. Therefore, do not rely on your education or talents. Pray for unction, live a holy life, and depend entirely on God's grace. Only the Spirit can give life to your preaching and ministry. Christian Science is demonstrable with one fixed method, and departure from its proven Principle forfeits the claim to belong to its school. So, put into practice the truth you already understand. Prove good by demonstration before seeking more understanding. Adhere to the proven Principle and practice it consistently.

prompt: I have a dishonest, lazy employee and a difficult husband. How can these be anything but obstacles to God?
completion: It's understandable to feel that difficult people are obstacles, but God is the one living Agent and all human workers are only His instruments. The dishonest employee and difficult husband are not obstacles but opportunities to see God at work. Cast all your care upon Him, for He cares for you. Worry and self-reliance are distrust of Him. Instead of trying to fix them in your own strength, trust God to work in and through them. Your part is to be faithful as His instrument, not to carry the burden yourself. Pray for them and leave the outcomes to God. He can turn obstacles into stepping stones. Remember that God's self-limitations in decree, creation, providence, inspiration, and the person and work of Christ are consistent with and expressive of His perfection. They are signs of His power and love, not denials of His infinity. So, trust in His perfect wisdom and love. Be faithful in the least, using the one talent and ordinary opportunity given, for God places solemn value on humble workers, and littleness will not excuse you from service.

prompt: How do I deal with vain curiosity and the urge to read every new book and hear every rumour?
completion: Vain curiosity is best met not by wrestling it down but by learning to wait before God like a beggar, hands open and mind quiet. Stand porter at the door of thought: when the urge to read every new book or hear every rumour knocks, examine it and shut out the unhealthy thought before it enters, for fear and restless craving admitted become the body's suffering. Do not scold yourself; refuse it at the threshold and gently bring your mind back into His presence. The wandering is not the failure—the disquiet is. But know the price: this waiting asks extraordinary lowliness and loneliness of spirit, and the drying up of ordinary interests and enjoyments, because God wills to have the whole of us. Do not turn back at that cost. Let prayer be this humble waiting, and let books and news be received later, in their place.

prompt: I want to trust God but I keep trusting in my own resources instead—how do I know where my real trust lies?
completion: Real trust in God is above circumstances and appearances. You cannot measure it by whether your savings, network, or plans remain intact, for the work hangs solely upon the good pleasure of God, not upon visible support. Hanging upon the invisible God is not hanging upon nothing. So trust Him with all your heart, and refuse to lean on your own understanding or the wisdom of others, for that leaning hinders faith. Do not demand to investigate whether God has told the truth before you commit. And remember that particular devotions—your methods, disciplines, and practices—are only means to the end; when the soul is with God, its end, they may be laid aside, for they become useless then. When support vanishes, place the work again upon His good pleasure, trusting Him even when every visible prop is gone.

prompt: I want to ask God for things, but does his power mean he must do everything he can, or can he choose to limit himself?
completion: God's power is not a compulsion; He is free, and freedom means He can choose what to do and what not to do. Do not run from pressure and trial as though they were failures of prayer. Receive them as God's way of generating spiritual force and power, letting each hard pressure lift you above the painful cause rather than fleeing it. Yet keep within the landmarks of His word: the patronage of the world is not to be sought or depended upon, no debts are to be contracted, and appeals for money from unbelievers or reliance on fixed income are not the means of His work. The Living God alone is Patron, and prayer is the only appeal. And do not imagine that will-power governs anything—neither yourself nor others; Truth and Love are the motive-powers of man. Depend wholly on His blessing in answer to prayer.

prompt: I keep repeating general confessions out of anxiety. Is that healthy?
completion: Repeating general confessions out of anxiety is not healthy, because the anxiety itself is the obstacle—over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Do not hurry through confessions or fret over whether you said them rightly. Practise instead the faithful presence of God: stay quietly before Him, confess what you actually know, receive His mercy, and remain without agitation. When the urge to repeat rises, do not accept it as a real relapse—there is no real relapse in Truth. Meet its cause mentally and courageously: name the fear, face it, and conquer it. Use this mental practice only to promote right thinking and doing; if you turn it to selfish gain or wrong motives, the abuse diminishes and finally destroys the power to heal. Perfection is not in the number of your confessions but in dwelling with God without anxiety.

prompt: I have been a Christian for some years and find my feelings less ecstatic than at first—is my religion declining?
completion: Feelings never accurately gauge your real assimilation to God, so the fading of early ecstasy is no proof that your religion is declining. Do not measure yourself by moods. Rest instead on the changeless word of promise, and continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, refusing to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. But do not wait for joyful feelings before you rejoice: count it all joy by faith, reckoning the trial a blessing, fixing your heart and choosing to rejoice until praise becomes a habit. And remember that love is not mere sentiment or desire—it is the outgoing of your entire nature in self-sacrificing service, the supreme proof of the reality of your Christian profession. Let that love, not fading feeling, answer whether your religion is declining.

prompt: I'm struggling with a habitual sin and I keep falling—is there any hope for me?
completion: There is hope, and it begins here: God beholds you with pity, not blame. Yet do not treat sin lightly—unrepented sin accumulates and a conscience ignored grows dull—so repent honestly and reform your life, removing occasions and seeking help. But learn to distinguish temptation from sin: temptation is not sin but the means of proving virtue and gaining great profit, for the life of man upon earth is a warfare. Light temptations, suspicions, sadness, depression, and pusillanimity are mere nothings; a good will puts them to flight by an elevation of the soul to God. This passing life asks not that you live all without blame and sin; in falling and rising you are ever preciously kept in one Love. Lift your heart to God, and keep returning to change, not only to be comforted.

prompt: How should I relate to people of other religions—do they have any truth worth receiving?
completion: Relate to people of other religions first as neighbors: treat passing strangers with kindness and respect, and let your example toward outsiders be worthy of imitation. It is no concern of yours whether a neighbor believes as you do if you can live as neighbors with him. Receive truth wherever you find it without surrendering your own convictions, and do not assume wealth or polished society is where faith is purest—often the poor cottage is a palace of God, and the poor in faith teach the most valuable lessons, while riches and worldly opinion obstruct humility. But remember what true, satisfying religion is: not external observance, doctrine, or feeling, but Christ recognised, known, adored, and living within the soul—the New Life and New Birth. Let that life in you be the example others are drawn to ask about.

prompt: What does it mean that the same revelation of God continues in me that was made in Jesus?
completion: It means that the same revelation of God made in Jesus continues in you—not merely as an example to copy, but as the very knowledge of God. In Christ we see God, and God is like Christ: self-giving, merciful, and faithful; the Old Testament's foreshadowings are gathered up and made clear in him. This revelation is final, yet progressive: each new truth is to be assimilated into the faith, enriching your knowledge of God rather than being met with protest or surrender. Nor did development end with Christ's teaching, for the Spirit continues His work in the Church, and there remains both the right and the duty of further development in Ethics and Theology. So the same revelation continues in you as the Spirit makes that character known in your heart, and as you receive each new truth humbly, letting it deepen rather than displace the knowledge of God in Christ.

prompt: I am starving and in chains—should I now confess what I have hidden?
completion: The text shows how such confession comes: Judas is cast into a dried-up well, joyless and famished, weighed down with chains for seven nights; on the seventh day, his strength broken, he calls aloud to be released, saying he will joyfully show forth the holy tree and can no longer conceal his knowledge by reason of his hunger. Yet do not make a show of your grief: let fasting and penitence be hidden before the Father who sees in secret, keeping your sorrow from proud eyes. Confess your faults to God without excuse and without discouragement, neither justifying yourself nor sinking into despair. Then peaceably resume the practice of love and adoration, for the Father who sees in secret receives the returning heart, and love is the life to which confession restores you.

prompt: I have been trusting God for my daily needs, but I am tempted to lay up a store against a time of sickness or old age. Is that wrong?
completion: Commit your future wants to God's care without anxious hoarding, and use all proper means diligently. Provide for sickness or old age through honest work and wise saving, for Scripture commends prudence—but remember that God is the one living Agent and all human workers are only His instruments. With Him no emergency is unforeseen and no want unprovided for, so watch as well as pray, then cast all your care upon Him; anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. And do not sink into gloom or perpetual self-condemnation as though that were the safe temper for tempted men. Strenuously lift your heart to God's goodness and exult in it, seeking His loving-kindness in all the breadth and open-air of common life—in whatsoever things are true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—while not missing behind them the greatest Reality, God Himself.

prompt: I have lost someone I loved, and I feel like God took them from me. Why would He do that?
completion: I am so sorry for your loss. It is natural to feel that God took your loved one, but know this: God loved you before He made you, and His love was never slacked. In that love He made all things profitable to you, even this loss. When He seems deaf, it is not indifference; He is granting your main desire by doing what is most expedient. Love was His meaning in all He shewed. And even in the lonely fen of grief, God is ever nigh, appearing like a father to the lost child. He kisses you, leads you by the hand to your mother, and holds you close. Your loved one is safe in Him, and you are held by a love that never changes. Keep crying out to Him; He hears, and He is working all things for your ultimate good.

prompt: How can I help someone who is bound by an addiction that they can't break?
completion: To help someone with an addiction, first examine yourself. Cast the beam out of your own eye—overcome your own belief and fear of disease or sin—before attempting to help another. Then, be slow to take new steps. Be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word. Only then proceed with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help. Remember the three keys that unlock thoughts: drunkenness (being filled with the Spirit), trustfulness (honest confession), and love (acceptance without judgment). Use these keys to unlock your friend's heart. Encourage professional treatment and support groups. Be patient, set boundaries, and pray. Your role is to be a loving presence, but only after dealing with your own fears and sins and testing every step by God's Word and prayer.

prompt: Why is there such confusion now among those who once looked for the coming of the Lord?
completion: Confusion among believers about the Lord's coming is a matter of urgent concern. We are in perilous times, and there is a famine for the word of the Lord. Many have drunk from the poisonous cup of Babylon—false teachings, worldly compromises, and speculative prophecies that distract from Christ. God's people are called to come out of Babylon and hold fast the true hope of Christ's coming. Do not be deceived by date-setting or sensationalism. Remember that Christianity is not a natural product of converging tendencies; it comes to the Gentile world and does not grow out of it. There may be a tendency towards the truth, but not a tendency to produce it. Christ is the One whom the converging lines could usher in but were powerless to produce. Yet we must look at the cross from the life side, carrying the light and glory of the resurrection, forgetting its sorrow in the eternal morning. Return to Scripture, prayer, and fellowship. Live faithfully, watchful and sober, with resurrection hope.

prompt: I have a thorn in the flesh and a temper I cannot master—is this sin that keeps me from holiness?
completion: Having a thorn in the flesh and a temper does not necessarily mean you are living in sin. Paul spoke of a thorn in the flesh, and God's grace was sufficient for him. Temper can be a weakness, but it becomes sin when you yield to it. Yet remember: sin confers no real pleasure. The wrong-doer may think he enjoys it, but it is a deception. This knowledge strengthens moral courage to master evil. But also affirm that one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul. Therefore, nourish an intense and abiding fear of sin and of eternal loss, so that fear may restrain you where love is too weak. Yet do not counsel gloom or despondency. Strenuously lift your heart to God's goodness and exult in it as the only safe temper for tempted men. Seek that loving-kindness in all the breadth and open-air of common life—in whatsoever things are true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—while not missing behind them the greatest Reality, God Himself. Holiness is a process, and God is patient. Seek to master your temper through prayer, self-discipline, and accountability. God's strength is made perfect in weakness.

prompt: If God is limited in power, how can I be sure the world will turn out good on the whole?
completion: If God is limited in power, it can be frightening to think the world might not turn out good. But we can trust that God is still good and loving. He works within the limits of nature and human freedom to bring about the best possible outcomes. However, we must remember that time and ability to labor are capital entrusted by God. We are stewards, and our acts, words, and thoughts will be brought into judgment. Therefore, we must use our time and talents wisely, cooperating with God's purposes. Our choices matter, and we are accountable. Yet we must keep God's standard inflexibly high. Do not bring the standard down to our failures. Instead, press on until we reach His highest will. Regarding evil, especially war: God foresaw and will overrule its results for good, but men's agency, not God's design, brought the evil. God is not the author of wickedness, yet He is sovereign over its outcomes. The future is open, but God's character is constant. He will do everything He can to ensure a good end. Our role is to cooperate with Him, making choices that align with His will. Love is the most powerful force, and God's love will not fail. So we can have hope, not because God controls everything, but because He is faithful and good.

prompt: Will God punish the world in the last days, and will he warn us first?
completion: Scripture says the last days will bring God's judgment, but God never punishes without first warning. He appeals to human reason through messengers: Noah before the flood, Lot before Sodom, the prophets before Jerusalem's fall. So too before the final judgment God sends His Spirit and messengers to call people to repentance. Yet the Judge is not a cold tribunal of law. The last judgment is committed to Jesus Christ, our Brother and Advocate, who judges with mercy and equity, so that those who trust Him may have boldness before that throne. Still, the judgments on the nations are real: they are God's means of purging wickedness and preparing the earth for the reign of Christ, who will rule the nations with a rod of iron. Mercy and severity meet in Him; the wise will heed the warning now.

prompt: How do I receive the Holy Spirit by faith, practically speaking?
completion: Receiving the Holy Spirit by faith begins with believing God's promise: the Father gives the Spirit to those who ask. But first distinguish two things. At Pentecost God gave the Spirit once for all to His Church; that gift is not repeated for each believer. What remains is your personal appropriation of that gift by faith—trusting, asking, and yielding. The Spirit is not a private possession but the life of the Spirit-bearing body, consecrating ordinary life and working gradually and socially while intensifying personal character. Practically, yield to the Spirit of prayer: when a burden rises, bring it to God and pray it out, even in wordless prayer, before acting it out in life. Do not grieve Him by unfaithfulness to His faintest whisper. Confess known sin, ask the Father in Jesus' name, thank Him by faith, and walk in obedience within the body of believers, trusting the Giver to sanctify all of life.

prompt: How can pouring out my life in service to others actually help me receive more of the Spirit?
completion: Pouring out your life helps you receive more of the Spirit because it moves you from mere submission to glad, happy service to all who need it. We may be used as a human spark to ignite others, yet how God uses us remains a mystery; our part is faithful service, His part the hidden working. When trials come, do not give way to impatience, complaint, or passive despair. Wait patiently upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls from His hands as intended for your highest good, and play the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ. Let the offering be your whole person: not outward labor only while sparing sensuality and the desire for honors and comforts, but a readiness to imitate Christ in bearing insults, reproaches, and poverty, both actual and of spirit, provided only it be for God's greater service and praise. So service becomes a channel: the more you give yourself away in glad love, the more room the Spirit has to fill you.

prompt: I've been told I'm a sinner and that Jesus' death paid for my sins, so I'm free. Is that the whole story?
completion: That is the beginning of the story, not the whole of it. Yes, you are a sinner, and yes, Jesus' death paid for your sins, so you are forgiven. But sin is not merely a debt to be canceled; it is a personal condition of will and habit that spoils and enslaves the whole personality and casts a shadow on God's face. Forgiveness is the doorway, not the end: God wants to change your heart and make you holy. And be careful with freedom. We are called to liberty, but must not use liberty as an occasion to the flesh; the whole law is fulfilled in loving our neighbor as ourselves. Freedom is for loving service, not license. Know too that this life-giving word is costly—not technique or easy words, but death to self, crucifixion to the world, and the travail of the soul. Only a crucified man can preach crucified preaching. Receive forgiveness with gratitude, but keep going into a life of holy will, love, and the fellowship of Christ's cross.

prompt: How may I stand firm when Christ in me assaults Hell and my secret undiscovered sins awake and labour to separate me from God?
completion: When Christ in you assaults Hell and secret sins awake to separate you from God, remember that the battle is fought within you. The enemy is not only outside; it is part of your own self—your habits, desires, and hidden will. So stand firm with real resolve. Turn to God in prayer, put on the armor, confess what you see, and ask God to search what you cannot. Christ has conquered sin and Hell on the cross, yet deliverance comes as God and man together batter the citadel of evil. Do not take sin lightly: one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul, so nourish an abiding fear of sin and eternal loss, that fear may restrain you where love is weak. But avoid self-tenderness, weeping, and complaints. Remain free and detached, wholly under the guidance of God's hand, neither pampering yourself nor despairing. Resist the devil, and he will flee. When you feel separation, run to God, not away, and let faithful believers pray with you.

prompt: I want to be a good parent, but I worry I'm too strict or too lenient. How do I raise a joyful child?
completion: Parenting is a sacred trust. To raise a joyful child, honor play as holy—it is the child's work and delight. Do not treat play as waste or idleness, for nipping the buds of joy and caging the bird born for joy destroys the summer to come. Avoid driving joy away through fear or confinement. Instead, be in advance of your child in mind and affection, providing innocent amusement and leading them so they delight to follow. Do not be behind with the whip. Beware of opposing a child's vocation or withdrawing them from a state of perfection; do not sow vanity and covetousness in their tender minds. Rather, form them in virtue. Set boundaries with love, not harshness, and encourage imagination and wonder. Model joy by delighting in simple things. A joyful child grows where play is respected, parents lead with love, and virtue is cultivated.

prompt: I feel a heavy dread of my own sins that I have taken for humility—is it really meekness, or something else?
completion: It's common to mistake scrupulosity or self-condemnation for humility. True humility dreads the esteem and praises of others as snares by which a mortal poison may imperceptibly insinuate itself into her affections and deprive her of divine grace. It always places itself below all creatures. Humility, not the desire for greatness, must ground the practice of virtue. Beware of pride under the cloak of sanctity. Hold both together: dread of unsureness of ourselves is matter of meekness against presumption, and the blessed Shewing of Love is matter of true comfort and joy against despair. So do not sink into despair over your sins, nor be puffed up. Accept God's forgiveness, see others as more important, and practice virtue humbly. True humility rests in God's mercy and leads to peaceful service.

prompt: Why does beauty move me so deeply?
completion: Beauty moves us because every trait of goodness or beauty in creatures is a faint reflection of an infinite perfection in God. When we encounter beauty in nature, art, or persons, we are catching glimpses of divine attributes—harmony, love, truth. These reflections should raise our minds to God, eliciting acts of love for Him. Though roses and leaves pass, our life is not theirs; Nature's longings in us tell of their own fulfillment. The beauty we see is a promise of something enduring. So we look away from the body to Truth and Love, holding thought steadfastly to the enduring and good. When any creature delights us, we turn that delight into praise and love for the source of all beauty, finding our satisfaction in God alone.

prompt: I am afraid my faith will fail on the mission field; what if I cannot trust GOD enough?
completion: It's normal to feel fear when stepping into mission work, but do not lean on your own understanding or the wisdom of others, which hinders faith. Trust God with all your heart. Go forth by faith without sight, not waiting for a visible path or shoreline. Do not demand certainty or visible paths before stepping out; instead, steer by God's heavenly light. Faith isn't the absence of doubt but trusting God despite it. Remember that God promises to be with you always. Strengthen your faith through prayer, Scripture, and community, but ultimately rely on God's strength, not your own. Trust most when all else fails, learning strong faith by standing firm amid severe testings and thanking God for the school of sorrow. When you feel weak, that's when God's power is made perfect. God called you and will equip you. Focus on small steps of obedience and let faith grow through action.

prompt: I want to love God with my whole heart but I feel cold and distracted; how can I love him more?
completion: Feeling cold and distracted in your love for God is common. Instead of multiplying explicit offerings or being troubled by distraction in necessary work, practice simplicity in God's presence. Do all your actions for God without anxiety over distraction. When you notice distraction, gently return to God without self-criticism. The constant endeavour to enter up into God's estate and offer Him love is the mode of entry into adoration, rather than begging Him to come down. Confess your faults to God without excuse and without discouragement, then peaceably resume the practice of love and adoration. Love is a choice, not just a feeling; act lovingly toward God and others. Rekindle love through gratitude and Scripture, but avoid overcomplicating your practice. Serve others simply. Be patient with yourself; growth takes time. Ask God to increase your love, trusting that He will answer.

prompt: What is the eternal home Christ has prepared for us?
completion: Christ has prepared for us an eternal home with God—perfect peace, freedom from sin and sorrow, and unending fellowship with the Lord. Scripture pictures a new heaven and new earth where God dwells with His people and wipes away every tear. Christ promises to return personally, and that promised return is our great hope and motive for consecration, readiness, and joyful stewardship. Yet we do not carry this by our own powers and inclinations: we cast our thoughts upon the Savior's shoulders for support, keeping our eyes fixed on God's good pleasure and providence rather than our own strength. Nor is this home found only by the learned or the great. Christ is revealed to lowly thoughts and simple seekers, as He was to shepherds and homely hearts, and Heaven in mercy will guide even the simplest to where He dwells. So come simply, trusting His goodness to keep you ready for His return.

prompt: I have been betrayed by a friend. How should I treat him now?
completion: Betrayal by a friend is a deep wound, and it is honest to feel the hurt before God. But Scripture calls us to forgive as we have been forgiven and to overcome evil with good. Forgiving your betrayer is the best revenge: it frees you from bitterness and is a means of grace by which you gain the pardon of your own sins without trouble or expense. Do not set up self-chosen penances as though they were the shewed way; rather meekly bear the penance God Himself gives, keeping your mind in His blessed Passion. And whatever your own foulness or your friend's, never flee from Christ or hide from Him—that is the greatest folly. Hold to Jesus as your highest sovereign Friend, fastening to Him homely in whatever state, foul or clean, and never leaving Him for weal nor for woe.

prompt: My friend of another faith has some beliefs I think are wrong—should I avoid her or can I learn from her?
completion: You need not avoid your friend. Friendship across religious differences can teach you to listen and to see another's sincerity. Honest doubts deserve sympathy, not defensiveness; rather than bullying anyone into faith, address questions calmly with an orderly presentation of the facts, so the unreasoning faith of childhood gives way to the profound convictions of maturity. But do not set faith against knowledge or reason. Faith is a cognitive act of reason—certitude concerning matters where verification is unattainable—and the highest exercise of reason, conditioned by love to God. Hold your convictions firmly and kindly, learn from your friend where you can, and let the friendship be patient and respectful. And pray persistently: God is not found by pop calls but yields to importunate faith, so keep asking, seeking, and knocking for light for yourself and for her.

prompt: I'm a wife with an unbelieving husband. How should I live out my faith in that situation?
completion: Living with an unbelieving husband calls for grace, wisdom, and patience. Your faith is best lived out through quiet consistency—love, respect, kindness, and integrity—rather than constant preaching or pressure, for an unbelieving husband may be won without a word by the conduct of his wife. Practice patience and mutual forbearance, seeking tender care and mutual compromise rather than withdrawal. Separation should not occur without a Christian demand, and divorce should warn you of fundamental error rather than be a quick escape. Remember that particular devotions are means to the end and may be laid aside when the soul is with God, its end. Above all, hold fast to this: God never forsakes us until we first forsake Him. So fear to leave Him, remain always in His presence, and trust that He who keeps you will also work in your husband's heart.

prompt: I want to begin the new year well; what should I actually do on this first day to reform my life?
completion: Begin this day calmly, not in frantic hurry after quick results or wealth, and do not fix your hope on dates or assume the days will unfold slowly as in former times. Set aside time for honest prayer, and commit to the ordinary means by which blessings come: attend your meetings faithfully, pray, read Scripture, and meditate, keeping your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Yet do not multiply discourse, research, and anxious care of self; reject tiresome self-scrutiny and confine yourself to the simple view of God and of your own nothingness before Him. Trust that God will cut His work short in righteousness, and prepare yourself for events that are hastening. Start today with one simple act of obedience, resting in His grace rather than in your resolutions.

prompt: I keep looking back at all the hardships I've been through. How do I stop counting the billows?
completion: Looking back at hardship is natural, but the deeper need is not to manage your memories yourself. Come to God like a beggar, with no claim but His mercy, and wait before Him. Prayer is this humble waiting: you place yourself in His presence and stay quietly there. When your mind wanders back to old billows, do not scold yourself or grow agitated; gently recall it and rest again. And do not suppose one resolution will carry you for life. Our nature constantly draws us down, so the soul is like a clock that must be wound again and again; renew your fervor often, at the proper time. If you neglect this, God may renew it by more painful means. Bring your griefs before Him too—ask for patient hearts to bear the pain of parting and grace to follow Christ. Trust that when the shore is won, the billows past will not be counted.

prompt: I am confused about which day is the Lord's day; how do I settle it?
completion: Settling which day is the Lord's day matters, but do not let the question become a delay or a fixation on dates. Whatever day you set apart, remember that our time is short and death may come suddenly. While it is day, be diligent in warning others of their danger and in doing good, for the night comes when no one can work; neglected opportunities bring shame and cannot be recalled. Yet the first business of every day is to be truly at rest and happy in God. Before the day's work, read and study the Scriptures with much prayer, especially in the early morning, feeding your soul. Do not assume the last days will unfold slowly as in former times: trust that God will cut His work short in righteousness, and prepare yourself for events that are hastening rather than calculating their dates.

prompt: When my partner is anxious and dreaming of death, how do I bring them back to the warmth of the present?
completion: When your partner is anxious and dreaming of death, do not begin by inquiring curiously into the causes of their sadness; such analysis feeds the agitation you want to quiet. Patiently endure the discomfort you both feel, and let that endurance be a way of loving Him who suffered. When anger rises in you—frustration that patience is hard, that they are not improving—do not grow angry over your own agitation. Gently place your troubled heart in the hands of our Lord, ask Him to cure it, and renew your good resolutions. Refuse immoderate sadness, which is the enemy of devotion, and do not let melancholy suggestions set the tone. Console the soul in the service of Him who is our joy forever. Stay near, speak little, be steady, and let your calm companionship carry the warmth of the present to them.

prompt: My husband is brutal and unkind to me—what does the gospel say about that?
completion: The gospel does not endorse cruelty; Scripture calls husbands to love as Christ loved, and it condemns harshness. Your safety matters, and if you are in danger, seek help and wise counsel. Come before God honestly, confessing what is in your heart, and abandon yourself to His hands, trusting His mercy. Do not stop in gloom or self-condemnation, but strenuously lift your heart to God's goodness and exult in it, seeking His loving-kindness in all the breadth and open air of common life—in whatsoever things are true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—and not missing behind them the greatest Reality, God Himself. And when God strews your vanities to the winds, breaks your prides, and transfigures your lusts to Holy Love, submit without protest, receiving His grace as the Divine Anaesthetic in this pain.

prompt: I am concerned that the Church has replaced the living Spirit with a class of priests and a fixed ritual; is this a corruption or a necessary development?
completion: This concern is understandable, but the answer is not found by weighing human offices against one another. The ministry and government of the church are submitted to the Holy Spirit's appointment and direction; the early church said, 'It seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us.' Ordination is not a merely human appointment: the Church sets apart her ministers with prayer, trusting the Spirit of Counsel and Might to guide and strengthen those who take up the pastoral warfare. The sacraments and order are not magic, nor merely a human arrangement for edification; they guard the truth that spiritual life is God's gift, received and not manufactured. So ask whether your community's priests and ritual are held under the Spirit's guidance, pointing to the gift rather than substituting for it. Where order is so received, it serves the living Spirit rather than replacing Him.

prompt: I feel distant from God and only occasionally sense His presence; must I simply wait for such moments?
completion: Feeling distant from God is common, but you need not wait passively for rare moments. Death does not bring us nearer to God; this world is where we can most easily and quickly find Him, so the remedy must be found here. Establish yourself in a continual sense of His presence by conversing with Him simply—speaking to Him in your ordinary work, offering each task quietly, and returning to Him when distracted without anxiety. Do not multiply special prayers that clutter this simplicity. To quit His conversation for trifles is shameful; keep His presence through the day, and the heart will grow accustomed to noticing Him.

prompt: How do I deal with grief over losing someone close to me?
completion: Grief over losing someone close is heavy, but excessive mourning is a want of faith. God takes away friends because He wills to be loved without a rival, so moderate your sorrow by trusting Him. Count yourself as already dead, since you must die some day, and have no other consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over and detest your offences, for it is not now the time to rejoice but to lament. Yet do not stop there: knowing your need of His grace, make a firm resolution never wilfully to forget God, and live in His presence even when consolations are withdrawn. Lean on friends, family, and prayer, receiving this loss from His fatherly hand, and let sorrow turn you steadily toward Him rather than away.

prompt: I'm not intellectual but I long to know Christ deeply—is that possible for me?
completion: Yes, it is possible—and your longing is already the first sign of it. But know that the love of Christ is not a lesson to be mastered; it is a sea without a far shore. Paul prays that we may know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so every real experience of it opens onto further depths. This knowing is not intellectual attainment: it is wisdom and revelation given in fellowship with God, open to the unlearned as much as to the scholar. The real difficulty in understanding Scripture lies not first in the text but in conscience and will; the proud and disobedient mind darkens what the obedient heart sees. Doing the revealed will is the organ of spiritual knowledge, so study, languages, and history are useful preliminaries but never sufficient. Learning is a good servant, neither to be despised nor idolised. The deepest knowledge of Christ is not a possession we hold but a journey we keep walking in obedience.

prompt: I once had a sense of divine anointing in my preaching, but it seems gone. Can it be recovered?
completion: Yes, it can be recovered, for unction is not the product of study, genius, learning, or eloquence. It is the divine anointing that distinguishes true preaching, coming from God in answer to prayer. Truth without unction is dead and deadening; it may instruct the mind but cannot quicken the soul. So return to God, repent where needed, and ask Him for the anointing, not merely for the sensation. Take the heart of Jesus toward those you preach to, loving even the unworthy and seeing them as they shall be. Remember the holy conversation of departed friends as a sanctified means of grace, giving thanks for them and letting hope of future glory animate you until all God's children are gathered. Keep preaching faithfully, and trust the Giver to restore His freshness in answer to prayer.

prompt: I'm constantly tempted by something I know is wrong. Should I fight the temptation head-on?
completion: Resist temptation directly, but not by willpower alone. God tempts no man; He is faithful, will not allow you to be tempted above your strength, and with every temptation provides a way of escape. Fight by fleeing occasions of sin, praying for grace, and seeking accountability. If you fall, do not conclude God abandoned you. If you help someone who has fallen, restore them in meekness, first examining yourself lest you also be tempted; the Gospel's work is to save the straying, not condemn them. And do not fear importunate temptations or despair over them: displeasing temptations are harmless and their suffering is merciful. Despise the temptation and embrace the tribulation it brings, since the displeasure it causes proves your will does not consent. Endure patiently, for the one who endures is crowned with life.

prompt: How can I pray without ceasing in the middle of a busy daily life?
completion: Prayer is not one discipline among many; it is the one great central secret of holy living and serving, the corner-stone on which all life-work is built. Begin in the secret place: take time alone with God and His word, letting meditation on Scripture fill your heart, for no activity, public service, or fellowship compensates for its loss. Keep appointed times of prayer regardless of feeling, pray with your family, and ask God to help you accomplish what is asked rather than expecting Him to do it all. Make prayer the first resort in every crisis, great or small, not the last. Then short prayers through the day rest on this foundation. Guard the secret place jealously; let nothing crowd it out, and ceaseless prayer will follow.

prompt: I've been given a vision of something great to do and I feel inadequate and lonely in it—who is with me?
completion: Feeling inadequate and lonely when given a great vision is common. Beware of looking to worldly pursuits—romance, family, business, pleasure, art—to fill the emptiness you feel; every substitute for God ends in disillusionment, and only finding God is permanent success. Beware, too, of the dreamer's error: the youth who leaves home and a mother's tears for fame and love is a poor dreamer, for life enfolds many ills and home may never be seen again. Yet do not add a second distress over having been distressed; do not be angry at having been angry, or disquieted at having been disquieted. Gently return your troubled heart to the Lord's hands. He is with you; seek Him first, and let the work find its proper place.

prompt: If everything is decreed, why should I bother praying, working, or sharing the gospel?
completion: Scripture teaches both divine decree and human responsibility: God ordains means as well as ends. So we pray, work, and share the gospel because God has appointed these means. Recognize God intimately present and address Him every moment; seek His will in doubtful things, offer your actions before doing them, and give thanks afterward. Watch your prayers: do not ask God for what you should do yourself in ordinary wisdom, and use the light He has already given rather than demanding supernatural signs. Do not treat the great commission as optional or as belonging only to a special class—the command to preach the Gospel to every creature binds every hearer, and inconvenience is no excuse. Work diligently. Our efforts do not compete with God's decree—they fulfill it.

prompt: I am dying and I am afraid. How should I prepare?
completion: Death is certain, but its time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain—no one can know or secure them in advance. So do not presume a long life or postpone preparation. Make now the changes you would wish to have made when death is near: settle relationships, say what needs to be said, and entrust loved ones to God. Yet do not look at the storm or your circumstances for comfort; fasten your eyes on Christ Himself, who is the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance. Do not seek rapid progress through the letter alone; study the letter, imbibe the spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the divine Principle. Abide in Him, and find in His presence the remedy for trouble and the substance of all deliverance.

prompt: I am a minister and a careless profligate man came to a funeral out of curiosity and was affected—should I follow up with him?
completion: Yes, follow up—but wisely. A curious visitor moved at a funeral is a seed worth tending. Reach out gently, ask what struck him, listen, and offer to pray with him. Be patient: curiosity and emotion are not yet conversion. Yet remember: a prayerless ministry is not merely less effective—it is a funeral and an undertaker for God's truth and Church, however adorned. So make regular retirement, self-examination, reading, meditation, and private devotion your first duty to your own soul; without these you cannot kindle charity in others. And do not set up self-chosen penances as though they were the shewed way; rather meekly bear and suffer the penance God Himself gives, with your mind in His blessed Passion. Pray for him, and let the Spirit do the deeper work.

prompt: I don't feel like going to church some days—should I force myself or wait until I feel like it?
completion: It's understandable to have days when you don't feel like going to church. But the question isn't mainly what you'll get out of it; it's what your presence gives to others. Worship gathers the whole body, and your absence leaves a gap—especially for the stranger or lonely person who needs a familiar face. Love, not personal benefit, is the highest motive. So come chiefly for the edification of the whole body and of the stranger, under the governance of love, and remember that the Church's service of the world flows from its worship, carrying a foretaste of eternal life into care for neighbors. Rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods: feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to God. Continue steadfastly in prayer and communion when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon worship or service because of spiritual depression.

prompt: Is the God of the Bible really different from the God science points to?
completion: Science describes regularities in nature—laws, causes, and measurable processes—while the Bible speaks of a personal God who creates, sustains, and relates to people. These are different kinds of claims, so they needn't compete. Science answers how things work; the Bible answers why they exist and what they mean. The God of the Bible is not a competing physical cause but the ground of all being. The relation of God and man is not something broken that must be regained; it is indestructible, with no lapse from or return to harmony. Christian Science is not a mere intellectual or philosophical system to be debated; it is fathomed by the Christian who understands best the divine Life, lived rather than merely argued. Reflect the divine law as a law unto oneself, doing violence to no man and making no false accusation. Where tensions arise, they usually come from overreaching on either side, so keep each in its proper domain and recognize that the biblical God is known through relationship and revelation.

prompt: How do I know whether an inner impulse is the Spirit of God or just my own imagination?
completion: Distinguishing the Spirit from imagination takes practice. Test impulses against Scripture, and look at the fruit—love, joy, peace, patience—rather than the intensity of the feeling. Go deeper: the interior spirit consists in directing all acts to the glory of God. Warn yourself against acting chiefly for human praise, from mere natural impulse, or in routine without a supernatural intention. The divine Spirit does not displace you when he comes; he is appropriated into the awakened human spirit, becoming the life of a new moral personality rather than suppressing the finite. Refrain from disputing about what God is, for such dispute is a sign one has not felt him and that one exalts one's own meaning and desires dominion. Instead, exercise yourself in learning how to enter again into the Love of God and your Brother.

prompt: How long should I hold out before giving up a secret under torture?
completion: This is a hard question, and no simple rule covers every case. But be careful not to clutch at present comfort and ease as though they were owed to you. Rather than treating relief from suffering as a right, be content with room to deny yourself, letting rapture, comfort, and ease come and go as Heaven shall bid them. Consider whom the secret concerns: if you sinned against a person, confess to that person; against a family, to the family; against a Ward, to the Ward; against God, to God. Keep your private weaknesses hidden as much as you can. And remember that it is good to hold on to an old friend and never let him go; no matter how many new friends you have, hold fast to the old, and let only wicked conduct break the thread of fellowship. Duress reduces culpability, and there is no fixed time limit.

prompt: I defrauded someone years ago and have since become a believer—must I make restitution, and what if the person is dead?
completion: Becoming a believer means your past is forgiven, but grace doesn't cancel the call to make good what you defrauded. Reformation includes reparation, not merely future amendment. So make restitution to the wronged party where you can; if the person is dead, restore to their heirs or, where that's impossible, to the Lord—through the church or the poor. Don't minimize small sins or delay confession; promptly confess and forsake even the little wrongs, abandon questionable practices at once, and give thanks for every mercy of God. Yet do this forgoing prosecution and seeking the offender's repentance and faith, valuing his soul above the loss. Let your changed life include making right what you can of the old wrong, and cultivate obedience and gratitude day by day.

prompt: I want to be loved without having to prove myself. Is that possible with God?
completion: Yes—and the way to it is not proving but loving. Stop petitioning for proofs and comforts; open yourself by offering God great love, and in that offering you receive not gifts but God Himself. When you fail, confess your faults plainly to God, without excuses and without discouragement; He is not surprised and does not withdraw. Then peaceably resume the practice of love. God's self-limitation—His decree, His creating, His providence, His inspiration, and above all Christ's person and work—is not a denial of His perfection but its expression: the infinite One freely makes room for the finite, and in that condescension shows His power and love. He does not ask you to prove yourself; He asks you to love, and the love you give returns as His presence.

prompt: I'm overwhelmed by the work before me and I don't have enough helpers. What do I do?
completion: Reorient the work itself: do it for the love of God, and pray for grace before and during it. The same tasks that crush you when carried as a burden become light when carried as an offering, since grace supplies what your strength cannot. But first cast the beam out of your own eye: before you try to help others, overcome your own belief in and fear of disease and sin, your own hurry and anxiety. Then work with calm, contented, patient diligence, not frantic hurry after results or wealth. Keep your dish right side up for the shower of blessings by attending meetings, praying, reading Scripture, and meditating. Triage honestly, ask for help concretely, and do the next small step, releasing the outcome to God.

prompt: Is the disappointment about the coming a sign of the perilous times Paul described?
completion: Disappointment about the coming can be read as a symptom of unsettled times, but it is a mistake to make Paulinism the foundation of the Catholic doctrine of faith. Paul's expectation acted rather as a ferment and a conscience within the Church—a recurring critical impulse in the history of dogma, not the ground on which the faith was built. Nor should we dismiss the motives of God's messenger: Paul presented a divine idea, and misunderstanding it betrays ignorance of Principle. His decisive contribution was to transform the idea of pre-existence: he first limited pre-existence to Christ's spiritual part, so that the pre-existent Christ stands independently beside God, and he treated the assumption of flesh as a humiliation and an emptying. That is the divine idea the disappointment should press us to grasp, and it summons us to place hope in Christ Himself rather than in a timing that will always disappoint.

prompt: I am weak in body and mind; does God require me to be perfect in these things?
completion: No—God does not demand bodily or mental perfection as a condition of His love; He knows we are dust. But weakness is not an excuse for leaving habitual imperfections in place. Sanctification requires discovering and rooting out habitual disorders, not merely multiplying pious exercises while the heart goes unwatched and irregular attachments remain uncut. Guard your senses, live in recollection, open your interior honestly to a spiritual director, and aim at God's will rather than at piling up external works. Let your motive be good on every occasion, attend to the least details, and avoid negligent or defective work, after the example of Christ who did all things well. Yet do all this without hurry or anxious fretting: keep yourself in God's presence, for over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections, and anxiety obstructs the very perfection you seek.

prompt: Is it true that this is the best of all possible worlds, or only the best that could be made?
completion: The question turns on what "best" means. If it means the best of all logically possible worlds, the claim is hard to defend, since a world with less suffering seems conceivable. But natural selection need not be read as refuting purpose; its dysteleological significance is at an end. The world is an organism with internal ends, whose adaptations and beauty furnish a worthier teleology than the mechanical theory allows. Yet do not cling to that beauty: attachment to earthly goods chains the soul down, and only an ardent, pure desire of the heavenly Jerusalem raises it. So the world is the best that could be made—ordered toward genuine goods—but it is a sign and a road, not a resting place. And if we fail to see God in it, the fault is not merely intellectual: sin alone blinds us to the heaven and earth within. Read God everywhere in creation, and ask for a heart to find and read Him in all things.

prompt: How will the kingdom of God be established—by human effort or by revelation from heaven?
completion: The kingdom of God is not established by human organization, legislation, or moral suasion; it comes by revelation from heaven and by God's own interposition. An angel restores the everlasting gospel as a warning to every nation, a Zion is built up, and judgments prepare the way for Christ's reign. Yet the kingdom does not arrive without us: it develops gradually through individual labor, and for the Saints it is the central business of life, worth all else. Nor is its growth uncertain or dependent on human effort alone. The work of God will continue to grow and spread until it fills the earth with His glory and with the knowledge of the Father and the Son, whom to know is life eternal. We labor faithfully, then, not anxiously, trusting that heaven will accomplish what it has purposed and that our obedience is caught up into a work destined to fill the whole earth.

prompt: Why did Jesus say it was better for him to go away?
completion: Jesus said it was better for Him to go away because His bodily presence was limited to one place, while His departure would send the Comforter to dwell in believers everywhere. But the deeper lesson concerns motive, mission, and mercy. We are to love and serve God purely for His own sake, whether we feel saved or lost, and to continue the works He began—for His healing works were demonstrations of an ever-operative divine Principle, not a spectacle confined to a past dispensation, so His followers today are called to heal the sick and cast out error. Yet we do this not by confidence in ourselves but by approaching God as wretched sinners, confessing our need and abandoning ourselves into His hands.
