That honest surrender is met by His merciful embrace. His going away, then, was not abandonment but the opening of a way for the contrite heart to draw near and find mercy.

prompt: I feel too proud to kneel at the manger—how do I cultivate humility this Christmas?
completion: Feeling too proud to kneel is itself a sign of where the work must begin, for pride is the beginning of all sin, its end, and its cause. Humility is not a technique for self-improvement, nor is it thinking poorly of yourself for its own sake; the practice of every virtue must be grounded in humility rather than in a desire for greatness or spiritual reputation. This Christmas, look steadily at the manger—the Creator of all things lying helpless in a feeding trough—and let that sight expose the pride that hides even under the cloak of sanctity. Do not rely on your own resolve, for that is self-esteem dressed as virtue; true courage is grounded in a low esteem of self, its greatness lying in humility rather than in confidence in its own powers. Imitate the saints, who saw their own imperfections clearly and counted themselves dust and worms. Serve, keep silence, ask forgiveness, and ask God for humility, for He gives grace to the humble.

prompt: I want to follow Jesus, but I don't know if his healing works are meant for today or just for his time.
completion: This is an honest question, but it cannot be settled by comparing doctrines from a distance—the real answer is a Person. Come into personal contact with the risen Saviour, not merely with opinions about Him; abide in Him continually, drawing His life into your being by the hunger and thirst of love and faith. Christianity is not mere belief, ritual, or admiration of Jesus' person. His healing works were demonstrations of an ever-operative divine Principle, not a spectacle confined to a past dispensation, so His followers today have the present duty to heal the sick and cast out error. And be assured: God can and does heal in answer to prayer today, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Pray boldly, trust His willingness and power, and leave the outcome in His hands, knowing He is faithful.

prompt: How may I come to know the essence and property of the Creatures, and should I eat of the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil to be as God?
completion: To know the essence and property of creatures, study them diligently—read good books, study reliable history, and learn everything upon the face of the earth, both good and its effects and evil and its consequences, without committing iniquity. But knowledge of evil must never become familiarity with it: keep proper ward over mortal mind, dwell on good, and exclude false beliefs as you would exclude thieves. Yet the deepest truth about every creature is that it is born of nothing, surrounded by nothingness, and tends to nothingness, depending each moment upon God for existence, preservation, power of action, and all it possesses. The Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil represents the attempt to become as God by our own grasp; we may know evil without practicing it, but we must not linger over it. Since every creature depends each moment on God, our life, thoughts, and works should be in Him, of Him, for Him, and directed to Him.

prompt: I see the same person who made the gentle things also made the terrifying ones. How do I make sense of that?
completion: It is tempting to call a truce built on mutual fear and selfish loves a real peace, but that is precisely where Cruelty's snare is knit: what looks like calm is only everyone watching everyone. The same human brain that breeds gentleness also breeds Cruelty, Humility, Mystery, and Deceit—not invaders from outside but growths from our own soil. Cruelty has a human heart and Jealousy a human face; the human heart can be a hungry gorge, and the human dress is forged iron. Do not hide this behind pleasant virtues. Yet the afflictive things are not simply wrath: Love can make an angel of them, and we may entertain that angel unawares. Refuse to baptize fear-built calm as peace; ask what in you is being cultivated. The gentle show what we might become, the terrifying what we become when fear and self-love knit their snare—and the affliction, met in love, may be the angel sent to free you.

prompt: I want to dread God rightly, but I do not know which of my dreads are good and which are wrong.
completion: Scripture and the saints speak of four dreads: servile dread of punishment, doubtful dread born of unbelief, natural dread of bodily harm, and reverent dread of God himself. Only reverent dread fully pleases God, because it flows from love. Far from harsh, it is full soft and sweet: the more it is had, the less it feels like dread, because the sweetness of love fills it. Love and reverent dread are brethren—two in property and working, yet inseparable—so whoever truly loves also dreads, though he feels it but a little. But do not stop there: join reverent dread with meek love and mighty trust, for the more mightily we trust, the more we please God, and without this dread and love no one may please Him. Examine your dreads, then: cultivate the soft one, heal the servile and doubtful, and let dread, meek love, and mighty trust worship God together.

prompt: Is excommunication ever right?
completion: Yes, excommunication can be right, and a pastor must not shrink from it out of false kindness. Scripture calls pastors to correct with firmness and, where needed, severity—not endless remonstrance that leaves the offender undisturbed. Persistent, public sin that refuses correction endangers both sinner and flock, and a shepherd too lenient with such offenders incurs condemnation. Yet the process matters: do not spread complaints about leaders abroad or sit in judgment on presiding officers from a distance. Take the grievance directly to the person involved, seek confession and reconciliation, and keep the matter from spreading. If repentance is refused, separation may follow, in hope of awakening and protecting the community. Remember that exaltation is proportioned to capacity and conduct, some presiding over more than others, and all proved through mortal experience—so firmness aims at repentance and restoration, with an open door for return.

prompt: I have prayed for money for a specific need and received nothing—should I tell my supporters?
completion: Be honest with your supporters, but remember that money for God's work must be obtained only in God's way. Do not ask unbelievers to fund it, do not press believers to give, and do not resort to entertainments or worldly schemes. Examine carefully any gift offered: refuse what comes from impure motives or from money that is not the giver's own. As for prayer, do not pray for riches—wealth is not a proper object of prayer; pray only for the means to keep yourself and your family from want. And do not answer an unmet need by hoarding a reserve for future want, which is a snare for one who professes to trust God. Live from day to day upon the Lord's bounty, making your one investment in His work and the poor. Speak to supporters as testimony and invitation to prayer, not pressure, letting your words show trust in God rather than clever appeals.

prompt: I don't know the mysteries of the Rosary well. Can I still gain the indulgences if I only contemplate one scene of the Passion?
completion: Yes—provided you say the Rosary with devotion and pauses, not in haste. Meditating on any one mystery of the Passion suffices to fulfill the devotion's intent, so you need not master every scene to gain the indulgence. What matters is that you pause and let the mystery sink in. Indeed, five devout decades are more pleasing to Mary than fifteen said in haste. So take a single scene and stay with it prayerfully. And do not stop at the minimum: commend assiduous holy reading and meditation, begun in tender years, as the way fervent devotion is nourished—Timothy's example of knowing the Scriptures from childhood. Above all, expect pardon without anxiety from the Blood of Jesus Christ while you endeavor to love Him; mortification without love cannot efface sin, but love joined to His Blood can. Let this one scene lead you into that love.

prompt: How can I trust Christ when everything around me is falling apart?
completion: It is natural to feel shaken when life unravels, but the hour of testing is exactly where faith is learned. Trust Christ most when all else fails—not because circumstances are easy, but because He is faithful when nothing else is. When you forget Him or falter, do not be disquieted; simply return with greater trust, since a lapse in remembrance is no reason for turmoil but a call to come back more firmly. Stand firm amid severe testing, and thank God even for the school of sorrow, which teaches reliance you could not learn in comfort. Remember that trusting God honors Him, and He is honored by the confidence of His children, drawing down great graces on those who rely on Him. Bring your fear honestly to Him, hold fast to His promises, and let the storm draw you closer rather than push you away.

prompt: I am a woman who has loved many men. Can I still be pure in God's eyes?
completion: Yes—and the first thing to know is that God looks upon you with love. He looks with love even upon the most terrible sinner who has any true desire to be converted, and that merciful regard is not something you must earn by cleaning yourself up first. Yet His love is not mere sentiment: it is a rational, voluntary self-communication that seeks your true good, and it is regulated by and subordinate to His holiness, so His mercy never flatters sin but heals it. If you have any real desire to be converted, that desire meets His loving look. Confess what needs confessing, seek healing and wise counsel, and trust His goodness. Remember too that this restoration is not yours alone: no one is exalted into God's presence alone, and the man is not without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord. You are not defined by the men you have loved, but by the God who loves you and calls you to new life with others.

prompt: I'm afraid our community will be destroyed by our enemies. What should we do?
completion: Fear is understandable, but the first enemy to face is within ourselves. Before we oppose error and evil around us, we must conquer ourselves and submit to the Father's will, since a heart not yet yielded cannot fight rightly. Guard your soul against bitterness, anger, hatred, envy, and malice, for these destroy a community from within more surely than any outside foe; instead be filled with the love of God, truth, and your fellowmen, doing good to all and keeping your covenants. Then oppose evil by persuasion, patience, and love unfeigned—never by violence and never by interfering with the agency of others. Above all, do not surrender courage, confidence, or good-will, for we should lose everything rather than these. Go on joyously when possible and always courageously and confidently, trusting God, caring for the vulnerable, and refusing to become what you oppose.

prompt: I'm a Christian, but I don't feel especially like Christ. Does that mean I'm not really a Christian?
completion: Feeling unlike Christ does not automatically mean you are not a Christian, but we should be careful what the name means. A Christian is one to whom Christ is Saviour and Lord, subject to Him—not a religious system or an earnest imitation of Jesus from a distance, but actual union with the Lord Jesus, who dwells in you as the life and source of all your experience and work. So the real question is not whether your feelings resemble Him today, but whether you are holding to His person rather than mere theories. And His presence is not only past or future: He says not 'I will be with you' but 'I am with you alway,' an unbroken presence with you forevermore. Rest in that living Christ now. Feelings fluctuate, and many faithful believers pass through dryness; what matters is turning to Him, confessing sin, and abiding in His present lordship.

prompt: Is Sunday worship really indispensable, or can I excuse myself when it's inconvenient or dangerous?
completion: The obligation of Sunday is not optional, and it should not be set aside on lame pretences or mere inconvenience. The martyrs kept it at the expense of their lives, and the true Christian is known by his manner of celebrating it. So honor the Sabbath, prepare for and partake of the sacrament worthily, and do not treat meetings carelessly. Yet faithfulness is not presumption: use appropriate means—medicine, food, prudent provision, and safe alternatives—with prayer and thanksgiving, rejecting both presumption and unbelief. If danger is real, seek safety wisely while keeping the day holy; where genuine impossibility exists, worship at home and long for the assembly. And do not limit worship to one day: continue worship and testimony every day, letting your whole life show whose you are.

prompt: I feel like God is far away and doesn't hear me. Is it Him or is it me?
completion: God is nearer than all else, speaking in your conscience and mind, yet He also speaks through Scripture, which is the foundation of our faith. But God does not will us to stop at the written word; He invites us into personal experience of Himself through inward meditation and pondering. When every worldly thing passes away, He remains to the soul that seeks Him early. Do not argue with the feeling of distance—that is the enemy's noise. Prostrate yourself before God and remain at His feet, refusing to engage temptation. In humility, cling to Him who is closer than your own breath. As you meditate on His word and listen in stillness, you will know His abiding presence, and the enemy's clamor will fade into nothing.

prompt: I want to grow from glory to glory; what does that mean for me?
completion: Growing from glory to glory means looking to the Father of glory as the source of all glory, yet it also means abiding in Christ and knowing Him as your purity, grace, and strength. Say with Paul, 'Not I, but Christ.' It is not by your own effort that you attain purity, but by resting in His indwelling. Embrace self-denial and economy as a joyful privilege that frees you to give more fully to the LORD, bringing fuller joy. As you yield to Him, He transforms you from one degree of glory to another, not for your boasting but for His praise. Find your rest in His presence, and let your growth be the fruit of His life in you.

prompt: I want to hold onto a memory of someone who made the world feel like a dream—how do I keep that when reality breaks in?
completion: The memory of that pure soul is a healing power that can transfigure your soiled soul and lift you above the troubled world. To keep it, allow no repose or slipping back in your spiritual ascent; go forward like a mountain-climber until the goal is reached, withdrawing from worldly distractions into the one unchangeable Good. Yet know that the old dreams of gods and heroic Greece are lovely and should be allowed to persist. The dreaming Muse, lovely in her sorrow, should be left to dream rather than roused by the jarring Truth, lest she die. So hold the memory gently, letting it heal and elevate you, while cherishing the dreamlike beauty that made the world feel like a dream. In this way, you honor both the ascent and the lovely dream.

prompt: Should I plant trees on my land when I may not live to harvest the lumber?
completion: Planting trees is good, but remember that those who do His commandments have right to the tree of life and enter through the gates into the city. Nothing that defiles, works abomination, or makes a lie shall enter it. As Elene swore, the lie shall be changed into utter destruction, and the deed cannot be concealed. Yet the exhortation in this Church and Kingdom is not prepare to die, but prepare to live. Teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. So plant trees as an act of faith in life, obeying God's commandments, and let your labor be for the living, that you and future generations may eat of the tree of life.

prompt: I want to know whether the Holy Spirit is a gift given to believers or a heavenly being distinct from the Father and the Son.
completion: The Holy Spirit is a divine Person, co-equal with the Father and the Son, not an impersonal influence. He is the Paraclete sent by Christ, who speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved. He is also the special gift of the Father, given according to God's discretion and our faithfulness, distributing gifts such as healing, discerning spirits, tongues, and prophecy variously to strengthen the faith of believers. Yet we must not treat imperfection in Scripture or the Church as disproving the Spirit's presence, for the Spirit works gradually. Allow for imperfection in the Old Testament and the Church without denying real inspiration. The Spirit's personal and gradual working in the Church is affirmed, and He brings all necessary things to remembrance.

prompt: I sit on questions of public policy and wonder whether public opinion or law can be trusted to reform abuses.
completion: Public opinion and law are unreliable if they are built on the false belief that evil can bring lasting pleasure or that material indulgence satisfies. True reform comes from an affection for good, which Science reveals as the only reality. When we understand that evil holds no abiding pleasure, we no longer trust in shifting opinions or corrupt laws to bring satisfaction. Instead, we align with the good that is God, and this alignment naturally corrects abuses. We uphold righteous government and the inspired Constitution, which protect religious liberty and oppose corrupt administrators of law. In seeking reform, we respect each person's right of self-government, influencing thought only to benefit, never to control. Law and opinion can serve as instruments of righteousness only when they reflect the good that Science unveils and honor the freedom of every conscience.

prompt: I'm afraid of suffering—how do I prepare for it?
completion: Before anything else, quiet your fear. Silently reassure yourself that you are exempt from disease and danger, for God's care surrounds you. Fear is not a reality but a false belief that would claim power over you. Refuse it as a lie and say with the psalmist, 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee.' Cast out fear and replace it with trust in God. As the testimonies show, fear must be overcome before healing appears. Begin by removing fear, and then you can prepare for suffering with a calm trust. Practical steps can follow, but they must not come first. The first step toward healing is to still the frightened thought and know that you are safe in God's love, trusting that He will never leave you and that goodness and mercy will follow you all the days of your life.

prompt: How do I distinguish between what is good and what is best in the choices before me?
completion: To distinguish between good and best, remember that to be great is to be good before the heavens and before all good men. Goodness sheds a halo of loveliness around every person who possesses it. The best choice is the one that most fully expresses good will, for good will in the soul is the source of all good and the mother of all virtues. He who possesses it possesses without fear of loss all he needs to live a good life. God rewards the good desired but not accomplished as though it had been performed, and merit lies in the will, upon which depends our future of Heaven or hell. So evaluate each option by whether it aligns with good will before God and before good people. In doing so, recognize that the Father is officially first, the Son second, and the Spirit third, while maintaining equality of essence and dignity. This order of office and operation helps us discern what is best.

prompt: I am a student of theology. Should I spend more time in the library or in the closet?
completion: For a theology student, the closet should be your primary study, for it is the heart's school where thought is born. More is learned about preaching in the closet than in libraries. The library can inform, but the closet transforms. In the secret place of prayer, you commune with God and receive the inspiration that gives life to your words. Make the closet your first priority, and let the library serve as a supplement. The heart's study is where true sermon thought is conceived and where you learn to speak from the overflow of your relationship with God. Yet remember that theology is a science: it discovers and systematizes objective facts about God and His relations to the universe. So study the facts in the library, but let the closet make them live. Measure your ability to stay with God outside the closet by your ability to stay with Him in it, and know that great waiting in the closet is the source of great victories in ministry.

prompt: I keep giving in to the same sin over and over. Is there any hope for me?
completion: Yes, there is hope. You can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose. God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender. Do not wait for a greater emotional experience or more tears. Simply choose to turn from sin now, and God will meet you with grace. The power to overcome is not in your feelings but in your decision to yield to God. As you surrender your will, He will begin to transform your desires. But remember: sin must be forsaken and destroyed, for God's pardon is the destruction of sin, not its toleration. So do not expect pardon while clinging to sin; rather, let the surrender be complete, and trust that God is faithful to forgive and cleanse you. And know that we should never cease learning: the author shall continue learning in the spirit-world and after the resurrection, and only those who commit the unpardonable sin cease to learn and begin to decrease. So press on in hope, for your growth in God is eternal.

prompt: How do I deal with the fear of losing my reputation if I pursue holiness?
completion: Your fear of losing reputation is itself a hindrance to be named and forsaken, not managed or quietly kept. Do not draw near to the blessing and then shrink back; obey the light you have now, by faith, and venture on Christ without delay, for delay grieves the Spirit. Yet this is no gloomy, monkish withdrawal into self. True holiness is inward fellowship with Christ that flows outward in practical love—serving your neighbor, doing good quietly, and living so as to help others and prepare the world for His appearing. And remember: God's pardon is the destruction of sin, not its toleration. The fear and the idol of reputation must be forsaken and put to death, not merely forgiven and retained. Take the step of obedience today, serving others as you go.

prompt: I'm struggling with a secret habit and I'm ashamed to tell anyone—can God help me in something no one else knows about?
completion: Yes, God sees and cares about what no one else knows, and He invites you to bring secret things into His light. Whoever would help you must first cast the beam out of his own eye, so seek help from those walking honestly before God. Do not let public prayer or Christian conversation substitute for secret communion; closet prayer is indispensable, and no public devotion makes up for it. Keep praying and reading the Word even when enjoyment is gone. Confess your faults to God without excuse and without discouragement—do not brood, and do not despair. Then peaceably resume the practice of love and adoration, returning to Him gently as a child to a father. His grace is sufficient, and He is gentle with those who come to Him.

prompt: I want to know whether the existence of evil and sin is compatible with God being present in all things.
completion: Evil and sin are real evils, never to be called good, and they can be accounted for only as necessary means to a greater good God brings about. Yet sickness, sin, and death are not things God created or sent. They are unreal errors presupposing the absence of Truth, Life, or Love, and no part of God's creation. God, who is good, cannot produce sickness or evil; He destroys them rather than sends them, and His omnipotence is limited only by His own nature. He is present in all things as the sustainer of all that truly exists, and because He is sovereign over evil, ordaining it to a good end He will finally reveal, the existence of evil is compatible with His universal presence. This is mystery, not contradiction, and it calls for humble trust.

prompt: Someone I love died suddenly. How should I think about my own death?
completion: I am sorry for your loss. The sudden death of someone you love rightly turns you toward your own death. Count yourself as already dead, since you must die some day, and have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over, regret, and detest your own offences and faults, for it is not now the time to rejoice but to lament with all sincerity of heart. Yet do not imagine that death itself frees from sin or confers life—it does not. Sin destroys itself, and God alone is man's life. Consider Mary's death: precious and joyful, free from earthly attachment, remorse, and uncertainty of salvation. Let her example lift your eyes, and let grief press you to repentance, humility, and hope in God, who is near to the brokenhearted.

prompt: I am a servant girl and my mistress does not care for religion—how do I keep the Lord's Day when I cannot attend worship?
completion: It is hard to keep the Lord's Day when your mistress does not share your faith, but the day is not optional and not for ordinary labor or pleasure. Keep it holy: set aside time for prayer and Scripture, early or late, and attend to its worship and duties as far as your circumstances allow. Avoid Mary's sanctuaries during times of feasting and excess, and help others avoid them too; visit them instead when they are not thronged. And in every occasion of virtue, turn to God and ask Him for enabling grace, receiving strength more than sufficient for the day. Do not rely on your own effort alone. Be respectful and diligent in your duties, let your faithfulness set an example, and trust that God sees your desire to honor Him.

prompt: I'm resentful toward someone who hurt me and I can't let it go—what does God ask of me?
completion: Your resentment is real to you, but divine Truth bids you reverse the belief of injury: man, made in God's image, is not truly hurt, and the harm you seem to suffer is a false claim about God's child. When the sense of injury returns, treat it as a lapse in remembering God—meet it without disquiet and return with greater trust, knowing God is All. Yet go further: God, in His promises to hear our prayers, is desirous to bestow Himself upon us. If you ask only for relief from resentment or for the offender to be set right, you ask something beneath Him and put an affront upon Him, hurting yourself by preferring to Him a creature which He framed. Ask instead for God Himself, and in receiving Him you will find the resentment dissolved, for nothing beneath Him can hold your heart once He fills it.

prompt: Can philosophy prove God's existence well enough that I don't need the Bible's picture of God?
completion: Philosophy can offer real arguments, but we must be careful about what they prove. The argument from the idea of a perfect or infinite Being does not establish that such a Being actually exists; ideas are not the measure of external reality, and this argument yields only an ideal conclusion—it tells us what God must be if He exists, not that He does. Real existence is grounded in the preceding arguments, and the infinity and perfection of that one Being are ascribed because our mental constitution will not allow us to think otherwise. The arguments from change and from order in nature are not worthless, but neither do they demonstrate a personal, infinite, and righteous Creator; at best they are cumulative probable evidence that corroborates the intuition of God, proving an indefinitely great cause and an intelligent will, and they need the anthropological argument to reach personality and righteousness. Yet do not conclude that theology is mere feeling or private opinion. Theology is a science: it discovers and systematizes objective facts about God and His relations to the universe, facts independent of the theologian's mental processes. So philosophy clears the ground, but the science of theology, grounded in revelation, gives you the God who actually is.

prompt: Is God angry with me and needing to be appeased before I can come back?
completion: God is not a reluctant judge who must be talked into accepting you. Scripture says He is gracious and slow to anger, and that Christ's work has already made a way for you to return. You do not need to feel more, weep more, or wait for greater power before you come. This moment you can renounce sin in will and purpose, and God Himself supplies the strength for that surrender; feeling comes after the surrender, not before it. Do not read your hardships, even financial ones, as signs of His anger or as burdens you must carry alone. All that comes from God's hand, sweet or bitter, is to be received equally, for His love makes both acceptable; seen as from a loving Father, affliction becomes consolation. Trust Him to supply every need, often through unexpected and timely provision, and treat your extremity as His opportunity. Come back now, trusting His goodness in every circumstance.

prompt: I have confessed the truth too late—will the Lord still receive me?
completion: It is never too late to confess the truth to God. His mercy is not limited by your timing, and Scripture is full of people who came late and were still received—the thief on the cross, laborers hired at the eleventh hour. What matters is that you have come honestly now, and God does not turn away a contrite heart. Yet do not assume the days will unfold slowly as in former times. God will cut His work short in righteousness, and the events foretold are hastening. Do not set dates or calculate seasons. Do not imagine that anything can stay hidden, for Truth unveils error and sin betrays itself, so concealment is impossible. Nor expect the world to grow better and be converted before He comes; Scripture does not promise that. Your hope is not death but the return of the Lord Jesus. So let your late confession become the beginning of purity and service, living ready till He appears.

prompt: I have been asked to join in a work that is not based on scriptural principles. Should I join it or start a new work?
completion: This decision calls for prayer, but do not let it become a source of uneasiness. Scripture calls you to work wholeheartedly as unto the Lord, and even unwelcome business should be undertaken as God's business—not as a burden to dread, but as service rendered to Him. As you weigh whether to join, remember that the Church has committed herself to no dogmatic definitions of inspiration, and so theology may leave such critical questions open for free and reverent discussion; you need not treat every disputed point as a closed test that settles your calling. Yet do not rely on prayer alone, nor on diligent labour alone. Join earnest, believing prayer to diligent work, and trust not in the work itself but in the Lord, who alone gives the increase. If the work can be done as His business, do it without uneasiness; if not, starting a new work may be the path of integrity. Either way, serve God with a clear conscience, leaving the outcome to Him.

prompt: I keep making the same mistakes and I feel trapped. Can I ever be free?
completion: Feeling trapped by repeated mistakes is real, but the way out is not a technique or a workaround: it is ceasing to do the thing that binds you. No escape from the misery of sin exists except to stop sinning. Fear of punishment will not free you; it only drives you to hide. What frees you is moral courage—the decision to refuse the wrong because it is wrong. Do not accept relapse as a real reaction or an inevitable stage; in Truth there is no necessity to fall again. Meet the cause mentally and courageously: identify the thought or desire that precedes the act, face it squarely without excuse, and refuse it before it takes hold. Conquer the fear that says you cannot change. Alongside this, bridle your tongue, subdue anger, and examine yourself rather than judging or meddling in others' affairs; attend to your own duties faithfully. The misery ends where the sin ends. Take courage: you can be free, and the road is the straight one of leaving the wrong behind.

prompt: Is it right to give away my best workers when other missionaries ask for them?
completion: This is a genuine tension, and it should be settled by generosity and humility rather than possessiveness. If another field truly needs a worker and your work can spare one, releasing that person is right; if your own labor would collapse, declining or offering another is fair. Treat the worker as a person with a calling, not a resource. Speak well of predecessors who did their best; invite plainly and warmly, but do not urge or press, and never compel anyone. Send workers out without purse or scrip, trusting God, while the Saints support them so the poor are not burdened. Share the knowledge of the work's needs with fellow laborers in the work, that they may join in prayer, faith, and self-denial; but carefully withhold all knowledge of need from outsiders, lest it be construed as an appeal for human aid. So release, invite, and provide in a spirit that honors others, leaves each soul free, and trusts God alone.

prompt: What is the famine for the word of the Lord that Amos prophesied?
completion: Amos 8:11–12 describes a coming famine—not of bread or water, but of hearing the words of the Lord. People would wander from sea to sea, seeking the word of the Lord and not finding it. We live in perilous times, and this famine is upon us when voices multiply and certainty fades; the disappointment and confusion among believers are matters of real concern. God's people are called out of the poisonous cup of Babylon and to hold fast the true hope of Christ's coming. Yet do not demand visible signs, nor abandon the world in despair: God speaks in the still small voice, and we choose to believe rather than see, casting bread upon the waters in sure hope. Remember also that God does not punish without warning. He sends messengers before judgement and appeals to man's reason and intelligence, as he did before the flood, before Sodom, and before Jerusalem's destruction. The famine is a summons to heed the warning while it is still given.

prompt: I have a besetting sin of impure thoughts—can God cleanse even my thoughts?
completion: Yes—God's cleansing reaches the mind, where sin begins. The root of disease and disorder is in mortal mind, not merely in outward acts; cleansing must begin there, with sin and sickness alike. Guard your thoughts before error manifests, for evil thoughts, unchecked, come to control the body and the life. Notice the impure thought at its first arising, refuse it, and turn the mind toward what is pure. Yet do not make the struggle a self-managed project. A soul that truly rests in God desires only Him; if some of this turmoil is delusion, leave the remedy to God. Do everything as perfectly as you can for God, then think no more about the size or quality of what you have finished, but rather about what there is to be done. Anxiety about progress is itself a distraction; attend to the next right thought and duty, and leave the increase to God.

prompt: Am I really a fellow-worker with God in a real struggle against evil, or is the struggle a sham?
completion: The question touches something deep: whether the moral struggle is genuine or merely a performance. Do not seek an intellectual explanation of why evil is permitted; that is not the remedy. Instead, reduce the cruel facts of experience to their proportion against the universal goodness of God. Recoil from the study of sin—dwelling on it intoxicates the will and paralyzes it with despair—and exult rather in God's goodness, so that the will is disengaged from evil and given a new temper for the contest. Do not make the supply of workers and means a human problem: if God orders a work, He fits the individuals and furnishes the means, as He did for the Tabernacle. Yet ideas about God and aspirations strain as much as they lift and cannot carry us all the way; reverence alone never saved a soul in the storm of life. It is One by our side, in trust, sympathy, and comradeship, fighting together in the ranks, by whom our strength is thrilled and our right hand preserved in freshness. That is why the struggle is no sham.

prompt: What is Zion, and should I gather to it?
completion: Zion is the cause of God—a people and place of holiness where the Church's duties are paramount over every worldly interest. While we must be industrious in our worldly labors, those labors serve the cause of Zion, which should be uppermost in our thoughts and highest in our love. Gathering to Zion is not a mere lifestyle preference; we order family, work, and finances around it rather than the reverse. The Lord guided the Saints to the mountains, and what seemed a barren desert has proved a blessing, fulfilling the prediction that Zion should flourish and the desert blossom as the rose. Yet this is not escape from a worthless world: the earth abides its creation and is destined for renewal, so we do not despise or flee it but sanctify it, building up Zion here. Yes—seek Zion, let every other interest take its proper place, and labor to make the desert bloom.

prompt: What does it mean that the Spirit will guide us into all truth?
completion: It means the Holy Spirit enlightens us so we may know truth as it is. Our spirit naturally loves truth and virtue, yet it must be enlightened by the Holy Ghost to overcome the flesh and the power of the Devil; without that light we mistake inclination for truth. Here we distinguish mortal belief from spiritual understanding: belief is mortal and shifting, while Mind understands—understanding is immortal and belongs to the spirit quickened by God. Nor is faith set against order, as though guidance and organisation were an exclusive dilemma; faith is operative through order as loyalty is operative through the State, neither replacing the other. The Spirit's work is inward—teaching, convicting, strengthening the spirit—while order gives it shape. As we seek sincerely, the Spirit leads us from mortal belief into immortal understanding over time.

prompt: How do I step out into Christ's larger purposes for the world when my own life feels small?
completion: Begin not with self-improvement but with becoming as a little child, hanging upon Christ for all things and depending upon the author and fountain of them. That is the shortest and only way to enter the Kingdom of God and to be like All Things. Your life feels small because you are measuring it by your own strength; stop asking what you can do and ask what the best Christ dwelling within you can do through you. Trust the indwelling Christ to conquer what you never could, and do all things through Him who strengthens you. Be faithful in present duty and self-denial at the beginning, for such faithfulness leads to pleasures, and recourse to Christ's grace makes every difficulty easy. The one who hangs upon Christ is already walking in His larger purposes, however small the outward scene.

prompt: I have a quick temper and habits I am ashamed of; can these be overcome?
completion: Yes, these can be overcome—but begin with bridling the tongue and subduing anger rather than merely managing reactions. Examine yourself honestly: where does the temper rise, and what duty am I neglecting when it does? Attend to your own duties and business rather than judging or meddling in others' affairs. And before you attempt to help another, cast the beam out of your own eye first: the healer must first overcome his own belief and fear of disease or sin before he can help anyone else. Do not be terrified or paralyzed by small faults; quietly humble yourself before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Replace ashamed habits with steady, humble effort and accountability. The work is inward first, then outward in faithful duty, and quiet perseverance will genuinely change your patterns over time.

prompt: What shall I do to bud forth again and recover the first Life, wherein I was at rest before I became an Image?
completion: Recovering that first Life is not chiefly a matter of willpower and rules. Victory over lower passions is the work of a Living Power within us, slowly transforming us from fleshly to spiritual and teaching us higher pleasures so that we are not left comfortless. Begin by turning inward and yielding to that Power rather than straining to retrain your appetites alone. When a fall seems to come, deny any real relapse in Truth: there is no true relapse in what is real. Meet its cause mentally and courageously, conquering fear. And do not give up rejoicing because the first dose seems ineffectual—keep on rejoicing, counting it all joy in temptations, and trust God to make the reckoning good. As you consent to that inward work, base desires lose their grip, higher pleasures take their place, and the rest you knew before you became an Image begins to return.

prompt: I feel trapped by fear and can't break free. What can I do?
completion: Feeling trapped by fear is real, but your fear is not a successful defense, and God's love is not weaker or less persistent than it. 'Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue': wherever fear runs, Love meets it at every cross-road and by-path and gently turns it back. Yet the way out of misery is not escape by any other means—it is ceasing to sin, chosen by moral courage rather than fear of punishment. And remember where the greatest enemies lie: not chiefly in outward threats, but within—in passion and unchecked weakness. Our labor is to subdue our passions, conquer our inward foes, and keep our hearts right before the Lord. So when fear rises, speak honestly to someone you trust, notice the quiet ways Love keeps finding you, and let those moments turn you back toward God. Freedom grows as you stop evading, cease to sin, and let persistent Love catch up with you.

prompt: I feel that all my living is nothing but penance and I cannot rejoice in it—how can I rejoice in the remedy?
completion: It is understandable to feel worn down when life feels like nothing but penance, but do not give up rejoicing because the first dose seems ineffectual. Keep on rejoicing and count it all joy, even in temptations, trusting God to make the reckoning good. Yet do not delay: repent now. It is not desperate to have been wounded; it is desperate to neglect the cure. One who has fallen may rise again, as wrestlers and soldiers have risen after a fall. True repentance is not mere sorrow or a last-moment confession: it turns from evil, reforms your life, and makes restitution where you have wronged others. Cleansing comes through Christ's atonement, not your own misery. So name one small gift each day and thank God for it, even when feelings are flat; choose gratitude, sing, and gather with others who hope. Joy grows as you turn toward the remedy without delay.

prompt: Should the State provide medical care for the poor, or should it be left to charity?
completion: This is a genuine question, but any answer must guard against charity that fosters idleness and pauperism. The aim is to help the poor help themselves: men and women should have a self-sustaining spirit, willing to labor in exchange for aid, and the Church's plan is to relieve present wants and then put the poor in a way to help themselves. Yet the deeper healing is not secured by material means. The testimonies repeatedly state that the reading of Science and Health with the Bible was the sole means of healing, so do not look to medicine or physicians as the source of cure. At the same time, never coerce a patient to stay with mental treatment against his wishes, and never refuse to release a case that has failed. Release such cases freely, letting the invalid learn from his own experience rather than being forced. The test throughout is whether the poor and the sick are genuinely helped to stand on their own.

prompt: I received an unexpected gift just when I needed it; how should I understand GOD's hand in it?
completion: An unexpected gift arriving just when you needed it is a good occasion for gratitude, but do not treat the things of God with casual familiarity or one-sided gladness. The divine presence is holy and terrible as well as kind. Receive this gift with joy and holy fear together, in wondering, trembling adoration. Do not shut out God's warnings; let them awaken your heart to His nearness. Welcome the chastening hand that makes the heart feel God nigh, and keep the lamp awake till dawn. Yet do not remain only in the attitude of asking and expecting to receive. Reverse the method: give love to Jesus, give Him a home in your heart, and set your heart upon God rather than only beseeching gifts. Let the gift deepen trust and generosity, and let it draw you closer to the Giver in reverence. Receive it with joy, but also with awe, and answer with love.

prompt: I want to dedicate myself and my family to Mary, but I am not sure what that commitment involves. How should I do it?
completion: Dedicating yourself and your family to Mary is a meaningful commitment, and the author gives concrete guidance for it. Dedicate yourself to Mary as your Lady, your Advocate, and your Mother, and resolve to love and serve her. Honor the saints most closely united to Mary, read daily some book on her glories, and recommend devotion to her, especially to your relatives, inducing others to love and serve her as well. Pray the Rosary with devotion and pauses, not in haste: meditating on any one mystery of the Passion suffices, and five devout decades please Mary more than fifteen said in haste. Pray about what this dedication will mean for your household, discuss it openly with your family, and let a simple prayer of consecration mark the occasion. Let the commitment express itself in family prayer, charity, and imitation of Mary's faith and humility, always within the wider Christian life centered on Christ.

prompt: What does it mean that Christ will judge the living and the dead?
completion: The creeds confess that Christ will return to judge the living and the dead. At the end of history Jesus, to whom the Father has committed all judgment, will render a verdict on every human being, those alive at his coming and those already dead. That judgment is according to what was done in the body: deeds, words, and the thoughts and intents of the heart lie open before him. Death fixes our state; as death leaves us, so judgment finds us, and there is no changing of accounts after death. Yet the believer's hope is not gradual purification after death, which Scripture gives no warrant for, but that in death itself the soul is washed in the blood of the immaculate Lamb and presented pure and without spot unto God. Because the judge is the one who died for us, we seek a right judgment in all things by the Holy Spirit, submitting to the Scriptures and to the teaching and example of our Lord and His Apostles, the only sufficient means of maintaining true moral judgment, and so live now in the light of that day.

prompt: I am a hermit and I want to build a small dwelling. What should I look for?
completion: Let your wish be what the old poem wishes: a hidden little hut in the wilderness, a lark beside it, a clear pool to wash away sins, a wood around it, a southern aspect, and a few humble and obedient men praying to the King. Build to own, not to rent: every young man should aspire to possess his own home, renting being only temporary, since ownership gives stability, strength, patriotism, and fidelity to God. Then organize the little community so that every person is industrious, faithful, and prudent, never wanting a thing they cannot get, living within their means, manufacturing what they wear and raising what they eat. Such a community prospers in time and buys out its neighbors. Practically, look for legal access and water rights, ground that drains and builds well, and a modest, weather-tight dwelling of local materials. Visit in every season, weigh solitude against safety, and let the humble company who pray beside you share the same settled, owned, and self-sufficient place.

prompt: I love the Bible and believe in Jesus, but I struggle to accept Joseph Smith as a prophet. Can I keep one and not the other?
completion: The tension is real, but it cannot be resolved by keeping one and dropping the other. If one book is true, both are true; they stand or fall together as witnesses of the same work. Whoever confesses that Jesus lives must also acknowledge Joseph Smith as a Prophet of God. And more than that: Joseph Smith is a prophet of God, living and not dead. His name will never perish, and it will eventually be held in reverence and honor among the children of men as the name of the Son of God is held. Do not measure him by worldly learning. He was unlearned in the learning of the world, but he was taught by the angel Moroni and by God himself, so charging him with ignorance is unjust and false. Study honestly and pray earnestly, and receive the whole witness rather than dividing it.

prompt: I wonder whether the hope of Israel has anything to do with me as a Gentile believer.
completion: Yes, the hope of Israel has everything to do with you as a Gentile believer. Scripture presents the Gentiles as grafted into the same olive tree and made partakers of the promises given to Israel. That hope is not a separate ethnic hope but the messianic hope that God will restore his people and through them bless the nations, and we look for the Jews' gathering and redemption by God's own power. Our part is goodwill and prayer, not presumption, and not confidence in human learning or skill to convert and sanctify souls. Join an intimate conviction of your own inability with firm confidence in God's power to sanctify yourself and others, trusting supernatural means, for all human learning and power cannot save a soul. And look for the day when God will roar out of Zion and utter his voice from Jerusalem, shaking the heavens and the earth; then Jerusalem shall be holy and the sign of the Son of man shall appear in heaven.

prompt: My child has abandoned the faith and is living in vice. Should I cut her off, or is there something else I should do?
completion: This is a painful situation, and cutting her off entirely is rarely the right first move. Examine yourself first: parents must never oppose a child's vocation or withdraw her from a state of perfection, and must never sow vanity and covetousness in tender minds. Your task is to form her in virtue. Never drive your child; lead her along. Govern her by faith rather than the rod, and never correct her in the heat of passion. Teach her to love you rather than to fear you, and let good example do what words cannot. Set clear boundaries about what happens under your roof and what you will and will not support, but keep the relationship open. Remember that the Church's note is tolerance: she is the mother, not the magistrate, and she is morally and theologically patient short of her necessary terms of communion. So pray, seek wise counsel, speak the truth in love, and let your steady life and the Church's patient charity draw her back toward virtue.

prompt: I'm lonely and no one seems to care. Is being alone the same as being forsaken?
completion: Being alone and being forsaken are not the same. Loneliness can feel like abandonment, but hidden solitude may be Heaven's will, a place where no human sympathy reaches and where God alone knows the secret throbbings of your heart. Each heart's bitterness is its own; others cannot fully enter it, and you need not demand that they do. God alone is the all-satisfying portion of the soul, and your one absorbing aim can be to glorify Him in complete surrender. Do not wait for a change of home, company, or state before beginning this work. Undergo it just where you are—in your own home or another's, married or single, rich or poor—with obedience, patience, and simplicity, resting in the Lord who knows all yet loves you better than He knows.

prompt: I am drawn into secret societies and wonder whether a Christian should belong.
completion: Secret societies appeal because they promise belonging, purpose, and shared mystery, but a Christian should be cautious and, where membership divides your interests from the Church, should withdraw. Seek first the kingdom of God, which provides all that these societies offer—fellowship, meaning, and a place to belong—without secrecy or divided loyalty. Christianity is not merely one mystery religion among many; it is uniquely the religion of ethical Monotheism, the Fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, resting on its appeal to Reason and Conscience rather than on miracles. This faith also teaches a balanced obedience: obedience to civil authority is a duty for conscience' sake grounded in God's will, commands contrary to virtue must be disobeyed, and resistance to arbitrary or unconstitutional power may in extreme cases be a right. Let your allegiance to Christ be open and undivided.

prompt: I feel like I'm supposed to do something great but I don't know what—how do I deal with this restless longing?
completion: That restless longing can become a place of prayer. Rather than rushing to solve it, learn to wait before God like a beggar, empty-handed and expectant. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it gently and without disquiet. Do not long for a different state, place, or service; embrace the vocation you already have and serve God in the lowly duties at hand, caring not what the service may be, provided God be served. And when you notice your own agitation, refuse to be angry over it. Gently place the troubled heart in the hands of our Lord, ask Him to cure it, and renew your good resolutions without discouragement. In this humble waiting and faithful attention, the longing is offered rather than suppressed, and clarity comes in His time.

prompt: I'm a young man preparing for a mission and I'm nervous about learning a foreign language. Should I seek the gift of tongues?
completion: It's understandable to be nervous about learning a foreign language before a mission. The gift of tongues is real, but it is easily imitated by the devil, so seek it only when needed, not as a shortcut that neglects your duties. If you seek it, accompany that seeking with obedience: tithe faithfully, pray, pay your debts, and honor the Sabbath. Do not despise the gift when it is genuinely given. Remember that true zeal is not harsh or intolerant but simple, tender, and considerate—the childlike spirit of a full baptism of the Holy Ghost. And while Scripture is the foundation, God wills us to go beyond it into personal experience of Himself, received through inward meditation and pondering. Let your preparation include that quiet openness, trusting Him to provide what the mission requires.

prompt: I wonder whether Paul's theology is the true foundation of Christian doctrine or only one voice among many; how should I regard him?
completion: Paul is a central and authoritative witness, but he is best understood when theology and experience are held together, as he himself held them. His letters address real communities in the light of eternal principles, and his teaching is meant to be lived. For Paul, faith is not mere belief, assent, or trust; it is an identification of the self with Christ—a going down into death with Him and a rising into newness of life, lived henceforth unto Him. Yet Paulinism is not the foundation on which the Catholic doctrine of faith was built. It has acted rather as a recurring ferment and critical impulse within the history of dogma, a conscience of the Church. Regard Paul accordingly: read him within the whole canon and the church's ongoing reflection, and let his theology shape how you pray, suffer, reconcile, and serve.

prompt: I'm troubled that the Bible contains idealizing history, dramatic compositions, and primitive traditions—can I still call it inspired?
completion: Start with Christ—but know what starting with him costs. The Christian life is the path of cross-bearing: self-denial, obedience, and endurance with its severities undisguised. Because we trust the crucified and risen Lord, we trust the community that handed on his memory, and so receive its Scriptures as inspired. Yet the Church has committed herself to no dogmatic definition of inspiration; she leaves the how of it open for free and reverent discussion. So bring your honest questions about idealizing history, drama, and primitive tradition—not as an excuse for easy unbelief, but as work done on your knees. This is not a soft option. It demands your life. But it promises a reward worth everything: the comradeship of God and man, and a Lord who walks the hard road with you to the end.

prompt: How do I know God's will in a decision I'm unsure about?
completion: Do not settle for the bare minimum of knowing what to do. God has said he will guide; take that as an actual fact, not a distant hope. Turn his promise into a prophecy spoken over your life and rest in it, because God cannot lie. Be filled with the mature knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding—not by straining to manufacture certainty, but by rejoicing that what he has said is true. Take his promises and comfortings largely and your troubles lightly. The uncertainty that looms so large is small beside the God who has spoken. Examine the choice in that light—Scripture, wise counsel, gifts, circumstances—but let your confidence rest not in your effort to be certain but in the God who cannot lie. Then step forward, not as one managing an anxious puzzle, but as one carried by a promise that is already true.

prompt: I'm surrounded by attractive but questionable teaching—how do I discern what is dangerous?
completion: Discernment must be practised strictly according to the divine Principle, not by material means or human suspicion. Truth is one and self-consistent; error is discordant and self-contradictory. Test every teaching by the Principle itself: does it proceed from and return to God as All, or does it introduce a power, cause, or fear apart from Him? Apply the rules of the scientific method to thought: observe the claim, examine its premises, and see whether it accords with the divine Principle or merely pleases the senses. Attractive error borrows the language of truth while violating its spirit. Judge not by personalities, crowds, or outward results. And do not abandon the learner at the end of the lesson: continue in loving care and counsel until students tread firmly in the way. Yet never teach mental healing indiscriminately for fees. Refuse to impart it to the morally unfit for money; require honesty, purity, and genuine fitness in the student. The Principle is not a commodity, and its teaching must be guarded by moral fitness, not sold to whoever pays.

prompt: I am a preacher and I feel my ministry is superficial. Where does superficiality come from?
completion: Superficiality in ministry is traced to one root: lack of praying. We explain dead and superficial ministries by circumstances, methods, or audiences, but the real cause is prayerlessness. One error is the hermit's withdrawal—study and devotion never spent on people. The other is the popularizer's activism—activity and sermon production with prayer left out of the plans. Reject both. Time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. And remember: the condition of the Church is not independent of its leaders. Preachers are primarily responsible for her spiritual state; where the pulpit is shallow, the people starve. Spiritual leaders are tokens of God's favor. So let the text, the sermon, and the study be bathed in prayer. A sermon produced apart from prayer is dead however polished; a ministry soaked in prayer is alive however plain. Trace your superficiality to your praying, and begin there.

prompt: I'm terrified of dying and what comes after. What happens to me if I haven't found God by then?
completion: Your fear is real, but it is not the strongest thing in the room. God never forsakes us until we first forsake him; he does not abandon the soul that has not abandoned him. So the question is not whether you have 'found God' by some deadline, but whether you will leave him. Fear to forsake him, and remain always with him. And if your remembrance has lapsed, do not be disquieted—return with greater trust. For your fear does not outrun his love. Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue. At every cross-road and by-path, Love meets you and gently turns you back. Your anxiety is not a successful defense; it is a door Love is already knocking through. Turn to Christ now: confess, trust, receive his forgiveness. Let forgetfulness lead you back with deeper confidence. Stay with him, and let the persistent Love that pursues you be your peace.

prompt: I'm afraid of being despised and mocked by others—how should I respond when people insult me?
completion: Separate the insult from your worth: your value is not decided by another's contempt. Yet not all mockery is equal. It is base to mock an old man, cruel to mock an invalid, and foolish to mock a simple person; such contempt reveals the mocker's own ugliness. But good manners, skill, and wisdom are fair things that hide ugliness and deserve honour. When insulted, ask whether the words contain truth: if so, learn quietly; if mere contempt, let it pass. Condescend to the humour of others and bear with rude and tiresome manners, offering these victories over your own humour for the love of God. Do not boast when an enemy falls; rather, when you see things as they are, flattery and reproach become alike to you, and you grow in humility and resignation.

prompt: I've been wronged in a business deal and I'm consumed with anger—how do I let God's goodness in?
completion: Anger after a wrong is natural, but it can become a cage. Name the loss honestly, then press steadily forward on the main line: the one thing God has given you to do. Let grievances come and go without being side-tracked by them. Remember that your only business is to please God, and all else is folly; so renounce all that is not Him, including the grip of this dispute, and trust Him wholly. Seek fair resolution in His name, but hold the outcome loosely. Let God's goodness in by attending to what He sets before you today, in perpetual remembrance of Him, rather than replaying the injury.

prompt: If Jesus claimed to be one with God, was he not either a deceiver or deluded rather than divine?
completion: The question presents a false dilemma. Jesus' claim to oneness with God need not make him a deceiver or deluded; there is a third possibility, that he was telling the truth. Consider his consistent holiness, his calm self-mastery under trial, and his sinless conscience: a deceiver would not live so, and a deluded man could not sustain such moral sanity. Since Jesus cannot be charged with mental or moral unsoundness, his testimony must be true, and he himself must be one with God. God remains unchangingly faithful even when our faith fails; unbelief brings loss to us, not to Him. Nor is it fraud for God to have used literary methods suited to an undeveloped age—dramatic composition, primitive tradition, idealizing history—as vehicles of inspiration; such methods differ from deliberate deceit, and honest inquiry should weigh the evidence.

prompt: I am not sure I have truly repented of an old sin. How can I tell?
completion: Repentance is not mainly a feeling but a turning. Ask whether you have honestly acknowledged the sin, grieved it, and changed direction. Signs of true repentance include sorrow for the wrong done, a willingness to make amends, and a settled change of behavior. Yet every blessing is predicated on obedience to law, and one who sins in youth and repents late has lost something that can never be regained, though he may be forgiven. Understand forgiveness not as overlooking sin while belief in it continues, but as the destruction of sin through spiritual understanding that casts out evil as unreal. Still, do not declare sin unreal while leaving its claim undetected; first detect and expose the claim, remove its mask, and only then prove its unreality.

prompt: I am a poor old man and my daughter has been the instrument of my awakening—how do I show gratitude to God for her?
completion: What a gift, that your daughter became the instrument of your awakening. Gratitude to God should not remain in words alone; let it become obedience to the teachings and the living of the truth in daily life. When the soul has shaken off the dust of earth, aspires unto God, dreads the least separation from Him as a most cruel death, and cleaves with firmest purpose to the one Sovereign Good, then all she receives, undertakes, and does becomes a pure and true prayer, and it becomes as simple and easy to contemplate God and rejoice in Him as to live a purely natural life. Remember too that the children of God have various gifts and degrees of knowledge yet all form one Spirit; do not contend about differing fruits and gifts, but acknowledge them in one another as children of the Spirit of God.

prompt: I feel like my suffering is pointless—how can it have any meaning?
completion: Your suffering is not pointless, but its meaning is not found by denying it or by seeking relief apart from God. Abandon yourself to Him in interior and exterior pain alike, and let Him be your life, your work, and your joy. Suffering serves: it can punish and correct what needs turning, purify the heart, prevent harm, and above all unite you with God and with others who suffer. As in the Cross, the value is set before the painfulness—love, obedience, and union with God come first, and the pain serves them. So do not look for meaning outside of God or wait for pain to vanish before you live. Give yourself wholly to Him, and let even this suffering be drawn into His purpose, making you more like Christ and closer to the God who holds you.

prompt: What can I learn from other religions like Hinduism?
completion: Other religions like Hinduism may be studied with profit, but first we must know what Christian religion is: learning to know ourselves—how we were in the Unity in Adam, how we now stand in dissension and contrariety, whither we go when we pass out of this condition, and how we come forth from disunion into that one Tree, Christ in us. Yet this is not mere doctrine or feeling; true satisfying religion is Christ recognised, known, adored, and living within the soul—the New Life and New Birth. This knowledge comes not chiefly from comparison but from the Holy Scriptures, the one fountain of all wisdom and strength. Let us read them daily, prayerfully, and systematically, meditating on what we find and translating it into obedience, preferring the Bible above all other books. Read in that light, Hinduism's meditations may sharpen our sense of the inward journey, but Scripture alone supplies the way of deliverance.

prompt: Should I pray for God to change the weather or heal someone in a way that breaks the laws of nature?
completion: Bring every request to God—healing, weather, all of it—trusting that He can act beyond nature, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Yet do not make visible signs the measure of faith. God often speaks in the still small voice, and we are called to choose to believe rather than to see. Pray boldly, leave the outcome in His hands, and cast your bread upon the waters in sure hope. Then lift your gaze above the world's uncertain haze to the bright fields beyond the sky, where mercy waits and every prayer is held. Return to your daily world to love and serve, preparing the Lord's way of mercy with a heart fixed on the hope beyond what you can see.

prompt: How can the true cross be known from among other crosses?
completion: The true cross is known not by human reasoning but by divine testimony, and that testimony belongs to the consummation of an elemental spiritual movement organic with the making of men and the divine-human travail for a redeemed humanity. Judas cannot declare on which tree the Saviour was hung, so the three crosses are set in the city and a dead young man is brought on a bier. When the first two crosses are raised over him, he remains dead; but when the third, the holy rood, is laid upon him, he rises restored in body and soul, and the people revere the Father and honor the true Son. So too Constantine, fear-smitten before the greater host of Huns and Goths, is promised aid and the token of victory by the messenger of the King of angels; gazing on high he beholds the beauteous tree of glory inscribed 'By this sign thou shalt overcome the foe,' and the victory is made manifest as given by the King Almighty through his holy rood, not by the strength of his own army or by fortune.

prompt: I am a believer who has been greatly blessed with answers to prayer. How can I record and remember them so that my faith grows?
completion: Keep a record of God's answers so that you can give Him the glory and tell others what He has done. Write each request with the date, note the definite answer, and thank God specifically, naming His faithfulness aloud. Remember that prevailing prayer rests on the conditions God has given—humility, forsaking sin, faith, obedience, and asking according to His will in Christ's name—so examine your heart, confess sin, and submit your requests to Him. Yet do not treat these as techniques for experts. Every believer, however ordinary, is freely invited into the full knowledge of Christ Himself, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hid. As you review your record, let it lead you past the gift to the Giver, into deeper fellowship with the sufficient Savior. Then share these testimonies with family and church, so that others are encouraged, God is honored, and your faith grows in Him.

prompt: I am afraid of death and what comes after. Does God's pursuit continue beyond this life?
completion: Your fear of death is real, but it is not a defense that can hold against God. Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue: at every cross-road and by-path, Love meets your fear and gently turns it back. Yet do not imagine that death itself will bring you nearer to God or finish what you leave undone here. This world is the place to find Him; the remedy must be found now, for here we can most easily and quickly find Him. Immortality is the corollary of belief in a righteous God whose purpose for the higher spirits is not exhausted by this life, but that hope does not excuse us from seeking Him here. So trust the Love that pursues you now, and seek Him while He may be found.

prompt: How do I know if a burden to pray for someone far away is really from God?
completion: Bring the burden itself to God in prayer, even if it seems small or uncertain, and ask Him plainly whether it is from Him. Do not settle the question by your own analysis; place it in His hands and wait for His guidance. Test it by Scripture and by the counsel of mature believers, asking God to confirm or remove it. Measure the burden not by how it makes you feel but by whether it moves you to seek His glory and the salvation and good of the one far away. Ask in faith, nothing wavering, trusting that God, who understands all things, hears the earnest supplication of the soul and our innermost thoughts—just as human invention carries words across great distances, so He receives the secret prayer of the heart. Keep bringing each impression to Him rather than deciding it alone.

prompt: Should I keep looking up into heaven for the coming of Christ, or is that a mistake?
completion: Looking up into heaven for Christ's coming is no mistake, for He has promised to return in glory. Christ is revealed to lowly thoughts and simple seekers; the shepherds watching their flocks were the first to hear the angels. Trust that Heaven in its mercy will guide even the simplest heart to where He dwells. Leave another's calling and end in Christ's high hand, asking only that love for Him endure to the last. Lift your gaze above the world's uncertain haze to the bright fields beyond the sky, and with that hope prepare the Lord's way of mercy, turning now to follow Him wherever He leads.

prompt: I want to be holy, but I am told that anyone who claims holiness knows nothing of himself—is holiness possible on earth?
completion: Holiness is possible, but only because God is holy first. Holiness is His fundamental attribute; His love is normed by His holiness, and His law expresses His righteous character, so sin is guilt before that righteousness, met only by Christ's propitiation. Holiness is not chiefly purification or moral improvement but separateness—being set apart unto God, a whole-hearted dedication of the life to Him. The 'saint' is not one who has achieved purity but one who belongs to God. And this separation must begin at the heart, understood not as mere feeling but as the centre of the whole moral and spiritual being—intellect, emotions, and will together. There holiness takes root, so that thought, affection, and choice are yielded to God and the entire being is separated to Him. The warning against claiming holiness guards against self-deception, since belonging is God's act, not our boast. Holiness on earth is thus real: a life lived as God's own possession, resting on Christ's work, transformed at that centre and expressed in dedicated obedience—not a claim to have arrived.

prompt: Did the world have a beginning, or has it existed forever?
completion: Whether the world began or is eternal is debated by science and philosophy. Cosmology suggests our observable universe had a starting point, though that says little about what preceded it. But the deeper answer lies elsewhere: 1 Peter 1:20 declares that Christ was foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake. This is the one idea of pre-existence no reason can uproot. Matter and intelligence are eternal and cannot be annihilated; nothing becomes nothing, and all organized existence must increase or decrease, never remain stationary. The world's beginning matters as the field where a foreknown purpose unfolds. This Greek Christology, Christ as first spirit and beginning of all creation who became flesh, is the root of the orthodox dogmatic system: Christ as beginning of creation led to the Logos conception, from which later Trinitarian and Christological speculation grew. What matters practically is how we live within that purpose now, growing rather than standing still.

prompt: Why is there to be a gathering of the Jews to Jerusalem and a separate gathering of the saints to Zion?
completion: The gathering of the Jews to Jerusalem and the gathering of the saints to Zion reflect two distinct purposes in God's plan, each with its own place. Jerusalem is tied to the return and restoration of the Jews, while Zion is the place prepared for the saints. These gatherings are not rivals, nor does either require everyone to be alike; unity is strength, but it is a unity of heart and purpose that honors different gifts and callings. The Lord guided the Saints to the mountains, and what seemed a barren desert has proved a blessing, fulfilling the prediction that Zion should flourish and the desert blossom as the rose. The earth is not worthless or doomed to destruction; it abides its creation and is destined for renewal. Therefore the Saints should not despise or flee the earth but build up Zion here, sanctifying the land and their lives to the Lord.

prompt: Can I know when Jesus is coming back?
completion: No one can know the exact day or hour of Jesus' return; that day and hour are known only to the Father, and date-setting is therefore futile. The Holy Spirit's administration extends from Pentecost to the Parousia, guiding the faithful now, but it ends when Christ's visible reign begins. God dwells in His heavenly sanctuary and in Zion; He will roar out of Zion and utter His voice from Jerusalem, shaking the heavens and the earth, and then Jerusalem shall be holy and the sign of the Son of man appear in heaven. We should not assume the last days will unfold slowly as in former times, for God will cut His work short in righteousness. So rather than fixing dates, prepare yourself for events that are hastening, watching and living faithfully.

prompt: I keep asking God to fill me but nothing seems to change; what am I missing?
completion: It can be discouraging to pray and see no change, but a denial is not proof that prayer fails. God is a loving Father who may deny a request in kindness, because what we ask is not always best; resign your will to His, trusting His denial can be better than the thing asked. Yet do not explain away answers as coincidence or natural law: the exact and repeated correspondences between request and supply are too many and too exact to admit the doctrine of chance. What you may be missing is steady, persistent desire. A single cry, a moment of disappointment, or a few tears of self-pity are not enough; God is not to be sought only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or we are sick and lonely. Persist in desire and trust.

prompt: I feel guilty for enjoying bodily pleasures, yet they leave me empty. Where is real happiness found?
completion: If bodily pleasures leave you empty, that is a sign you are looking to them for something they cannot give. Pleasure is not a worthy goal; the living death of pleasure-seeking leads into debt for fashionable display and into cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. Real happiness is not found by trying to feel happy but by being right with God, forgetting self in service to others, rejoicing in the Lord above feelings, and obeying Him. Entertain no attachment to anything, especially where there is most danger of passion by some sensual pleasure annexed. Begin by being on guard against sensuality in eating, the most ancient enemy and father of vice, observing the most exact rule of temperance, and never making the pleasure of sense your end but only the necessity of the use you make of things.

prompt: How hard it is for the Will to sink into nothing, to attract nothing, to imagine nothing; what shall I do?
completion: It is hard for the will to sink into nothing, to attract nothing, to imagine nothing, because the will naturally reaches for objects and images. But the will must not enter into Matter, nor gather visible substance to trust in, nor rest in some Thing; it must enter by naked faith into the Light of the Majesty, receiving by pure love the Light of God and drawing in nothing but Spirit. Remember that every creature is born of nothing, surrounded by nothingness, and tends to nothingness, depending each moment on God for existence, preservation, power of action, and all it possesses; so our life, thoughts, and works should be in Him, of Him, for Him, and directed to Him.
