completion: The pressure to conform to fashion is a temptation to pride in outward adorning. Scripture commends humility and the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, of great price in God's sight; pride in dress was the very sin by which Elizabeth was awakened, and the love of finery can be turned from by grace. Dress modestly and simply, honoring God and neighbor, and honor the duties of the housewife and the service of Relief Societies in caring for the poor and needy. Yet go further: vain and immodest dress is a snare that wounds others' souls, and the excuse of meaning no harm will not do, for the one who prepares the poison is more guilty than the one who drinks it. Let your adorning be good works, not a stumbling block.

prompt: I am not sure the miracles in the Bible really happened—can I still believe the rest?
completion: Yes, you can still believe the rest. A miracle is not a violation of natural law but an extraordinary event in nature wrought by the immediate agency of the immanent God, coinciding with the word of a religious teacher; it suspends no law of nature, for God is always at work in His creation. Miracles are for the consolation and confirmation of the Saints, not the proper means of convincing unbelievers; no good, honest person requires one to believe. Meet experience with experience: the real burden of proof lies in the present spiritual miracle of forgiveness and regeneration in your own life. That abiding evidence does not depend on settling every historical question, so hold to the core message of love, justice, and hope while honest questions coexist with genuine commitment.

prompt: I have to correct someone who is doing wrong—how do I do it without driving them away?
completion: Before correcting another, remember that if every person in the community would correct his own errors each day, the errors of the whole would be continually corrected. This is an individual business over which each must preside until every fault is corrected. So begin with yourself: examine your own faults daily and set your own house in order. Then approach the other with humility, as one sinner to another, in private and with patience, and do not abandon them when instruction ends; continue loving care and counsel until they tread firmly in the way. If your grievance concerns a leader, take it directly to the person involved, seeking confession and reconciliation, and do not spread the matter abroad or sit in judgment upon presiding officers from a distance.

prompt: I'm anxious about the future and want certainty. Is it wrong to want to know what will happen?
completion: Wanting to know the future is human, and the desire isn't wrong—but it often rests on an assumption that time is guaranteed. Death is certain; its time, place, and manner are utterly unknown, and no forecast can secure them. Yet this uncertainty is not a summons to frantic haste or self-willed resolution. The safe guide in every crisis is believing prayer joined with the word of God, and continued uncertainty is itself a reason for continued waiting; delay is God's means of drawing you to prayer and keeping self-will in check. Make now the changes you would wish to have made when death is near, but make them patiently, refusing all carnal or chance methods of determining the mind of God. And do not await the accidents of life with fear, but with perfect hope, trusting that God, whose child you are, will deliver you according as they come.

prompt: I have been told that the cross is only something that happened long ago—how can Christ crucified be present to me now?
completion: The cross is no new thing, invented to replace the old pieties of the human heart; it is the putting of the love of God into those old fundamental pieties—the realizing in Jesus Himself of the dearest truths about God: that He is Father, that He cares, that He will not abandon us. In Christ crucified we see the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He assumes for its eternal issues. This is not the improving of the old nature but death and resurrection: the old self is crucified with Christ, and a new creation rises into God. Nor is the cross only long ago or a figure of speech—Christ is openly set forth crucified before your eyes and in you, bearing the curse wherever sin is. Wherever sin is acknowledged, there He is crucified; faith may lay hold of the deliverance already accomplished and receive the new life.

prompt: I feel a deep restlessness that nothing earthly satisfies—is that a flaw in me or a sign of something more?
completion: That restlessness points to something real—you are made for more than earth can give—but be careful: over-eagerness and restlessness are the mother imperfection of all imperfections. They masquerade as spiritual hunger while scattering the soul. Notice, too, that the sensation is not a fixed fact but the effect of a belief: believe that nothing can satisfy you, and the restlessness persists; root out that belief and replace it with the truth that God is near, and the sensation changes or lifts. Yet do not be astonished at finding miseries in yourself, as though perfection were a finished work. The work is never done; it must always be recommenced with a good heart. Let your seeking be a sweet, peaceful, and amiable effort, accepting each new beginning without dismay.

prompt: I'm a young woman wondering whether I should form a definite purpose in life—what should it be?
completion: Yes, form a definite purpose—but let it be shaped by three convictions. First, every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way; ask where you can do good and how to make yourself capable of doing at least a little good. Second, set before you as the goal of all your efforts and desires the possession, even in a mortal body, of an image of the happiness to come and a foretaste of the delights, life, and glory of Heaven, so that your hopes, thoughts, and prayers breathe only God. Third, remember that the intention determines the true value of every act: actions done for merely natural ends, or only to be seen by men, lose their supernatural reward. So do all things for the glory of God, and let that intention order your studies, work, relationships, and prayer.

prompt: I am told that Catholicism grew out of a compromise between Jewish and Gentile Christianity; should I accept that my church's doctrine is a mixture of two parties?
completion: That claim oversimplifies a complex history. Tensions between Jewish and Gentile believers were real, but the original principle of distinction between Jewish Christianity and the main body of the Church lay in policy rather than doctrine: how far the Church would bind observance of the Mosaic law—circumcision, diet, and table fellowship—as a condition of fellowship. Justin Martyr distinguishes two tendencies among Jewish Christians: the strict, who insisted on the law for all, and the tolerant, who did not. He recognizes the tolerant as brethren, and the evidence shows the matter had ceased to be a burning question for the main body of Christendom in his day. The decision of the majority in councils and conferences rightly prevailed; minority dissent may permit conscientious withdrawal, but not internal war against the Church's decisions. So you need not accept the framing of Catholic doctrine as a mixture of two parties: the core faith was shared, the dividing line was policy, and the Church's working harmony was upheld.

prompt: Should the Church take sides in politics, or stay neutral about forms of government?
completion: The Church is not a partisan political body: it endorses no candidates or parties, for its mission is spiritual. Yet the Saints are taught to be good citizens, loyal to the Constitution and the laws of the land. Non-partisanship concerns factions, not the nation, and there is no conflict of loyalty between Church and nation. As a family serves the nation by being a good family, so service of the Kingdom builds up the land. Citizens should therefore support the nation in its acts, unless the nation is capable of something better, or demands what is intrinsically immoral or a repudiation of the spirit of Christ. Only then does faithful citizenship require refusal. Otherwise loyalty and faith work together, and the Church forms members whose devotion makes them better citizens, not rivals to the country.

prompt: How do I stop being anxious about my spiritual progress?
completion: Anxiety about progress comes from over-eagerness, the mother imperfection of all imperfections, and the remedy is keeping yourself in God's presence. Do not mistake calm for complacency: not advancing is going back, so keep steadily advancing without hurry or fretfulness. When storms of worry rise, call on the Lord present within you; awakening Him calms the soul's storms. And when you stumble into small faults, do not be terrified or paralyzed. Humble yourself quietly before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Over-eagerness breeds anxiety, and terror over trifles blocks perfection; but a calm, advancing soul, calling on Christ within and rising gently after each fault, finds both peace and growth.

prompt: Is Christ's presence in my heart just a feeling or an idea, or something more?
completion: Christ's presence in your heart is more than a feeling or an idea; it is a living relationship in the atmosphere of His love. Believe that He ever loves you and claim His sweet approval and tender regard. His words are spirit and life, applicable to all time, coming to us still brightened with that same spirit and life. When you behold His Passion, do not see pain alone. Behold in three manners: the hard pains He bore, the love that passes them, and the joy and bliss of the Trinity within it. That same loving, joyful presence is what dwells in you. So rest in His living word, remain in prayer, and let His presence shape your life, confident that you are loved, accompanied, and held in joy.

prompt: I pray for my congregation, but only that they be saved. Is that enough?
completion: Praying for your congregation's salvation is good, but the question is whether your commitment matches it. The author teaches that members join the confraternity solely to serve God and Mary and save their souls, not for worldly advantage, and must not forsake its appointed days for worldly business. Real prayer is scarce, and helping bring preachers and the Church back to prayer is the greatest work a benefactor could do. Do not neglect congregational worship because you get nothing out of it; love is the highest motive. Attend chiefly for the edification of the whole body and of the stranger among you. Keep its days, serve God and Mary, and let prayer and presence together seek the salvation of all.

prompt: I'm exhausted and overwhelmed by everyday duties. How can I keep any awareness of God through all of it?
completion: When duties overwhelm you, do not multiply techniques; simplicity is the heart of practicing God's presence. Do each action for God without anxiety over distraction, for a wandering thought in necessary work is not a failure. Beware of hurry and over-eagerness, the mother imperfection of all imperfections, for anxious fretting blocks perfection. Remember that God is the one living Worker, and all human workers are only His instruments. Cast all your care upon Him, for anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. So keep yourself in His presence calmly, doing what lies before you as His instrument, and return gently when you drift. Awareness grows through simple, repeated intention and trust in the one who works in you.

prompt: How do I resist the devil's attempts to distract me through cares and anxieties?
completion: Distraction through cares and anxieties is one of the devil's favorite tactics, because it scatters the mind and keeps it from resting in God. But the remedy is not frantic self-management; it is to come before God like a beggar, with nothing to offer but your need, and simply wait in His presence. When your mind wanders into worries, do not be terrified or paralyzed by the lapse. Quietly humble yourself, recall your attention without agitation, and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Small faults are not catastrophes; they are occasions for humble return. Cast all your care upon Him, for He is the one living Agent who works in you; your part is only the instrument He uses, and anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. Let the cares pass through, bring your attention back in tranquility, and trust that God is present and at work even when thoughts scatter.

prompt: I've been trying to be good on my own strength and I'm exhausted—is there another way?
completion: Yes, there is another way, and your exhaustion is a good sign that the first way was never going to work. Trying to be good on your own strength treats goodness as a project you must complete by willpower, which inevitably leads to burnout. But before you try to fix others or even fix yourself, cast the beam out of your own eye. Look honestly at your own fear and sin, and let God deal with those first. Then, in every occasion of virtue—each temptation, each decision, each small act of love—turn to God and ask for enabling grace, receiving strength more than sufficient. Strength of character is not fixed by temperament; it is the will's power to control your actions independently of inclinations and human opinions. It grows by repeated virtuous acts and shrinks by yielding to passions, and progress is proportioned to self-victories. When you fail, return to God for the next occasion and keep steadily on.

prompt: I'm told to love my neighbor, but why should I be moral at all—what makes right actually binding on me?
completion: The question of why we should be moral is answered most deeply not by a menu of options but by the nature of God Himself. Right is right because God is it; His moral perfection is the law of our being, and conformity to Him is what we were made for. We are not bound by arbitrary commands, by utility, or by an abstract nature of things apart from God. We are bound because He is the Sovereign Good, and our flourishing consists in conformity to His character. Loving your neighbor is therefore not arbitrary; it is part of what it means to live rightly before the God whose very nature is love. Because love is the law of His being, we must compel the heart to suffer tranquilly and remain kind to the neighbor even when rebellious murmurings and sudden impatience rise within us. Avoid contention and unmerciful judgment; show mercy and charity, for that generous nature marks a true lady or gentleman.

prompt: I am too busy to pray much. Is that a valid excuse?
completion: Being busy is a real constraint, but 'too busy to pray much' is not a valid excuse in the deepest sense. Prayer should be kept at appointed times regardless of how you feel; feelings are not the measure of faithfulness. Set fixed times each day and keep them, even briefly, and establish family prayer as a regular practice. Do not imagine prayer is easy or naturally congenial; it is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy before God. When you pray, do not merely ask God to do everything while you remain passive; help God accomplish what you ask by acting in accord with your prayer. Little praying is a deluding make-believe, worse than no praying. Above all, take time to be alone with God and His word. Constant activity, public service, and Christian fellowship do not compensate for the loss of the secret place; secret prayer and meditation are indispensable to fruitful service, so refuse to let activity crowd out communion.

prompt: I am a parent and my child has died in the faith—how do I think of her body in the grave and her soul with Christ?
completion: I am so sorry for your loss. It is a profound grief to bury a child, even one who died in the faith. But do not think of her death as a hopeless loss. She has shaken off the dust of earth, she aspires unto God, and she dreads the least separation from Him as a most cruel death. She cleaves with firmest purpose to the one Sovereign Good, and all she receives, undertakes, and does is pure and true prayer; it is as simple and easy for her to contemplate God and rejoice in Him as to live a purely natural life. Such children are redeemed and beyond Satan's power, and you will have the joy of nurturing her after the resurrection. Your grief is real, but her soul is safe and at prayer. And let this hope renew your responsibility: teach and watch over your children in the gospel, and guard them from the wickedness of the world, for that charge remains.

prompt: I find it hard to be gentle with myself when I fail—how do I practice self-compassion without excusing myself?
completion: Self-compassion without excuse begins in God's presence, not in a rush to repair. When you fail, slow down; anxiety and over-eagerness to fix yourself are the mother imperfection, closing you off from peace. Be wary too: pity would be no more if we did not make somebody poor, and the tree of Mystery and Deceit grows in the human Brain, so kindness to yourself can quietly excuse harm. Yet do not heal from self-condemnation or guilt. Stand in the moral might of Mind and firm trust in Truth: name the failure honestly, condemn the wrong and not your whole self, and let mercy arise only where you truly own the harm done. Keep standards patiently, free from fretting, and dwell calmly with God, trusting that unhurried, examined kindness lets you learn without collapsing or self-deception.

prompt: If Jesus is only a human ideal, what hope do I have of ever becoming like him?
completion: If Jesus is only a human ideal, there is no hope—an ideal cannot lift you to itself. But the Christ-ideal is a revelation of the God-life, supplying the dynamic for striving. Yet do not settle for a righteousness merely credited to you: salvation is an actual redemption of the entire self, made righteous by living in Christ's power the life He lived. And do not cling to your own good works or best attainments, as though striving or real change were your achievement. Give up the good as well as the bad, and take Jesus in place of your own self, receiving His divine impulses instead of your best attainments. Then the unattainable ideal becomes ground of hope, not despair: not you imitating a distant pattern, but Christ living His life in you.

prompt: What does it mean that Christ died for me—did he take my punishment so I don't have to face it?
completion: Christ's death bears sin's consequence on our behalf, but we must be careful what that consequence is. Death is the law of physical nature, yet death as known among men—with its fear and estrangement—is the penalty of sin; sin altered our attitude toward things. Christ abolishes death, so it becomes the gate of life immortal. Understand the curse rightly: the curse is disobedience, not obedience; transgression, not law-keeping. Christ was made a curse for us on the tree, and thereby loosed us from sin so that we need not sin any more—redemption is not liberty to disobey. Let consolation rest wholly on Christ: his sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. Looking at self clouds the view, but his promises leave no room to doubt his power and will to save. Turn from yourself to the altogether lovely Saviour.

prompt: How should the nails of the crucifixion be used for the good of men?
completion: The finding of the nails is no matter of digging and guesswork. Elene's heart mourns until they are found; Cyriacus bows his head on Calvary and prays the Lord of angels to reveal the unknown mystery. A sign in the form of fire rises where the nails were hidden—a leaping flame brighter than the sun—and the nails glitter from their burial-place like stars or gems set in gold. The people say with one accord that the miracle is of God, whom they formerly withstood. Only then does Elene inquire of the wise man and choose his advice: the nails are set upon the bridle as a bit for the horse of the most noble among kings, a guard invincible against stress in war, a holy sign of God, and she sends the bridle to her son over the sea as an offering. So too should study begin with morning meditation, implore divine light in all reading, season learning with aspirations to God, and seek resolution of doubts at the foot of a crucifix—for studies without humility, simplicity, and prayer nourish vanity and error rather than virtue.

prompt: I am a servant of God, and I have been tempted to be jealous for my own reputation in the work. How do I become jealous only for God's glory?
completion: Jealousy for your own reputation is a snare, and jealousy itself is corrosive: jealousy and mistrust destroy affection. The work is not your possession. But the remedy is not to manage your image or retrain your heart over time—it is to be jealously and habitually occupied with Jesus. When a trifling word or distracting thought turns you aside, do not lose your peace over a straw; turn from every conflicting thought and look steadily up to Him. Practise mutual freedom and confidence, give others room, and let benevolence grow more diffusive. And refuse to seek riches, greatness, or honour in a world where Christ was poor and despised; such seeking is not compatible with discipleship. Embrace being despised, poor, and mean with Christ as your true glory. A heart fixed on Jesus and content with His lowliness has no room left for jealousy over its own name.

prompt: I have given up on my dreams because they all failed. Is there anything left to hope for?
completion: There is no true relapse in the Truth: the dream that failed was never your life, and failure has no final claim on you. Meet the cause mentally and courageously: name the fear that said one failure was the end, and refuse it. Pity the smallest and lost—even the little emmet matters—and know a watchman is set to light the ground: the glow-worm bids the wanderer hie thee home. But first examine your own heart. Do not blame the hardness of hearers or of circumstances while your own love has grown cold and your distress for souls has faded. The results you desire come by intense distress for souls and by tears, not by complaint. Let your heart be softened, weep for the lost, and then rise with courage to the work still waiting.

prompt: I've been praying for a family member's salvation for years. Should I keep going?
completion: Yes, keep going. Pray at appointed times whether or not you feel the spirit of prayer, and pray together as a family where you can. Do not confine prayer to a set hour or place: join it to every ordinary action—at work, in the shop, abroad, sitting, or lying down—keeping God always before your eyes. Let your asking be joined to action, helping God accomplish what you ask rather than expecting God to do it all. Above all, make prayer your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress. Pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it, for the same grace that reforms you is what you ask for your family member. Prayer woven through the whole day, with willing labor and a searched heart, is powerful and never wasted.

prompt: What is the shaking of the powers of heaven, and when will it happen?
completion: The shaking of the powers of heaven is God's own declaration from His dwelling: He will roar out of Zion and utter His voice from Jerusalem, and the heavens and the earth shall shake. His dwelling and voice are in His heavenly sanctuary and in Zion. When it happens, the Lord will be the hope of His people; then Jerusalem shall be holy, and the sign of the Son of man shall appear in heaven. This is a future shaking, sure because God has spoken. Until then, longing and seeking are our common working, not a fault to be cured now; we do not claim fullness of rest in this life. Nor does faith exempt us from anxiety and assault: the Kingdom of Heaven is in the Saints, operative by faith, even while the natural life is encompassed with flesh, blood, the World, and the Devil. So the soul sinks into the hope of the Grace of God and stands like a rose among thorns until the body's death.

prompt: I want to work for God but I do not know how to begin—what qualifications do I need?
completion: Wanting to work for God is a good beginning. The first thing necessary is earnestly to search His holy will by devout reading, listening to, and meditating on His eternal truths, which enlightens the divine law and guides us to every duty. Trust God to provide both the individuals and the means for any work He orders, as He fitted the workers and furnished the materials for the Tabernacle. Carry on the work within the landmarks of His word. Do not seek or depend upon the patronage of the world, do not appeal for money from unbelievers, and contract no debts; let the Living God alone be your Patron and prayer your only appeal. Bring a willing heart, humility, and faithfulness in small things, and depend wholly on His blessing in answer to prayer.

prompt: If I am a part of God, how can I worship Him, and how can He be good when wicked men are also parts of Him?
completion: Take all generally and behold God in all—do not cling to any special shewing or singular insight. Worship is the general beholding of God in all things: in creation, in neighbor, in ordinary life. Understand God rightly: He is not a corporeal person with human passions, located in space, or influenced as a human being is influenced. God is incorporeal, infinite Mind and Love, and material conceptions of Deity impede spiritual growth and obscure man as God's image. As for wicked men, behold God in all and see that His goodness is not divided by creaturely misuse of freedom. Yet do not fall into either self-reliance without God or dependence without effort. Fight your own battles with confidence and personal effort, while acknowledging constant dependence on God. Know yourself, cherish good character, and let worship be the grateful, undivided beholding of God in all.

prompt: What is the meaning of the stone cut out of the mountain without hands?
completion: In Daniel 2 the stone 'cut out without hands' strikes the statue of world empires and grows into a mountain filling the earth. Cut 'without hands,' its origin is wholly divine—not human power—signifying God's everlasting kingdom, inaugurated in Christ. It also teaches us to pray: we present ourselves as a stone before the Carver, yielded and passive, asking God to form His own image in the soul. Yet being carved is not a resting place; our rest must be 'no rest below,' and we press onward to Sion, trusting the pillar and the living waters. The chisel that shapes us is often the cross—not an accident but fitted to our stature, measured to what we can bear. Rightly understood, all God does shall work our final good, and the stone He carves He will bring at last into the mountain of His kingdom.

prompt: Why does the church seem so divided—does that grieve the Spirit?
completion: Church division is real and painful, and it grieves the Holy Spirit, who prays for the unity of Christ's body. Yet membership in the Church is no loose affiliation: it is a real bond carrying personal obligation, for we are members one of another. Divisions arise from pride and lack of love, and their cost is grave—the Church has become less actual to men than the nation, and therefore less powerful. The remedy is not human machinery of votes and officials but submission of the ministry and government of the church to the Holy Spirit's appointment and direction, echoing 'It seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us.' The text shows a twofold organisation: prophets and teachers, bishops and deacons, each with their own charism, ordered around the diakonia tou logou and the economy of the church. The Churches' independence rested on the Spirit in their midst—not on uniformity. Where each gift serves under the Spirit's guidance, division is healed and the Church becomes actual and powerful again.

prompt: Why does the Holy Spirit seem so limited in His work in my life?
completion: Feeling that the Holy Spirit is limited in your life is common, but He is no impersonal influence or emanation. He is a divine Person, co-equal with the Son, the Paraclete sent by Christ, who speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved. He is also the life of the Spirit-bearing body, the Church, working through means—Scripture, sacraments, fellowship—consecrating nature rather than bypassing it, never setting spirit against matter or grace against nature. His work is gradual and social: He forms us within a body, over time, through ordinary means, while intensifying personal character. Do not conclude from imperfection that He is absent. The Old Testament bears marks of its age, and the Church is not flawless, yet the Spirit truly inspired and truly indwells, bearing with the imperfect while He forms it. So draw near to the Church and the means of grace, and do not grieve the Person who dwells there, working patiently until His image is complete.

prompt: I'm afraid of what people will think if I follow these ideas. Should I hide my beliefs?
completion: It's natural to fear what others think, but fear is not a trustworthy counselor—it is Satan's falsehood, and the answer to it is trust. So do not hide your beliefs out of fear. Say with the psalmist, 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee,' and trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life. The deeper issue is moral clarity: moral ignorance and sin hinder demonstration and must be overcome. For the early Christians the decisive objects of conviction were the judgment, heaven, and hell—the general judgment and the final condition after it were the clear goal of all meditation, and this proves the moral character of the religion. Discretion may sometimes be wise, but it must never become a hiding place for sin or a surrender to fear. Be honest without being needlessly provocative, and let trust, not fear, govern your openness.

prompt: Shall all then have eternal joy and glorification alike?
completion: Scripture suggests that all the redeemed share eternal joy, though its measure may differ—'one glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars'—and the parables tie reward to faithfulness. Yet we must not consign to endless torment those who lived by the best light they had. All except those who sin against the Holy Ghost will inherit some kingdom of glory, and those who live by the best light they have will receive glory beyond expectation. None of this rests on our faithfulness as its ground: the cross of Christ is our sole ground of glory and our constant theme, for Jesus tasted death for me, in time and in eternity. Nor is the Christian life without bearing on how Christ is seen. Christ shines forth from the believer's life to others, and the believer is glorified in union and communion with Him—a reciprocal glory in which He is seen in us and we are made like Him.

prompt: I feel like my life is a burden to others. Is there any point to my suffering?
completion: Your life is not a burden, for you are God's beloved child, whole and free. The belief that you are a burden is a false sense of injury; in divine metaphysics, man is unhurt and perfect. Keep yourself in the love of God by constant trust and constant obedience. Then hard things become easy and sorrow is silver-lined with hope. Trust God as All-in-all, and know that suffering has no real power over you. See yourself as called to represent God to others: be dependable, true to your word, always giving, and self-forgetful in love. As you live toward others as God would, you will find your life rich with purpose and blessing.

prompt: I love someone who seems to be falling away from good living—should I keep begging God for a special sign about them?
completion: Abandon yourself to God in this suffering, trusting His wisdom and love. Do not seek special signs; instead, live, work, and rejoice in God alone. Your loved one's path is in God's hands. Keep your hope in God, not in signs. Rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods. Continue steadfastly in prayer even when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Expect God to reveal Himself as a present help in trouble, and let this difficulty deepen your knowledge of Him. God is faithful, and He will guide you and your loved one according to His perfect will.

prompt: How can I present Christ to others as a compelling figure rather than a mild one?
completion: To present Christ as compelling, recognize that the gospel portrait is not a product of human imagination. No mere human genius, least of all Jewish fishermen, could have originated such a figure. The portrait of Christ, free from puerility and self-contradiction that mere imagination produces, can only be explained by granting His person and character were historical realities. Present Jesus in the richness of His mysterious person as Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, man and God, as the Gospels do. The manifold Gospel picture is a self-evidencing fact. Be simple, human, approachable, and childlike, reaching others by simple human sympathy and love, so that they see in you the same Christ you proclaim.

prompt: I feel the burden of unreached millions and cannot sleep—what does GOD want me to do?
completion: God wants you to practice His presence simply. Do not multiply explicit offerings or be troubled by distraction in necessary work. Do all your actions for God without anxiety, avoiding the multiplication of explicit offerings that would interfere with simplicity. Present early seeking of God as the practice of those who do most for God; a desire for God unable to break the chains of sleep is weak. Connect the morning's seeking with the day's seeking, so that your whole day is lived in His presence. Come apart and rest awhile, finding rest in harmony with God's will and in trust, and learn to be still before Him. Then your burden will be lightened by His peace.

prompt: I have a friend who is dying in sin and refuses the sacraments; can Mary still obtain mercy for him?
completion: Perseverance in true devotion to Mary until death gives secure confidence of salvation. Your friend's refusal of the sacraments is serious, but Mary's intercession is powerful. Her prayers have the force of a command with her Son, and it is impossible for her not to be heard. If your friend has any devotion to Mary, even if imperfect, we may trust that she will obtain for him the grace of final perseverance. Moreover, Mary assists the souls in purgatory, consoling them, alleviating their pains, and delivering them through her intercession. Keep praying, and trust that Mary will not fail to help those who persevere in devotion to her until death.

prompt: How do I keep from being consumed by the pursuit of pleasure and comfort?
completion: Entertain no attachment to anything, and be most on guard where passion is most dangerous—where sensual pleasure is annexed. Begin with eating, the ancient enemy and father of vice: keep the exact rule of temperance, taking food for necessity, never making the pleasure of sense your end but only the use you make of things. Behold this in Christ's Passion: the hard pains, the love that passes them, and the joy and bliss of the Trinity within it. But know that pleasure-seeking is a living death: it drives men into debt for fashionable display and into illegitimate schemes, until the hunt for pleasure breeds cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. Flee it, and let necessity, not craving, rule you.

prompt: I am a woman whose husband has died in battle. How do I go on?
completion: Do not turn curiously inward to ask why your sadness is what it is; cease that inquiry. Patiently endure the aversions and repugnances that come, bearing them as a way of loving Him who suffered for you. Yet do not sit idle waiting for the Lord to guard you while you make no effort: take every precaution, order your affairs, and strive to help the Lord—being as willing to fight your own battles as to have Him fight them. And do not make the removal of pain your chief good or resist His correction. Ask rather for a wise and thankful heart, yielding your will to God's rod, rather than wishing the pain away.

prompt: I want to make my home and community beautiful, but others say it's a waste of time. What does God want?
completion: Beauty is a duty, not a waste: God made the earth and its elements good when rightly used, so beautify your garden, house, farm, and city, and let every improvement serve the good of others. Yet do not settle into earthly comfort or plant and build for long rest, for this is no time for planting and building while souls wander and judgment nears. Steel your heart to let bright hopes fade; count over God's mercies and your own sin. Abandon yourself to God in interior and exterior suffering, and live, work, and rejoice—but in God, not in the things you make.

prompt: I have been told that the gospel is just a set of timeless moral teachings—is that really what it is?
completion: The gospel is not simply a code of morals. It is not enough to live an honest life; the gospel requires obedience to rites and ordinances, and observing these is indispensable. Faith itself is a gift obtained by obedience, as all other blessings are. Nor is the gospel only for the already righteous: it is designed to make Saints of sinners, to make good men better, and to give power to overcome weaknesses. Yet do not keep this to yourself or look down on others. Desire that all honest-in-heart come to know the truth and be saved, share what you know freely, and welcome others rather than excluding them.

prompt: I study and read constantly, but I feel proud of my learning and dry in prayer. How should I study as a Christian?
completion: Do not seek rapid progress through the letter alone, nor trust methods other than adhering to the divine Principle. Study the letter, but imbibe the spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the Principle they express. Let historical study of the New Testament be a means to a more stalwart and intelligent faith, pursued with prayer and crowned by reverent obedience. And know that Christian Science is both preventive and curative: when temptation or illness arises, turn to the textbook and let it renew your mind before the error takes hold, not only after. Where pride rises, return to the Principle, which is not yours to boast of.

prompt: I've been given a position of authority in the church. How should I carry it?
completion: Congratulations on your new calling. In the church, authority is not coercive power but moral and spiritual weight—the kind that carries our judgment because it is earned by character, service, and fidelity. Remember also that you hold this office because a free and independent people, acting by conscience and not by coercion, chose and sustained you by voluntary vote. That democratic order is part of the authority's dignity. Carry it with humility and prayer, leading by example rather than by command. Your role is to serve, not to be served. And do not treat ordination as a merely human appointment: the Church trusts the Spirit of Counsel and Might to guide her ministers, so receive your setting apart with prayer that the Holy Spirit will guide and strengthen you in the pastoral warfare. Coercion adds nothing to the Church's true authority; a belief secured by threat is not submission but mere compliance. Keep your own devotion warm.

prompt: I wonder whether the sermon on the mount is relevant to my life today or only to people centuries ago.
completion: The Sermon on the Mount is absolutely relevant to your life today, but not as mere theory or fine words. Jesus' teaching is Truth to be practised and demonstrated—proving Christian power by the destruction of sin, sickness, and death. The Beatitudes, love for enemies, and trust in God are not abstract principles but commands that, when lived, break the hold of sin and bring healing. The saints show this: their example is itself a perpetual and moving sermon, and the sight of their relics is a strong incentive to virtue. So don't merely admire the sermon; obey it, and look to those who have lived it. And teach it to children from their early years, as a mother once taught her son to read the Bible in the tent and on the prairie, telling him the story of Jesus' death and resurrection. Ask how each passage calls you to put down sin, to forgive, to heal and comfort. Read it prayerfully and act on it.

prompt: I want to believe that love is the only thing that gives the soul rest—but I'm afraid of being ruled by it. How do I reconcile this?
completion: Your fear is understandable, and part of it should be kept. The soul shrinks from the whole great surrender, seeking instead a love on its own plane where no upward effort is needful; that lesser love feels safe but returns empty and unsatiated. Yet do not dismiss the fear of God: one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul, and an intense, abiding fear of sin and of eternal loss should be nourished, so that fear may restrain us where love is too weak. But the true Quiet of the Soul, which no creature can disturb, is not reached by your own reason, self-direction, or comforts. It is attained only by wholly giving yourself up to the life of Christ and resigning your will to him, desiring and willing nothing without him. Let fear guard you and love draw you, until surrender becomes rest.

prompt: I'm a returned missionary and feel ignored by my ward—what should I do with my time now?
completion: It's painful to feel ignored after serving so intensely, but respond with the Lord's own patience rather than quick condemnation. He pleads long with his people, and so should you. Keep reaching out with kindness whose smiles are better than cursings. Remember that elders are sent out without purse or scrip, trusting God rather than begging from the Saints or leaning on the poor for support; trust God, and let the community support you as it is able while you serve freely. Speak well of predecessors who did their best, and never disparage them. Invite others to come and serve, but do not urge or compel anyone; let them respond freely. Give yourself time to adjust, then get busy: attend activities, help the bishop and ward leaders, volunteer, and build friendships one at a time. Your service still matters.

prompt: I am a teacher who wishes to prove from the prophets that Jesus' birth, death, and resurrection were foretold; is this the right use of the Old Testament?
completion: Yes, prophecy is a valuable teaching tool, but be careful where you place the decisive evidence. The case for Christianity rests on the New Testament witness to Christ—above all the bodily Resurrection, which is the historical justification of his Divine claim. That resurrection is established on evidence as conclusive as that for any ancient fact: the empty tomb, the objective appearances, and the rise of Christianity together refute the swoon, spirit, and vision theories, and Christianity is inexplicable without it. Yet the Old Testament was itself treated as a Christian book, containing the explanations necessary for every occasion, and used under the six points of view the author lists. So teach it as the early Church did: as a source of the knowledge of faith, with prophecies like Isaiah 7:14, Micah 5:2, and Isaiah 53 confirming Christ, while grounding your students' faith in the risen Lord.

prompt: I have been told that miracles are impossible because they contradict experience. How should I weigh that against the claims of the Gospel?
completion: The objection that miracles contradict experience assumes a closed system, but experience is limited and God is not bound by its regularities. Still, do not think a miracle is required for honest faith; no good, honest person needs a sign to believe. Miracles are for the consolation and confirmation of the Saints, not to compel the skeptic. Assurance of the Gospel rests not on human testimony or wonders but on the witness of the Holy Ghost within: ask God in the name of Jesus and receive that witness which cannot be mistaken. Test every wonder by the text's criteria—whether it confirms revealed truth, glorifies Christ, and accords with God's nature and word—and reject counterfeits like faith-healing and Christian Science, which neglect means and God's revelation in nature. God answers prayer for healing by special providence and by strengthening the soul rather than by miracle; neglecting means is presumption against God.

prompt: How do I keep from being distracted by useless thoughts?
completion: Useless thoughts are not harmless; they spoil all, because they crowd out communion with God, your true life. So when you perceive one, reject it and return to God—but calmly, not with hurry or anxious fretting. Over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections; anxiety about every stray thought only multiplies them. Keep yourself quietly in God's presence, and let your return be gentle and steady. Crucially, guard your mind's wandering at other times, not only in prayer: the soul that practices God's presence through the day becomes calm and recollected when it comes to prayer. What you do outside prayer shapes what happens within it. So cultivate a steady awareness of God in ordinary tasks, and recollection in prayer will come more easily.

prompt: How do I let Christ actually rule in the deepest parts of my life?
completion: The deepest parts of your life are not conquered by your own resolve but by Christ dwelling within you. Stop asking only what you can do in your own strength and ask what the best Christ can do through you; trust the indwelling Christ to conquer what you never could, and do all things through Him who strengthens you. Do not think you must be learned or great to find Him: Christ is revealed to lowly shepherds and homely hearts, and Heaven in mercy will guide even the simplest to where He dwells. Nor try to attain purity and grace by your own effort; know Christ in you as your sanctification and strength. Abide in Him, say with Paul 'Not I, but Christ,' and find rest in His indwelling. His life in you is the rule you seek.

prompt: I am a preacher and I am discouraged by my lack of results. What is the secret of fruitful ministry?
completion: Discouragement over results is common, but the secret of fruitful ministry lies in holding together what the world separates. Reject the hermit's withdrawal, which keeps a man from the people he is called to serve; equally reject the popularizer's activism, which fills the calendar while leaving prayer out of the preacher's plans. Time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. Keep the order right: prevailing with God precedes pleading with men, and the mightiest in the closet are the mightiest in the pulpit. Yet do not attribute life-giving power to truth itself, to orthodoxy, or to human ability. All life-giving power is the Spirit of God upon the preacher and the word; truth unquickened by the Spirit deadens rather than gives life. So pray for the Spirit's anointing on both messenger and message, and let prayerful dependence shape all your labor.

prompt: I'm a very rational person. Can't I reason my way to God?
completion: Reason is a genuine gift, but it is not the measure by which revealed doctrine must be approved, nor is it to be confused with mere reasoning. Rightly ordered—conditioned by holy affection—reason prepares the way for revelation, examines its credentials, and systematizes its facts; once revelation is given, reason implicitly trusts what is above it. Yet do not make reason a supreme, self-sufficient arbiter, nor demand that argument alone produce belief; reason is faith's guide and instrument, and faith is a personal venture of trust that reason can justify but never create. Moreover, in our present state of sin, unaided reason and natural religion are not sufficient for the knowledge of God and duty. Reason and intuition fail on matters of utmost importance; natural truth needs divine confirmation; and only a revelation of God's merciful nature can break the power of sin. So use your reason, but seek the revelation that reason cannot supply.

prompt: How do I commit everything—my past, present, and future—to God's Providence?
completion: Commit your past, present, and future to God by entrusting yourself and all that concerns you to His unfailing and most sure Providence, in silence and peace. Accept all things, whatsoever their cause, as from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence, and set aside vain and wandering thoughts that weary soul and body. Learn to trace His leadings: even a chance meeting or a gathering of the serious and the careless at a grave may hold a manifest connection in His purpose of grace; adore rather than scoff. And remember that all evil of whatever kind happens only by God's permission and ever for some good end: it could not be except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him Who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. Therefore commit all things without fear to the Providence of God.

prompt: I'm afraid that if I really look at my sin I'll be paralyzed—how should I think about my own evil?
completion: Do not seek an intellectual solution to why evil is permitted; that is not the remedy. Begin by cleansing your mortal mind of sin and sickness, guarding evil thoughts before they control the body. Then refuse to dwell on sin in a way that intoxicates the will or paralyzes it with despair. Reduce the cruel facts of experience to their proportion against the universal goodness of God; recoil from the study of sin and exult in His goodness, so the will is disengaged from evil and given a new temper for the contest. And know this: sin confers no real pleasure. Seeing that clearly strengthens moral courage to master evil, for you no longer fear losing a good you never truly had.

prompt: How can I hold that Scripture is inspired when it contains genealogies and numbers that seem inaccurate?
completion: Consider the Bible's remarkable internal unity: roughly forty writers across some seventeen centuries, from every rank of life, speak with one subject, one spirit, and one aim. Such agreement could not come from collusion across so vast a separation of time and station; it requires a superhuman intelligence as its author. Take up Science and Health as a key to the Scriptures, whose honest study with the Bible enables you to prove all things, testing apparent inaccuracies against the spiritual sense. Yet hold the Holy Scriptures as the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, preferred above all other books. Read daily, systematically, and prayerfully; meditate on what you find and translate it into obedience.

prompt: I am in a position of authority and people criticize me. How should I respond?
completion: When criticized in authority, appeal from the practice of the past to its indwelling principle: ask what earlier leaders sought and carry that work forward rather than repeating or discarding it. Listen carefully, separate useful feedback from hostility, and respond calmly. Do not boast when critics stumble; the brethren should not exult over an enemy's downfall. When you see things as they are, flattery and reproach become alike, increasing humility and resignation. And toward those who wrong you, apply the precept 'Resist not evil' and the teaching of the Sermon on the Mount: read the precept together with the offender, refusing retaliation and legal vengeance, and let the principle, not reaction, guide your response.

prompt: I am a Christian and wonder whether funeral singing and solemn music are proper in religion—may they be used?
completion: Yes, funeral singing and solemn music may be used, but remember that a prayerless ministry is a funeral and an undertaker for God's truth and Church, however adorned it may be. Singing in the church is not a professional performance but the Spirit-filled, mutual worship of the regenerate body. Nor does devotion belong only to cloisters or solemn occasions: it suits every state of life. Amid exterior business the heart must remain on God in interior recollection and prayer, and the spirit of the world must be shunned. So let funeral music be joined to prayer, with texts of faith and resurrection hope, sung by a congregation whose daily lives are already offered to God.

prompt: I'm angry at God for something that happened to me—is it okay to tell Him that?
completion: Yes, you can tell God you are angry. But don't demand a sign or give up in despair. God often speaks in a still small voice, not in dramatic displays. Choose to believe rather than see. Cast your bread upon the waters, trusting that God is at work even when you can't see it. Return to your daily life with hope. Remember that God is good and cannot produce sickness or evil; He destroys them rather than sends them. Suffering and evil often come from human agency, indiscretion, or ignorance, not from God's design. God's hand is in all things as permission and overruling, but He is not the author of evil. Trust that He hears you and will guide you as you trust Him.

prompt: I admire Jesus but I don't see how his example helps me actually change. What am I missing?
completion: You're missing that Jesus' example is not just about admiration but about transformation through following his demonstrations. Jesus didn't just teach; he healed the sick and cast out error by beholding the perfect man. To change, you must do the same: see yourself and others as God sees them—perfect and whole. Prove the Principle by works. Also, forgive injuries after the example of the good thief and of Christ on the cross. By forgiving, you become a true imitator of Christ and heir of his disciples' privileges. Christianity is not mere belief or ritual; Jesus' works demonstrate an ever-operative divine Principle. His followers today have the present duty to heal the sick and cast out error. Start by studying Jesus' healing works and applying the same correct view of man to your own life, and practice forgiveness daily.

prompt: What does it mean that God's will could become my will without me losing myself?
completion: It means that your will, as the mistress of your faculties, must recall your roving mind and carry it to God. You don't lose yourself; rather, you find your true self in Him. Your will becomes an instrument of God's will by governing your thoughts and bringing them back to God as their last end. Sin arises when the human will opposes the Divine will; this friction generates forces baneful to man. Therefore, aligning your will with God's is essential for wholeness. Take comfort mightily in God's promises and take your troubles lightly. God's promises are great and sure, and He will guide you as you surrender to Him. This is a process of transformation where you discover your identity in Christ and experience His peace and joy.

prompt: Is it right to set a holy relic upon a king's bridle for victory in war?
completion: Using a holy relic as a talisman for victory in war is not appropriate. Relics are meant to inspire faith and devotion, not to be used as magical charms. Trusting in a relic for victory rather than in God's will is misguided. Christians are called to peaceableness, submission to existing authorities, and patient waiting for the Lord. We must give due honor to rulers as far as religion allows, but we must never blaspheme Christ or sacrifice to idols even to escape death. Above all, we place supplications, prayers, and intercessions for kings and all in authority in the forefront. The peace of the world depends on rulers who need God's wisdom and the good hand of God upon them. Prayer, repentance, and seeking God's guidance are more important than physical tokens. Ultimately, victory comes from God, not from relics.

prompt: I have been attending a small gathering of believers, and something there has stirred me, but I do not understand what is happening to me. What should I do?
completion: It's great that you're attending a small gathering and feeling stirred. That stirring is likely the Holy Spirit, but you should be slow to take new steps. Be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word. Test every proposed step by Scripture and prayer. Then, with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help, move forward. Walk in sweet confidence yet with holy, humble watchfulness, trusting God to keep the feet of His saints. The narrow way requires despairing of your own strength, giving yourself up to the Mercy of God, and sinking into the Passion and Death of Christ. Watch your mind against evil, put away all unrighteousness, forgive your enemies, and esteem yourself a servant of God and of your fellow-Christians. Talk to mature believers for guidance. Don't rush in self-will. God will reveal His will as you seek Him humbly.

prompt: I feel like I am being stripped of everything I relied on. Why is this happening?
completion: It sounds like you're going through a painful time of loss. When everything you relied on is stripped away, it can feel like God has abandoned you. But remember that God sometimes allows these trials to draw us closer to Him. Do not think that a single cry or a moment of disappointment is enough to obtain His gifts. God requires steady, persistent desire—a continual seeking of His face, not only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or we are sick and lonely. Keep knocking, keep asking, and trust that He will answer in His time. Guard your tongue against angry complaints, and examine yourself to see if there is any sin hindering your prayers. Attend to your own duties and do not meddle in others' affairs. Yet above all, remember that self-renunciation is the foundation of all perfection. Without renouncing your own will and embracing humility and compunction, exterior practices bear little fruit. Lay that foundation first, and God will be near to you.

prompt: How do I handle it when the home church tells us to retrench and cut back the work?
completion: When the home church tells you to retrench, it can be disappointing. But remember that God's work must be done according to God's mind, not according to worldly wisdom. The church leadership may have discerned that certain activities have become mixed with worldly establishments and need to be separated. Trust their decision, but also pray for discernment. Support the retrenchment by helping to purify the work, ensuring it is done in God's way and not merely according to human plans. Avoid mixing the church with worldly partnerships or business methods, for such mixtures lead to departure from the Word. At the same time, do not neglect mutual confession and pastoral visitation. Open your heart to trusted brethren and welcome the pastor's visits and inquiries, for an unvisited church becomes an unhealthy church. Above all, cleave meekly and mightily to Holy Church, finding solace in the unbroken blessed Common. Do not set your own feelings above the Church's common teaching, but submit in humility, trusting that Christ guides His Church.

prompt: When will Jerusalem be made holy, and where will God dwell then?
completion: Jerusalem will be made holy when God roars out of Zion and utters His voice from Jerusalem, shaking the heavens and the earth. At that time, the sign of the Son of man will appear in heaven, and Jerusalem shall be holy. God will dwell in His heavenly sanctuary and in Zion, and His voice will go forth from Jerusalem. We look forward to that day when the Lord will shake both heaven and earth, and the holy city will be established. This city is a real city, measuring fifteen hundred miles square, with many mansions prepared by Christ for His saints. There is abundant room for all who are written in the Lamb's book of life. Until then, we should live faithfully, trusting in God's promises and showing goodwill toward the Jewish people, looking for their gathering and redemption by God's power, not by human effort alone. We pray that God will hasten the day when all Israel shall be saved.

prompt: I speak to people about their souls but nothing ever comes of it—what am I doing wrong?
completion: It's frustrating when you pour your heart into speaking to people about their souls and see no results. But do not be impatient or complain. Instead, wait patiently upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls you from His hands as intended for the highest good. Play the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ, co-operating with His grace. Your labor is not in vain in the Lord. Keep speaking the truth in love, and leave the results to God. He will bring forth fruit in His own time. Do not despair or give up, but continue faithfully, trusting that God is at work even when you cannot see it. Name your piteous futility honestly: you can do nothing of yourself. But God alone makes much of naught. It is precisely in your nothingness that His love works, so offer your weakness to Him and let Him work through you. Receive kindly and amiably any censures upon your condition, life, and conversation, and offer this acceptance to God as fruitful for your soul.

prompt: Can I know God directly in my own experience, without argument or inference?
completion: Yes, you can know God directly in your experience, but our knowledge of God is partial and not exhaustive. We know substance through phenomena, and we know the infinite as the absence of all limit. So while you can experience God's presence, that experience is not a full comprehension of His essence. It is real knowledge, adequate for the purposes of science and faith, but it remains partial. Seek Him in prayer and meditation, and He will reveal Himself to you, but always remember that your knowledge is a finite participation in the infinite. Rejoice that you can know Him truly, even if not fully. Moreover, seek to know God and your own soul together, for the soul is known where it is, in God. Find yourself in Him, and you will find Him in you. When difficulties arise, do not treat them merely as problems to escape, but as occasions to know God more deeply. Expect God to reveal Himself as a present help in trouble, and let every trial deepen your knowledge of Him.

prompt: Was Christ's kingdom set up at his first coming, or is it still future?
completion: The kingdom of heaven is not the visible church, and Christ has not yet set up his everlasting kingdom on the earth; his people still wait and pray for it. Nor can it be built by human organization, legislation, or moral suasion: it must be revealed from heaven and established by God's own interposition, with an angel restoring the everlasting gospel as a warning to all nations, a Zion built up, and judgements preparing the way. Yet this is no mere inward state. The kingdom of God is a literal kingdom on the earth, composed of living and resurrected saints, with laws and administrators, and Christ will reign over all the earth. Believers therefore labor faithfully now while awaiting that visible, literal reign.

prompt: How should I respond when I feel the Spirit prompting me to speak in a meeting?
completion: When you feel the Spirit prompting you to speak, respond prayerfully and humbly. Speak plainly so the whole congregation can hear and understand, say what you have to say and then stop, and do not darken counsel by many words. Remember that talking to God for men ranks above talking to men for God; learning to intercede is the precondition of speaking well. Scripture is the foundation, but God wills us to go beyond it into personal experience of Himself, received through inward meditation and pondering. So let your words to the congregation flow from a heart that has first learned to plead with God and to commune with Him inwardly, then speak clearly and briefly as the Spirit gives utterance.

prompt: How do I give the Holy Spirit my undivided affection when I'm so drawn to worldly things?
completion: The Holy Spirit is a jealous, loving Friend who dwells in you and is grieved by divided affection; friendship with the world is enmity with God, so give Him undivided and unbounded affection. Do not separate the Spirit from the Church or set spirit against matter and nature against grace: He is the life of the Spirit-bearing body, consecrating nature and working gradually and socially while intensifying personal character. Our commonness lies in un-Godlike thoughts of heart and mind, and their alteration is the work of the Holy Spirit, set in motion by taking Christ into the heart. So do not rely on willpower or self-improvement; surrender your thoughts to Him, remain in fellowship, and let Him transform you from within.

prompt: I'm trying to understand God, but I picture Him as a person who gets angry. Is that right?
completion: It is understandable to picture God as angry, but keep always in mind that God is present, sees and hears all things, and penetrates the heart; by this remembrance you guard your soul against anger and dissolute mirth. Do not demand visible signs or abandon the world in despair: God often speaks in the still small voice, and we choose to believe rather than to see, returning to the world and casting our bread upon the waters in sure hope. His anger is His settled opposition to sin, not human temper. And do not think you must first feel more, weep more, or wait for greater power. You can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender.

prompt: How would my body be maintained in the World, and how could I maintain those who are mine, if I incurred the displeasure of all the World?
completion: This is a real fear, but the answer begins with industry, thrift, and wise use of time and resources. Labor is indispensable; the elements of wealth are already around us. If you incur the world's displeasure for faithfulness, do not imagine idleness or dependence on others will sustain you. Work diligently and spend thriftily, yet live as if your mind were in heaven and your body in the tomb, withdrawing your heart from amusements and vanities that turn it from blessed eternity. Remember that the spirit world is not idleness or annihilation: all go there, and the faithful continue their labors with the same Priesthood and identity they had in mortality. So trust God to bless honest effort now, and commit your way to the Lord, who sustains you and those entrusted to you.

prompt: I want to help the poor, but I don't know if my charity is genuine or just for show. How do I know?
completion: Your worry is sound, but charity is not first a human feeling to be audited. Charity unmade is God; charity made is our soul in God; charity given is the virtue by which we love, keeping us in Faith and Hope until all shall be Charity. Practically, do not let fear of being deceived make you stingy: it is better to give to ten beggars and be sure of helping the one truly needy, for giving with a single eye to assist the needy brings a blessing regardless. At the same time, never give to the idler who is able to work; set the able-bodied to work. Relieve present wants, then put the poor in a way to help themselves, and let your giving build up rather than weaken.

prompt: I am afraid of the devil and of evil thoughts that press on me at night; how do I stand against them?
completion: Nighttime fear is real, but fear is often Satan's falsehood, and the answer to a lie is trust. Say with the psalmist: 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee.' Trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life. Remember that the devil is not almighty: his power is limited by divine permission and by our own sloth. He cannot go beyond what God allows, and much of what we suffer comes from our own negligence—so watch, pray, and keep a calm routine before bed. Guard your thought against the inoculation of evil suggestions and be careful of evil associates. Treat temptations as occasions of advantage when well used, letting each one drive you to trust; and if fear persists, speak with a pastor.

prompt: What is the right order of my loyalties?
completion: Begin with God above all, then the household, then the wider circle. In the household, the father is head and master; he should treat his family as an angel would—affectionate, kind, leading by example—and wives and children should be subject to his dictates rather than dictating to him. Hold humility and charity as the mother virtues to which all others attach, choosing solid virtues over showy ones. And do not hide your faith to avoid opposition: openly confess your convictions, as the young missionary did when asked if he was a Mormon—'dyed in the wool; true blue, through and through.' Loyalty to God is not a private preference but a public confession. Beyond the home, serve your faith community, neighbors, and work in due measure, never neglecting those entrusted to you.

prompt: I am too busy with my own affairs to go to the mission field—is that a valid excuse before GOD?
completion: Busyness can be a real constraint, but it is often self-made. Much of what fills our days is superfluous occupation multiplied by curiosity and restlessness; limit yourself to legitimate employments and refuse the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that create more impediments than works. Then, if real duties hold you, remember that the mission is GOD's own work through many hands, and the hidden contribution of prayer and sympathy is no small part of it. God is the sole Patron of the whole work: do not abandon or contract one branch because another is in straits, and do not treat lack of funds as reason to cease trusting him. Trust him to supply each part according to his will, and share the work by giving, praying, and freeing others to go.

prompt: I want to know whether Mary is truly free from all sin, or whether she too needed to be saved from sin like the rest of us.
completion: Mary was truly free from all sin, not as one opinion among several. She was conceived without original sin from the first moment, preserved by a singular grace anticipating the merits of Christ, fitting because she is the Father's daughter, the Son's mother, and the Holy Spirit's spouse. She was saved preventively rather than remedially, and this is entirely God's gift. She is also the gate of heaven: no one enters except through her, and she introduces whom she wills into paradise. Her intercession is morally necessary for salvation, because God has ordained that all graces be dispensed through her hands. Yet this takes nothing from Christ: Jesus Christ alone is the mediator of justice, and Mary's mediation is entirely his gift and subordinate to him.

prompt: Why has attendance at worship and family prayer declined, and does it matter?
completion: Attendance at worship and family prayer has declined for several reasons: long working hours, scattered families, Sunday recreation, and loss of confidence in institutions. But one common excuse is unworthy: that we do not feel the spirit of prayer, so we wait. Scripture teaches that we should pray at appointed times whether or not we feel like it, and that family prayer should be kept as a household habit. Prayer is not asking God to do what we are unwilling to do ourselves; it is asking with a willing heart to help accomplish what is asked. And what we ask must be purged of selfishness: not chiefly comfort, reputation, or earthly advantage, but the glory of God and the salvation of souls, and what we ourselves could become for God and His kingdom. Does it matter? Yes. But the remedy is not to squeeze prayer into leftover time. Give the best of your time and strength to prayer; let the closet come first, and let study and activity come second, freshened by the closet. Then worship and family prayer will be where faith is passed on and where people find moral direction.

prompt: I am a young woman and I have fallen in love with a man I have just met. Is this love wise?
completion: Falling in love quickly is common, but love is not blind, and it should not be set against discernment. Scripture prays that love may abound more and more in knowledge and all discernment, so that we may distinguish things that differ and approve the things that are excellent. So test this affection. Do you know his character, honesty, temper, faith, and how he treats those who cannot help him? Is this love good, or merely pleasant? Is it better than your other callings, and is it the best and most excellent path for your life? Remember also that love is not chiefly a feeling but the will to please and benefit the beloved at the cost of sacrifice, and it grows by repeated acts of service. The same is true of love for God: it grows by frequent service and by considering what He has done for us. And the more you know God, the more your desire and love for Him increase, so that great love loves Him equally in pains and pleasures. Let that deeper love order your affection for this man.

prompt: I want to know for myself whether this work is true. Should I rely on the testimony of the elders, or seek a witness myself?
completion: You should seek a witness yourself, and you may rightly begin with the elders. Their testimony is a reasonable starting point, and it would be arrogant to ignore it. But do not stop there. Each person may obtain a witness of the truth by the Spirit through prayer, study, and obedience, and that testimony rests not on any man but on God. So ask Him to confirm the truth to you. As you do, remember the Lord's patience: He is long-suffering with those slow to hear and continues to plead with His people. Do not quickly condemn those who do not yet see. Let your kindness be such that your smiles are better than cursings. Respect the order of office: an elder may know his own duties by the Spirit, but he must not dictate to his superior or counsel him unless called upon, and then only to make suggestions. And remember that it is a duty to listen to the truth, wherever it comes from.

prompt: I'm tempted to think that if I just improve social conditions, that's enough—that religion is really about making the world better. Is that true?
completion: Improving social conditions is good and important. Religion that has nothing to say about poverty, injustice, and suffering is empty. But religion is not only about making the world better. If that were all, religion would be reduced to politics and charity and would leave the deeper problem untouched: our separation from God. Much of our religion keeps the curtains drawn, treating faith as our feelings and thoughts about ourselves. Tear down the curtains and let in the sunshine. The leal love of God is every day, as near as the open air and as free as the sunshine. Religion is not man's feelings about religion; it is the love of God, objective to our hearts, to be received freely. When the soul receives that love, it grows like an olive-tree green in God's house. And be assured: if you love God, all things, even grief and sin, will turn to your good, even when the means are unseen. Remember too that religion appears purest among the poor. The poor cottage may be a palace of God, and the poor in faith can teach us the most valuable lessons, while riches and worldly opinion obstruct humility and spirituality. So work for justice, but let God's mercy be the foundation.

prompt: I believe the truths of my faith, but they feel distant and don't move my heart. How can I make them real to me?
completion: It is common for believers to feel that the truths of their faith are distant. The remedy is not to force emotion but to attend to the truths themselves. Set aside regular time to read and reflect on them. Pray honestly about your dryness. Consider how these truths connect to your daily life and to the people around you. Talk with trusted friends and mentors who can help you see them more clearly. Be patient with yourself; feelings often follow faithful practice rather than preceding it. But be clear about one thing: do not seek comfort in illusion or in feelings sustained by a spirit of illusion. Foster the idea of Truth. Only what is real is sustained by the Spirit. And understand that casual reflection is not enough. By serious and frequent meditation divine truths must be concocted, digested, and turned into the nourishment of your affections before they can be powerful and operative enough to change you and produce the necessary fruit in your life. Finally, trust God with all your heart. Do not lean on your own understanding or on the wisdom of others, and do not demand to investigate whether God has told the truth before you trust Him. Such leaning hinders faith. Trust Him, meditate on His truth, and let it become real in you.

prompt: I feel God's discipline in my life and it scares me. Is He punishing me or warning me?
completion: What you're feeling is common, and Scripture speaks to it. Discipline in Hebrews is a father's correction of a beloved child, not the wrath of a judge. But notice the posture Scripture commends: meek waiting before God, hands off the scales. Do not rush to diagnose yourself or let fear drive you to scheme a way out. Bring the pressure honestly before Him and wait. What looks like a hindrance is often the very place where God intends to show Himself. He sways the judgment and removes the obstacle in His own way and time. And remember: all He requires He also gives. His precepts are promises—'Thou shalt not' is His assurance to preserve you from sin as you trust Him. Most importantly, God is good and cannot produce sickness or evil; He destroys them rather than sends them. So this fear is not His voice. Let His goodness, not dread, define your waiting.

prompt: A brother in my church has fallen into sin—should I confront and condemn him, or is there another way?
completion: Scripture gives a clear pattern. Matthew 18 tells you to go to him privately first, then with one or two witnesses, then involve the church. The goal is restoration, not condemnation; Galatians 6:1 says to restore gently. And here is your comfort: Christ promises to be a Brother to the forsaken—when earthly fathers forsake, He takes us up. Trust that for your brother. Yet restoration must not become indulgence: the holy table is not for notorious sinners without repentance, and the priest is accountable for the sacred blood, an authority above an emperor's. But do not let that harden you. Forgive as you hope to be forgiven, looking to the Lord who resigned all to earn your pardon. Refuse to mete out love by your own narrow rule.

prompt: I'm haunted by a dream of someone I lost and it heals me—should I trust that comfort or call it illusion?
completion: Dreams are strange territory, but the test is Truth. God is Spirit, and only what is real is sustained by Spirit; illusion has no such support. Ask whether this comfort draws you toward what is true—toward God, honest grief, and real love. Foster the idea of Truth rather than dwelling on whether the dream is illusion. But do not force the matter; release it freely and let the person learn from his own experience. And remember where the fulness of the Spirit is given: along the line of duty and obedience to Christ's command to reach the world. God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment.
