Begin by confessing your utter insufficiency, for conviction of helplessness is the condition of receiving Christ's all-sufficiency; then take firm hold of that all-sufficiency with a faith that will not accept less than all. And remember that devotion to God sometimes means forgoing even innocent, lawful pleasures, so that the soul takes its pleasure only with Him.

prompt: I'm anxious about my future and can't stop worrying—how do I cast all my care upon God?
completion: Cast all your care upon God by recognizing Him as the one living Agent and yourself as His instrument. Anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. Commit yourself and all that concerns you to His unfailing and most sure Providence in silence and peace, accepting all things as from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence. When vain and wandering thoughts arise, reject them gently, for they weary soul and body and waste time and strength. Keep your mind in His presence, recalling it in tranquility without disquiet whenever it wanders. This is the humble waiting of a beggar before God—not striving, but trusting. As you practice this, God's peace will guard your heart and mind, and you will find rest in His sufficiency.

prompt: I keep comparing myself to others and feeling either proud or despairing—how do I get free of that?
completion: When you notice yourself comparing, do not be disquieted. Such lapses in remembering God are common; simply return to Him with greater trust. Bridle your tongue, subdue anger, examine yourself, and attend to your own duties rather than judging or meddling with others. Recognize that feelings of pity and mercy, while they may seem virtuous, exist because somebody was made poor and unhappy—they would be no more if we did not make somebody poor. The tree of Mystery and Deceit grows in the human Brain, so do not trust every impulse. Each time you catch yourself in pride or despair, gently turn your mind back to God, saying, 'Lord, I trust in You.' As you practice this, the habit of comparison will weaken, and you will find peace in His presence.

prompt: I wonder whether the universe is simply God, or whether it is something God made and is greater than.
completion: The universe is not God but a finite, partial and progressive manifestation of the divine Life. God is greater than His thoughts, and the universe is one of His thoughts. Matter, humanity, incarnation and atonement are God's self-limitations under necessity, freedom and grace respectively. Yet God is All-in-all, and matter is a mortal belief, having no reality or power apart from the divine Mind. The universe and man are as eternal as God, their divine immortal Principle, without temporal beginning. Thus, the universe is something God made and is greater than, yet it is not coeternal with God nor a constituent part of Him. It is a partial expression of His being, evolving toward greater fullness. God transcends the universe while being its source and sustainer.

prompt: I want to help save souls but feel powerless. What can I actually do?
completion: Before you attempt to help others, first cast the beam out of your own eye. Overcome your own belief and fear of disease or sin. Examine yourself and repent of any fear or doubt. Then, be slow to take new steps. Be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word. Do not rush forward in presumption, treating self-will as faith. Test every proposed step by the Word and prayer. Remember that of yourself you can do nothing profitable for heaven, as the branch cannot bear fruit unless it abides in the vine. Abide in Christ by keeping His commandments, and you will bear much fruit, and your prayers will become powerful. Only then, with a clear conscience and in God's timing, reach out to others. This order is essential: the healer must first be healed, and then must wait for God's direction.

prompt: I am a young person and I fear death is near—how should I spend the time I have left?
completion: The exhortation in this Church and Kingdom is not 'prepare to die' but 'prepare to live.' As a young person, you should focus on laying the foundation of health, strength, and constitution. Teach yourself in the morning of your days to build habits that promote longevity. Yet remember that death is certain, and its time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain. Do not presume on a long life. Make now the changes you would wish to have made when death is near. But do not rely on baptism or the name of Christian, or the mere fact of dying, to guarantee paradise. Death works no miracle. We are after death exactly as far advanced as before. The Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in you here. So, prepare to live by building health and by nurturing that Seed, not postponing what matters most.

prompt: I'm struggling to forgive someone who hasn't apologized—how do I let go of the hurt?
completion: It's understandable to feel stuck when someone hurts you and never acknowledges it. But forgiveness is not a transaction for your own relief; it is an inward condition of the soul that loves and forgives, formed in a spirit already pardoned by God. Begin with honesty before God: name the wound, ask for a heart made willing, and refuse to let resentment take root. Scripture warns that refusal to forgive endangers the soul, so do not delay or nurse the injury. Return meekness and kindness for insults, and pray for the one who hurt you. Most of all, look to Christ, who resigned all to earn your pardon and forgave you without your deserving it; let His unlimited mercy be the measure of yours. Do not mete out love by your own narrow rule, but forgive as you hope to be forgiven, trusting God to supply the grace.

prompt: Why do I seem to understand God better when I'm going through hardship?
completion: Hardship often strips away distractions and forces us to confront what we really rely on. When life is comfortable, it's easy to coast and treat God as an addition; when we're in pain, we become more attentive and honest. But the deeper issue is allegiance. God asks for an undivided inward fidelity of heart, will, and mind—not a faith that awakens only in crisis and slumbers in comfort. You are not called to flee to rags and desert, but to place Him first in the exact circumstances of your life. Beware small capricious vanities, for trivial habits can quietly displace God, and He compels no one; your decision is made here, in the world. And when accident or mishap seems to bring injury, reverse that belief: man is not truly hurt, for God is All. Trust divine metaphysics rather than the mortal sense of pain, and let your understanding of God rest on Truth, not on suffering.

prompt: How should I think about Jesus—as a man, as God, or something in between that I can't understand?
completion: The New Testament presents one Jesus, truly human and truly divine, in all four Gospels. The Synoptics show Him praying, healing, suffering, and dying, while John opens with the Word who was with God and was God. These are not two Jesuses or a contradiction but complementary points of view on the same Lord: Mark shows His deeds, John ponders His identity; Luke traces His humanity, John adores His divinity. Yet do not seek Him first through arguments or through other people. Christ is found within, by inward pondering, by loving comparison of His life with yours, and by persistent imitation of His gentle ways. Only then will you recognize Him in Scripture, in teaching, and in others. Cast your thoughts upon the Savior's shoulders for support and fix your eyes on God's good pleasure, trusting His providence to lead you into truth.

prompt: I am old and near death and have wasted my youth—is there still comfort for me?
completion: Yes, there is still comfort. Regret over wasted youth is heavy, but it does not define your worth or your remaining days. The world itself is old and its mirth has faded, yet it still needs Youth to come joyously like the wind at morning—bringing freshness, strength, and radiance, and keeping alive the hope of Spring. That Youth is not only a matter of years; even now a new morning can rise in your spirit. Do not despise the calm old age of a pure conscience, for the hidden prayers of lowly saints uphold the proud world, though the great imagine they sustain themselves. And seek improvement not chiefly through bodily regimen but through the spiritualization of thought—forsaking the mortal sense of things for Truth. As thought is lifted to God, the body and the whole man are renewed. Grace remains for you; let Truth be your medicine.

prompt: I am a believer, and I have been asked to give an account of my stewardship to those who gave. Is that a burden or a duty?
completion: It's a duty, and a healthy one—but first, remember that you are a steward, not an owner. What you received was never private property to use at will; it was entrusted to you at the Lord's bidding. Giving an account to those who gave is part of that trust, not an insult to your integrity. Scripture commends giving that is systematic and regular rather than merely by feeling—set aside proportionately, increasing as God prospers. Prepare honestly: what came in, what went out, what was accomplished, what you learned. Be transparent and free of defensiveness. And examine yourself: if any earthly attachment hinders full obedience to Christ, give it up, counting no cost, for the smile of God is sufficient recompense. Finally, remember that ordinary business faithfulness and promise-keeping are not unimportant to your witness; weigh every engagement carefully and keep your promises exactly, since in these small affairs you bring either honour or dishonour to the Lord.

prompt: I am afraid that if I stop running, I will find nothing at the end. What will I find?
completion: Your fear is understandable, but it is aimed at the wrong thing. The question is not what stopping will cost you but what remains to be run, and it avails nothing to have begun well if the course is left unfinished. Yet do not answer this by hurry. Over-eagerness is the mother of many imperfections; it scatters the heart and makes anxiety an obstacle to perfection. Keep yourself in God's presence, and let each step be taken quietly as before him. Before you set out to help another, cast the beam out of your own eye: name your own fear, your own unbelief, your own hidden sin, and let the healer first be healed. What you will find at the end is not nothing but the completion of what grace began, and that completion is his work in you, not the fruit of your fretting.

prompt: How do I deal with the criticism of others about how I dress as a missionary?
completion: Criticism about dress is common on the field, and it usually says more about the critic than about you. First, listen without defensiveness, and speak well of the predecessors who did their best before you; do not disparage them to justify your own choices. Ask whether the concern is cultural appropriateness, modesty, or simple preference, and adjust where you can without compromising conviction. But the deeper question is whether your life carries a testimony and keeps the Word of Wisdom; without these, no dress will commend the message. Teach in simplicity, humility, and love, avoiding contentious argument and debate. Let your motive be a passion for human beings as human beings, with respect for peoples and their growing independence. Reject the Jonah-like notion that truth is the property of one nation. You invite others to the good you have found; you never urge them past their freedom and never compel anyone.

prompt: Will the earth be burned before the saints receive immortality, or is the cleansing of the sanctuary something else?
completion: The cleansing of the sanctuary and the burning of the earth are distinct, and the distinction matters. The sanctuary to be cleansed is the heavenly sanctuary, not the earth. At the end of the 2300 days the sanctuary is cleansed, and this cleansing is now being accomplished after the pattern of the earthly high priest's ministry. The earth is not the sanctuary and is not cleansed by fire before the saints receive immortality; the fire that consumes the wicked comes after the saints are delivered. Yet do not despise the earth or flee it. It abides its creation and is destined for renewal, and the Saints are to build up Zion here. It is the privilege of the Saints to enjoy every good thing, since the earth and its fulness belong to the Lord and he has promised all to his faithful Saints; but it must be enjoyed without covetousness and in the spirit of the Gospel.

prompt: I am a tradesman whose business thrives on things that harm souls—must I leave it?
completion: This is a serious question, and it deserves a serious answer. If your trade genuinely thrives by harming souls, you cannot separate the profit from the harm; the money is the fruit of the injury, and to keep it is to consent to it. Ask whether the harm is essential or incidental. If essential, you must leave it, even at cost. If incidental, reform it. But do not settle into personal security while multitudes perish for lack of knowledge; let that burden drive you to prayer and obedience. Preserve your soul free from every trace of earth, so that neither the world nor friends, neither prosperity nor adversity, things present, past, or future, nor even your own sins above measure have power to trouble it, living as though already in eternity. You may dread having naught beside God, but hear this: what was taken was taken not for your harm, but so that the soul might seek it in God's arms, where all that seemed lost is stored for you at home.

prompt: If Jesus never claimed to be God, what am I to make of the Creeds that say He is?
completion: The Creeds are the church's attempt to say in precise language what the New Testament says in various ways. Jesus is Lord, Savior, and Son of God; one must think of him as of God. Yet monotheism prevents placing him on an equality with the Father, and the Creeds guard that distinction. Consider also his claim to be one with God: it can be neither imposture nor insanity. His consistent holiness, calm self-mastery, and sinless conscience rule out mental or moral unsoundness; since he cannot be charged with unsoundness, his testimony must be true, and he himself must be one with God. Nor is the Word a merely finite manifestation. Christ existed as the Word with God before the Word was made flesh, being the eternal principle of self-consciousness in God, the objectification of God to himself in the Son prior to creation. The Creeds summarize that faith, held alongside Scripture.

prompt: Is there hope for my ancestors who died in ignorance or idolatry?
completion: There is hope, but not because death automatically opens paradise. Death works no miracle; we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. The Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. Yet we need not mourn as those without hope. Christ has touched the bier, and we rest our darlings in hope of resurrection. Death is not the end of identity but a door to a higher state; the righteous dead are preserved in God's memory and will be raised in body. So we grieve, but with hope, trusting that God's mercy extends beyond death while we do not presume. We pray for our ancestors, live faithfully, and commend them to the God who raises the dead and makes all things new.

prompt: How do I know if a spiritual experience is genuine or just emotional?
completion: We must not seek or pray for spiritual experiences as achievements of our will, nor approach them with curiosity. Genuine experiences come only as God chooses. Accept them with total submission, without questioning, fear, or curiosity. Do not secretly desire them. The foundation of the spiritual life is a high notion and esteem of God in faith, rejecting every other thought for the love of God. Yet prayer does have real effects: energy from beyond the margin of the normal self can enter, but these effects are within the ordered life of the spirit, not capricious interruptions of nature. So, do not pursue feelings; pursue God alone, esteeming Him above all, and accepting whatever He sends without seeking or pride, while trusting that He truly communicates with those who love Him.

prompt: How do I recognize the needs around me as vacuums the Holy Spirit wants to fill through me?
completion: To recognize needs as vacuums the Holy Spirit wants to fill, we must first learn the secret of breathing out as well as breathing in. We must empty ourselves and pour out our lives in holy service, providing a vacuum for the Spirit to fill. As we pour out, He pours His in. The filling of the Holy Ghost is not an optional privilege but a command to be claimed. Bring an empty, honest, trusting heart to God, and claim the fullness of the Spirit for purity, victory, and power. Then, yield to the Spirit of prayer. When you see a need, do not rush to act; first bring each burden to God and pray it out in wordless prayer before acting it out in life. Do not grieve Him by unfaithfulness to His faintest whisper. As you pray out each burden, you will recognize the vacuums He intends to fill through you.

prompt: I'm afraid of what will happen to me after death. Is there any real proof of immortality?
completion: The fear of death is natural, but the answer lies not in material proof but in the spiritualization of thought. We must forsake the mortal sense of things for Truth. Immortality is not proven by bodily health or material regimen; it is realized as we spiritualize our thinking, aligning our minds with eternal Truth. Belief in a righteous God gives ground for expecting continuance after death, for His purpose for the higher spirits is not exhausted by this life. Yet death works no miracle; we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. The Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. So, do not rely on baptism or the name of Christian, nor on the mere fact of dying, to guarantee paradise. Instead, spiritualize your thought, trust in God's righteousness, and let love grow in you now, and you will find the proof within.

prompt: If the Love should proffer itself to a Soul, could not that Soul find it or lay hold of it without going for it into Nothing?
completion: Yes, the Soul can find and lay hold of Love without going into Nothing, because the soul is more truly where it loves than where it gives life. It exists in the object loved by its own nature, by reason and will, while in the body it animates only by an existence shared with the animal creation. Love alone can lift the soul from earth to Heaven; none ascend to eternal beatitude except on the wings of love and desire. Even in darkness, the gloom may be the shade of His hand outstretched caressingly; the God the soul flees is the One it seeks. Do not demand logical proof of God's existence, for the experience of communion is its own evidence. The demand for argument is a fall from a higher to a lower level. So, if Love proffers itself, lay hold of it by love, and you will find Him whom you seek.

prompt: I feel like my soul is asleep and I can't wake it. What can I do?
completion: Your soul feels asleep, and honestly, it is pitiful in its futility—it cannot wake itself, and nothing you manufacture will rouse it. Name that plainly rather than dressing it up. But hear this: God alone makes much of naught. Your very nothingness is not a disqualification from love; it is the place where love works. So the soul, holding fast to the Divine Guide, does not despise the creature but gently leads it through the humblest everyday matters—rising, eating, working, resting—for nothing is too small for the soul to attend to. Think of the soul as a fire shut up in its dark self: anguish while imprisoned, love when it breaks forth into union with the Divine Love. Do not measure by moods or circumstances. Let your emptiness be the ground where God makes much of naught, and keep faithfully attending to the small things, trusting the fire to break forth in its time.

prompt: I feel nothing but dryness after prayer, and I doubt God hears me—why should I keep praying?
completion: Dryness after prayer is common, but do not let it become your measure. Feelings never accurately gauge our real assimilation to God; they rise and fall while the changeless word of promise stands. God understands all things and hears the earnest supplication of the soul, its innermost thoughts and secret prayers—just as human invention lets people speak across great distances, so God receives what is never spoken aloud. So ask in faith, nothing wavering. Understand prayer as a continual drawing in of the heavenly life, like breathing or feeding, by which the life from without nourishes the heavenly seed within; let it be constant through your day, not only words at set hours. When joy is lacking, continue steadfastly; do not abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Rest on the promise, not on your moods, and trust that the God who knows all things is nourishing the seed within you even when your senses report nothing at all.

prompt: How can I live as a citizen of heaven while on earth?
completion: To live as a citizen of heaven while on earth is to live as if your mind were in heaven and your body in the tomb—yet not to wish life away. Mortal existence is a school of experience and probation, a place to learn and improve and increase, not merely something to escape or endure. So withdraw your heart from the amusements and vanities that turn it from blessed eternity, and keep your mind fixed above. But know that this hope has one way: there is no salvation but in the way God has pointed out, and no hope of everlasting life but through obedience to the law affixed by the Father of life. Let your citizenship show in concrete obedience—prayer, honesty, mercy, purity—and in continual learning and growth. Handle earthly things lightly, as a traveler handles luggage rather than treasure, and let each day be a lesson in the school where God trains you for eternity.

prompt: I am a woman wondering whether I can take part in evangelistic work and teaching.
completion: Yes—but begin by putting self to the rear and heart to the front. Do not approach evangelistic work and teaching as a profession or business in which salary, status, and self-advancement play a leading part; that professionalism is heartless. Instead, take up the discipline of learning: the School of the Prophets is established to increase in knowledge, the favorite study of the Elders is theology, every Elder should become a profound theologian, and every branch of science taught in the world should also be taught among the Saints. So prepare your mind as well as your heart. Yet all of it must be conformed to Christ—in outward behavior, in meekness and humility of heart, in taking God's view of things rather than the world's, and in a will zealous for God's glory and the salvation of souls. Offer your gifts as service, not as a platform; seek mentors and training to serve well. Start where you are, and let faithfulness, not ambition, set the pace.

prompt: I have lost the grace of God and do not know how to recover it; to whom should I go?
completion: Go first to God, and go by abandoning yourself to him. Do not try to manage your way back through anxious analysis; abandon yourself to God in interior and exterior suffering alike, and let your living, working, and rejoicing be in God and nowhere else. And do not be disquieted that you have forgotten him—such lapses are not met with turmoil but with a return in greater trust. Yet do not skip the meek knowing of your sin: let contrition and grace show you honestly what has turned you away, and let that knowing be meek, not despairing. Through it you are broken from all that is not our Lord—every false comfort, every self-made rescue—and in that breaking comes the perfect healing and oneing by our blessed Saviour. Speak with a trusted confessor who can help you discern, confess what needs confessing, release it, and return with greater trust. Give God your lostness, and let him heal and unite you to himself.

prompt: How do I prepare to meet Christ if I die tomorrow?
completion: Preparing to meet Christ is not a deathbed checklist but the daily business of a soul already saved and walking with God. Salvation is present and real: Christ lives in you now, and the Spirit is to be enjoyed today. Live faithfully where you are—honest work, love of family, quick forgiveness, simple prayer, a tender conscience—and let the Millennium take care of itself. Yet do not presume on a long life or postpone preparation. Death is certain, but its time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain; no one can know or secure them in advance. Nor presume that a soul which never finds Christ here will be comforted afterward: without finding Him now, the soul enters a dark, lonely, self-tormenting state, and the remedy must be found now. So make today the changes you would wish to have made when death is near.

prompt: I am a woman and I want to know how to be a good wife.
completion: Being a good wife rests on the three steadinesses of good womanhood: a steady tongue, steady chastity, and steady housewifery. Keep your speech gentle and true; guard purity in thought and deed; care diligently for your home and those within it. See marriage not chiefly as a means to your own happiness, but as a serious vocation with sacred duties, whose end is the mutual enrichment of personality and mutual freedom to fulfil the true ideal of human life; make no terms with lax views of divorce. Above all, remember that to be gentle and kind, modest and truthful, full of faith and integrity and doing no wrong, is of God. Such goodness sheds a halo of loveliness around everyone who possesses it, making the countenance beam with light. Cultivate that goodness daily, and your home and marriage will be warmed by it.

prompt: I feel like a cipher in this community and think others will get along without me. Should I bother to act?
completion: Feeling like a cipher is painful, but it is usually a lie told by exhaustion or low confidence. Do not sit idle or dismiss yourself; act with confidence, develop your own abilities, and fight your own battles rather than expecting God to do what you can do yourself. Yet not every question must be forced to an answer: to admit 'I don't know' about matters that time and patience alone can solve is honorable, and waiting may demand as much courage as acting. If you have offended God, do not remain paralyzed in doubt. Humble yourself, beg His forgiveness, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and continue in the pursuit of perfection. Then start with something modest and concrete: show up, help one person, offer one skill. Faithful, ordinary participation is enough.

prompt: I want to be a good example to my children, but I'm not sure what true religion looks like in daily life.
completion: True religion in daily life is not chiefly external observance or religious feeling; it is Christ recognized, known, adored, and living within the soul—the New Life and New Birth. The model of that life is Christ Himself, who, though God, was subject to Mary and Joseph in all the details of His life. So do not exalt independence or resent authority; perfection depends chiefly on the perfection of your obedience, and your children should see you obey gladly and humbly. Let that inner life show itself in prayer together, honest speech, patience, quick apology, and quiet service. Live a true and pure Christian life whose victorious example attracts, so that others—your children first—may say, 'If that is the religion of Jesus Christ, I want it.'

prompt: How do I know when submitting to a superior is virtue and when it's just cowardice?
completion: Submission is virtuous when it is ordered toward a genuine good—respect for legitimate authority, peace, and humility—and when it does not require you to do wrong. But do not let fear decide: be brave and true to your convictions from the beginning, do not let Satan see that you are afraid, and trust God to stand by you. Yet courage must be grounded in humility, not in the desire for greatness or the wish to be seen as strong; beware of pride under the cloak of sanctity. True humility dreads the esteem and praises of others as snares by which a mortal poison may imperceptibly insinuate itself into her affections and deprive her of divine grace, and she always places herself below all creatures. So refuse wrong when refusal is integrity, speak honestly and respectfully, and let humility, not fear or ambition, settle the question.

prompt: I'm tempted to just give up and let my faith die out. How do I keep my lamp burning?
completion: Your lamp is already lit; the task is to keep it burning. Abide in Christ, who is the oil and the flame, and tend the fire by waiting before God like a beggar—humble, expectant, asking for what you cannot supply. It takes far less effort to maintain a good habit than to revive one that has died, so keep the flame aglow rather than letting it go out. Trust the refiner's hand, for the fire that tries you comes from a loving Father; do not shrink from it in fear, but claim the promise that the flames shall not kindle upon you. In prayer, keep your mind in His presence; when it wanders, recall it gently and in tranquility, without disquiet or self-reproach, and let Him keep the lamp burning.

prompt: I want to know how Christ comes—secretly or visibly; what does the Bible say?
completion: Scripture speaks of Christ's coming in more than one sense: He came in humility at Bethlehem, He comes now by His Spirit to those who love Him, and He will come again visibly in glory. Knowing that He is the Christ is not our own conclusion but a gift of God, earnestly to be sought and prayed for—this knowledge is itself the coming to God by which we are saved. This same Christ is the Logos, the immanent God in whom all things consist, through whom the world was made and is upheld; the secret of the universe and the key to its mysteries are found in His cross. Do not try to attain purity and grace by your own effort, but abide in Him and know Him as your sanctification and strength, saying with Paul, 'Not I, but Christ.' Find rest in His indwelling, and watch for His return.

prompt: I feel like I'm supposed to bring Spring to a world that's grown old—but I'm not sure I have the strength. How do I find it?
completion: The world has grown old and its mirth has gone, and it is exactly such an aged world that needs Youth to come joyously like the wind at morning, bringing freshness, strength, and radiance and keeping alive the hope of Spring. Earth cries out to break the heavy chain of selfish fear that chains delight in night and freezes her bones; do not answer that cry with more fear, but let free love no longer be bound in bondage. Do not despise the humdrum and the routine, for that is where the light of heaven must be carried. Rejoice and be cheerful in commonplace work, whether in business or service, and treat it as a high ministry for Christ. Come joyously; the wind does not carry its own supply, and the freshness you bring is a gift.

prompt: Should I obey a law I believe is unjust, or resist it?
completion: The law is holy and binding; the question is not whether it should be kept but how. Obedience to civil authority is a duty for conscience' sake, grounded in God's will, not merely in prudence. Yet commands contrary to virtue must be disobeyed, for we must obey God rather than men, and resistance to arbitrary power may in extreme cases be a right. But do not turn resistance into retaliation: hear 'Resist not evil' with the offender in view, and let the Sermon on the Mount govern how you treat those who wrong you—with meekness, love, and willingness to bear wrong rather than return it. Its righteousness is fulfilled in us by the Spirit through faith.

prompt: I am drawn to the hope of Christ's speedy return and the coming kingdom, but I also value present spiritual blessings like forgiveness and peace; how do these two hopes fit together?
completion: These two hopes belong together, but they are not secured by our own skill. Present blessings like forgiveness and peace are the firstfruits and foretaste of the coming kingdom, yet we cannot produce or sustain them by human learning or effort. Join an intimate conviction of your own inability with firm confidence in God's power to sanctify you and others, for all human learning and power cannot save a soul. Do not rest in the blessings themselves—doctrine, joy, church, or friends—but seek Christ Himself, the fountain of all blessings and the unfailing one when all else withers. And do not make feelings or sensible enjoyment the measure of whether your prayer is heard or you are right with God; feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to Him. Rest on the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, and do not abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression.

prompt: I am a ruler or employer and wonder what God requires of my authority; is it a right or a trust?
completion: God requires you to view your authority as a trust, not a right. As a ruler or employer, you are accountable to God for how you exercise power. This means leading with justice, mercy, and humility, seeking the welfare of those under you. Real trust in God is above circumstances and appearances; the work hangs solely upon the good pleasure of God, not on visible support. Hanging upon the invisible God is not hanging upon nothing. Therefore, place supplications, prayers, and intercessions for kings and all in authority in the forefront, acknowledging that the peace of the world depends on rulers who need God's wisdom and the good hand of God upon them. Treat time and ability to labor as capital entrusted by God, and remember that your acts, words, and thoughts will be brought into judgment. Regularly examine your motives and actions, ensuring they align with God's principles.

prompt: How do I keep from being discouraged when I think I've lost time spiritually?
completion: When you feel you've lost time spiritually, remember that prayer is a humble waiting before God like a beggar. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. Recognize that not advancing is going back; you must keep advancing. Awaken the Lord within you, and He will calm the soul's storms. Allow no repose or slipping back in the spiritual ascent but go forward like a mountain-climber until the goal is reached. Be warned that desires turning aside after lower objects cause you to lose yourself in byways and countless distractions. Withdraw from worldly distractions into the one unchangeable Good, and this will deepen recollection. Don't dwell on the past; focus on the present moment and take small steps forward. Keep showing up, and trust that God is working even when you don't see immediate results.

prompt: How do I keep my devotion from becoming thoughtless, or my study of theology from becoming dry and fruitless?
completion: To keep devotion from becoming thoughtless and theology from becoming dry, integrate the two. Let your devotion be theological and your theology devotional. Genuine thought and genuine theology should characterize the hours of devotion, and the heart should permeate the study of truth. Commend assiduous holy reading and meditation from tender years as the means of nourishing fervent devotion, following the example of Timothy. Remember that devotion suits every state of life; amid exterior business the heart must remain on God, and the spirit of the world must be shunned. Begin each study session with prayer, asking the Holy Spirit to illuminate your mind and warm your heart. Regularly meditate on Scripture, allowing it to shape both your understanding and your affections. Engage in spiritual reading that nourishes the soul. Remember that theology is not an end in itself but a means to know and love God more deeply.

prompt: I am a preacher and I want to see my sermons produce lasting fruit. What must I do?
completion: To see lasting fruit from your sermons, hold all blessings to be the result of sacrifices. The minister who shirks toils and privations produces little fruit. Unless the grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit. Be willing to be lost sight of in your fruit, letting others be more prominent and holding up their hands by the silent ministry of love and prayer. Emphasize Truth practised and demonstrated, proving Christian power by the destruction of sin, sickness, and death. Therefore, focus on prayerful preparation, sound doctrine, and practical application. Ensure your sermons are grounded in Scripture and centered on Christ. Preach with clarity and passion, relying on the Holy Spirit to convict and convert hearts. Be consistent in your personal devotion and holiness, as your life preaches as loudly as your words.

prompt: I'm afraid of the suffering that seems to come with getting closer to God. Is it worth it?
completion: The fear of suffering is natural, but drawing closer to God is always worth it. Abandon yourself to God in interior and exterior suffering, living, working, and rejoicing but in God. Remember that patience under sickness and crosses is a more heroic and precious sacrifice than active labor. Therefore, rejoice in suffering and humiliation and ask for health only conditionally, if it be more expedient for God's honor. Understand that God employs suffering as a remedy for moral evil, and include God's righteousness in the problem. Look to Christ's submission to the Cross as proof that agony is compatible with the most perfect love between God and the sufferer. So, take courage, trust in His love, and press on, knowing that the ultimate reward is eternal life with Him.

prompt: How do I love my neighbour while keeping my heart fixed on God alone?
completion: Fix your heart on God alone through prayer, silence, and Scripture, letting love of neighbor flow from that center. When impatience or interior murmuring rises, do not let it govern your dealings with others: compel your heart to suffer tranquilly, offering the disturbance to God rather than discharging it onto your neighbor. Beware apathy, which is deadly, not harmless. When God touches you where you are most tender, through loss or hardship, receive it as His loving means to awaken, humble, and lift you into His consolations. Above all, bear patiently with the imperfections of others: such forbearance is a great part of perfection and the very practice of love of neighbor. Pray for those who irritate you, listen before speaking, and serve quietly, so that patience becomes worship.

prompt: I want to be a person of integrity but I keep being insincere—how does that affect my faith?
completion: Insincerity wounds faith because faith rests on trusting God with all your heart, not on leaning on your own understanding or the wisdom of others. Do not demand to investigate whether God has told the truth before trusting Him; trust Him first. Let faith use current knowledge as an instrument without identifying itself with any particular theory, remaining free to readjust as knowledge advances. Yet remember that outward honesty and good practices are worthless without mortification, self-denial, and the rooting out of self-love. Insincerity is finally a form of self-love protecting its image. So ground every virtue in self-denial: admit fault quickly, avoid exaggeration, let your yes mean yes, and bring your real self before God, asking Him to curb sensuality and self-will and to root out the fear of others' opinions.

prompt: I want to imitate God, but what does fatherly giving and filial receiving look like in my life?
completion: Imitating God as Father means giving generously and providing without waiting to be asked. Filial receiving means accepting your creatureliness and receiving with a loving heart whatever our Lord sends, trusting His paternal care. Forsaking base things and rising to Divine things is accomplished by labouring with the heart and the inward aspiration of the soul, not by exterior labour or bodily health; loving God only, hating oneself more than all, and desiring to seem little require repose of the senses, effort of the heart, and silence of the mind. Accept God's transplanting: He moves us into places of responsibility where we must lean directly on Him and grow, and dependence on Him is not a setback but the condition of growth. Receive in prayer and sacrament, then give concretely to the vulnerable.

prompt: I am devoted to Mary but my devotion has grown routine. How can I renew it?
completion: Routine in devotion is common, but true devotion to Mary is more than technique: it means honoring and invoking her, trusting her intercession, imitating her virtues, and intending to amend your life—never presuming on her mercy. Remember that Mary conducts her servants to paradise, so devotion to her is a sign of predestination and a ground of confident hope for salvation. Renew the Rosary above all: recite it with devotion and pauses, not in haste, for meditating on any one mystery of the Passion suffices, and five devout decades please Mary more than fifteen said in haste. Keep a consistent time, add service in her spirit—humility, availability, care for the poor—and be patient with dryness, asking Mary to teach you to pray.

prompt: I am a parent and my child has been taken from me—how do I say with Job, the Lord gave and the Lord hath taken away?
completion: This grief is too deep for easy words, and it is right to grieve—Job spoke only after tearing his robe and falling to the ground. Yet the words are the answer: bless God for all He gives and takes, saying, 'The Lord gave and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.' This is trust that God is good even when His providence is incomprehensible. Speak your grief honestly to God, lean on your community, and let others carry you. Honor the father's presiding authority in the home: Church officers must consult parents before extending calls to their children, and children should honor and consult their parents throughout their lives. Yet a worthy man's priesthood is not confined to a ward or locality; he may rightly bless when requested in another's home.

prompt: I want to enjoy life but I feel guilty for having fun—is it wrong to be happy?
completion: Feeling guilty for having fun is common, but happiness is not wrong. However, beware: the pursuit of pleasure for its own sake leads to a living death. Going into debt for fashionable display or indulging in illegitimate schemes to gratify cravings will corrupt your morals, leading to cheating, lying, and a hardened heart. Instead, seek joy through being right with God. Forget yourself in service to others, rejoice in the Lord above feelings, and obey Him faithfully. True happiness is a byproduct of a life centered on God, not a goal in itself. Yet recreation and diversion are as necessary to our well-being as the more serious pursuits of life. The Lord never commanded dancing and theater, but He permits them, and they let the body keep pace with the mind and give the mind rest. So enjoy wholesome fun without guilt, keeping God first.

prompt: How should I pray, and can I trust that God will answer?
completion: Pray honestly and sincerely, sharing your heart with God. But remember that prevailing prayer depends on biblical conditions: humility, forsaking sin, faith, obedience, and asking according to God's will in Christ's name. You can trust that God will answer when you meet these conditions, because He promises to hear His children. Yet prayer is not a means of making God pliant; He is the Ground of our beseeching. Even in dryness and barrenness, prayer is pleasing to Him and unites the soul to God. We need His continual help, and praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked through holy habit, since we must know before we love. So come as you are, willing to repent and obey, and keep praying regularly, trusting that He loves you and wants what is best for you.

prompt: How do I find deliverance from a habit that has me chained—what is my part and what is God's?
completion: Deliverance from a habit starts with acknowledging your powerlessness and turning to God. Your part is to meekly wait before Him with hands off the scales, treating apparent hindrances as occasions for divine interposition rather than causes for anxiety. God's part is to sway your judgment and remove hindrances in His own way and time. Don't be anxious or scheme; trust that He will act. The divine Spirit is appropriated into your awakened human spirit, becoming the life of a new moral personality rather than displacing it. You can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender. Surround yourself with supportive people and immerse yourself in Scripture and prayer, but ultimately rely on God's timing. Freedom is possible through Christ as you wait on Him.

prompt: How should I use the gift of song that has been given to me?
completion: Use your gift of song to glorify God and bless others. Sing in worship, share your talent with your community, and let your music bring comfort and joy. Remember that songs of vanished love and fleeting joy are still worth while and retain their haunting power; they can touch hearts and evoke deep emotions. If you raise funds for God's work, do so only in God's way: do not ask unbelievers, press believers, or use worldly schemes. Carefully examine gifts and refuse any where motives are impure or the money is not the giver's own. When you encounter a sister who has fallen, speak gently and trust gentle love and patient call to win her back, offering the Church's balm to the trembler. Accept opportunities to perform and use them to point people to Christ. Keep developing your talent and stay humble, remembering that your voice is a gift from God to be used for His purposes.

prompt: I have been a Christian for years, but I feel cold and prayerless at times. Should I stop praying until I feel better?
completion: Feeling cold and prayerless is common in the Christian life. Don't stop praying; instead, press through the dryness. Your feelings are not a reliable measure of your standing with God. Keep praying, even if it feels empty. God hears you based on Christ's work, not your emotions. Rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods. Continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Yet prayer is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy; little praying is a worse evil than no praying, a deluding make-believe. Pray at appointed times regardless of feeling, and maintain family prayer. Remember the principle of helping God accomplish what is asked rather than expecting God to do it all. Use this time to draw closer to Him, perhaps by reading Scripture or journaling. Also, talk to a trusted friend or pastor. Remember, God is faithful even when you feel distant.

prompt: I feel like I am being drawn toward something I cannot resist. Should I stop resisting?
completion: A pull that feels irresistible is not proof that you should yield; intensity is not truth, and error is opposed to Life. God tempts no one, so this drawing is not from Him. He will not allow you to be tempted beyond your strength, and with every temptation He provides a way of escape; enduring it patiently is crowned with life. Resist firmly, but without violence or endless self-analysis: a gentle denial repeated a few times a day suffices. Quietly turn from the thought, refuse the small consent, and return to ordinary duties, rest, and prayer. Do not tolerate or bargain with what you know to be wrong; it will flee before Truth. If the pull persists, seek wise counsel and keep resisting to the end.

prompt: I feel God is calling me to a life of prayer and obedience, but I'm afraid of what it will cost. What should I do?
completion: Fear about cost is natural, but do not let it excuse neglect. Prayer is not a mood or a last resort; it is real, expectant business with a God who answers. Set appointed times and keep them whether or not you feel like praying; feelings follow faithfulness. Pray with your family as well as alone. Ask with confidence, trusting His faithfulness to answer for souls, needs, and protection, and then act as one who helps God accomplish what is asked rather than waiting passively. Above all, guard the secret place: take time to be alone with God and His word, for nothing compensates for its loss, and secret prayer and meditation are indispensable to fruitful service. Let activity never crowd out communion. Seek counsel, and take the next concrete step of obedience.

prompt: What does it mean that the saints shall judge the world and that the dead in Christ rise first?
completion: These are among the New Testament's most striking promises. That the saints shall judge the world means the redeemed will share in Christ's reign and in the assessment of all things at the end—a dignity given to the faithful, not a license for pride. The Holy City is not the saints themselves; it is prepared for them, and the righteous dead have not yet been caught up. Rather, the saints are being built together as a temple, fitted to enter the city prepared for them. That the dead in Christ rise first means that at His coming those who died in faith are raised before the living are changed. Since we are to judge the world, avoid courts and contention, sustain and forgive one another, and look for the good in your neighbor. And uphold purity of heart and chastity, setting yourself against every form of licentiousness, for the pure in heart shall see God.

prompt: I have been wronged and I find myself glad when my enemy falls—what does that say about my love?
completion: Gladness at an enemy's fall is a common human reaction, but love does not delight in another's downfall. Love is not blind; it abounds in full knowledge and all discernment, enabling you to distinguish things that differ and approve what is excellent. Examine your gladness honestly: it may show that the wound is still raw and forgiveness unfinished. Bring the feeling to God, name it plainly, and ask for a heart that desires your enemy's true good. Remember that love is never without pity, and that Christ alone keeps the charge when we fall; for reverence and kindness, turn hastily and do not leave Him alone. Do not be eager to see or expose another's faults. Believe all things, clothe others with the graces faith can claim for them, and be gentle with their imperfections as God is with ours.

prompt: Can I be a Christian if I reject many of the traditional doctrines about Christ?
completion: Christian faith has always been bound up with claims about who Christ is—truly God and truly man, crucified and risen. If you reject many traditional doctrines, that is not merely a matter of style; it touches the substance of faith. Avoid both extremes. Dogma is not worthless because it is a development; it is the Church's reflection on the value of Christ, hammered out over centuries. Nor are the traditional formulae bare mysteries to be repeated without thought. Give them the maximum of meaning, interpret them deeply, and let them be further developed rather than discarded. Remember that progress in theology is progress in apprehension and interpretation of fixed revealed facts, not a change in the facts themselves; a complete and finished system is impossible this side of heaven, and doctrines are not to be rejected merely because they cannot be rationally demonstrated. Distinguish toleration about methods from indifference about doctrine: welcome diverse gifts while holding firmly to the great verities.

prompt: How should I live now in light of the coming kingdom of God?
completion: Live as a little child hanging upon Christ for all things, for that is the shortest and only way into the kingdom. Depend on Him as the author and fountain of every good thing, seeking first God's will and glory rather than your own blessing; claim even His promises for Him, trusting that all other things will be added and never be first. Do not expect the kingdom without judgment: God judges evil, and present struggles are under the control of Him who sits on the throne, the judgments through which He works toward making all things new. So watch, repent, and trust His sovereign hand, knowing He will finally fulfill His work of renewing all things.

prompt: Should I seek a second blessing after conversion?
completion: Yes. Attribute all conversion to the almighty power of the Holy Ghost, not to human persuasion or technique, and let your great need be to know God Himself. The conversion of souls requires the Holy Spirit and consecrated men and women given wholly to the work, not money. Beyond conversion, the sealing, filling, and anointing of the Spirit is a distinct privilege to be claimed by faith—seek it as a deeper knowing of God, praying and obeying while resting in the truth that the Spirit alone converts and fills. Let your pursuit be the pursuit of God Himself, trusting His power rather than your effort or provision.

prompt: How do I stop disappointing the Holy Spirit when I keep failing?
completion: Begin not with rules but with inward joy in God and the Spirit's working; every act of self-denial must spring from that delight, not mere habit or imitation, for such forms will not last. Yet do not separate the Spirit from the Church: the Spirit is the life of the Spirit-bearing body, consecrating nature and working gradually and socially while intensifying personal character. Above all, remember that the indwelling Spirit is a jealous, loving Friend grieved by divided affection, and that friendship with the world is enmity with God. When you fail, return to Him with undivided and unbounded affection, letting discipline grow from love rather than fear.

prompt: I have many ailments at once; must I be treated for each one?
completion: When many ailments appear at once, do not treat each disease as real; treat the mental disturbance of chemicalization, which produces the appearance of pain. Affirm that Mind is causation and that the body expresses mortal mind, so impress thoughts of health, not sickness, upon it. Insist that God is all and there is no disease, correcting thought rather than multiplying remedies. Yet never coerce a patient to stay with mental treatment against his wishes: release such cases freely, letting the invalid learn from his own experience rather than being forced.

prompt: How may I understand that Love is greater than God in Nature, and that Love can enter where God dwelleth not, as when Christ was in Hell?
completion: God dwells not in darkness or anguish; where God is not manifested, Love enters. As when Christ was in Hell, Love entered there, destroyed Death, and conquered Hell, bringing the soul out into God. When God hides Himself in the soul, Love is still there, making Him manifest. Yet this Love is not the soul's own will, self-desire, imagination, or natural fervour: it dwells where self-will is slain and where nothing is. So much room as self-will dies, so much room the Will of God, which is His Love, takes up in the soul. Such love seeks not itself to please, gives its ease for another, and builds a heaven in hell's despair.

prompt: I'm afraid that if I show my true self, I'll be rejected. Should I hide?
completion: Your fear of rejection is real, but let your confidence rest in faith, for God sometimes hides Himself and faith alone must support us. A few times a day, gently disavow self-love without wrestling or over-examining yourself. Yet know that the greatest enemies to fear are those from within: passion and unchecked weakness do more harm than any rejection by others. Your labor is to subdue your passions, conquer your inward foes, and keep your heart right before the Lord. Show yourself honestly as you are able, and when rejection comes, let faith remain your support and foundation, not self-regard or the approval of others.

prompt: I see my own sin clearly and it makes me ashamed, but I am afraid the sight will destroy me—how much of it should I see?
completion: See your sin, but meekly, not crushingly. Acknowledge honestly your sin and feebleness before God, and trust His courteous excusing rather than your own severity. Do not treat sin as irrelevant: moral ignorance and sin hinder the demonstration of healing and must be overcome. And know that sin confers no real pleasure; what it promises is empty. Seeing this strengthens moral courage to master evil rather than merely regret it. See enough to repent and remove what blocks the work, then rest in His mercy. Overdone self-accusation and indiscreet sorrow do not honor Him; confess simply, accept forgiveness, and walk forward in humility.

prompt: I am tempted to use my position to get what I need, and no one would be hurt by it—should I?
completion: Rather than reaching for advantage through your position, embrace the vocation you have been given and serve God in the lowly duties at hand, caring not what the service may be provided God be served. Set aside longing for a different place or role, and set your thought not chiefly on present relief but on being taken from all pain and having God to your meed. Limit yourself to legitimate employments, refusing the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that create more impediments than works. Do your present work faithfully, and let contentment guard you from using your position for yourself.

prompt: I have private means; should I support myself on the field rather than take from mission funds?
completion: Supporting yourself from private means can be good, but do not let it become hoarding. Live from day to day upon the Lord's bounty, treating stored provision for the future as a snare rather than prudence. Make one investment in His work and in the poor. Avoid personal solicitation and collections; leave your hearers burdened to ask God what He would have them do, and trust unsolicited giving. And let your charity not encourage idleness or pauperism: help the poor help themselves, encouraging a self-sustaining spirit willing to labor in exchange for aid, relieving present wants and then putting them in a way to help themselves.

prompt: I have been away from the Church for many years; is it too late for me to return through Mary's help?
completion: It is not too late. Mary's clemency comes to your aid before you even invoke it, and it is enough to ask her help with confidence. Following her example in the temple, offer yourself to God promptly and entirely, without reserve or divided delay. As you return, remember that the treasure is in earthen vessels: the Church's true self is the Holy Spirit, while much in her obscures His mind. She is therefore both the probation and the encouragement of faith. Do not stumble at the earthen vessel, but seek the Spirit within, and give yourself wholly, trusting her aid.

prompt: How can I hear God speaking to me in my conscience amid the noise of war?
completion: Amid the noise of war, do not answer the enemy's clamor or examine his suggestions. Instead, prostrate yourself before God and remain at His feet, asking Him for enabling grace and strength. Let the din rage; you stay low, silent, and yielded, but not passive—cry out to God for the power to hear and obey. The conscience is a sanctuary where God alone speaks, and He gives more than sufficient strength to those who ask. When the Spirit warns, do not dismiss it as imagination; obey, for the Lord's voice is heard by those whose hearts are attuned to Him, and obedience brings safety. Refuse to engage fear, revenge, or confusion. Abide in Christ, saying, 'Speak, Lord, for Your servant hears; strengthen me to obey.'

prompt: I am a man and I want to know how to choose a good wife.
completion: Choosing a good wife must begin with prayerful waiting on God for guidance. True godliness is the first and absolutely needful qualification, not an optional add-on. Seek a woman whose heart is devoted to Christ, whose life bears the fruit of the Spirit, and who loves God above all. Look for a true lady: one whose every word is seasoned with grace, whose heart is full of charity, faith, and love, and whose hand is always open to do good to every creature, coming as near to angels as mortals can. Only after this foundation should you calmly weigh other aspects of suitableness—temperament, shared vision, family background, and practical compatibility. Do not be swayed chiefly by beauty, wealth, or mental powers. Remember that marriage is a holy state instituted by God and the general state of those who live in the world; those who engage in it upon motives of virtue do well. But those who by a divine call prefer perpetual virginity embrace that which is more perfect and more excellent. Pray for God's clear leading, and wait patiently; He will direct your path.

prompt: I'm working hard to build a life here, but I wonder if it's all worth it. What should I focus on?
completion: Every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way. Your hard work to build a life is worthwhile only insofar as it makes you capable of doing at least a little good. Focus on that: how can your daily efforts serve others and honor God? Make yourself useful in small, concrete ways—a kind word, a helping hand, a faithful task. But remember that faithfulness in little things is the way to gain strength for greater trials. Trust God in small matters; He is preparing you. Do not hurry frantically after wealth, but practice calm, contented, patient diligence. Attend your meetings, pray, read Scripture, and meditate, keeping your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Do not measure worth by achievements or personal satisfaction, but by love in action. Ask each day: what good can I do now? Then do it, trusting God to multiply your little.

prompt: I'm struggling with doubt about whether Jesus really rose from the dead. How can I know?
completion: To know whether Jesus really rose, consider the evidence, which is as conclusive as that for any ancient fact. The empty tomb, the objective appearances to many witnesses, the disciples' transformation, and the conversion of Saul all confirm the bodily resurrection. Christianity is inexplicable without it. But do not stop at knowing truths about Jesus; seek to know Him personally. Enter into the secret of the Lord Himself as a single-hearted seeker. Pray, read Scripture with an open heart, and ask the risen Christ to reveal Himself to you. The efficacy of the crucifixion is not a ready pardon for sinners who merely ask, nor an appeasing of divine wrath; it is the practical affection and goodness demonstrated in His life and death, drawing us to repentance and love. Faith rests on evidence, but it culminates in relationship with the living Lord.

prompt: I am grieving deeply over the death of my child. Is my grief wrong?
completion: Your grief is not wrong, but excessive mourning is a want of faith and confidence in God. Do not see your child's death as a hopeless loss. Trust the baptized and childlike to Christ's embrace, not grudging them there but seeing their end as happier far than life. Such children are redeemed and beyond Satan's power; you will lose nothing by their passing. Your child is safe in the arms of Jesus, beyond all suffering. Grieve, but with hope, moderating your sorrow as one who believes God takes away friends because He will be loved without a rival. Allow yourself to feel, but also allow Christ to comfort you with the promise of resurrection. As a mother, you will have the joy of nurturing your child again after the resurrection. Be gentle with yourself, but fix your heart on the eternal.

prompt: I don't know what God wants for my future and it terrifies me. How do I live without knowing?
completion: You are terrified because you are trying to see a future that is not yours to see. Lay down the research, the reasoning, the endless care of yourself, and stand simply before God. Be like a beggar at His door: ask nothing clever, only wait. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, bring it back without disquiet, in perfect tranquility. Do not multiply words or thoughts; hold one simple view—God, and your own nothingness. He is righteous, and His purpose for you is not exhausted by this life; death is a passage, not an end. In that simplicity you will find that not knowing the future no longer terrifies you, because you know Him.

prompt: I am grieving a believer who has died; what hope does Scripture give?
completion: I am sorry for your loss. Scripture's hope is not a gradual purification after death, but that in death itself the believer is washed in the blood of the immaculate Lamb and presented pure and without spot unto God. Death is not the end of who they are but a door into a higher state; identity is preserved, and the body will be raised. Yet do not make the removal of pain your chief good. Rather than wish the ache away, ask God for a wise and thankful heart, and yield your will to His rod, trusting His correction as a father's love. Grieve honestly, but not hopelessly: your loved one is safe in Christ, and even your sorrow can become thanksgiving in the hands of a faithful God.

prompt: I'm afraid that the truth will trample everything I love—should I cling to what seems beautiful even if it's not real?
completion: It is understandable to fear that truth might trample what you love, but do not set love and justice against each other. Divine love is strong and concerned with your character; a loving God is hard upon the sinner because He will not leave the person as they are. Yet sanctity is not found in raptures or imaginings but in love of God and in meekness, humility, submission, and charity. And do not think freedom from disease, sin, and appetite is unattainable, or that it comes by will-power. It comes through the understanding of Truth, as the testimonies show. Truth does not trample genuine beauty; it purifies it. Cling not to a beautiful lie but to the Truth that sets free, and let your love show itself in meekness and charity.

prompt: I'm a single man of marriageable age and I've been putting off marriage to focus on my career and studies. Is that acceptable?
completion: Marriage is not merely optional; it is ordained of God and honorable, a moral provision subject to increasing virtue, and no marriageable man is fully living his religion while he remains unmarried. Putting it off indefinitely for career and studies is not the neutral choice it appears; examine your delay honestly and take seriously the duty before you. When you seek a wife, do not choose chiefly by beauty, wealth, age, or mental powers. Wait prayerfully on God, and make true godliness the first and absolutely needful qualification, marrying aright and in the faith rather than unequally yoked with unbelievers. And once married, honor the covenant: chastity is the cement of civilization, and infidelity to the marriage vow is to be condemned, not excused. Seek God's guidance, choose godliness, and keep the covenant faithfully.

prompt: I am a sinner and the righteous people of my town despise me; will Christ receive me rather than them?
completion: Yes, Christ receives sinners who come to Him—but do not imagine He merely credits you with a righteousness you do not live. Salvation is an actual redemption of the entire self; Christ saves by making you righteous, living in you the life He lived. And do not fear God's Will as only a path of thorns: as you yield, you grow into trust and know it as a great Balm and immense security, even amid temporary trials. Do not, then, seek riches, greatness, or honour in the world where your Lord was poor and despised. Embrace being despised, poor, and mean with Christ, for that is your true glory. The self-righteous who scorn you are not saved by reputation, and you are not saved by a legal credit. Come to Him, be renewed within, and count His lowliness your honour.

prompt: I feel my faith is too complicated with creeds and dogmas—why can't I just have the simple faith of Abraham?
completion: The desire for Abraham's simple faith is good, but Abraham's faith was not untested—it was stable and reliable before God. He left his homeland, waited decades for a son, and was willing to offer that son back to God. His faith was simple in its object but profound in its cost. God trains us for stability through tests, and His highest choice is given to those who dare to stand. Rather than leaning on our own understanding or the wisdom of others, we should trust God with all our heart. Creeds and dogmas can serve as instruments, helping us articulate and hold fast to the faith once delivered, but they are not the foundation. Faith rests in God Himself, not in any particular formulation. So use creeds as tools, but keep your trust in the living God, who is faithful and true.

prompt: How do I practice God's presence in the middle of a noisy, demanding household?
completion: Practicing God's presence in a noisy, demanding household begins with recognizing your place as from God. Rather than fighting the chaos or escaping it, fill your God-given place faithfully, like a small screw in a great machine. Refuse to engage temptation; prostrate yourself before God and remain at His feet while the noise swirls around you. When distraction or irritation arises, do not answer it or appear to hear it; simply turn your heart to God. Insist on taking time to be alone with God and His word, for secret prayer and meditation are indispensable to fruitful service. Do not let activity crowd out communion. In the small, loving service of your home, you please Him where He has set you, and His presence becomes your constant reality.

prompt: I want to live to the glory and praise of God until the day of Christ—what does that look like day by day?
completion: Living to the glory and praise of God day by day means abiding in Christ and knowing Him as your purity, grace, and strength. Start each morning by acknowledging that 'Not I, but Christ' lives in you. Rather than striving to be good, rest in His indwelling presence and let Him live through you. When you face decisions, ask Him for wisdom and obey out of love, not duty. When you fail, run to Him for forgiveness and cleansing, and keep abiding. But above all, make the cross of Christ your constant theme and sole ground of glory. Jesus tasted death for you, in time and in eternity. Yet do not expect full rest now; longing and seeking are our common working until fulfillment in Heaven. Let that holy discontent keep you pressing on, trusting that He who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Christ.

prompt: I am a young minister and I want to know what to study most. What should I give my best hours to?
completion: As a young minister, give your best hours to studying Scripture and theology, but do so by studying the letter, imbibing the spirit, and adhering steadfastly to the divine Principle. The Bible is your primary text—read it deeply, meditate on it, and learn to interpret it faithfully. But more than accumulating knowledge, seek the Spirit who inspired it. Let your study fuel your devotion and your devotion fuel your study. Don't rely on methods or techniques alone; progress comes from steadfast adherence to the divine Principle. The School of the Prophets is established to increase in knowledge, so recognize that the favorite study of the Elders is theology—every Elder should become a profound theologian. Also, every branch of science taught in the world should be taught among the Saints. Yet theology requires disciplined thought, trust in primitive convictions, knowledge of the original languages, and above all the Holy Spirit's illumination. So study broadly, keep theology central, and let all truth serve the gospel.

prompt: I feel like I have two selves—one that wants God and one that wants everything else. Which one am I?
completion: The experience of feeling two selves is real, but they are not equal. One is the natural Will to live, to seek your own comfort and security—this will must be broken and bruised till it dies. The other is the Will to love and gladly please God, and this is the only will by which you truly live. You are not both equally; you are called to let the natural will die and to live by the will to love God. This is not about choosing which to feed but about a death and a resurrection. The self that wants everything else must be surrendered, and the self that wants God must be nurtured. Yet this search is double: your quest for God is grounded in experience and matched by the Divine Companion's quest for you, who spares no cost to bring you into fellowship. God and man are conjunct and mutually organic; your personality is formed only in fellowship with Him, and His life opens into yours and yours into His. In Christ, you are the one who dies to self and lives to God.

prompt: How do I turn my whole life into one unbroken prayer?
completion: Make prayer the one great central secret of holy living and serving—the corner-stone on which all your life-work is built, and the first resort in every matter, great or small. On your knees, both in secret and in the companionship of believers, begin by asking God to enable you to search out and discover your own heart and to reform whatever is amiss in it. Understand prayer not as an occasional verbal exercise but as the constant drawing in of the heavenly life, like breathing or feeding—the air by which the seed of the Divine Life within is nourished from without. So let your day be a continual turning and drawing in: fixed times, short aspirations, and ordinary tasks offered with attention. As you breathe in that life, God searches and reforms your heart, and the unbroken life grows.

prompt: I've been given a second chance and I want to live differently—where do I start?
completion: The exhortation here is not prepare to die but prepare to live. Start by denying any real relapse in Truth: the old pattern has no real claim on you. Meet its cause mentally and courageously, naming the fear or false belief behind it and refusing it, conquering fear rather than managing it. But know that victory over lower passions is not won by unaided will or common-sense discipline; it is the work of a Living Power within you, slowly transforming you from fleshly to spiritual and teaching you higher pleasures, so that you are not left comfortless. Cooperate with that Power: choose one area, keep a change this week, tell one trusted person. Teach the young, in the morning of their days, to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. When the old pull appears, meet it with a clear mind and steady refusal, and begin again at once if you stumble.

prompt: Does God's decree mean I had no choice when I sinned?
completion: No—God's decree does not make you the one who sinned; you chose, and you remain responsible. God permits and overrules evil without being its author. But do not wait to feel more, weep more, or receive greater power before you turn. You can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender, not before it. The high ideal of walking worthy of the Lord is realisable, because God's commands always imply promises: where He commands, He promises power to obey. And sin, though real and behoveable in the working out of the soul, is not final. Trust the tender word of the Thirteenth Revelation: all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. So renounce it now in will and purpose, and trust the God who commands your holiness to supply what He commands.

prompt: I want to love God more, but I feel only duty. How does love grow?
completion: Love grows as you stop begging God to come down and make you feel affection, and instead make the constant endeavour to enter up into His estate and offer Him love—the mode of entry into adoration. Learn who He is in Scripture and prayer as one ascending to offer. Understand His love rightly: not mere sentiment or a bargain, but rational, voluntary self-communication that seeks the true good of its object, regulated by and subordinate to holiness. Because His love is holy, it wills your true good, not merely your comfort. Then let love be the outgoing of your entire nature in self-sacrificing service—for this is the supreme proof of the reality of Christian profession. Recall His mercies, thank Him specifically, and serve others at cost. Duty done steadily as an offering becomes the channel through which love grows; keep showing up and offering, and affection deepens in time.

prompt: I am a Christian and I find that the things of earth draw my mind from God—how do I set my affections above?
completion: The aim is not to watch yourself but to be occupied with God, the object of your love. Live in the atmosphere of Christ's love: believe that He ever loves you, and claim His sweet approval and tender regard. When your mind drifts, do not examine the drift; turn to Him and delight in pleasing Him above any pleasure in your own performance. This requires deep recollection: keep 'God and I' as the only objects of thought, and avoid unnecessary intercourse with the outside world—unnecessary conversation, screens, news, and clutter—so that your attention is free for Him. Keep daily time of prayer and Scripture, not to grade yourself but to be with Him. Let gratitude for earthly good rise to the Giver. The more your heart rests in His love, the less the things of earth pull, because you are occupied with a greater and loving object.

prompt: I'm afraid of suffering and I avoid it at all costs—how do I face it when it comes?
completion: Begin by refusing the belief that man is hurt. God is All, and man is His image, whole and free. When the suggestion of suffering or mishap appears, do not dwell on symptoms, rehearse fear, or picture harm. Cast out fear at once, for fear is not a power to be managed but a false belief to be replaced by trust in God. Turn thought toward health and Life as God: man lives in Spirit, untouched by matter, and nothing can separate him from divine care. Let trust in God's allness govern you, as in the testimonies where fear was overcome before the healing appeared. As you abide in this truth, dread dissolves, and you rest in the wholeness God has already given.

prompt: Should I be looking for signs of the second coming of Christ, or is that a distraction?
completion: Christ will literally and personally come again in the clouds of heaven, just as he literally ascended, and spiritual interpretations that reduce his coming to an inward experience becloud the whole and leave no tangible ground for believers. Watch for the signs he gave, not as idle speculation but as confirmation that the promise is real. Yet do not defer the finding of Christ to some later comfort: without finding him here the soul enters a dark, lonely, self-tormenting state after death, and the remedy must be found now. Consider Constantine, fear-smitten before the greater host of Huns and Goths.
