The messenger of the King of angels promised aid and the token of victory; the emperor gazed on high and beheld the beauteous tree of glory inscribed, "By this sign thou shalt overcome the foe." The victory was made manifest as given by the King Almighty through his holy rood—not by the strength of his army nor by fortune. So too our hope rests not on signs alone but on the King who gives the victory.

prompt: How do I deal with the feeling that God is a stern judge rather than a loving Father?
completion: God the Father is not a vague spirit diffused everywhere without a habitation; he is a person who dwells in a place, and the Son is the express image of his person. The Father and the Son are two distinct persons together in heaven, as John saw the Lamb take the book from the hand of him that sat on the throne. When you feel God as a stern judge, remember that this personal Father is ever nigh. Think of the lost child in the lonely fen: the father appears ever nigh, kisses him, and leads him by the hand to his mother. So God draws near to you as a loving Father. Let parents take heed too: warn them against withdrawing children from a state of perfection or opposing a child's vocation, and against sowing vanity and covetousness in tender minds. Instead, form children in virtue, that they may know this Father's love and never mistake him for a stern judge.

prompt: What becomes of wealth and the beauty of the field when this world passes away?
completion: The Lord has done his share by surrounding us with the elements of wealth—wheat, meat, wool, and all things needful. The earth is full of resources, and it is our business to mold them to our wants by knowledge and labor. There is enough for all, without contending. Riches are no sin in themselves, but a very great and dangerous temptation. Beware of hoarding: keeping riches unused brings leanness of soul and darkness of mind. Put every dollar and every ability out to use for the good of the community. And understand that the temper which trusts in wealth or success does not merely soften and emasculate; it nurses meanly cruel and aggressive tempers, so that the prosperous man strengthens himself in active wickedness. When this world passes away, what passes is our misuse of God's provision, not the provision itself. Receive these gifts thankfully, mold them to your needs, and circulate them in service.

prompt: I am considering marriage—how should I choose a companion, and how much should godliness weigh against beauty or money?
completion: Begin with prayerful waiting on God for guidance in marriage. True godliness is the first and absolutely needful qualification; without it, no beauty, wealth, or brilliance can make a marriage right. Having sought that first, weigh other suitableness calmly. Understand marriage as a serious vocation with sacred duties, not merely a means to private happiness: its end is the mutual enrichment of personality and mutual freedom to fulfil the true ideal of human life. Make no terms with lax views of divorce. Commend mutual tender love and the bearing of each other's faults, for forbearance is the daily bread of marriage. And beware of making marriage a matter of traffic or a money job; a union formed for gain is no true marriage. Make godliness the foundation, let love and forbearance be its walls, and let the rest be weighed in calm, prayerful judgment.

prompt: I have been searching for love in all the wrong places. How do I find the love that lasts?
completion: It is good that you recognize the pattern. Do not settle for a love that merely tolerates flaws; aspire constantly to the perfection of holy love. True love is strong and concerned with character: it corrects, purifies, and refines, and in God justice and mercy are one. Yet love cannot rest until it has sounded all the depths and learnt the perfections of its Beloved and become one with Him. It suffers nothing to intervene between itself and God, springing forward and finding no peace till it has overcome every obstacle and reached the Beloved, for love is strong as death and carries the lover out of himself into the heart of the beloved. Seek first that love; let every human affection be ordered toward it, and no lesser love will finally satisfy you.

prompt: How do I respond when someone asks me why God saved me and not others who were killed?
completion: This is one of the hardest questions. Say honestly that you do not know why God spared you, but do not let the mystery breed disquiet: when we forget God, we need not be troubled, but return to Him with greater trust. Acknowledge the grief and point to Christ, who shares our death and promises resurrection. Then let your answer be a total self-oblation, holding back no secret exception, asking, 'Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?' Do not merely ask what sacrifices are bound, but what sacrifices can be made to God in gratitude for Christ mocked, scourged, crowned with thorns, and dying for our sins. Let a life offered without reservation be your answer rather than words alone.

prompt: How can I be ready to enter into the celestial city when it comes down from God out of heaven?
completion: Readiness begins with a life ordered toward God: prayer, repentance, love of neighbor, and faithfulness in small things. Know that the heavens are literally opened at the place where the Cherubims and the flaming sword keep the way of the tree of life; this is the gate of heaven, and by this way the Holy City will descend. God will roar out of Zion and utter His voice from Jerusalem, shaking the heavens and the earth; then Jerusalem shall be holy and the sign of the Son of man appear in heaven. Yet do not be unsettled, driven by every wind of doctrine, or looking for Christ here and there. Come to God's rest: a settled conviction of the truth, freedom from doubt and fear, and a refusal to chase after every new claim. Keep your conscience clear, trust His grace, and let the promise of the city give you peace.

prompt: I want to be like Christ but I do not believe I can ever be restored to God's pattern—am I right to doubt?
completion: Your doubt is understandable, but you need not wait for a better feeling or greater strength. This very moment you can renounce sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender. Do not languish over the number and magnitude of your sins: all is possible to God, and it is as easy for Him to forgive and blot out innumerable and heinous sins as to forgive one. Of ourselves we cannot even think what is right; all comes to us from God. And with Jesus, affirm that God is the Life of man: individualized existence is restored, not lost in death, which is only a seeming vanishing that Truth restores. So pray, obey, and trust that He will complete what He begins.

prompt: Is the doctrine of the Trinity a meaningless formula, or can it still mean something to a modern person?
completion: The Trinity can feel like an abstract formula, but it is inscrutable, not contradictory, and it still speaks to modern people. It says that God is not a solitary power but a communion of love, and that love and relationship lie at the heart of reality. The Trinity is the necessary complement to God's attributes: within God there is the eternal object of knowledge, love, and will. Yet the Three are not separate individuals like three Gods; the word 'Persons' must express mutual inclusion, so that in the Spirit's indwelling is the indwelling of the Father and the Son. Christian doctrine is the Church's reflection on the value of Christ; it is to be given the maximum of meaning and further developed, not discarded. Approach it prayerfully, and let it shape how you think about God and neighbor.

prompt: Why should I wait patiently for the Lord instead of trying to force change myself?
completion: Waiting on the Lord begins with a willingness to have no will of your own. Be slow to take new steps; do not presume that strong desire or an open door is faith. Bring each step to God in prayer and test it by His Word, yet go further: the true workman waits for the Master's beck, glance, or signal in the time, the way, and the associates of His work, accepting the helpers God provides rather than those preference would choose. And do not despise mere presence before Him. Like a statue placed for the King's pleasure, remain before God content to wait upon His will even when you can do nothing. Prayer is not measured by output but by devotion. When He signals, move with patient, believing expectation; until then, stay.

prompt: How does the Spirit transform me into Christ's likeness?
completion: The Spirit transforms you by turning you again to God, out of whom you proceeded. This is not self-improvement but conversion: becoming as a little child, forsaking all your own imaging and lust, and coming again to the Divine Vision. The Spirit is also the first-fruits and earnest of the coming redemption of the body—not wholly future, nor already complete in the flesh. And do not seek power as your own possession. Receive the Holy Spirit within and upon you, letting Him be the power that causes you to walk in God's statutes. You have no power of your own; the power is His, coming upon you. So turn, renounce your self-made centres, and let Him—not your grip—be the strength that conforms you to Christ.

prompt: I feel God is watching to see if I overcome—what happens if I fail?
completion: God is watching, and His watching is jealous love. All your experiences come as tests, and every step is decisive for your eternal future. He is looking for tested pattern men and women—those who overcome. Let His eye stir you to overcome rather than to despair. Yet when you forget Him, do not be disquieted; a lapse in remembrance is a call to return with greater trust. And go further: abandon yourself to God in interior and exterior suffering alike. Do not seek life, work, or joy outside of Him. Live, work, and rejoice—but only in God. Then failure loses its terror, for you are not carrying yourself. The Father who watches receives the child who returns, and in that abandonment every test becomes a place of His jealous love.

prompt: I want to know how to pray aright; can this book teach me?
completion: Yes, a book can help—if it teaches you the divine model Christ gave. In that model we are bound to recommend to God, before all other things, the exaltation of His own honor and glory, and to beg that the kingdom of His holy grace and love be planted in all hearts. Prayer must also be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress: pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own hearts and reform whatever is amiss in them. And do not think the deep knowledge of Christ is for an intellectual few. In Him all treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hid, and the full, free, open opportunity of knowing Him in His divine fulness is offered to every believer. Read prayerfully, test by Scripture, and press into Him.

prompt: How may I come to be as a little child, hanging upon Christ for all things, and so enter the Kingdom of God?
completion: To become as a little child is the shortest and only way to enter the Kingdom of God and to be like All Things. It is not a technique you cultivate in your own strength but a turning: hanging upon Christ for all things, depending upon the author and fountain of them. Cast all else out of your heart, because God would possess it alone—beg this favor and do your part. Yet do not stiffen your will against His guidance. Keep a will of wax, pliable in His hand, and go on boldly like a child held by God's hand. When you stumble in little things, do not be daunted; rise and continue. The child who hangs upon Him, whose heart is emptied for Him alone, and who rises undaunted from stumblings—this is the one who enters.

prompt: I want to be remembered for something good, but I feel insignificant. Does my life matter?
completion: Your life matters, but not as the world counts mattering. Count yourself as already dead, since you must die some day, and have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over, regret, and detest your offences and faults; it is not now the time to rejoice but to lament with all sincerity of heart. Yet do not fear that God abandons you. The eternal Father who cares today will care tomorrow, either withholding trouble or giving invincible courage to bear it. Knowing your need of His grace, resolve never wilfully to forget Him and to live in His presence even when consolations are withdrawn. Your significance rests not in a legacy but in that faithful presence.

prompt: I fear God's punishment so much that I want to hide from Him rather than run to Him—how should I flee?
completion: It is natural to want to hide when you are afraid, but hiding from God never works. Flee by committing yourself to GOD's protection in danger and finding His Word sweet and sufficient in peril. Then resist the devil boldly on holy ground, armed with the breastplate of righteousness and the shield of faith, claiming the promise that he will flee. Remember that God never forsakes us until we first forsake Him; the real danger is not His anger but our own departure. So fear to leave Him, and remain always with Him. He is not a tyrant waiting to crush you but a Father who welcomes the returning child; confess your fear and sin honestly, and let His forgiveness calm you.

prompt: Is a minister of another denomination truly ordained?
completion: A minister is an ambassador and messenger of God, judged by faithfulness rather than popular approval. He must reprove sin sincerely, without softening the Gospel to soothe hearers, and visit all the sick, esteeming a man's immortal soul above his present favor and fearing none but Him who can destroy both soul and body. He must avoid both extremes: the hermit's withdrawal and the popularizer's prayerless activism, remembering that time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. Yet honor both kinds of ministry: the voice that speaks for God and the hidden force that supplies power through holy sympathy and silent prayer. Each should be true to his own ministry, and where such faithfulness is found, its orders bear good fruit.

prompt: I am afraid of the day of judgment—how can I be ready to give an account of my stewardship with joy?
completion: Fear of judgment can be a healthy wake-up call, but do not wait for joyful feelings before you rejoice. Count it all joy by faith, reckoning the trial a blessing, and choose to rejoice even when feelings fail until praise becomes a habit. Live in daily readiness for the LORD's return, able to give an account of your stewardship with joy, using time, money, and gifts faithfully and keeping short accounts with God. Yet do not make gloom or perpetual self-condemnation your safe temper; strenuously lift your heart to God's goodness and exult in it, for that is the only safe temper for tempted men. Seek His loving-kindness in all the breadth and open air of common life—in whatsoever things are true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—while not missing behind them the greatest Reality, God Himself.

prompt: I am afraid that God is too angry with me to hear my prayers; is there someone who can plead my cause before him?
completion: Yes—Jesus Christ is the one who pleads your cause before the Father; He is your advocate, and His finished work is why you may come at all. Come with reverence, approaching prayer with trembling, shutting your senses to distractions and observing strict silence of tongue and body. Yet come with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, for God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask. Remember that of ourselves we can attain to no good thing and have nothing to offer God that was not already His. Our one recourse is to turn to Him in every occurrence in prayer as guilty, poor, and needy beggars, weak and miserable, yet as His children, with holy fear mingled with love, peace, and recollection.

prompt: What is the one thing that will remain to me if I lose everything in this war?
completion: If you lose everything in this war, the one thing that remains is your courage, your confidence, and your good-will. These are indestructible because they are of God. Even when all else is stripped away, you can go on joyously, courageously, and confidently. But do not merely endure evil—resist it firmly. Error is opposed to Life and will flee before Truth. Stand firm against every form of evil, knowing that Truth is omnipotent. Moreover, remember that Christ is the stronger who divides the spoils; He claims the world's beauty and learning for His service and tunes them to celestial melody. So even in loss, you gain the treasures of heaven, and all that is true and beautiful becomes yours in Him. Hold fast to these gifts, for they are the essence of your being and cannot be taken from you.

prompt: I am a person of faith and I want to know how to pray.
completion: To pray, begin by entering the inmost chamber of your heart and shutting the door of your senses. Adore God in spirit and in truth, with an intelligence and will purified from every phantom of earth. Approach Him with a pure heart, a free conscience, and unfeigned faith. But do not leave your mind behind—seek the full assurance of understanding and an abundance of conviction. Let your heart be made strong and full of love, and engage your mind in loving God. Remember that continual help of God is needed, so cultivate a holy habit of thinking of Him often. Since we must know before we love, let your prayer be a continual being with God, and He will draw near to you.

prompt: I've been told the spiritual and temporal should be kept separate in the church. Is that true?
completion: The idea that spiritual and temporal matters should be kept separate is false. All things are spiritual before God, and He has the right to guide temporal as well as spiritual affairs. Business, labor, and daily life are not outside His counsel. The church should not divide life into sacred and secular compartments, but should acknowledge God's sovereignty over every aspect of existence. Moreover, one need not be always at church to be with God; you can make an oratory of your heart and hold familiar conversation with Him in meekness, humility, and love. The sacraments and order of the church guard the truth that spiritual life is God's gift, received and not manufactured—not as magic, but as means of grace that keep us in the gift. Thus, in all places and tasks, you may commune with God and seek His guidance.

prompt: I am a recent convert and feel overwhelmed by all the doctrine I do not yet understand—where should I start?
completion: As a recent convert, begin by making a total sacrifice of yourself to God. Ask, 'Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?' and hold nothing back in your heart. Conversion is not merely learning doctrine but an entire oblation of self. So start by surrendering your will completely to Him, without secret exceptions. But remember that conversion is wrought by the almighty power of the HOLY GHOST, not by human persuasion or effort. Your great need is to know GOD as the worker, and to yield to His Spirit. As you study doctrine, seek a genuine readjustment between faith and modern knowledge—a fresh correlation that does not tamper with principle on either side. Let your first priority be to give yourself wholly to God, and He will lead you into all truth.

prompt: I am in a position where I could quietly help a poor person who is ashamed to ask—how should I do it?
completion: If you are in a position to help a poor person who is ashamed to ask, do so discreetly and respectfully. But first, never oppress the poor or take advantage of their vulnerability. The Scriptures warn that those who oppress the poor will come to nakedness, thirst, and hunger without means of supply. So let your help be pure and without any hint of exploitation. Offer assistance in a way that preserves their dignity, perhaps through a third party or by making it seem like a natural opportunity. Be sensitive to their feelings and avoid drawing attention to their need. Provide practical help, such as groceries, paying a bill, or offering employment opportunities. Do it without expecting anything in return, and keep the matter confidential. Your kindness should be an expression of love and compassion, reflecting God's care for the poor. And if the person is sick, support their trust in the power of Mind, telling them that their strength is in proportion to their courage. Finally, encourage the poor to be honest, thankful, and frugal, and remind them that coveting another's goods is as wicked as miserly hoarding.

prompt: I've been hurt by the church and want to leave. Is there still a place for me among God's people?
completion: I'm sorry you've been hurt by the church. While you can make an oratory of your heart and converse with God in meekness, humility, and love apart from church, do not treat your membership in the Church as a loose affiliation. It is a real bond carrying personal obligation. Cleave meekly and mightily to Holy Church, for she is the unbroken blessed Common, the body of Christ. Yet acknowledge that the Church's divisions have made her less actual to men than the nation, and therefore less powerful. Your pain is real, but the Church is not broken; she is holy and beloved. Find solace in her common teaching and in the communion of saints. Even if you step away for a time, remain united in heart to the Church, and let your heart be an oratory where you meet God and His people in love.

prompt: I want to know the true church; how can I identify it?
completion: To identify the true church, look for a visible, unified body that witnesses to the central truths of the faith with authority. It honors both enthusiasm and sanity, valuing religious fervor while maintaining sound instruction and order. The true church is a permanent community whose conservative and educational functions supplement its evangelistic zeal. It holds firmly to essentials like the Trinity, the deity of Christ, and salvation by grace, and it allows freedom on non-central points. Importantly, this Church cares only that the individual is pure in heart and the nation honourable; it is indifferent to personal success and national expansion. It is ready to suffer for its testimony. You can recognize it by its fidelity to the gospel, its love for one another, and its balanced life of worship, teaching, and service.

prompt: I want to spend my one life well—how do I balance the joy of the present with the fear of what's coming?
completion: To spend your one life well, do not seek a middle way of serving both God and the world; such a compromise brings gloomy wretchedness. Instead, follow Christ all the way, that He may complete His process in you. Seek joy not by trying to feel happy but by being right with God. Forget yourself in service to others, rejoice in the Lord above feelings, and obey Him faithfully. Cling steadfastly to God and His likeness, trusting that harmonious Life destroys the belief in what Life is not. Do not let fear and doubt overshadow your clear trust in God. The joy of the present is found in recognizing that God is Life, and in Him there is no sickness, sin, or fear. Calmly trust that His harmonious Life is your life, and that whatever seems to threaten it is a false belief. As you hold to this truth, fear dissolves, and you can enjoy the present as a reflection of God's goodness, knowing that your future is secure in Him.

prompt: I feel too shy to attend Mutual Improvement—how can I be reached?
completion: Feeling shy about attending Mutual Improvement is normal, but do not let anxiety rule you. Keep yourself in God's presence and avoid hurry and over-eagerness, for over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Withdraw as much as possible from acquaintance and from men, and abstain from affairs that hinder your purpose. Seek with jealous care the place, time, and means most suited to quiet and contemplation. Lovingly embrace silence and solitude, and fly the agitation of a world never at rest. When self-love stirs, gently disavow it a few times a day without violent resistance or excessive introspection; the gentle denial suffices. In this way, you will be reached by God's peace and guided in what to do about Mutual Improvement. Trust that He will open the way in His time, and do not force yourself beyond what is peaceful.

prompt: I wonder whether the differences among Christians today are as serious as those in the early centuries, and what the history of dogma can teach me about them.
completion: The differences among Christians today are serious, but the history of dogma offers insight. Dogma is the product of the Greek spirit working on the soil of the Gospel, preserving both the Christian content (monotheism and the significance of Christ) and the philosophic form. It did not simply continue New Testament theology or the whole richness of early Christian preaching. Its presuppositions were the fundamental motives of the Gospel, the common preaching concerning Christ, the Christian use of the Old Testament, and the Greek spirit. Today's differences often reflect similar underlying issues. By studying the history of dogma, we can see how the Church articulated its faith in response to these presuppositions. Moreover, we must not reduce Jesus to a figure small enough to be fully comprehended; the Gospels present Him in the richness of His mysterious person as Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, man and God. That manifold picture is a self-evidencing fact. Learning to distinguish central truths from secondary matters, we engage present divisions with humility and charity.

prompt: I worry that Christ's own words about Jonah and the flood settle the historical questions; am I bound to read them as strict history?
completion: You are not bound to flatten Christ's words into a strict chronicle, but neither should you dismiss the historical question. The earliest testimonies present Jesus appealing to real events in Israel's memory—Jonah and the flood—as signs of judgment and mercy. These sayings were recorded within the apostolic age, too soon after the events for myth to form, and in an age of historical inquiry rather than credulity. Critically examined, they belong to a first-century Jewish prophet speaking to a skeptical generation; they are not slow legendary growth. From the faith that Jesus is Messiah, we read them as authoritative teaching about repentance and judgment. Far from dissolving him, honest criticism leaves the historical Christ more firmly established as the central fact of history, and the luminous reality of his Life is affirmed rather than explained away.

prompt: How do I love God equally in pain and in pleasure?
completion: Loving God equally in pain and pleasure begins by settling why you come to him: not for the comfort or pleasure the practice brings, but from love and because God wills it. Worldly pains and pleasures are not comparable to spiritual ones, so do not weigh them against each other or bargain for relief. Be careful for nothing and fear nothing; desire only not to offend God. This is possible because God is not a distant sovereign sitting apart in ease: he is passible, grieved over sin, and his holiness requires and his love provides atonement. The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world expresses an eternal fact in God's nature. In pleasure, receive the gift and turn it into obedience; in pain, do not let it purchase your devotion. Keep a steady rhythm of prayer and service, and let blessedness—God's own joy—be the controlling element of your love.

prompt: I'm at peace with the world and my life. Why would I need God at all?
completion: Your peace is worth taking seriously, and it is not wrong to enjoy a settled life. But consider what your peace is made of. We are not isolated selves who happen to need a God alongside us; human personality is formed only in fellowship, and God's life opens into ours as ours opens into his. A peace built on the world's goods alone is a truce, not a homecoming. God is a God of deliverances who keeps his people in answer to prayer—yet his purposes are fulfilled in the death of some as in the deliverance of others. So do not seek him only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or you are sick and lonely, as though a single cry or petulant demand could obtain his gifts. He asks steady, persistent desire. Ask honestly what your peace rests on, and whether there is a longing in you that only fellowship with him can finally meet.

prompt: How do I stop being distracted by images and fantasies when I try to pray?
completion: Distraction in prayer is common, and the first step is not to panic. Come to prayer like a beggar waiting at a door: you have nothing to offer and everything to receive, and you need God's continual help. When images or fantasies arise, do not scold yourself or wrestle with them; gently notice them and recall your mind to God's presence in tranquility, without disquiet. Praying, being with God, and thinking of him often are linked through holy habit—we must know him before we can love him. But do not imagine prayer is easy or naturally congenial. It is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy, and little praying is a worse evil than no praying, a deluding make-believe. A short phrase of Scripture can serve as a quiet anchor, and stillness beforehand helps, but do not make technique the point. With practice your capacity to stay present will grow.

prompt: I'm afraid that my past will always define me—can God really come between me and it?
completion: Your fear is understandable, and the past can feel like a weight that follows you. The Christian answer is that God offers forgiveness and a new beginning, but this is not a purely spiritual transaction kept apart from daily life. All things are spiritual before God, and he has a right to guide your temporal affairs as well as your inner life—your work, your relationships, and the practical outworking of your past. And the past's hold is not merely external: the flight from God runs down the labyrinthine ways of the mind, through memory, shame, and fantasy. Yet God follows there too, with unhurrying chase and unperturbed pace. When you confess your past, he does not hold it against you. Beyond the records and the witnesses, the Spirit of God bears record in your heart of the living Redeemer, and that witness exceeds all other evidence. Your identity is no longer finally determined by what you did.

prompt: I was raised to believe in God, and the arguments seem only to confirm what I already held; is that a legitimate way to believe?
completion: Yes, and this is closer to how faith actually lives. Religion is not produced by proof, nor destroyed because proof is insufficient to some minds. Faith springs from the soul itself, and the arguments are corroborations that awaken, explicate, and confirm an intuitive conviction already present—not a complete demonstration. Logic itself presupposes God, and finite premises cannot reach the Infinite; the bridge of argument is entered and left only by leaps of intuition. Nor need you fear a clash with science: our religion will not contradict the facts of science, whose leading principles are eternal facts, and God never made something out of nothing but organized the earth from existing matter. So let proofs confirm what your soul holds, resting your belief on that deeper ground.

prompt: I am afraid that if I give everything to God I will lose myself. What should I do?
completion: Your fear is understandable, but notice what it assumes. Of ourselves we can attain to no good thing, and we have nothing to offer God that was not already His; so surrender cannot impoverish you, for all you give was His gift first. When you forget God—and we all do—that lapse need not cause disquiet. Let every lapse become a return with greater trust. Nor fear that surrender leaves you destitute: God supplies all need, often through unexpected and timely provision, and extremity is His opportunity. Our one recourse is to turn to Him in every occurrence in prayer—guilty, poor, and needy beggars, weak and miserable, yet His children—with holy fear mingled with love, peace, and recollection.

prompt: I am a poor old man near seventy and my sight is dim and my strength fails—what promises are mine in old age?
completion: Your age and frailty are real, but hear the true exhortation of this Church and Kingdom: not prepare to die, but prepare to live. Children should be taught in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. The aged world, whose mirth has gone, needs Youth to come joyously like the wind at morning, bringing freshness, strength, and radiance and keeping alive the hope of Spring. And do not despise your hidden place: the calm old age of a pure conscience and the hidden prayers of lowly saints are what uphold the proud world, which is not self-sustaining. So tend what strength remains, welcome the renewing spirit, and let your quiet prayers and clear conscience be your lasting gift.

prompt: I feel like I'm not doing enough for my community—how do I know when I'm doing what God wants?
completion: It's good that you care, but be careful: curiosity, ambition, and restlessness multiply occupations and create more impediments than works. Limit yourself to legitimate employments—the plain duties already before you—and refuse to add more out of anxiety. Do not imagine you can meet the need by your own sufficiency: confess your insufficiency, for the conviction of helplessness is the condition of receiving Christ's all-sufficiency. Then take firm hold of that all-sufficiency with a faith that will not accept less than all. Yet watch your prayers: do not ask God for what you should do yourself in ordinary wisdom, nor demand signs. Use the light God has already given, and let your asking be for grace to do faithfully what lies in your hands.

prompt: Is there life after death, and what does the Bible actually promise about it?
completion: The Bible speaks of life after death, but go deeper: mortality is not real as such. Being is immortal and inseparable from Deity, so belief in a righteous God gives reason to expect continuance—His purpose for the higher spirits is not exhausted by this life. Immortality is a corollary of that belief, not a mere wish. Scripture then treats death not as an end but as a door to a higher state; it comforts rather than despairs for the righteous dead, affirms that identity is preserved, and promises the resurrection of the body. So the biblical hope rests not on the reality of death but on the immortal being that is never separated from God.

prompt: How do I tell the difference between a living faith and a dead conception of God that's making my prayers empty?
completion: The emptiness you feel is not mainly a technique problem; it is a revelation problem. A dead conception of God makes prayer empty because you are speaking to a figure of your own making—distant, transactional, or merely moral—and no amount of raised voice, multiplied words, or refined method will make that figure answer. Living faith flows from a fresh sight of who God actually is: holy, near, faithful, and speaking. That sight calls for worship in spirit and in truth, with an intelligence and will purified from every phantom of earth. So enter the inmost chamber of your heart and shut the door of the senses, coming with a pure heart, a free conscience, and unfeigned faith. And take courage: God, who understands all things, hears the earnest supplication of the soul and your innermost thoughts, just as human invention carries messages across great distances. Ask in faith, nothing wavering, and your prayer will not be empty.

prompt: I am a minister and wonder whether I should be bound to one place or go wherever doors open—how do I know the Spirit's leading?
completion: The question is not finally settled by committees, votes, or officials, but by the Holy Spirit's appointment and direction. Begin in prayer, asking the Spirit to make His will plain, and let your decisions echo the early church's discernment: 'It seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us.' Human counsel is valuable, but it is not the rule of the church; the Spirit is. The servant of Christ has one Master, and He is guided by the Spirit as to time and place, not bound by human direction or fixed rules. Yet remember where the promised power lies: along the line of duty and obedience to Christ's command to reach the world. The fulness of the Spirit is given as we obey and step out into His plans for the world, not for selfish enjoyment. So ask not where you will be comfortable but where obedience to the gospel takes you, and there expect the Spirit's power to go before you.

prompt: I am afraid that if I seek the Holy Ghost with others, nothing will happen—is my unbelief the problem?
completion: Unbelief may indeed be part of the problem, but it is not the only thing to examine. Keep holy vigilance: the enemy sows suggestions and discouragements, and we must never consent to them in the will. When fear says nothing will happen, call upon the indwelling Holy Ghost to expel every evil suggestion at the command of faith, refusing to agree with the lie. But do not seek power as your own possession. Receive the Holy Spirit within and upon you, letting Him be the power that causes you to walk in God's statutes; you have no power of your own. Remember that your spirit naturally loves truth and virtue, yet it must be enlightened by the Holy Ghost to overcome the flesh and the power of the Devil. So gather with others in expectant prayer, not as a technique but as obedience, asking in faith and trusting God to give the Holy Spirit to those who ask.

prompt: If Christianity keeps developing, how can I be sure it will not one day be outgrown?
completion: Honest questions deserve sympathy, not scolding. Doubt is not rebellion; it is often the doorway from the unreasoning faith of childhood to the profound convictions of maturity. So do not be afraid of the question, and meet it with an orderly presentation of the facts. Christianity has developed across centuries—doctrine, worship, and practice have changed—and that does not mean it will be outgrown; it means it is alive. But do not explain it wholly by its historical antecedents or human causes, as though it were merely a natural product of its environment. It is a new beginning by divine power, even as we examine honestly the conditions under which it arose and the men on whom it operated. And remember that advancing stages are gained through growth, not accretion, and through the scientific work of proving God individually. Accumulating reading will not carry you; proving God for yourself will.

prompt: What does it mean to walk in the Spirit day by day?
completion: Walking in the Spirit is not a technique for pleasant days; it is a vow to espy God in all things and deny self in all things, counting the cost. That means finding Him not only in worship and consolation but in the common, the dull, and the unwelcome—the commute, the chores, the difficult person, the unanswered prayer. Self-denial is the daily shape of it: saying no to the flesh so that the Spirit's life can flow. But do not seek power as your own possession. Receive the Holy Spirit within and upon you, letting Him be the power that causes you to walk in God's statutes; you have no power of your own. And remember how He comes: in power and love, gentler than the morning gale, lighting crowns on sainted heads and proclaiming life to come. The dullest walk becomes lit with wisdom when we look for that God there. So begin each day asking not for comfort but for eyes to see Him in everything, and for grace to deny yourself in everything.

prompt: I feel empty after receiving a fresh touch from God—do I need to be filled again already?
completion: Feeling empty after a fresh touch of God is not failure but an invitation to the next step: we must learn to breathe out as well as breathe in. The Spirit fills a vacuum, and vacuums are made by pouring ourselves out. Look around—needs and hungers are empty spaces waiting for the Spirit to fill them through you. Do not settle for a vague doctrine of filling or suppose it impossible: being filled unto all the fulness of God is the climax of the Spirit's strength and Christ's indwelling, a matter of personal experience as the proper conditions are fulfilled. And remember that the touch you received was never a possession to keep in idleness. Nearness to God is a capacity to be perpetually renewed by active enthusiasm toward Him, not a condition retained in laziness. Pour out, and He pours in; stay eager, and the emptiness becomes room for His fullness.

prompt: I feel guilty resting when I'm ill, as if I've broken some law of health and must pay for it. Is that true?
completion: No, it is not true that resting when ill breaks a law of health that demands payment. But be careful of two errors. Do not affirm sickness as your identity—you are not "the sick one," and illness is no part of who you truly are. Nor refuse to acknowledge sin where it is present, for sin must be faced and destroyed, not excused. These differ in kind and effect: sickness is a condition to be healed, sin a wrong to be forsaken. Let the healing be done not from self-condemnation, guilt, or doubting trust, but from the moral might of Mind and firm trust in Truth. If this startles you out of the dream of suffering, understand the motive: the shock is given to facilitate recovery, not to condemn you. Rest without guilt, since rest is not payment for sin; let illness be healed and sin destroyed, each according to its nature, and let neither define you.

prompt: How may I find the Love of God when I seek it in my own will, self-desire, images, opinions, affections, and natural devotion, and lose the substance by hunting after a shadow?
completion: You are seeking God in your own will, desires, images, opinions, affections, and natural devotion, and so you grasp a shadow instead of the substance. Yet do not read your darkness as proof that God is absent: the gloom may after all be the shade of His hand outstretched caressingly, and the God you seem to flee is the very One you seek. To forsake base things and rise to Divine things is accomplished by labouring with the heart and by the inward aspiration of the soul—not by exterior labour or bodily health. Loving God only, hating oneself more than all, and desiring to seem little in others' eyes require repose of the senses, effort of the heart, and silence of the mind. And know that finding God increases both joy and the power of suffering; yet joy becomes greater than pain, and Good so much greater than Evil that Evil becomes negligible. Turn inward, then, and labour there, trusting the hand that casts the shade.

prompt: I see people worshipping in different ways and I wonder if any of it is true. How do I know?
completion: It is understandable to wonder about truth when worship looks so different. But spiritual worship is not vague inward sincerity detached from form; it was realized in definite institutions. In the Lord's Supper, the ruling idea is sacrifice—the sacrifice of thanksgiving offered by the community. So look for worship that embodies this: a community gathered around a definite institution, offering itself in thanksgiving and sacrifice to God. Yet do not prize some singular special shewing above the general beholding of God in all; take all generally and behold God in all, not clinging to any special thing. And beware the cold, prohibitive religion that binds joys and desires with briars, the Chapel of "Thou shalt not" that fills the Garden of Love with graves. Choose rather the worship where souls are pleasant and happy as God their father, and let warmth and gladness be your test of truth.

prompt: I am fixed on the pain I feel and cannot lift my heart to the bliss I am to trust.
completion: It is hard to lift your heart when pain holds your attention, and that struggle is real. But do not let your longing settle for mere present relief. Set your thought higher: on being suddenly taken from all pain and having God to your meed. The Fifteenth Revelation lifts the soul above its suffering to this—that pain will not have the last word, and God Himself is your reward. Yet do not live outside the sense of His love, letting hardness and sorrow remain unlit. Keep yourself in the love of God by constant trust and constant obedience; then hard things become easy, and sorrow is silver-lined with hope. And do not measure progress by claims or words, but by fruits: test yourself by whether you live the supreme good and demonstrate healing, letting your fruits prove your understanding. Let that hope pull your heart upward, above the pain you feel.

prompt: Is liberty simply being left alone to do as I please?
completion: Liberty is not simply being left alone to do as I please. We are called to liberty, but we must not use it as an occasion to the flesh; instead, we serve one another in love, for the whole law is fulfilled in loving our neighbor as ourselves. Christian liberty is not a license to sin but a freedom to love. Government must protect the Saints' religious rights equally with other denominations and not interfere with worship. Yet true rest is not found by removing trouble or stopping our heart; it is found by giving everything up to Christ, even our work, believing He has taken it all. We keep still and trust while He bears the government on His shoulder.

prompt: I am tempted to doubt GOD's faithfulness when I fail to trust Him—does my unbelief change His faithfulness?
completion: No, your unbelief does not change God's faithfulness. God remains unchangingly faithful even when our faith fails, for He cannot deny Himself. Our doubt does not alter His character or His promises. Yet unbelief brings loss: it robs us of peace and hinders our experience of His blessings. But we must learn to trust most when all else fails, learning strong faith by standing firm amid severe testings and thanking God for the school of sorrow. Our confidence rests not in our feelings or efforts but in the divine faithfulness of Him who calls us, being confident that what He has promised He is also able to perform.

prompt: I am tempted to despair because of the number of my sins; can I still hope for pardon?
completion: Yes, you can still hope for pardon, but do not treat sin lightly. Unrepented sin accumulates and destroys the ability to do right, and a guilty conscience can weigh you down. Therefore, repent sincerely and reform your life. God's mercy is greater than your sins, and if you confess and forsake them, He will forgive. Remember that God tempts no man, and He will not allow you to be tempted above your strength; He provides an issue with every temptation, and enduring temptation patiently is crowned with life. Indeed, temptation is not sin but the means of proving virtue and gaining great profit, since the life of man upon earth is a warfare. Light temptations, suspicions, sadness, depression, and pusillanimity are mere nothings which a good will puts to flight by an elevation of the soul to God.

prompt: How do I seek God early, as the Psalmist says, when I am exhausted and afraid?
completion: Seeking God early means prioritizing Him at the start of your day and in your life. When you are exhausted and afraid, turn to God first. See God on the skyline in the attitude of a sentinel: the Lord is thy Keeper, thy Watchman, who neither slumbers nor sleeps. He assumes responsibility for thy life, making thee feel thy responsibility for things within thy power while relieving thee of things too great for thee. So life is hallowed by being watched and peace is secured by His guard. Aim at cheerful and willing waiting, for pining savours of unwillingness and discontent; the lover of God should be serenely glad. Remember that God is nearer than all else, speaking in conscience and mind, and when every worldly thing passes away, God remains to the soul that seeks Him early.

prompt: I am a person who has sinned greatly. Can I still be saved?
completion: Yes, you can still be saved. No matter how great your sins, God's grace is sufficient. But let the restorer identify with the sinner, confessing his own faults, and point to the fountain opened for sin. Following Christ, who took our sins and made them His own, we approach not from superiority but in humility. There is no salvation but in the way God has pointed out, and no hope of everlasting life but through obedience to the law affixed by the Father of life. Remember that man is a potential child of God, not meant for a dark chaotic life; the full nature may break forth in one life, and power is given to become sons of God. So do not give up hope; turn to Christ and accept His forgiveness.

prompt: There are poor families in my ward, including my own relatives, and I feel overwhelmed. What is my duty toward them?
completion: Feeling overwhelmed is understandable, but the care and instruction of the poor is the pastor's first obligation, so it must not be pushed aside for other concerns. Feed the flock with the word of God, teaching plainly that the poor are to be cared for, and serve your own relatives without favoritism or neglect. Keep prayer at appointed times whether or not you feel the spirit of prayer, gather your family in prayer, and help God accomplish what you ask by visiting, giving, and organizing the ward rather than expecting God to do it all. Require those who receive help to be honest, thankful, and frugal, and teach that coveting another's goods is as wicked as miserly hoarding. Let instruction and care go together, so the poor are both fed and taught.

prompt: I'm rich and I feel guilty about my wealth. What does the gospel ask of me?
completion: Guilt about wealth is not unusual, but remember that your wealth belongs to the Lord and is uncertain; you hold it as a steward, not as an owner. The gospel asks you to use it for the Gospel and the poor, providing for your family and paying fair wages, and to warn yourself against covetousness and the idolatrous love of property. Do not hurry frantically after more wealth; practice calm, contented, patient diligence, attend your meetings, pray, read scripture, and meditate, keeping your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Do not measure worth by public display, and do not despise the prayers of the poor and desolate, for their intercessions rise with more than royal pomp. Give generously and deliberately, letting your goods serve God's work rather than your reputation.

prompt: I have been given a large inheritance—should I keep it or give it away?
completion: A large inheritance is a significant responsibility, and no one should pressure you with solicitations or collections for God's work. Instead, let yourself be burdened to ask God what He would have you do, and trust that giving which is unsolicited and freely offered is the right kind. Remember that it is all the Lord's and we are only his stewards: the faithful pattern is to put in ten dollars where one is taken out, and to pay more tithing rather than less. Do not press to know the hidden counsel of God or treat its hiddenness as a failure of faith; trust the hidden Deed to God's goodness and occupy yourself only with what is open—providing for your family, deciding before God how much to keep and give, and acting in freedom rather than under pressure.

What are the potential obstacles to adopting the Phonebloks concept, including economic and aesthetic factors? Answer according to: We all know that the cycle of electronics consumerism is broken. Because it's an endless money drain for consumers to keep their gadgets current. Because the never ending desire to show off new features leads to bloat and complexity of design. And because all our outdated, abandoned gadgets have to go somewhere. According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, we Americans threw away 310 million electronic gadgets in 2010 alone. That's about 1.8 million tons of toxic, nonbiodegradable waste in our landfills.
At least somebody's expressing concern about this problem—nearly 15 million somebodies, actually. That's how many people have watched a viral YouTube video called Phonebloks, which touts a new phone concept by Dutch designer Dave Hakkens.
Hakkens wants the people of Earth to rise up and demand a new kind of cell phone, in which the various components—camera, processor, GPS, screen—snap together like Legos.
This system, he says, would let you build exactly the phone you want. If you keep your files online, you could remove the storage module and replace it with a bigger battery. If you are older, you could unplug the camera and replace it with a bigger speaker.
Above all, though, he suggests that the Phonebloks concept would dramatically cut down on e-waste. You wouldn't throw away a phone every other year; instead you'd own just one phone that's built—and rebuilt—to last. If one component broke or became obsolete, you'd just unplug it and replace it with a new one.
Clearly, this concept is consumer catnip. It offers the promise of staying current—without the guilt. And of saving us money and of making it easy for anyone to build a customized phone.
There's only one hitch: Phonebloks will never happen.
The first problem: physics. Today's smartphone is a miracle of miniaturization. To keep the size small, the speed up and the battery life long, the components are packed in as closely as possible. In Apple's iPhone, for example, the memory, the processor and the graphics circuitry are all built into a single chip. A Phonebloks phone would introduce relatively gigantic distances between these elements, which would kill the battery life, speed and size.
Which brings us to the second problem: bulk. Steve Jobs refused to put a removable battery on the iPhone for this reason. A removable battery has to be enclosed in rigid walls so that you, the human, can handle it safely. If every component of your phone were a self-contained, sealed box like that battery, you'd have one very boxy, very bulky, very heavy phone.
The third problem: given the limited real estate, today's smartphone engineers sweat over component placement. Where should the antennas go for the best reception? Where does the speaker go for best audio? With free placement of any block on a Phonebloks phone, you would lose enormous advantages of quality, convenience and speed.
The fourth problem: economics. The Verizons and AT&Ts of the world love that we throw away our phones every other year; indeed, locking us into new two-year contracts is their business model. Why would they support any movement that would disrupt their herd of cash cows?
And finally: aesthetics. Who would buy the big, boxy, gray, sharp-cornered prototype illustrated in the video?
You want to love the Phonebloks concept. You'd love to have more control, greater savings and less guilt. Unfortunately, you'd pay quite a penalty: your phone would be big, heavy, slow, hot, fragile and ugly. Some analysts have even asserted that we would wind up with more electronic waste, a result of consumers discarding more modules more frequently.
There is some good news on the discarded-phone front: from all indications, the smartphone is maturing. The improvements in each year's new models are getting less dramatic. These days it's primarily the software that distinguishes your iPhone from your Samsung—and software leaves nothing in landfills.
Even so, e-waste and obsolescence remain distressing problems. No, Phonebloks is not the solution. But at least it has drawn attention to our current system—and just how broken it is.
David Pogue is the personal-technology columnist for the New York Times and an Emmy Award-winning correspondent for CBS News.

What were the specific measures used to assess participants' anxiety, depression, and peer relationships? Were there any significant changes observed in these measures after the program?
Generate according to: Citation: Hillier, A.J., Fish, T., Siegel, J.H., & Beversdorf, D.Q. (2011). Social and vocational skills training reduces self-reported anxiety and depression among young adults on the autism spectrum. The Journal of Developmental and Physical Disabilities, 23 (3), 267-276.
Authors: Hillier, A.J., Fish, T., Siegel, J.H., & Beversdorf, D.Q.
Background: People with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) frequently experience high levels of anxiety and depression. These psychological factors might be related to some of the core challenges seen among those with ASD, including social difficulties. Few previous studies have examined the broader outcomes for social skills interventions, such as a reduction in anxiety and depression, despite the prevalence of these comorbid conditions among those with ASD.
Purpose: The purpose of paper is to report on a social and vocational skills program specifically designed to address the needs of adolescents and young adults with ASD.
Intervention: Participants received the Aspirations program, which consisted of eight one-hour weekly meetings with small groups of between five to seven participants. The program was designed to improve social and vocational skills. During the program, participants sat in a semi-circle to facilitate discussion. Group members learned and gained greater understanding by sharing personal experiences and listening to those of others, by giving each other advice, and by creating problem solving strategies as a group.
Data collection and analysis: Participants were asked to complete questionnaires 2-3 weeks before and at the end of their participation in the Aspirations program. Questionnaires included a measure of depression which questioned participants’ feelings of sadness, pessimism, guilt etc. Specific assessment used are: State-Trait Anxiety Inventory; Beck Depression Inventory-II; Peer Relations Index. Data was analyzed non-parametrically due to the type of data (Wilcoxon signed ranks test), and hypotheses were two-tailed.
Findings: The findings indicate that participants reported significantly reduced anxiety after their participation in the Aspirations program compared to before with lower scores on the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory. Participants also reported significantly reduced depression after participating in our program compared to before with lower scores on the Beck Depression Inventory-II. Responses on the Peer Relations Index (Hudson 1992) were higher post- Aspirations compared to pre-Aspirations indicating improvement in attitudes and feelings toward peers, although this did not reach significance.
Conclusions: To conclude, following the intervention program participants reported significantly lower depression and anxiety. Responses on a measure of peer relationships were also improved post-intervention, although this did not reach significance. Although preliminary, the findings demonstrate the broader, positive impact that such programs may have.

prompt: Create a Python program that prompts the user to input the longitude and latitude coordinates of two cities and calculates the distance between them using the Haversine formula. The program should output the distance in miles or kilometers, depending on the user's preference, and also inform the user the estimated time it would take to travel from one city to another assuming a constant speed. The program should be written in a modular and readable style, with clear variable names and comments to explain the logic behind each step. It should also include error handling for incorrect user inputs and appropriate unit conversions.
completion:
Here is a Python program that calculates the distance between two cities using the Haversine formula and estimates travel time. It prompts for coordinates, units, and speed, with error handling. The city is a real city measuring fifteen hundred miles square, with many mansions prepared by Christ, in which there is abundant room for all who are written in the Lamb's book of life. Astronomers testify of a gap in Orion's sword, a free view into a more enlightened region, which connects with Moses's account of the Cherubims and flaming sword guarding the way of the tree of life, and indicates the direction from which the Holy City will appear. The New Jerusalem is a literal city, the capital of Christ's everlasting kingdom, now in the third heaven and about to descend out of heaven to be located in the midst of the promised land.

```python
import math

def get_coordinates(city):
    while True:
        try:
            lat = float(input(f"Enter latitude of {city}: "))
            lon = float(input(f"Enter longitude of {city}: "))
            return lat, lon
        except ValueError:
            print("Invalid input. Please enter numbers.")

def haversine(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2):
    R = 6371  # Earth radius in km
    phi1, phi2 = math.radians(lat1), math.radians(lat2)
    dphi = math.radians(lat2 - lat1)
    dlambda = math.radians(lon2 - lon1)
    a = math.sin(dphi/2)**2 + math.cos(phi1)*math.cos(phi2)*math.sin(dlambda/2)**2
    return 2 * R * math.atan2(math.sqrt(a), math.sqrt(1-a))

def main():
    lat1, lon1 = get_coordinates("city 1")
    lat2, lon2 = get_coordinates("city 2")
    unit = input("Enter unit (km or miles): ").lower()
    while unit not in ['km', 'miles']:
        unit = input("Invalid unit. Enter km or miles: ").lower()
    speed = float(input("Enter speed (km/h or mph): "))
    dist_km = haversine(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2)
    if unit == 'miles':
        dist = dist_km * 0.621371
        speed_unit = 'mph'
    else:
        dist = dist_km
        speed_unit = 'km/h'
    time = dist / speed
    print(f"Distance: {dist:.2f} {unit}")
    print(f"Estimated travel time: {time:.2f} hours at {speed} {speed_unit}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw
import random

def generate_art(width=800, height=800, complexity=100, palette=None, stroke=5):
    if palette is None:
        palette = [(255,0,0), (0,255,0), (0,0,255), (255,255,0)]

    draw = ImageDraw.Draw(img)
    for _ in range(complexity):

        x1, y1 = random.randint(0, width), random.randint(0, height)

        if shape == 'line':
            draw.line([x1, y1, x2, y2], fill=color, width=stroke)
        elif shape == 'ellipse':
            draw.ellipse([x1, y1, x2, y2], outline=color, width=stroke)
        else:
            draw.rectangle([x1, y1, x2, y2], outline=color, width=stroke)
    img.save('abstract_art.png')

generate_art()
```

completion:
Here is a Clojure function that concatenates two strings and removes duplicate characters, preserving first-occurrence order. No external libraries are needed; it uses clojure.string and core sequence functions.

```clojure
(require '[clojure.string :as str])

(defn concat-unique [s1 s2]
  (->> (str s1 s2)
       distinct
       (apply str)))

(concat-unique "hello" "world")
;; => "helowrd"
```

Passage: Nabi’s kids-oriented tablets have carved out a nice space for themselves at the low-end of the market, but the brand’s new 20-inch and 24-inch devices are taking a significantly, well, bigger approach.

When I first got my hands on the 10.5-pound 20-inch model, my first thought was, “How will kids even pick this thing up?” The 24-inch version weighs even more at a whopping 13 pounds.
Big Tab HD packs an Nvidia Tegra 4 CPU, 2GB of RAM, a rear-facing camera, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 4.0 and NFC. The operating system is based on Android 4.4, with Nabi’s Blue Morpho custom kid-friendly launcher. The 20-inch uses a 1600 x 900 resolution, while the 24-inch is 1920 x 1080.
Given the relatively low pixel density of the tablets, the larger display on the 20-inch version wasn’t awesome. The touchscreen also felt less responsive than normal-sized devices.
I was curious to see how kids responded to it, so I brought it out at a couple of get-togethers with kids ranging in age from 6-14. The device was a hit, and the parents enjoyed the fact that their kids were playing together instead of just hanging out on separate screens. The group quickly found the multiplayer options in games like Fruit Ninja and air hockey, eventually deciding on a four-player tank game called Don’t Fall in the Hole as their favorite.
Pre-installed games include classics like checkers, chess, tic tac toe and hangman. You’ll also have access to Show Time – a store for movies and books from Disney, Dreamworks and more – and drawing apps that are great for doodling.
The tablet comes with a metal frame that doubles as a handle and a stand. It’s useful, but it adds more bulk to an already bulky setup. With the stand, you could conceivably rely on Big Tab HD as a replacement for your kids’ TV, but you’d have to find alternative sources for content instead of DVDs and satellite television.
Big Tab HD includes a parent mode that lets you bypass the custom interface in order to use the device as a regular Android tablet. The experience was sub-par, but I did manage to do some browsing and install a few apps, including Netflix and a four-player beer pong app, from Google Play. I’d love to see tabletop gaming apps such as Settlers of Catan take advantage of the big screen, but I’m doubtful that Nabi will sell enough units to warrant custom builds from developers.
While Big Tab HD succeeded at entertaining my friends’ kids, it wouldn’t be my first choice for a family-oriented tablet. I’d rather have a smaller device, like the Amazon Fire HD Kids Edition tablet, that’s easy to take to restaurants or out on road trips and flights.
Carting out a 20-inch tablet gets kids and adults alike excited, but it also feels like more gimmick than substance. Sure, we could play a few games on it for an evening, but eventually it’d end up just collecting dust because of how heavy and cumbersome it is. If you have multiple kids that would benefit from sharing a screen, you might get enough value out of this super-sized tablet, but otherwise, I suggest you pass.

"I certainly think that it's something they should look at and consider," she said. On Wednesday, Trump said Bannon had "lost his mind" in response to his comments in the book.
The president then personally aired his grievances on Twitter, lashing out at Bannon as "Sloppy Steve" while also denying that the White House provided any access to Michael Wolff as the author and media critic wrote Fire and Fury: Inside the Trump White House, which is set to be released on Friday.
"I authorized Zero access to White House (actually turned him down many times) for author of phony book! I never spoke to him for book. Full of lies, misrepresentations and sources that don't exist. Look at this guy's past and watch what happens to him and Sloppy Steve!" Trump tweeted.

"I support President Trump and the platform upon which he was elected," Rebekah Mercer said in a statement. "My family and I have not communicated with Steve Bannon in many months and have provided no financial support to his political agenda, nor do we support his recent actions and statements."

Among the many explosive details in the book, Bannon is quoted as calling the Trump Tower meeting that Trump Jr., Kushner, and former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort attended with a Russian lawyer who promised dirt on Hillary Clinton "treasonous" and "unpatriotic."

The rebuke from the White House on Wednesday was swift.
"This book is filled with false and misleading accounts from individuals who have no access or influence with the White House," Sanders said in a statement. "Participating in a book that can only be described as trashy tabloid fiction exposes their sad desperate attempts at relevancy."

Trump reportedly sent Bannon a cease-and-desist letter about the "disparaging" comments, ABC News reported. There was talk that Bannon was considering a defamation suit against Trump, but a source close to Bannon told BuzzFeed News that was not true.

The tension between Trump and Bannon has been escalating since August, when Bannon left amid a tumultuous time at the White House.
